title: Democrats more trusted on healthcare costs, survey shows
text: WASHINGTON — Democrats are more motivated to vote in November’s midterm elections than Republicans, potentially giving the party an advantage to flip at least one chamber of Congress, according to a poll released Tuesday by the nonpartisan health organization KFF.Democratic candidates also held an edge with voter confidence in their ability to address the rising cost of healthcare and everyday goods as well as abortion policy, though the parties were mostly tied when it came to addressing fraud in government programs. Republicans are trusted “to do a better job handling” immigration. “Of all the cost-of-living worries hitting voters now, a big health care bill is the least predictable, and that’s a big reason why health care costs are right up there with gas prices and the costs of food and housing on voters’ minds,” KFF President and CEO Dr. Drew Altman said in a statement. A majority of respondents, 66%, said they favor a candidate who supports a national health plan, which Democrats often refer to as Medicare-for-all. That support, however, fluctuates depending on how the question was asked. Seventy-six percent of those polled said they support a nationwide health plan when told it would “guarantee health insurance for all Americans.” The level of support was about the same, 75%, when people were told it would “eliminate all insurance premiums and reduce out-of-pocket costs for most Americans.” A slight majority, 52%, of respondents said they’d support a Medicare-for-all type plan when told it would “eliminate private health insurance companies.” Approval dropped to 38% when those polled were told it could “threaten the current Medicare program” and then to 35% when informed it would “require most Americans to pay more in taxes.” Support for a nationwide health plan decreased to 24% when those polled were told it could “lead to delays in people getting some medical tests and treatments.”When broken down by political party, far more Democrats, 84%, than Republicans, 35%, supported a nationwide health plan like Medicare-for-all.  Voters seek changeRegardless of which party secures control of the U.S. House and Senate following the November midterm elections, a significant number of those polled want to see lawmakers work to change the country’s healthcare system. Forty-nine percent said that “there are some good things about our healthcare system, but major changes are needed.” An additional 36% said “there is so much wrong with our healthcare system that it needs to be completely overhauled.” Another 13% said the country’s health system “works pretty well, but minor changes are needed.” And just 2% said there should be no changes. When asked what motivates people to vote in this year’s election, 20% of those polled said they wanted to bring about change, 19% said to stop President Donald Trump, 15% said they believe the country is in a crisis, 11% said the rising cost of living, 10% said to vote out Republicans, 9% said to protect democracy, 8% said to keep Democrats out of power, 7% said to end corruption and 6% said it was due to concerns about socialism or communism. Dems hold enthusiasm edgeForty-seven percent of those polled said they were more motivated to vote in this year’s elections than they were in the past, while 41% said they were about as motivated and 12% said they were less motivated. Democrats had a clear motivation advantage over Republicans with 63% of Democratic supporters saying they were more motivated and 28% saying they were about as motivated as they were during earlier elections. Thirty-eight percent of Republicans are more motivated and 53% said they were about as motivated as past elections. KFF polled 1,328 U.S. adults, including 1,013 voters, in English and in Spanish between Sept. 16 and Sept. 21. The margin of error is plus or minus 3 percentage points.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: It’s time to celebrate the sacred rite of voting in America
description: It was an early November day, cold and snowy. My father, Walter, was 85 and recovering from cataract surgery gone bad. He did the things an 85-year-old did – he read his newspaper daily despite an 8th grade education, told WWII stories, and doted on his grandchildren. But there was one more thing he did […]
text:
Kentuckians will got to the polls again on Nov. 3, 2026. (Austin Anthony for The Kentucky Lantern)It was an early November day, cold and snowy. My father, Walter, was 85 and recovering from cataract surgery gone bad. He did the things an 85-year-old did – he read his newspaper daily despite an 8th grade education, told WWII stories, and doted on his grandchildren. But there was one more thing he did on that cold, snowy November morning.
 Moving slowly with a patch securely over his left eye, he sat down at the dining room table as I arrived. 
“Daddy, it’s time to go vote,” I said. 
“I don’t think I can this time,” he replied. 
His answer was not unexpected but shocking nonetheless. I pondered for the longest moment and came up with this: “if you don’t vote, daddy, your guys won’t win”!  He looked at me for a moment with a look of deep concern and a sudden sense of urgency.  Slowly, he rose from his chair and headed toward the door. As if there was never a moment of hesitation, he walked past me at the door with these words, “What are you waiting for?”
 Looking back, it was a teaching moment that voting was something the weather or a bad eye could not stop. It was that important. We are reminded that democracy is sustained not only by historic figures and grand speeches, it is the stuff of ordinary people who put on their coats, learn about the candidates and the issues, and go vote.
 In honor of people like my dad and the most sacred rite of freedom, voting, The League of Women Voters of Lexington, Global Lex, and CivicLex are launching “Make Democracy Social,” and “Celebrate Democracy,” a two-part, nonpartisan voter engagement initiative, designed to help Fayette County residents become informed voters, make a plan to vote, and build community around civic participation.
The initiative, launched this September, will provide a toolkit where information instructs on how to conduct and host Democracy Potlucks. The potlucks will feature community forums where citizens gather to make democracy social with a meal and conversation. Community groups, churches, neighborhood associations, clubs, workplaces, language communities and friend groups are encouraged to consider hosting a Democracy Potluck before early voting begins. Sponsoring organizations will provide nonpartisan resources to help people research what is on their ballot, understand the offices being elected, and make a voting plan.
 Following these activities, all will be invited to Democracy Celebration opportunities where voters gather after voting to celebrate community participation.
 Visit www.lwvlexington.com for more information and look out for League of Women Voters of Lexington, Global Lex, CivicLex, and partner organizations out in the community throughout the fall.
 Let’s remember that our fundamental freedoms were the result of sparks of passion and the act of voting that underpins our most basic freedoms. They include freedom to worship as you wish and separation of church and state, freedom of speech to voice opposing opinions and enjoy a free press, due process and the right to counsel sparked by one man who spoke up and demanded representation in our courts (Gideon vs. Wainright, 1963).
 Let us remember that our most fundamental right to speak up and vote lay at the root of all our freedoms. The many battles throughout American history were ones of expanding the right to vote through many means including constitutional amendments that afforded voting status without discrimination regardless of gender, race, and age.
 Let’s honor the legacy of those who have gone before us. Voting is not something my dad did when convenient, when weather cooperated, or when he felt particularly inspired. It was a part of being a citizen and fighting hard every day to be informed and go vote. It is the act that not only preserves democracy but something we should celebrate. Let’s celebrate democracy together!

title: Workforce training program earns another No.1 ranking for Virginia
description: Virginia’s workforce training program has earned another No. 1 national ranking as the commonwealth competes for companies looking for workers trained for specialized jobs. Area Development, a major national trade publication, ranked Virginia first for workforce training programs in its 2026 Top States for Doing Business report. The recognition highlights th[...]
text:
The Virginia Economic Development Partnership oversees the Talent Accelerator Program, which provides customized recruitment and training services at no cost to qualifying employers. Virginia ranked first for workforce training programs in Area Development’s 2026 business rankings. (Photo courtesy of VDEP)Virginia’s workforce training program has earned another No. 1 national ranking as the commonwealth competes for companies looking for workers trained for specialized jobs.
Area Development, a major national trade publication, ranked Virginia first for workforce training programs in its 2026 Top States for Doing Business report. The recognition highlights the Virginia Talent Accelerator Program, which provides customized recruitment and training at no cost to qualifying companies opening or expanding operations in the commonwealth. 
Since its launch in 2019, the program has supported projects representing more than 22,000 announced jobs across the state, according to Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s administration. 
Virginia placed eighth overall in Area Development’s nationwide rankings and also finished fifth for innovation and research, sixth for site readiness programs and seventh for logistics and transportation infrastructure. 
The workforce recognition comes after Business Facilities ranked Virginia first for customized workforce training for the fourth consecutive year this summer.
“Workforce is one of the most important factors in any company’s location decision, and Virginia continues to distinguish itself nationally,” Virginia Secretary of Commerce and Trade Carrie Chenery said in a statement Monday. 
“The Virginia Talent Accelerator Program is a clear competitive advantage because it drives business growth by customizing talent solutions. This recognition reinforces that the commonwealth is not only attracting investment but also preparing Virginians for the jobs those investments create.” 
Created by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership in collaboration with the Virginia Community College System, the Talent Accelerator receives funding support from the governor’s administration and the General Assembly. Its services are offered as an incentive for companies creating jobs in Virginia. 
The work varies from project to project. Before training begins, the Talent Accelerator assesses a company’s recruitment processes and workforce needs. That can lead to assistance before an employee is even hired, including brief training sessions and assessments that give applicants a look at the work while allowing employers to evaluate potential hires. 
Recruitment help can include digital advertising and campaigns on streaming and podcast platforms. The program’s in-house team also produces videos, websites and 3D animations to help companies recruit workers and demonstrate workplace tasks. 
Once workers are hired, training can range from safety and basic skills to detailed instruction on production processes and individual jobs. Teamwork, conflict resolution and leadership training are also available. 
Manufacturing projects are paired with a regional community college, while the program also works with universities, including historically Black colleges, according to VEDP. 
Spanberger said Virginia’s latest rank shows the value of connecting economic development with workforce preparation. 
“Virginia is building the best workforce in America, and industry is taking notice,” Spanberger said in a statement. “The Virginia Talent Accelerator Program gives businesses a powerful reason to choose the commonwealth by delivering customized training that prepares Virginians to succeed from day one.”
Area Development has covered corporate site selection and relocation since 1965. Its 2026 rankings are based on a survey of 50 site consultants who evaluated states across 20 categories affecting corporate location and investment decisions. 
The magazine then weighted those results based on the importance of each factor in corporate site selection.
Virginia finished behind Georgia, Texas, Tennessee, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Alabama in the overall ranking. But it took the top spot for workforce training, ahead of Georgia and South Carolina. 
VEDP President and CEO Jason El Koubi said the Talent Accelerator’s value lies in building recruitment and training around an employer’s particular operation rather than offering a standard package. 
“Our team works directly with companies to design recruitment and training strategies that reflect their operations, culture and long-term growth plans,” El Koubi said in a statement. “Area Development’s recognition underscores the program’s impact and the value Virginia delivers to companies creating jobs across the commonwealth.” 
Several companies that announced Virginia projects this year are using the program.
Avio USA plans a roughly $500 million manufacturing facility in Hurt that is expected to create more than 1,000 jobs. RINGANA, an Austrian skincare and nutritional products company, announced an $85 million U.S. headquarters, production and distribution operation in Roanoke with 435 jobs. Jabil plans a manufacturing facility in Prince George County expected to create 352 jobs. 
Merck & Co. also plans to use Talent Accelerator as part of its $3 billion expansion in Elkton. The project is expected to create 500 jobs and will serve as the company’s Center of Excellence for Pharmaceutical Ingredients and Small Molecule Manufacturing. 
The Spanberger administration’s figure of more than 22,000 jobs reflects announced positions associated with projects supported by the Talent Accelerator. It does not indicate how many of those jobs have been filled or how many workers have completed training through the program.

title: Virginia Board of Education reinstates adult education advisory committee after 3 years
description: The Virginia Board of Education recently reestablished its adult education advisory committee after a three-year hiatus to guide how the state uses resources to improve its adult education and literacy program. The programs combine education and job training that can help enrollees earn recognized industry credentials and provide academic and parenting suppo[...]
text:
A college student leaving a lecture hall. (Photo by Getty Images / ferrantraite) The Virginia Board of Education recently reestablished its adult education advisory committee after a three-year hiatus to guide how the state uses resources to improve its adult education and literacy program.
The programs combine education and job training that can help enrollees earn recognized industry credentials and provide academic and parenting support for adults and their children. They also help learners strengthen English proficiency, develop civic and workplace skills, and improve basic academic skills through in-person or remote classes.
The committee’s return follows a three-month listening tour led by Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s administration, where educators, school leaders and parents spoke about strengthening Virginia’s K-12 system. 
At the board’s Aug. 27 business meeting, Superintendent of Public Instruction Jenna Conway said the committee helps the board by gathering feedback from stakeholders, considering adult learners’ access to rigorous programs and making effective use of funding, while keeping adult education and literacy moving forward. 
The board voted to re-establish the committee on Sept. 24.
“We can’t always have all those folks represented here on the board, and so we welcome reestablishing this committee to think through how we make sure that these students are having access to sort of equal rigor,” said Conway.
She added, “We want to make the most of every dollar, and we want to make the dollars go as far as possible.”
Virginia serves over 17,000 adults annually and has awarded $18 million to local adult-education providers for 2026-27 program year, according to the Virginia Department of Education.
Over the past three years, the agency said recipients reported over 52,000 student enrollments, and 7,400 secondary and industry-recognized credentials have been earned.
On June 20, 2001, a previous board created the first 14-member committee. However, the agency said the board’s action did not specify seat requirements, meaning seats could be added or taken away in future years.
Staff recommended no changes to the number of members, but asked that the ex officio role be reserved for the Adult Student of the Year, chosen through the Virginia Association of Adult and Continuing Education.
VDOE said it will seek nominations using the agency’s form and processes, review them for a balance of stakeholder groups and geographic representation, and then the board will review and approve recommendations.
The agency did not immediately respond to questions about the reason for the committee’s three-year break.

title: Democrats could win majority of governor’s offices for first time in 16 years
description: As the political prospects for Republicans worsen ahead of November’s midterm elections, the GOP is increasingly playing defense over its yearslong grip on state governments. That’s particularly true for gubernatorial elections, as Democrats could win a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010. Currently, Republicans boast  a 26-24 gubernatori[...]
text:
Iowa Auditor Rob Sand, the Democratic nominee for governor, campaigns at a September town hall in West Des Moines. Democrats in November could win a majority of governor’s offices for the first time in 16 years. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)As the political prospects for Republicans worsen ahead of November’s midterm elections, the GOP is increasingly playing defense over its yearslong grip on state governments.
That’s particularly true for gubernatorial elections, as Democrats could win a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010. Currently, Republicans boast  a 26-24 gubernatorial advantage over Democrats.
This November, voters will choose governors in 36 states. Thirteen of those races are considered competitive by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, which ranks the competitiveness of races for governor, the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House.
Some of this cycle’s most competitive races are in politically divided states such as Nevada and Wisconsin. But Republicans also are playing defense in several deeply conservative states, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.
Last week, the Cook Political Report moved its ratings of the Florida and Texas governor races from Likely Republican to Leans Republican. That means the GOP candidates are still favored in those states, but “given the grim political environment for the GOP, we can’t rule out the possibility of an upset in one or both contests,” wrote Senate and Governors Editor Jessica Taylor.
Democratic control of more governor’s offices could mean more bipartisan compromise — or gridlock — in state capitols. In Nevada, however, a Democratic governor could initiate a new era of progressive policymaking: Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo has vetoed more than 160 bills approved by the Democratic-controlled legislature during his term.
In states such as Alaska, Georgia and Ohio, Democratic governors could deliver new checks on Republican lawmakers who have enjoyed years of legislative control.
Trump’s Canadian trade war stirs up trouble for Republican candidates

The competitive races for state executives come as Democrats seek to rebuild state power after years of Republican dominance in statehouses. In addition to controlling a majority of governor’s offices, the GOP has held a majority of state legislative seats and chambers since 2010.
Democrats’ improving prospects are evidence of the broader political challenges facing Republicans across the country, said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston.
“It’s a rebuke of the Trump model, and especially the Republican Trump model,” he said. “But it’s also something that isn’t uncommon for midterms.”
With total Republican control of Washington, Democrats are benefiting from widespread dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump over the Iran war and the high prices of healthcare, housing, groceries and energy affecting nearly every part of daily life.


Despite winning his previous campaigns by double digits, Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott is facing a close competition with Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa.
“Our race is now a toss-up,” the subject line of a Sept. 29 fundraising email from the Abbott campaign reads.
Jones said the Texas Republican party is still reeling from internal bloodletting after Attorney General Ken Paxton ousted incumbent U.S. Sen. John Cornyn in a heated primary contest. Paxton, whose political career has been largely defined by scandal, now trails Democrat James Talarico in most polling in one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country.
To Jones, winning the Texas governor’s race is still a longshot for Democrats, but he said the president is the main reason it’s even competitive this cycle.
“It’s overwhelmingly a national phenomenon,” he said. “It has more to do with Donald Trump’s low approval ratings on both his handling of his job as president and his handling of the economy and just overall low favorability.”
More split governments?
Democratic wins for governor could bring divided government to some reliably conservative states.
While shared rule used to be common in states, most now are dominated by one party that controls both legislative chambers and the governor’s office. Power is split between the parties in only 11 states, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. 
Voters to decide fate of state taxes this fall

Last week, Democratic Iowa State Auditor Rob Sand pledged to bring “divided government once again” to Des Moines. Favored to win over Republican Zach Lahn, Sand said split power would bring more balance to state policymaking after years of GOP control.
If Iowa Democrats can prevent the GOP from winning back a legislative supermajority, they would hold more power over lawmaking and gubernatorial appointments than they’ve enjoyed for years.
Democrats flipped two Iowa state Senate seats in special elections last year to break the GOP’s veto-proof supermajority there. Senate Democrats have already used their newly won power by rejecting appointments, including a high-profile nomination for the leader of the state’s Health and Human Services Department.
Democratic wins for governor in November could bring divided power to Alaska, Ohio, Georgia, Florida and Texas. But divided government could vanish in other states.
In Kansas, Republicans are poised to gain even more control as state Senate President Ty Masterson leads in gubernatorial polling over Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher. If elected, Masterson would replace Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly, delivering a trifecta of Republican control to Topeka.
Voters to weigh different approaches to housing affordability in November

Vermont Gov. Phil Scott, a Republican, said this election cycle follows a familiar pattern for the party that controls Washington.
“We see this in every midterm: The party in power sometimes takes a beating, and I think that that’s what’s going to happen in this cycle,” he said.
Scott is favored to win reelection next month, which would keep power divided in Montpelier if Democrats continue to control the legislature as expected.
The Republican Governors Association did not comment on the party’s prospects for  maintaining its national advantage. In a statement, spokesperson Kollin Crompton said GOP governors and candidates remain focused on lowering taxes, unleashing American energy and keeping communities safe.
“Contrast that with Democrat governors who hurt working families with tax increases and stunt job growth with bureaucratic regulation; the choice in November is clear.” he said. “If Democrats gain control, these states will turn into hellscapes reminiscent of California and Illinois.”
A national move for power
In many states, the power of newly elected governors largely will be shaped by the partisan composition of legislatures.
Republicans have held a grip on state power across the country since 2010, when they won hundreds of legislative seats and picked up control of 20 legislative chambers during the first midterm election of President Barack Obama’s presidency.
Democrats hope to flip 500 seats across the country this cycle. But even with 15 legislative chambers identified as competitive this year, it’s unlikely Democrats will rebuild their legislative ranks to pre-2010 levels, when the party controlled 60 of 99 legislative chambers nationwide (Nebraska has a unicameral legislature).
Republicans currently hold 4,044 state legislative seats, compared with 3,227 for Democrats, according to Katy Owens Hubler, director of elections and redistricting at the National Conference of State Legislatures.
“Polls have been showing more Democratic enthusiasm,” she said,” but I think it’s likely Republicans will maintain their advantage in terms of absolute numbers of seats.”
States put criminal justice, marijuana policies before voters in 2026

Control of legislatures will not only affect state policymaking, but will likely shape the next wave of congressional redistricting, said Will Rusche, vice president of marketing and communications at the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, which works to elect Democrats at the state level.
Set off by a White House push to give Republicans more seats in the U.S. House, 10 states have completed mid-decade redistricting — a phenomenon unseen since the 1800s.
Rusche said the outcome of November’s governor and legislative races will play a major role in whether Democrats can win back federal power.
“It all runs through statehouses,” he said. “The majorities we win this year will determine what powers Democrats have, and you know the path to power in Congress and the presidency in 2028 and going forward.”
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org

title: Indiana reviews Medicaid waiver assessments amid scrutiny of new tool
description: The Indiana Family and Social Services Administration quietly paused determinations for disability Medicaid waivers in August to review how case managers were implementing the agency’s new interRAI assessment system, as advocates raised alarm about the tool’s accuracy. But after a break, the system is already back in place. Case managers started using the in[...]
text:
Concerns continue over a new assessment tool that is impacting disabled Hoosiers. (Getty Images)The Indiana Family and Social Services Administration quietly paused determinations for disability Medicaid waivers in August to review how case managers were implementing the agency’s new interRAI assessment system, as advocates raised alarm about the tool’s accuracy.
But after a break, the system is already back in place.
Case managers started using the interRAI algorithm in January to determine who is eligible for Medicaid waivers for intermediate care, a process known as level-of-care assessments.
The waivers allow disabled Hoosiers to stay in their homes, rather than an institutional setting.
FSSA used to approve nearly all disability waivers. But officials questioned the accuracy of those assessments after internal estimates suggested the approval rate should be closer to 90%, so the agency adopted interRAI.
Denials quickly surged, prompting alarm from Democratic lawmakers and advocates who worried the denials were in error.
Lawmakers want transparency in Medicaid waiver denials

FSSA paused level-of-care determinations Aug. 31 for assessments awaiting review by the Indiana Bureau of Disabilities Services, a spokesperson confirmed to the Indiana Capital Chronicle.
The agency undertook the review to “ensure case managers were conducting the assessment process consistently and in line with state standards,” the spokesperson said.
The Arc of Indiana, which advocates for disability rights, learned of the pause when it filed a public records request on Sept. 30 seeking clarity for how determinations were made.
Arc executives also found out FSSA had ordered new assessments for Hoosiers with pending level-of-care denials based on interRAI assessments, and that the agency had started rescinding denials currently in appeals and others who raised concerns to allow for reassessments of those cases.
“In practical terms, this process is essentially a fresh start,” said Karly Sciortino-Poulter, director of The Arc of Indiana Advocacy Network. “The new assessment replaces the previous assessment in its determination. If an individual is found eligible based on the new assessment, they will retain their waiver eligibility.”
She continued, “If they are found ineligible, they have the right to appeal the decision. Individuals should pay close attention to the new assessment and any notices they receive, particularly deadlines to appeal and steps to making the appeal.”
Determinations resumed Monday.
Indiana ‘fully confident’ in interRAI
An FSSA spokesperson said the pause on determinations was due to variability in how case managers were administering assessments, rather than an issue with interRAI itself.
InterRAI, also known as the international residential assessment instrument, started as an assessment tool for nursing homes.
“We remain fully confident in the interRAI tool and its effectiveness in evaluating individual needs,” the spokesperson said in an unsigned email statement.
Arc officials say FSSA informed them that new assessments will be conducted by mentors and specially trained assessors, alongside a persons’s assigned case manager — a decision praised by Arc CEO Kim Dodson.
Still, advocates from the Arc continue to raise questions about how assessment information is used to determine eligibility for waivers.
The group is seeking information about how FSSA maps interRAI assessment data onto Indiana’s level-of-care criteria, and how the agency uses that methodology to make eligibility determinations.
It’s also seeking records related to assessment training, quality assurance, implementation and outcomes.
“This is a sophisticated assessment that can have enormous consequences for an individual,” Dodson said.
While Dodson said the tool itself is not the fundamental problem, she remains concerned about how its implementation apparently differs from the “comprehensive, person-centered assessment” it was designed to be.
She added, “People with intellectual and developmental disabilities have a broad range of abilities and support needs. We need to understand what assessment information matters, how it is weighted, what criteria or thresholds are used, and how the methodology was developed and tested. We must have confidence that the process accurately identifies everyone who meets Indiana’s level-of-care requirements, not only people with the most significant or readily apparent disabilities.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: As oil prices soar, more NH residents are behind on their heating bills
description: High oil prices are teeing up a cold and stressful winter for many Granite Staters. “If we didn’t get heat assistance, for instance, we wouldn’t make it at all,” said Per Garp, a retired farmer from Loudon, during a roundtable event with heating assistance providers and Congressman Chris Pappas Monday in Concord. “… We’re going […]
text:
From left: Michael Tabory, chief operating officer of Community Action Partnership Belknap-Merrimack Counties; Per Garp, a retired farmer from Loudon; Jeanne Agri, chief executive officer of Community Action Partnership Belknap-Merrimack Counties; and Congressman Chris Pappas speak about energy costs during a roundtable event on Monday, Oct. 5, in Concord. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)High oil prices are teeing up a cold and stressful winter for many Granite Staters.
“If we didn’t get heat assistance, for instance, we wouldn’t make it at all,” said Per Garp, a retired farmer from Loudon, during a roundtable event with heating assistance providers and Congressman Chris Pappas Monday in Concord. “… We’re going to be cold, maybe even freezing. We need more.”
At a conference table at the headquarters of the Community Action Partnership Belknap-Merrimack Counties, the providers talked about what they have heard from residents as applications begin to come in across New Hampshire for this year’s heating assistance program. 
Inflated by pressure from the wars in Iran and Ukraine, the cost of oil is hitting Americans at the gas pump and, as cold weather sets in, inflating heating bills, too. In the Northeast, where reliance on heating oil is heavier than in the rest of the U.S., the impact on residents is likely to be especially severe: The average cost of a season’s worth of heating oil is projected to rise more than 31%, or $548, over last year, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors’ Association. That brings the average cost of heating a typical home throughout the winter to about $2,300.
Meanwhile, though the amount of assistance available to qualifying New Hampshire residents has increased since last year, it has not kept pace. The maximum amount of assistance a household could receive this year is $2,500, up $323 or about 15% from last year, according to figures provided by the New Hampshire Department of Energy. 
The average amount an applicant receives is approximately $1,200, said Terra Rogers, energy services director for Southwestern Community Services. 
Already, some of New Hampshire’s community action partnerships, which administer a heating assistance program for qualifying New Hampshire residents, have seen an uptick in new registrants, staff said. 
“We’ve seen a lot of people that are working families that are applying who are brand new,” said Rogers. Colleagues have commented on their surprise over the number of people submitting first-time applications this year, she said. 
“There was just a chat that went around the office, like, ‘Have you had a lot of new clients?'” she said. “And the next person says, ‘Yeah, we have. It’s been really high this year.'”
Assistance is available for households with incomes that range from $0 to approximately 60% of the median household income in New Hampshire, according to the New Hampshire Department of Energy. In 2024, the U.S. Census Bureau listed New Hampshire’s median household income as $99,031.
Assistance funding is not always enough to keep recipients warm, providers said on Monday. And some residents, they said, are scared. 
Given that assistance does not always cover a full delivery, and a single winter will typically require multiple fuel deliveries per household, some recipients are already carrying debt on their accounts, according to Kristin Bertrand, director of energy and area resource centers at Community Action Partnership Belknap-Merrimack Counties. 
The number of inquiries the agency has received this year from people concerned about overdue balances is higher than it was at this time last year, Bertrand said.
Rogers said she knows elderly program participants who keep their thermostats at 57 degrees throughout the winter because they cannot afford more fuel.
“All they can use is fuel assistance. For the whole season, that’s all they have, so they try to stretch their dollar, so they keep it really low. That’s quite cold, in the winter in New Hampshire,” she said. 
The high price of heating coupled with other ballooning costs eat up a fixed income, Garp said. 
As prices rise, “We have barely more money to pay with. … It doesn’t work,” he said. 
Garp pointed to the high cost of health insurance and medications as other factors straining his family’s budget, calling on Pappas to help lower Medicare premiums and other healthcare costs. 
This year’s sharp increases add to the financial stress many New Hampshire residents have carried over from last year’s heating season, providers said. They called for more funding and timely disbursement of federal dollars for the program, which is funded by the federal government and administered by states and local agencies. 
“Energy costs affect everything,” Bertrand said. 
Pappas said he was concerned about the impact of rising fuel costs on New Hampshire. He pointed to legislation he introduced this fall to increase funding for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program by redirecting $1 billion in funding for President Donald Trump’s “Board of Peace,” and legislation that seeks to allow states to increase eligibility for heating assistance dollars to include those making up to 75% of that state’s median income. 
Heating assistance directors said they want residents to be aware that they may be eligible for more help than they realize. 
“So many people that do have an income and are working actually are eligible,” said Heather Amer, chief operations officer at Southwestern Community Services. “So we try to let people know: If you’re nervous, just apply.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: The end is near for US hemp THC market. But uncertainty continues for Rhode Island growers.
description: On less than an acre of farmland in Hopkinton, rows of hemp plants were nearing harvest. Most of their “colas” — dense clusters of buds prized for smokable flower — had already been cut ahead of a nor’easter bound for southern New England on the last weekend of September. The rest will be harvested in […]
text:
Lovewell Farms co-founders Mike Simpson, left, and Ryan Plant, right, stand next to hemp plants nearing harvest on Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)On less than an acre of farmland in Hopkinton, rows of hemp plants were nearing harvest. Most of their “colas” — dense clusters of buds prized for smokable flower — had already been cut ahead of a nor’easter bound for southern New England on the last weekend of September.
The rest will be harvested in the next couple of weeks and turned into concentrate, destined to become products such as tinctures, 1-milligram THC gummies and 5-milligram THC lemonades, which Lovewell Farms launched earlier in September.
“We’ve leaned into the cans and beverages because the state regulations allow that,” Mike Simpson, co-founder of Lovewell Farms, said in an interview standing next to the hemp plants, joint in hand. “And we’re making hand over fist doing that.”
Rhode Island’s regulated hemp market generated $2.85 million in sales in 2025, according to data provided by the state’s Cannabis Control Commission. Drinks and seltzers infused with THC — the psychoactive component of the cannabis plant that can cause impairment— accounted for $2.36 million, or about 83% of the total. The state had 201 licensed hemp businesses as of Oct. 1, including 169 retailers.
But the market Simpson joined could soon be upended by a federal restriction that Rhode Island regulators say they must enforce. Starting Dec. 11, federal law will prohibit the sale of hemp-derived cannabinoid products containing more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container.
Existing regulations adopted by the Cannabis Control Commission in 2025 have allowed all products to contain up to 1 milligrams of total THC per serving, or 5 milligrams of total THC per package. 
A Sept. 11 bulletin from the Rhode Island Cannabis Control Commission warns any product over the new limit will be considered noncompliant and subject to administrative penalties “including but not limited to monetary fines.”
“Licensees are strongly encouraged to review their current inventory, assess their products against the new federal limit, and begin planning for the December 11 deadline,” the commission advised in an accompanying email.
Existing regulations adopted by the Cannabis Control Commission in 2025 allow all products to contain up to 1 milligrams of total THC per serving, or 5 milligrams of total THC per package. 
For Simpson, the commission’s guidance raises questions about what happens to the pallets of lemonade cans stored in a dark room on the farm, ready to ship to Rhode Island liquor stores, which have been licensed to sell hemp-derived beverages for the past two years.
“The idea that we would just kind of throw all that out without even engaging in a deeper conversation with the community or the industry is wild,” he said.
Mariana Ormonde, chief legal counsel for the commission, said she understands the difficult position the state’s hemp licensees are in. But the state’s hands are tied when it comes to changes made at the federal level.
“The reality of the situation is we can’t treat hemp like cannabis because it’s not cannabis,” Ormonde said in an interview.
Hemp leaves hang to dry inside a building on Lovewell Farms property in Hopkinton on Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
Lessons in chemistry
Hemp became legal at the federal level after the passage of the 2018 Farm Bill, allowing products with a THC concentration of 0.3% or lower by dry weight. The law was meant to allow an agricultural market for hemp-based textiles, animal feeds and human wellness products centered on CBD products.
But that original definition in the 2018 law did not account for ways to convert the plant to produce higher potency, paving the way for the proliferation of hemp-derived THC products like infused drinks — products which states have since scrambled to either regulate or ban.
“That’s kind of what opened up Pandora’s box,” Ormonde said.
Rhode Island’s hemp rules were formally adopted by the Cannabis Control Commission in 2025 — just months before Congress moved to close the potency loophole created by the 2018 Farm Bill as part of legislation to reopen the federal government after last year’s shutdown.
By itself, hemp produces little to no THC, the compound most commonly associated with cannabis intoxication. But that can change as the plant matures, explained Ryan Plante, Lovewell Farms’ director of cultivation.
“At 30 days of a harvest, it has almost non-detectable cannabinoids in most regards,” said Plante, who studied horticulture at the University of Rhode Island. “And then afterwards, it is common for hemp to get up to 0.5 milligrams, or 5.5 % to 1% of THC in that flower.”
Hemp’s THC potency can also be increased by chemistry. Methods include extracting cannabinoids from the plant and converting them into compounds such as delta-8 or delta-9 THC.



Quotation







The reality of the situation is we can't treat hemp like cannabis because it's not cannabis.


– Mariana Ormonde, chief legal counsel for the Rhode Island Cannabis Control Commission


THC drinks derived from hemp were illegal in Rhode Island until August 2024, when the state’s former Office of Cannabis Regulation began allowing the sale of products containing low levels of delta-9 THC at licensed retailers including vape shops, liquor stores, and some bars. 
The new federal definition was originally set to take effect Nov. 12, but Congress pushed the effective date back one month as part of a short-term government funding bill signed by President Donald Trump in September.
U.S. Sen. Jack Reed (D-R.I.) was among the 90 senators who voted for the one-month delay in August.
Ben Craig, a spokesperson for Reed’s office, said Rhode Island’s senior senator supported delaying what he called a nationwide hemp ban to give lawmakers more time to develop “balanced regulations” for hemp-infused products.
“He also wants to ensure responsible Rhode Island hemp businesses are not unfairly, adversely impacted by federal regulations,” Craig wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current. 
But Reed has also shared concerns raised by attorneys general from 39 states, including Rhode Island AG Peter Neronha, who last year sent a letter to Congress urging lawmakers to tighten the federal definition of hemp.
Neronha signed onto another multistate letter in August urging Congress to reject efforts to “delay, repeal, suspend, or weaken” the federal hemp restrictions enacted last year.
Simpson criticized the AG’s push for tighter restrictions, saying he has seen no evidence that hemp-derived products have increased youth access in Rhode Island. 
“Give me the evidence in the state of Rhode Island where we have increased youth access to cannabis,” Simpson said. “Show me the data that shows that, and then I will agree and believe you.”
Timothy Rondeau, a spokesperson for Neronha’s office, said the 2025 letter sought to close a loophole in the federal definition of hemp that allowed intoxicating cannabinoid products to be sold legally.
“The letter asserts that potentially harmful substances like this should be regulated, and where the regulation is patchwork across the country, federal regulation is best,” Rondeau wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current.
Lovewell Farms launched a THC-infused sparkling lemonade in early September 2026 — three months before the federal government is set to prohibit such products. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
Why is the cannabis market different?
Simpson sees a double standard in the Cannabis Control Commission’s decision to enforce the federal restrictions on hemp while continuing to allow the sale of recreational cannabis, which was never legalized under federal law.
“Why this, but not cannabis?” he asked.
Ormonde said the difference is that the federal government has imposed a new restriction on hemp that the state cannot simply disregard.
“Federal law is the supreme law of the land,” she said.
She said Rhode Island can regulate cannabis under state law because the state has chosen to do so, even though cannabis remains illegal under federal law. But with hemp, she said, the state is operating within a federal framework that Congress has now changed.
Keeping the hemp market would also pose challenges to the liquor retailers who have carried the drinks.
Nick Fede Jr., president of the American Beverage Licensees, said the changes could make it harder for retailers to process payments for hemp products because banks would no longer allow credit card sales — as is the case with regulated cannabis sales at Rhode Island’s retail pot shops.
“If it’s not federally recognized, they don’t want to touch that money,” said Fede, whose family owns Kingstown Liquor Mart in North Kingstown, which has a valid hemp retail license through March 2027.
Charon Rose, spokesperson for the Cannabis Control Commission, said her understanding is that the Trump administration is considering a new framework for hemp, but that the details remain unclear.
That uncertainty is one reason Ormonde said the commission is trying to avoid telling businesses to outright shut down before the federal deadline.
“We kind of have to wait and see what the federal government does before we can sort of act and advise our licensees in accordance with that,” Ormonde said.
In the meantime, Rose said regulators plan to revise its Sept.11 bulletin and issue updated guidance to licensees “in the coming days.”
Still, the ongoing uncertainty has made it harder for hemp businesses like Lovewell farms to plan for next year.
Simpson typically buys its 1,500 seeds from Oregon in February, ahead of the growing season. Seth Crawford, co-owner of Oregon CBD Seeds, told the Oregon Capital Chronicle he still expects to sell seeds to anyone who wants them, but anticipates demand will fall if the new federal rules reduce the market for industrial hemp processing.
“It’s very hard to run a business when you want to do investments in equipment and inventory when the regulations are changing,” Simpson said.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: We’ve tracked $80M of spending on almost 170 AI‑generated political ads this year — it’s weird
authors: Travis N. Ridout, Erika Franklin Fowler, Michael Franz
description: The 2026 U.S. midterm campaigns are the first in which AI-generated political ads are regularly appearing on people’s televisions and social media feeds. We are researchers who have been studying political advertising through the Wesleyan Media Project since 2010. This election cycle — using data from media reports, student coders and AdImpact, a firm that [[...]
text:
Republican sponsors — both candidates and interest groups — are much more likely to use AI than are Democratic sponsors. (Getty Images)
The 2026 U.S. midterm campaigns are the first in which AI-generated political ads are regularly appearing on people’s televisions and social media feeds.
We are researchers who have been studying political advertising through the Wesleyan Media Project since 2010. This election cycle — using data from media reports, student coders and AdImpact, a firm that tracks political ad spending — we’ve tracked about US$80 million in spending on almost 170 unique ads that use AI.
What we found has surprised us: AI use spans from hyperrealistic deepfakes to subtle enhancements; Republican sponsors — both candidates and interest groups — are much more likely to use AI than are Democratic sponsors; and, thanks to a patchwork of state legislation, many of these ads do not disclose the use of AI at all.
From deepfakes to subtle edits
An assortment of politicians and watchdog groups have expressed concern about campaigns using generative AI to produce deepfakes — synthetic videos showing people doing things they did not do — that might deceive voters.
We’ve noticed several ads containing hyperrealistic deepfakes of famous politicians, including Donald Trump, Nancy Pelosi, Barack Obama, Kamala Harris and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Ocasio-Cortez, in particular, is a favorite among Republican advertisers, appearing in at least five ads.
We’ve seen deepfakes in which a Republican Senate candidate from Louisiana drives a school bus full of undocumented immigrants, a Republican candidate for governor from South Carolina walks arm in arm with drag queens, and an ad in which Liz Cheney, Mitt Romney and Mike Pence are seen carrying pitchforks on the White House lawn.
People who are not politicians made appearances, too, including a fake Dr. Anthony Fauci, seen running around a state fair with a huge syringe, presumably eager to vaccinate everyone. We’ve also noticed several ads in which AI was used to generate crowds or constituents.
In several cases, AI was used to enhance visuals rather than generate something new. One ad from Chip Keating, a Republican candidate for governor in Oklahoma, includes an AI disclaimer, but it doesn’t specify exactly how AI was used. Ads that use AI to enhance visuals don’t necessarily look different from ads that were created in the pre-AI era, which makes it difficult for viewers to discern whether they depict something false.
A partisan gap
Republicans — both candidates and groups such as super PACs and 501(c) organizations — are much more likely to use AI in their ads than are Democrats, according to our research.
In fact, Republican candidates or pro-Republican groups were behind 80% of the ads we tracked and 83% of the spending.
We can only speculate as to why Republicans dominate the use of AI in political advertising in 2026. In general, Democrats tend to take on a regulatory mindset when it comes to political campaigns, favoring limits on campaign spending and required disclosures. In 2022, for instance, only Senate Democrats and two independents voted to advance the DISCLOSE Act that would have required additional campaign finance disclosures for super PACs, labor unions and corporations. Republicans, by contrast, tend to be more in favor of a free market approach.
These more general philosophies may be reflected in the parties’ use of generative AI for political advertising, something about which voters are worried. Polling shows broad support for more regulation, with 78% of registered voters favoring a ban on AI content that makes deceptive claims about candidates.
Disclaimers all over the map

AI-modified videos of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries posted by President Donald Trump were displayed at the White House in October 2025. (Alex Wong/Getty Images News via Getty Images)Because regulation of AI in advertising depends on a patchwork of state legislation, many of these ads are not required to disclose the use of AI. This lack of disclaimers makes tracking AI use in ads challenging. Our team has relied on media coverage and trained student coders to flag ads that are potentially AI-generated.
Across 35 states, only 31% of the ads we tracked — representing 22% of the spending — disclosed the use of AI tools. The wording of these disclaimers was all over the map. For example, one Georgia ad included the disclaimer, “This video has been manipulated or generated with artificial intelligence,” while an Oklahoma ad said, “Political satire. AI-generated images do not depict actual events.” A North Carolina state Senate ad said, “You guessed it! AI was definitely used to generate these silly video clips.”
Laws don’t drive disclosure
Some advertisers voluntarily disclose the use of AI even when they are not required to do so. Sometimes, the opposite occurs — advertisers don’t include disclaimers even when state law requires them to. In fact, we’ve found that a state law that requires disclaimers on ads that use AI has very little relationship with the actual use of disclaimers.
In states without laws governing the use of AI in political ads, 32% of ads contained a disclaimer; by contrast, in states with laws governing the use of AI, 29% contained a disclaimer. This comparison, however, is not perfect, as some of the ads in our database aren’t covered by their state’s law. Some states, such as Colorado, have laws that apply only to candidate deepfakes and thus exclude other uses of AI. In other instances, such as in Louisiana, an AI law was enacted after the ad aired.
Minnesota law generally bans deepfakes in political ads, but an ad featuring synthetic video of Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan aired in May 2026 anyway. Whether it violated state law is uncertain, as the law requires that the media be “so realistic that a reasonable person would believe it depicts speech or conduct of an individual who did not in fact engage in such speech or conduct.”
Moving forward, the real policy challenge will revolve around transparency, the enforceability of existing laws and simply figuring out what type of disclosure would be helpful to voters.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Some state leaders say changes to PJM’s electric grid governance aren’t enough
description: Democratic leaders in Pennsylvania, Maryland and other states have long called for PJM Interconnection, which administers the regional electric grid, to give more weight to state voices in its decision-making.
text:
Power lines cross a field in Snyder County, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Democratic leaders in Pennsylvania, Maryland and other states have long called for PJM Interconnection, which administers the regional electric grid, to give more weight to state voices in its decision-making.
But at the conclusion of PJM’s process to reevaluate its governance structure late last month, the lawmakers leading the charge were dissatisfied with the result. Critics said that while PJM members would give states some additional say, they kept most of the decision-making authority for themselves.
“The fact that companies that benefit from the current rules get to write and approve their own reform highlights the broken system Marylanders are footing the bill for,” said Rhyan Lake, a spokesperson for Gov. Wes Moore (D).
“FERC [the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission] gave clear direction to PJM and its members to give states a real voice, but PJM’s members responded with a term sheet that stifles the states by handing those same members a veto over any proposal the states bring forward,” Lake’s statement said. “Maryland strongly rejects this move, and the PJM Board and FERC should too.”
Workers monitor grid conditions in the main control room at PJM Interconnection in Valley Forge, Pa. Credit: PJM Interconnection
PJM was reevaluating its governance structure at the direction of the FERC, after Chair Laura Swett in July urged PJM to make “meaningful” reforms amid mounting pressure from states, including a leading state in Pennsylvania, and the White House.
“I want you all to hear this plainly: If the stakeholders cannot reach a set of credible, meaningful reforms or an agreement in principle by the end of September, then this commission is not going to hesitate to use the full extent of our legal authority to implement reforms necessary to restore confidence in PJM’s governance,” Swett said at the time.
The governance decision, announced Wednesday, was “PJM’s opportunity to show that it heard Chairwoman Swett’s warning,” said Pennsylvania State Rep. Danielle Friel Otten, part of the collaborative of Democratic legislators pushing for change at PJM.
Instead, PJM members, including transmission owners and generators, gave themselves “veto power over the very decisions at issue,” Friel Otten said in a statement Thursday.
The proposal advanced by PJM members, if approved by FERC, would let the state’s executive branches participate for the first time in the Organization of PJM States, or OPSI. It is currently made up of state utility regulators — in Maryland’s case, the Public Service Commission.
But PJM’s member committee would still get to make the final decision on the filing of key documentation before FERC, under Section 205 of the Federal Power Act. And two-thirds of members would need to support a proposal from OPSI for it to move forward.
PJM members also voted Wednesday to add one state seat to their nominating committee, which decides PJM’s board members. At least one competing proposal, from PJM staff, would have added two seats for states on the nominating board, plus the opportunity for an additional independent appointee.
Maryland Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery) said the governance plan offered by PJM members made states “spectators” to the process.
A map of the United States showing the nation’s regional wholesale energy markets. PJM Interconnection includes Pennsylvania and serves 67 million customers across its 13-state territory (FERC)
“PJM’s decisions shape what families pay for electricity, whether our grid is reliable, and whether states can carry out the energy policies their residents elected them to pursue,” said Hester. “States cannot be treated as spectators in a system whose decisions have such enormous consequences for our constituents.”
Hester has been among the Maryland legislators and climate groups criticizing PJM for slowing the arrival of clean energy to the grid and inadequately managing a data center boom, which has placed immense strain on the regional grid.
Jeff Shields, a spokesman for PJM wrote that Wednesday’s vote represents “an important step in the governance reform process and reflects substantial work by PJM members and stakeholders over the past several weeks.”
“At the same time, we recognize that differences remain, particularly regarding the appropriate role of states in PJM’s governance and stakeholder processes,” Shields wrote in a statement.
“PJM will continue working with its Board, FERC, and stakeholders towards meaningful governance reforms that improve decision-making, preserve PJM’s independence, and appropriately consider the perspectives of states, members, consumers, and other stakeholders,” Shields said.
For several Maryland legislators, Wednesday’s decisions from PJM were not enough.
“We have known for a long time that PJM is controlled by the for-profit energy and transmission companies that profit by slow-walking the clean energy transition and keeping consumer prices high,” said Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery). “Today’s vote by those same members made it clear that these members are willing to vote to protect their profits, even in the face of FERC directing them to reform the system.”
Climate group the Chesapeake Climate Action Network agreed.
“PJM proved once again that its governance is broken, and FERC needs to step in and force drastic governance changes within PJM,” said Jamie DeMarco, Maryland Climate Change Commissioner. “You cannot ask a broken system whether it wants change. Change must be forced upon it.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Madison officials say city is ready to manage clerk’s maternity leave during election
description: Madison City Clerk Lydia McComas took over her job in September 2025 with the city under heavy scrutiny from state election officials after nearly 200 absentee ballots were lost during the 2024 election. During the April 2026 state Supreme Court election, 23 late arriving absentee ballots nearly weren’t counted after a staff error.  Ann Jacobs, […]
text:
Madison officials say the city is prepared to manage Clerk Lydia McComas' maternity leave during the Nov. 3 election, even with the added scrutiny that comes with recent high-profile errors. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)Madison City Clerk Lydia McComas took over her job in September 2025 with the city under heavy scrutiny from state election officials after nearly 200 absentee ballots were lost during the 2024 election. During the April 2026 state Supreme Court election, 23 late arriving absentee ballots nearly weren’t counted after a staff error. 
Ann Jacobs, a Democrat on the Wisconsin Elections Commission, said at a meeting in April that the second error was “absurd.” The two problems made the city of Madison the subject of the first two investigations ever opened by WEC. 
In June, Votebeat reported that McComas told Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway that she would “firmly address the lack of communication” that caused the mistake and the clerk’s office would have more staff in place for the August and November elections. 
But McComas will be on maternity leave during the Nov. 3 election. 
Despite McComas’ absence, city officials say the processes put in place to avoid repeated errors, additional staff and help from other city departments will be enough to smoothly manage the midterm elections and the potential scrutiny that could come from WEC or the Republican Party of Wisconsin —  whose gubernatorial candidate this year, Tom Tiffany, has previously cast doubt on election results from Wisconsin’s largest cities. 
City spokesperson Dylan Brogan said of the recent errors in Madison that the city is “confident these things won’t happen again.” 
“This is a team process that involves 2,000 people,” he said. 
In McComas’ absence, deputy clerk Kaitlyn Bernarde is running the election. Brogan said that other city staff, such as City Attorney Mike Haas, who previously served as the WEC administrator, can help fill in. 
Bernarde spent more than four years as the clerk in Wausau, a credential that convinced WEC the transition wouldn’t be a problem. 
“[McComas] hired a new deputy who was the clerk out of Wausau. Based on that we didn’t have any concerns,” Jacobs told the Wisconsin Examiner. 
In an interview with the Examiner, Bernarde said prior to the August primary elections, the clerk’s office added a staff member who is responsible for managing the thousands of absentee ballots returned to the city, which she believes will prevent any further absentee-related errors. 
“That is one of our major new changes in our office, we implemented an absentee lead position before the August election, and so we have a full time staff member who’s in charge of that, as well as additional hourly staff and other city staff who are helping to ensure that we have checks in place in the system, that we can check in at different points to make sure that we’re on track to get ballots out on time to our AM delivery, our PM delivery, as well as any late deliveries throughout the day so that way some of those similar mistakes don’t happen again.” 
Bernarde also said that the city and election staff are prepared to run the midterms under scrutiny from WEC and outside observers.
“I think Madison always kind of is under scrutiny by the state, our residents and other people who are involved in the process, and so we’ve had experience working under that kind of pressure the last couple elections,” she said. “And we all want a zero [error] election, and so we talk through that with our staff, with our poll workers to ensure that we are trained and that we document any instances that happen. Because elections involve humans and so sometimes mistakes happen but we have processes in place to confront them, minimize them and then also respond to address them appropriately after.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Supreme Court’s recent ruling on voting means Kansans should check their registration status now
description: Last month, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that election officials can remove registered voters from their voter rolls using an inaccurate system called the SAVE database. If you are removed from a voter roll, that means you are no longer registered to vote. So, when you show up to vote on or before election day, […]
text:
Poll workers help a voter on Aug. 6, 2024, at a Lawrence precinct. (Photo by Maya Smith for Kansas Reflector)Last month, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that election officials can remove registered voters from their voter rolls using an inaccurate system called the SAVE database.
If you are removed from a voter roll, that means you are no longer registered to vote. So, when you show up to vote on or before election day, you can’t vote your regular ballot. Instead, you’ll have to cast a provisional ballot, which may or may not ultimately count. Election officials do not have to inform you if you are removed — you can be taken off the list and not know until election day, when it’s too late.
The SAVE database was created by Congress for states to check the citizenship status of people requesting government benefits. The database was used for decades for its intended purpose until last year, when Trump issued Executive Order 14248. Trump directed DHS to overhaul the SAVE database to add additional personal information about us, including our confidential Social Security records. Then, Trump directed states to have their election officials run their voter rolls through the SAVE database to find voters to remove from the eligible-voter list.
A glaring problem is the SAVE database is riddled with errors. It has flagged thousands of people as potential noncitizens to be removed from the voter rolls — people who ultimately turn out to be citizens. For example, using the SAVE database, 16,00 voters in Nevada were originally flagged by DHS as noncitizens. Then, the number dwindled to 185 noncitizens, then to zero — all of the 16,000 voters flagged by SAVE were citizens eligible to vote. The database is flawed.
Trump’s executive order was challenged, and a federal judge blocked his administration from using the SAVE database to remove voters from voter-registration rolls. The judge also found that the information obtained by the Trump administration and added to the expanded database violated multiple federal laws, including privacy laws.
However, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that Trump could move forward allowing election officials to use the expanded SAVE database to remove registered voters from their voter rolls. That means the federal government can proceed to add our personal, confidential information to the database and make it available to those officials running elections.
Presumably, election officials in red states will embrace using the SAVE database. Kansas is a red state.
Election officials in blue states who resist will face enormous pressure: The federal government has conditioned federal funding on whether an election office uses the SAVE database. Trump’s executive order also directs his Department of Justice to criminally pursue election officials who allow people to vote flagged by the SAVE database, and earlier this year DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullen specifically threatened criminal charges against election officials who don’t use the database.
We are less than 40 days from the midterm election. Federal law prohibits removing voters from voter rolls less than 90 days before an election. Theoretically, then, the midterm election should be safe from mass removal of registered voters. However, that’s not to stop some election officials from trying to remove registered voters before the midterms, and the National Republican Party has taken the legal position that mass removal of voters close to an election is permissible.
We don’t know what’s going to happen to the voter roll in Kansas in the coming weeks — who will remain on the list and who has been or will be removed without notice.
So now is the time — before Oct. 13 — to check that you are still on the list of registered voters. Go to the Kansas Secretary of State’s website to confirm that you are registered to vote. Tell your family and friends to check their voter registration, too.
Amii Castle is a professor at the University of Kansas, where she teaches at the law and business schools. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate.
