name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Tom Tiffany’s dam lies
description: The flyers that arrived in mailboxes in Oneida County, Wisconsin, just days before the April 1, 2014, county board elections, were nothing if not alarming. “Some County Supervisors have a Dam Plan which is much more than Water Over the Dam,” they warned. “Their plan would ELIMINATE DAMS!*”  Underneath this incendiary accusation, in tiny type, […]
text:
This is one of the flyers sent to Oneida County residents in 2014The flyers that arrived in mailboxes in Oneida County, Wisconsin, just days before the April 1, 2014, county board elections, were nothing if not alarming. “Some County Supervisors have a Dam Plan which is much more than Water Over the Dam,” they warned. “Their plan would ELIMINATE DAMS!*” 
One of the flyers sent to Oneida Co. residents in 2014
Underneath this incendiary accusation, in tiny type, was this asterisked elaboration: “*During the amendment process to the county master plan, Supervisor Martini proposed the removal of dams in Oneida County. The proposal did not advance.” The flyers, otherwise identical, each bore the names and photos of one of the four county board candidates who would heroically “Stop Their Dam Plan!”
Dams are critical infrastructure in northern Wisconsin, essential for lakefront homes and resorts, boating, fishing and other outdoor recreation. To seek their wholesale eradication, as Oneida County Board Supervisor Bob Martini allegedly did, is akin to proposing the expulsion of the Green Bay Packers. A 2013 report counted 42 dams in Oneida County, about half described as large, and half as small, some privately owned and some owned by utility companies, towns, the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, and the county itself. 
In the April 1 election, two targeted incumbents were defeated. Martini lost badly to challenger Robb Jensen, 213 to 128 votes, and Supervisor Candy Sorensen lost to challenger Lance Krolczyk by fewer than a dozen votes. A third incumbent, Bob Mott, beat a challenger by a narrow margin, while a fourth targeted candidate, Alan VanRaalte, won election to an open seat.
In February 2015, I wrote a two–part report on this matter for the Wisconsin Center for Investigative Journalism, now Wisconsin Watch, where I worked as a writer and editor. I noted that both Martini and Sorensen blamed the flyers for their defeats, and all four targeted contenders said the representations in the flyers were false. 
Martini, a former rivers protection coordinator for the state DNR, told me he had “never made an amendment or proposal to remove dams in Oneida County” and does not support a policy of doing so. He noted that counties don’t even have this authority, adding “It’s just wrong to lie to try to get elected.” Sorensen said that, during her time as a county board member, “there has never been any discussion or plan on removing Oneida County dams.” Mott and VanRaalte likewise denied any knowledge of a dam-removal plan, with VanRaalte exclaiming, “I live on a lake that’s created by a dam!”
What makes this story significant 12 years after the fact is that the flyers were produced with input from a Republican state senator who went on to become a member of the U.S. House of Representatives and is now his party’s nominee in the race for Wisconsin governor. His name is Tom Tiffany.
Tiffany’s explanation
When I interviewed Tiffany in 2015, he admitted to me that he helped craft the wording of this flyer, as well as another flyer aimed at boosting the candidacies of the same four candidates by accusing the county board of wanting to sell a county building at a substantial loss. He told me he was acting not in his capacity as a state senator but as a resident of Oneida County: “I care about my county. It’s important to be engaged.”
Tiffany provided a convoluted explanation for why the mailing, disclaimed by all four targeted candidates, was somehow still true. He argued that besides playing an “instrumental” role in past DNR dam removal projects, Martini served on the board on the River Alliance of Wisconsin, which Tiffany said is “associated with” a national group called American Rivers, which has “a bias toward removing dams.” The folks at the River Alliance said the two groups had no formal ties.
Tiffany also claimed that, during discussions on a county land-use plan, Martini had offered “some wording that was favorable to dam removal when possible.” Jensen, the challenger who beat Martini, also latched onto this thin reed for alleging that some board members had a plan to eliminate the county’s dams, saying a draft land-use plan favored by Martini included this language: “Support dam/drainage way repair and removal where appropriate.” Martini said he had no role in crafting this language, which was removed when some towns objected.
In a recent email exchange, Martini elaborated on the allegation that precipitated his electoral defeat: “The flyer said there was a plan to remove all the dams in Oneida County. There was no such plan. Even if there was a plan I would have opposed it on several grounds.” He went on to list some examples of dam-removal efforts he opposed during his time at the DNR.
DOJ investigation
In August 2014, a group formed in response to the flyers, Citizens for Democracy in Oneida County, filed a complaint against Tiffany and others with the state Government Accountability Board, an entity which at that time oversaw state election laws. The complaint alleged more than 70 violations of state elections laws, most dealing with whether the mailings met requisite disclosure rules and reporting requirements. It also accused Sen. Tiffany of causing “the dissemination of improper campaign information.”
The GAB declined to investigate, saying it defers to county district attorneys to investigate and prosecute such matters. And so the group sent its complaint to then-Oneida County DA Michael Schiek, who forwarded it to the state Justice Department, then headed by Republican Attorney General Brad Schimel. “We have received the information and it is under review,” DOJ spokeswoman Anne Schwartz told me in January 2015.
Recently, in response to an open records request and some prodding, the DOJ released to me its 91-page file on the case and associated documents. These records show that Special Agent Loreen Glaman was assigned in April 2015 to investigate the allegations, She interviewed at least a half-dozen people, including all four of the candidates the flyers were meant to assist. Tiffany himself does not appear to have been interviewed, but his role was described by Jensen, who “explained that Tom Tiffany approached him and suggested a mailing” and “assisted in designing the flyer.”
On July 15, 2015, Assistant Attorney General Jeffrey M. Gabrysiak wrote a “closeout of investigation” memorandum to Assistant Attorney General Roy Korte. The memo says the investigation found that while “some of the conduct in question appeared to constitute technical violations of the state’s election laws,” none appeared to be deliberate. Specifically, Gabrysiak concluded the flyers’ almost microscopic and bizarrely misspelled disclosure — “Authoized and pad for by candidate” — fell short of what the law requires, which is to include the name of the candidate or committee in this wording.
But Gabrysiak said the more significant allegations reported by Citizens for Democracy in Oneida County “lacked merit,” calling the one exception regarding requisite disclosure “minor” and “likely attributable to a lack of knowledge regarding campaign law or simple inadvertence.” He shrugged off the complaint’s allegations of untruthfulness, saying “Whether false statements have been made in campaign fliers is a subject of debate.”
Nonetheless, Gabrysiak recommended and ultimately sent warning letters to the four candidates, saying they “failed to properly name the sponsoring candidate or committee as required by law.” The letters said that while this failure was likely not intentional, the candidates would not be given “the benefit of the doubt as you were in this situation” should they again run for office. “This letter is meant to put you on notice that you will be expected [to] make yourself familiar with, and comply with, all applicable campaign laws and that failure to do so will subject you to criminal prosecution.” 
Far from the truth
What is most remarkable about this episode is the vastness of the gulf between the truth and what was stated in the flyers that Tiffany instigated and helped craft. While it may not rival other concerns about Tiffany, including his efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election results, Tiffany’s actions in connection with these flyers raise serious concerns about his honesty and integrity. 
The record shows that Tiffany set out, with some success, to kneecap candidates for local office with the blatantly untrue accusation that they had a “plan … to ELIMINATE DAMS” in Oneida County. And he stuck to this fabrication even after it was pointed out that none of the targeted candidates favored any such thing.
At the time I wrote about this episode, I remember being shocked by Tiffany’s apparent disregard for the truth, which I considered extraordinary. It was my impression, based on decades of reporting, that people in public office rarely say things that are flat-out and demonstrably untrue, as Tiffany did in this case. There is — or at least there was, back in the days before Donald Trump — too much danger that outright lies will be exposed and consequences will ensue. And indeed, the wounds opened by Tiffany’s conduct prompted some members of Oneida County to file a complaint that led to official investigation, however unsuccessful it proved to be.
In his current campaign for governor, Tiffany has also displayed a predilection for dishonesty. For instance, Tiffany has sought to distance himself from Trump’s wildly unpopular war in Iraq, saying it’s time to wrap things up, when in fact Tiffany has voted five times against resolutions to end the war. 
Tiffany, to his discredit, has recently been airing an ads blaming Crowley for allowing a county jail inmate to download child pornography. It features Crowley’s face alongside text that proclaims “Used the tablet to access child pornography,” as though it were Crowley who was doing the accessing.

But even this ad is arguably more defensible than the flyers that Tiffany devised in 2014; the county jail does have a program to provide tablets to inmates, some of whom got busted for misusing the privilege. The fairness of blaming Crowley for this is debatable, but at least the criticism is based on something that actually happened, unlike the plan to eliminate dams.
I suspect the current ads were created with input from campaign professionals who are mindful of just how far they can push the boundaries of campaign speech, while the 2014 flyers reflected Tiffany’s own unchecked inclination to deceit. Maybe that’s why he is no longer interested in trying to defend them. Tiffany’s campaign did not respond to requests for comment.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: How the Scarborough ICE facility is feeding the nationwide detention apparatus
description: The U.S. Immigration and Custom Enforcement facility in Scarborough had been set up as an administrative facility. But more detentions are happening there this year, including overnight, often just the first stop for people being detained in multi-state stays.  “This is one piece of the machine,” said Ruben Torres, advocacy and policy manager for the […]
text:
Dozens of people braved the rain outside the July 29 Scarborough town council meeting to protest the ICE facility in the town. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/ Maine Morning Star)The U.S. Immigration and Custom Enforcement facility in Scarborough had been set up as an administrative facility. But more detentions are happening there this year, including overnight, often just the first stop for people being detained in multi-state stays. 
“This is one piece of the machine,” said Ruben Torres, advocacy and policy manager for the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition.
The latest detention data obtained by the Deportation Data Project through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit paints a more complete picture of how the role of the short-term processing facility has changed under President Donald Trump’s second term. 
Unlike many other states, Maine does not have a standalone ICE detention center. The Scarborough facility is intended for routine check-ins and has just three small, short-term holding cells. This has meant local jails were often relied on for detentions — that is until last January when ICE pulled its detainees from the state’s largest jail in a rebuke to the sheriff, after he criticized the detention of one of his employees.
According to the data available through early August, detentions in the Scarborough facility increased after that change and now more directly align with overall apprehensions made by ICE in the state. 
More ICE arrests so far this year in Maine than previous two combined, data show

Eight people were held in the Scarborough facility overnight in 2026. That’s an increase from four in 2025 and zero in both 2024 and 2023, which is based on the number of stints listed between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., according to an analysis by the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition. 
Scarborough residents have requested the town look into whether ordinances and zoning are consistent with what is happening at the facility in practice. Last month, the town committee submitted a proclamation calling for Maine’s congressional delegation to review the facility and consider alternatives. 
Legality aside, Torres said the increase in overnight holds is particularly notable because it shows that increased demand has altered how the facility is used. 
Most people detained at the Scarborough facility are moved within six hours and taken out of state. The data also show that people who come through Scarborough are being moved much more frequently.
Two years ago, the average length of time between transfers was 46 days. Now, it’s an average of 12.6 days in a single facility during a detention stay, which often includes stints at multiple facilities.
“That makes it a lot harder for people to be able to secure legal counsel and to be able to get ahold of their loved ones,” Torres said. 
Overall in 2026, people processed out of the Scarborough facility had stints in a total of 30 other facilities in 11 other states. While detainees in the Scarborough facility used to stay in Maine, now they are mostly transferred to Massachusetts and New Hampshire, before often being sent to facilities in the South. 
“Those regions are typically much more conservative in their immigration court, which means that they have a higher chance to have claims denied and also have more rapid mega master hearings,” Torres said, referring to the bundling of immigration court cases — sometimes more than 100 at a time — into a single docket, which the Trump administration began doing in the spring to speed up proceedings.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Tribal communities respond to reports of euthanized wolf pack
description: The Great Lakes Indian Fish & Wildlife Commission is condemning what it calls a lack of communication between state agencies and tribal communities after nine wolves were trapped and euthanized in Price County. In a press release, the commission described the wolves as a pack consisting of four pups, three yearlings, and two adults.  “This […]
text:
A wolf makes its way across a road in Yellowstone National Park. (Jacob W. Frank/Courtesy of the U.S. National Park Service)The Great Lakes Indian Fish & Wildlife Commission is condemning what it calls a lack of communication between state agencies and tribal communities after nine wolves were trapped and euthanized in Price County. In a press release, the commission described the wolves as a pack consisting of four pups, three yearlings, and two adults. 
“This action damages existing relationships and fractures trust,” said GLIFWC Executive Administrator Jason Schlender in a statement. The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources said late last week that the wolves posed a threat to humans following incidents reported in July 2025 and August 2026. Non-lethal measures were unsuccessful in deterring the wolves, a DNR spokesperson said, according to Wisconsin Public Radio.
“We remind the WDNR and USDA Wildlife Services to involve GLIFWC and its member tribes in the decision-making process,” Schlender said in his statement. Wolves represent powerful symbols, spirits and teachers for many tribal communities. “Simply handing us the remains of our relatives after killing them does not constitute meaningful consultation.”
In 2021, when the DNR held a controversial wolf hunt, tribal communities opted not to hunt wolves on their lands. A quota of 200 wolves had been set by the DNR, a certain portion of which was allocated to tribal communities. Hunters in the rest of the state exceeded the quota in less than three days. 
The killing of the nine wolves represents the first time wolves were killed by officials in Wisconsin since a 2022 court ruling returning the animals to the Endangered Species List.
Earlier this month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to remove the gray wolf from the federal endangered species list. 
Wolves have come into conflict with rural and farming communities in Wisconsin, killing livestock and pets and triggering a campaign to restart Wisconsin’s wolf hunt. Wolf attacks on humans are rare, and only two fatal wolf attacks on humans have been documented in the last 20 years. 
Randy Johnson, the DNR’s large carnivore specialist, told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel that efforts to chase off the wolves using sound, lights and hazing were unsuccessful, and that “reports demonstrated a pattern of behavioral escalation, with the wolves showing less response to hazing and more acclimation to human presence.”
Investigative reports obtained by the Wisconsin Examiner describe three separate complaints made in August. The complaints describe wolves, sometimes collared, coming within close proximity of properties, such as in yards, driveways, or grassy areas. One of the reports mentioned chicken depredations. Another report stated that a wolf had come within 20 yards of a man mowing brush on his tractor in an effort to deter the wolves. The third report mentioned a person who saw a wolf near  five-gallon bait bucket for bears. The reports described the wolves as unafraid of people, and said efforts to deter them had been ineffective.
The Great Lakes Indian Fish & Wildlife Commission states that it was left out of the decision to euthanize the wolves, and that the Wisconsin DNR and federal government had met multiple times since 2025. “At no time during that period did WDNR or federal representatives contact GLIFWC staff to inform them of reported threats, share data, or provide decision-making criteria, bypassing consultation with GLIFWC and its member tribes,” the commission stated. 
It added that courts have ruled that the state of Wisconsin is required to co-manage resources within ceded Indigenous territories, such as those where the nine wolves were killed. This cooperation was reaffirmed in an executive order from Gov. Tony Evers in 2019, directing state agencies to consult with tribal governments on “matters that may directly or indirectly impact tribal nations.”
The commission says in its statement that the gray wolf is  known to the the Lake Superior Ojibwe as Ma’iingan, is considered a clan relative, and is a key cultural figure that has been mistreated and misunderstood. 
“People are often afraid of wolves, and wolves are too often mischaracterized,” said Conrad St. John, St. Croix tribal chairman and Voigt Intertribal Task Force chair. “Our elders relay that our communities have co-existed with Ma’iingan since the very beginning and we still don’t have any documented cases of attacks on humans in Wisconsin.”
Alex Bohman, GLIFWC biological services director, said that wolves strengthen deer populations by removing sick, weak, or old animals. “Tribes have coexisted with wolves for hundreds of years and can bring traditional ecological knowledge, as well as western science and data to these discussions.” Bohman said that state and federal agencies should engage with the commission and its member tribes on wolf management. “Ideally, this will lead to agreement on the most appropriate course of action,” she said.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: ‘It’s complicated’: A southwest Georgia district presents both opportunity, risk for Republicans
description: At first glance, a largely rural district that stretches across 30 counties in middle and southwest Georgia might not seem like friendly turf for a Democrat. But Congressman Sanford Bishop, a moderate Albany Democrat, has comfortably fended off GOP attempts to flip the seat in recent years. Bishop has represented the 2nd Congressional District for […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Sanford Bishop speaks at a rally for U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff on Aug. 18, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderAt first glance, a largely rural district that stretches across 30 counties in middle and southwest Georgia might not seem like friendly turf for a Democrat.
But Congressman Sanford Bishop, a moderate Albany Democrat, has comfortably fended off GOP attempts to flip the seat in recent years. Bishop has represented the 2nd Congressional District for more than three decades and is currently the longest-serving member of Georgia’s congressional delegation. The 79-year-old is expected to win another two-year term this fall.
Bishop is also the only Georgia Democrat to represent a congressional district that falls outside of metro Atlanta, and his district’s location, bordered by Republican-controlled districts to the north and east, makes it a prime candidate for partisan gerrymandering. 
US Supreme Court limits use of race in congressional district remaps, diluting Voting Rights Act

Earlier this year, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp urged lawmakers to redraw the state’s political maps ahead of the 2028 election after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling weakened part of the Voting Rights Act, and the 2nd Congressional district was widely seen as the likeliest target. Republican leaders in the Georgia Legislature ultimately backtracked on those redistricting plans, but lawmakers could still decide to redraw the boundaries in order to make Bishop’s district more friendly to a Republican candidate.
However, residents of Bishop’s district from across the political spectrum say drawing Bishop out of his seat is likely to be easier said than done.
‘I​​t’s not conservative, it’s not liberal’
This rural stretch of road in Lumpkin, Georgia, is part of U.S. Rep. Sanford Bishop’s southwest Georgia House district. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
If you drive through southwest Georgia, it’s hard not to notice the fields of cotton and peanuts that blanket the landscape during the growing season. Logging trucks and 18-wheelers roar by on the roadways, and vast irrigation systems stand over rows of crops. 
The district is an agricultural hotspot in the state, accounting for 19% of Georgia’s agriculture sales according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s 2022 census. 
It includes denser areas as well, encapsulating cities like Albany and most of Columbus and Macon. Though the district hasn’t been majority-Black since 2021, Black voters still make up nearly half of the district’s voting age population, according to Georgia’s legislative and congressional reapportionment office.
Seth Clark. Photo courtesy of the Clark
Seth Clark, a former Macon-Bibb County commissioner and Democrat who briefly launched a bid for lieutenant governor this year, said part of what makes the 2nd Congressional district unique is that the communities within it don’t always fall neatly along partisan lines.
“I​​t’s not conservative, it’s not liberal,” Clark said. “There’s a lot of people that are used to voting for Democrats and Republicans at the same time in this area.”
That swingy quality is perhaps more pronounced in Georgia’s 2nd Congressional District than anywhere else in the state. Of the state’s five “pivot counties” — places where voters chose former President Barack Obama in both 2008 and 2012 and President Donald Trump in 2016, according to Ballotpedia — four are in Bishop’s district. The district is also home to two of five Georgia counties that backed both Republican Gov. Brian Kemp and Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock in 2022, according to results from the secretary of state’s office.
The appetite for moderate politics is present even among loyal party members. At a rally for U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff in Columbus, real estate agent and Greater Beallwood Baptist Church pastor Adrian Chester said members of his community are increasingly squeezed by rising costs of living that stem from tariffs, increased gas prices and mounting cost of groceries. 
The district is one of the poorest in Georgia, with a median income of under $52,000 and 17% of families falling below the federal poverty level, according to the Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey. That makes the rising cost of living all the more keenly felt here. 
Democrats in the area, Chester said, should keep their focus on affordability issues and stay away from hot-button intra-party divides over ideology. 
“It’s time for us to move away from this whole ‘democratic socialism,’ things of that nature,” he said. “Let’s not be distracted. Don’t allow the Republican Party to dictate what our talking points are and what’s important to our people.”
Philip Kurland, owner of the political memorabilia store Plains Trading Post, poses for a photo on Aug. 19, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
Philip Kurland, a Plains resident who runs a political merchandise store called Plains Trading Post in the late President Jimmy Carter’s hometown, said the region boasts a number of politicians who enjoy cross-party support because of their strong presence in the community and responsiveness to their constituents’ needs.
“We want people that represent us and really don’t care if they’re Republican or Democrat,” Kurland said.
‘A true moderate’ 
A lawyer by training and self-proclaimed “city boy,” Bishop acknowledged that he had a lot to learn when he was first elected to represent the district in 1992. He has since become the dean of Georgia’s congressional delegation.
U.S. Rep. Sanford Bishop attends the 35th Anniversary celebration of the Macon Black Pages at the Tubman Museum on Aug. 18, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
A member of the centrist “blue dog Democrat” caucus, which emphasizes fiscal responsibility, Bishop has championed Democratic causes while also breaking with his party at times.
“Congressman Bishop is a true moderate, and he’s been a true moderate his entire tenure in Congress,” said Andra Gillespie, an associate professor of political science at Emory University.
Bishop’s congressional office did not respond to multiple interview requests.
Bishop is also a ranking member of an appropriations subcommittee focused on agriculture and rural development, and his longstanding relationships and institutional knowledge in Congress have allowed him to direct funds and resources to the district. During his tenure in office, Bishop has secured over a billion dollars in federal grants and loans for local communities across southwest Georgia, his office boasts on his website.
“I promised in 1992, that I would be like a sponge,” he told a crowd at the American Peanut Shellers pre-harvest meeting in Albany last month. “I would soak up that information and try to use it and arm myself so that I could be your advocate.” 
“You have helped me, and I am grateful,” he added.
That’s not to say that he hasn’t had bruising re-election fights. In 2010, he narrowly beat Republican challenger Mike Keown with 51.4% of the vote, the closest margin in his career. In 2022, he survived another tough contest after the district was redrawn by the GOP-controlled Legislature to be slightly more favorable for a Republican candidate, but he ultimately defeated Republican Chris West with nearly 55% of the vote. He will face Republican Matt Day in November. 
Part of Bishop’s success as a congressman, Clark said, is likely due to how attentive he is to the needs of his district, especially among constituents whose concerns are often less “nationalized” than those in other parts of Georgia.
“You’re not going to turn on MSNBC tonight and see Sanford Bishop on there,” Clark said. “But you might go to the high school football booster club, and he might be there. And that really matters.”
A deep knowledge of agriculture and the needs of farmers is also key to representing the district. Jimmy Wilson, a senior vice president at AB&T bank who attended the American Peanut Shellers’ meeting, said farmers across the state were desperately waiting on Congress to pass a long-overdue update to the farm bill, which he said would help stabilize farmers’ income amid rising costs, and modernize pricing standards that he says haven’t been adjusted in roughly 30 years.
US House passes ‘skinny’ farm bill that keeps big GOP cuts to food assistance

“We’re still working under a farm bill that was designed in 2018, so we need a current farm bill with current price support structures,” he said.
Bishop was one of only 14 Democrats who crossed party lines to advance the bill out of the House, and the only Democrat in Georgia to do so. The bill is now tied up in the U.S. Senate. 
Sandra Sallee, the Grady County Democratic Party chair, said that even people in her deep-red area can appreciate the work Bishop has done to bring funding and resources to the area.
“I think that there are people who grudgingly give him their respect, if not for his political leanings, but for the fact that they see, ‘oh, we got our street paved because Democrats worked for it and Sanford Bishop worked for it,’” Sallee said.
Signs mark a town square in Cuthbert, Georgia. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
State Rep. Gerald Greene, a Cuthbert Republican who has represented his southwest Georgia House District since 1983, said he has often worked with Bishop to help address the concerns of their shared constituents.
“Whatever benefits the people, then it benefits both of us,” he said. “It’s real easy to work with someone that has been involved in government as long as he has.”
What would it mean for the district to be redrawn?
Cheers erupted at the state Capitol when Speaker Jon Burns, a Newington Republican, announced at a press conference this summer that Republicans would not move forward at that time with redrawing political maps for the 2028 election as instructed by the governor. 
Georgia Republican lawmakers drop plans to redistrict, citing pending legal cases

The potential for redistricting intensified after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling earlier this year diluted a key provision of the 1965 Voting Rights Act by ruling that plaintiffs must prove that there was “intentional racial discrimination” in order to get gerrymandered districts overturned. 
Though redistricting is generally conducted once every 10 years following the U.S. census, that decision kicked off a spate of mid-cycle redistricting among Southern states seeking to pass maps that were more favorable to Republican candidates. 
In Georgia, those efforts have so far been unsuccessful. But Democrats quickly cautioned that the decision should be seen more as a delay than a cancellation. 
“I think most people presume that we are going to go back into special session after the election is over,” said Rep. Michelle Au, a Johns Creek Democrat. 
Rep. Michelle Au. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Republican state lawmakers, she added, likely held off on their plans to avoid energizing Democratic voters by redrawing the maps ahead of a big election. But depending on how the election results play out, lawmakers could call another special session to address redistricting after the midterms or take it up during next year’s regularly scheduled legislative session, which begins in January.
“I have no doubt that they are going to do it because why wouldn’t they, right?” Au said. “I think the only question mark for most people is just when.”
Federal appeals court voids ruling that Georgia’s political maps violated Voting Rights Act

For now, all eyes are on the courts. Last month, 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals sent a 2021 lawsuit over Georgia’s legislative and congressional maps back to a federal district court, ordering the judge to reexamine the case in light of the new Supreme Court precedent. 
Multiple political science experts and voting rights advocates say it seems likely that Republicans in the state Legislature will attempt to redraw the maps again ahead of the 2028 election, which could include newfound efforts to target Bishop’s seat and draw Black voters into other districts. 
“Although it’s not technically competitive, it’s the most competitive one we have in Georgia as a congressional district,” said Ken Lawler, the chair of Fair Districts Georgia, an organization that advocates for a nonpartisan redistricting process. 
During the 2024 general election, the most recent contest in which Bishop was on the ballot, he won re-election with over 56% of the vote. That margin, and the district’s location between other Republican-controlled districts, Lawler added, make it “a target for manipulation” which could ultimately weaken the electoral power of Black voters in southwest Georgia.
‘Prepared for the worst’: Black lawmakers brace for losses as Georgia GOP eyes new political maps

The new Supreme Court precedent also makes it much more difficult for courts to intervene in gerrymandering disputes.
“Because of the old interpretations of Section Two of the Voting Rights Act, people were going to be somewhat loath to redraw those district lines because you could get credibly accused of trying to disenfranchise Black voters,” Gillespie said. “Right now, you can change the lines on account of partisanship and not really be held to account about what the racial impact would be on African American voters.”
Kurland, the owner of Plains Trading Post, said he doubted Bishop would be easily defeated, comparing him to figures like the state lawmaker Greene, who have repeatedly survived tough election cycles in districts not seen as favorable to their party.
“Bishop has really come through for this district,” he added. “Even if they reapportioned it, I can’t imagine him not carrying it away.”
What’s next for redistricting? 
Burns, the state House speaker, said in a statement that lawmakers have not considered any proposals for reapportionment, but left the door open on redistricting.
“Given recent court decisions and ongoing litigation, we are continuing to examine the legal landscape not only here in Georgia, but across the country,” he said.
But Charles Bullock, a political scientist at the University of Georgia, who has written a book on redistricting, says Bishop’s district may not end up being the GOP’s top target.
“These are rural folks who very much appreciate what Bishop has done and the influence he has,” Bullock said. In his conversations with House leadership, he added, “at least one of them has said, rather than going after Bishop, maybe Republicans would look to trying to pick up a district in metro Atlanta.”
If Republicans do push forward with redistricting efforts, they will have to consider all of these factors, and may even need to drum up enthusiasm within their own ranks. 
Rep. Mike Cheokas. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
State Rep. Mike Cheokas, an Americus Republican who represents a handful of rural counties just south of Columbus that fall within Bishop’s congressional district, expressed relief that Republican leadership in the state House and Senate chose not to pursue redistricting during the June special session.
“This is an election year, and I’ve got opposition,” he said. “I sure didn’t want to be in Atlanta drawing district lines when I needed to be out campaigning.”
While Cheokas said he didn’t feel there was much appetite for redistricting during the special session, he didn’t rule it out for later this year.
“I’m not saying that it ain’t going to happen in the future, but I am saying that when it does happen — if it does happen — it’s complicated.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Judge dismisses lawsuit against Tosa cops for 2022 shooting
description: A federal judge has dismissed a civil rights lawsuit stemming from the non-fatal shooting of Damiso Lee by Wauwatosa police officers in April 2022. In a court document filed in late September, U.S. District Judge Brett Ludwig said that among the reasons he issued the summary judgement were the fact that  Lee was armed with […]
text:
The Wauwatosa Police Department (Photo | Isiah Holmes)A federal judge has dismissed a civil rights lawsuit stemming from the non-fatal shooting of Damiso Lee by Wauwatosa police officers in April 2022. In a court document filed in late September, U.S. District Judge Brett Ludwig said that among the reasons he issued the summary judgement were the fact that  Lee was armed with a handgun, disobeyed officer commands and attempted to run. 
A month before the shooting Lee, who was 17 years-old at the time, had reported his car stolen to the Milwaukee Police Department. Lee never called the department to say that he found the car, so it was still listed as stolen when Wauwatosa officer Evan Olson noticed it driving around one evening.
The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
 “The [automatic license plate reader] alert was categorized as ‘high,’ indicating that the vehicle had been involved in a felony offense,” a court document detailing Ludwig’s reasons for dismissing the case stated. The document mentions that Lee was returning home after picking up a Doordash order when he drove past Olson. He acknowledged in a deposition that he was in possession of a Glock Model 22 handgun. 
After his squad car’s automatic license plate reader system flagged the car, Olson radioed dispatch and followed Lee before deciding to conduct a felony traffic stop. He requested another nearby officer, Dexter Schleis, assist him. Lee drove into an alley behind an apartment complex and parked. “Officer Olson observed Lee open and close the driver’s door without exiting, turn the engine off, and then open the driver’s door a second time and leave it open,” Ludwig wrote. 
Body camera footage released by the Wauwatosa Police Department in 2022 shows that Olson got out of his squad and told Lee to “show me your hands” as Lee exited his own vehicle, holding the food container he’d picked up. Olson told Lee to stop and to not reach for his gun, the outline of which he said he could see in Lee’s pocket. In a report from district attorney’s office, explaining the decision not to charge Olson, Olson describes Lee as wearing a black hooded sweatshirt with a Glock logo in large lettering on the front. 
The footage shows that Lee dropped the food and turned to run away. Schleis was waiting on the other end of the alley. Olson yelled that Lee was armed and as he ran, Lee fell causing his gun to fall out of his pocket. He got back up, picked up the gun, and both Olson and Schleis fired. 
A Wauwatosa police squad on the scene of a officer-involved shooting. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
In his decision to dismiss, Ludwig states that while the officers believed that “their use of deadly force was objectively reasonable under the circumstances,” Lee argued that it was not reasonable because he was running away. “Lee’s position is contradicted by the evidence presented, including video recordings of the incident,” Ludwig wrote. The judge questioned whether Olson and Schleis “reasonably believed Lee posed a threat of death or serious bodily harm based on the information they knew at the time.” 
Ludwig ruled that the license plate reader flagging Lee’s car, Olson confirming the car’s stolen car status through dispatch, and Lee’s decision to flee while armed rather than explain that it was his car led to the shooting. “Indeed, the officers gave Lee multiple opportunities to surrender before resorting to deadly force, including after he retrieved the handgun,” Ludwig wrote. 
The judge discounted arguments by Lee’s attorney, William Sulton, that video shows that Lee was facing away from officers and running when he was shot. Ludwig wrote that Lee “changed directions multiple times during his brief attempt to escape.”
Attorneys offer opposing perspectives
Sulton wrote in an email statement to the Wisconsin Examiner that Lee is considering his options for appeal but that no decision has been made. “Suing law enforcement officers is not like suing other members of society because they have qualified immunity,” Sulton wrote. “I disagree with the judge’s conclusions about what the videos show. The videos show Damiso running away from the officers. The judge saw things differently and ruled that Damiso was running towards one of the officers, justifying lethal force.” Sulton continued, “there are too many cases of officers shooting civilians who are running away from them. This will continue until different decisions are made.”
Attorney Jasmyne Baynard, who represented Olson and Schleis, wrote that she disagrees with Sulton. “Plaintiff’s counsel took no depositions and did not serve any discovery,” Baynard wrote in an emailed statement to the Examiner, noting that Ludwig’s dismissal relied on “substantive law” rather than qualified immunity. “The idea that a police officer is required to wait until a suspect points or shoots a gun before they can act in justified self-defense is contrary to the law and common sense. Police officers are also not mind-readers and can only respond to a suspect’s action.”
The Wauwatosa Police Department (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
The Examiner asked Baynard whether there was anything the officers and Lee could have done differently.
Baynard said that Olson was not mistaken in stopping Lee because his car had been reported stolen and was still flagged that way in a police database. She added that “there is something Lee could have done differently —  he could have not gotten high, illegally possessed a firearm, and ignored multiple clear commands to STOP, not reach for a gun and most importantly AFTER dropping the gun, he could have just continued to run off and not picked it back up. No rational and objective review of the video (or Lee’s sworn testimony and recorded statements) supports the view that he was not a threat.”  
Lee being under the influence is not mentioned in Ludwig’s dismissal, Wauwatosa Police Chief James MacGillis’ summary of the incident, or the district attorney’s decision not to charge. A check of online circuit and federal court records also turned up no charges or citations listed under Lee’s name. 
Baynard stressed that “of course we should question an officer’s actions in these situations — in Wisconsin that is done in EVERY officer-involved critical incident.” In 2025, Baynard helped defend former officer Joseph Mensah during a federal civil trial over the shooting of Alvin Cole, Mensah’s third fatal shooting in five years. Olson and Schleis were called as witnesses during those trials, which ended in two hung juries before a confidential settlement was reached. The 17-year-old ran from police while carrying a handgun, but officers also provided contradictory statements about what happened. Mensah recently received $95,000 from the city of Wauwatosa for a PTSD claim.
Baynard wrote in a statement that “cops are subject to the court of public opinion and unable to respond. But we should also start questioning the behavior of the public. Until we stop forgiving criminal behavior, we will unfortunately continue to see cases like this where officers are forced to make difficult decisions so that they get to go home to their families.”
In 2022, after the district attorney decided not to issue charges in Lee’s shooting, Chief MacGillis spoke to the gravity and responsibility that comes with an officer’s decision to use force. “We all experience trauma when an officer-involved shooting occurs,” said MacGillis. “The injured subject, the subject’s family, the officers involved, the police department, and the community as a whole.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio Democratic candidates Amy Acton and Marcy Kaptur make “anti-transgender remarks”, face backlash
description: Ohio Democratic candidate for governor Dr. Amy Acton and Ohio Democratic U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur have faced backlash from comments they have made about transgender people during the lead up to Election Day.  Acton said she agreed with a U.S. Supreme Court ruling saying its constitutional for states to ban transgender women and girls from […]
text:
(Stock Photo by Vladimir Vladimirov/Getty Images)

Ohio Democratic candidate for governor Dr. Amy Acton and Ohio Democratic U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur have faced backlash from comments they have made about transgender people during the lead up to Election Day. 
Acton said she agreed with a U.S. Supreme Court ruling saying its constitutional for states to ban transgender women and girls from playing women’s and girl’s sports.
Kaptur has come under fire for an ad she recently put out touting her vote for H.R. 2616, which would require schools to out transgender students and jeopardizes school funding if schools “teach or advance concepts related to gender ideology.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
“I voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools because parents know what’s best for their kids, and boys should not play in girls’ sports,” Kaptur said in her ad. 
Kaptur was one of eight Democratic members of Congress to vote for the bill earlier this year, which is now in the U.S. Senate. 
“Marcy supports parents having more insight into their children’s education,” said Kylie Blitzer, spokesperson for Kaptur’s campaign, on why Kaptur voted for the bill. “That’s why she set the record straight on her vote with Republicans to give parents more say in the classroom.” 
Kaptur, the longest-serving woman in congressional history, is going up against Republican candidate Derek Merrin. Kaptur defeated former state legislator Merrin in a close race during the 2024 election.
U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-OH) speaks at a press conference urging the inclusion of the Civilian Climate Corps., a climate jobs program, in the budget reconciliation bill, outside of the U.S. Capitol on July 20, 2021 in Washington, DC. The program puts people to work by completing federally-funded green energy projects that will help communities respond to climate change. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images.)
LGBTQ+ advocacy group Equality Ohio gave Kaptur a “D” and Merrin an “F” on their candidate scorecard. 
“Transgender Ohioans should not be used as political talking points,” Equality Ohio said in a statement. 
“Ohioans are worried about rising costs, making rent, having food on their table, seeking medical care, and that’s where real leadership should be focused. Real leadership means refusing this culture war bait, not reaching for it.” 
Ohio enacted a law in 2024 that bans transgender women and girls from competing in K-12 and college sports after Republican lawmakers overturned Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine’s veto. Merrin voted in favor of the bill when he was a state representative. 

“There is no difference between whether Marcy Kaptur or Derek Merrin serves as out next Congressperson — you are both united against the LGBTQIA+ community,” Lucas County Stonewall Democrats wrote in a letter they sent Kaptur, calling on her to remove her ad.

Ohio governor race
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled over the summer that states like Ohio can continue to ban transgender women and girls from playing women’s and girl’s sports, and both Ohio candidates for governor agreed with the ruling. 
Acton told The Blade she does “not support boys playing in girls sports” and Ohio Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy said the ruling was a “win for common sense.” 
Ohio Democratic governor candidate and former director of the Ohio Department of Health, Dr. Amy Acton, looks on during a rally on April 28, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Jon Cherry/Getty Images.)
In response, Equality Ohio dropped Acton’s “A” to a “B” on their candidate scorecard.
“Equality Ohio has decreased the scores of Amy Acton and Marcy Kaptur in our 2026 Candidate Scorecard following anti-transgender remarks made by their campaigns,” Equality Ohio said in a statement. 
On her campaign website, Acton says all Ohioans deserve to be treated fairly. 
“As governor, I am committed to standing up against discrimination and ensuring that every Ohioan — including members of the LGBT community — receives equal protection under the law,” Acton’s campaign website says. 
In Ohio, 11.2% of people identify as LGBTQ+, according to a new report from the Human Rights Campaign.
Transgender issues are the latest hot-button topic in politics, said Equality Toledo Executive Director Brent Rabie. 
“For years it was gay marriage, and that was the boogeyman that everybody was trying to use,” Rabie said. “Now, they’ve targeted trans people and used them, and are doing false campaign ads. … Anytime people use any community for political points or to be a political punching bag, I think it’s dangerous.” 
Dara Adkison, Executive Director of TransOhio, said the political ads targeting transgender people are exhausting and infuriating. 
“Trans people aren’t an ideology. We’re not an issue,” Adkison said. “All issues are trans issues because trans people are just people, and Ohioans trying to exist like everyone else. To see ourselves ending up as the targeted minority group for so much of this current election cycle is a lot, to put it mildly.”
Other ads
The Senate Leadership Fund recently put out an ad saying former Democratic Ohio U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown “supports sex change surgery for kids, permanent surgical decisions with devastating consequences.”
Brown is going up against Ohio Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted in a competitive Senate race and Brown released his own ad in response. 
“Here they go again. Those same attacks against Sherrod Brown. With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about. In Ohio, it’s against the law to perform transgender surgeries on kids. That’s right. It’s illegal,” Brown’s ad said. 
PolitiFact rated the Senate Leadership Fund ad as “false” and “found no evidence that Brown has ever said he supports forcing gender-transition surgery for children.”
Gay marriage
A new Gallup poll from earlier this year shows support for gay marriage is down six percentage points from its peak in 2022 and 2023. 
Today, 65% of people support same-sex marriage compared to 71% in 2022 and 2023. 
In 2021 and 2022, 55% of Republicans said they support legal same-sex marriage, but this year that figure dropped to 37%. Democrats’ views have remained the same with 87% in favor.  
“Same-sex marriage is still legal,” Rabie said. “It’s still the law of the land. So we hope that that continues.” 
The U.S. Supreme Court legalized gay marriage in 2015 through the Obergefell v. Hodges case (which originated in Ohio), but as part of the 2022 decision that overturned Roe v. Wade’s abortion protections from the 1970s, Justice Clarence Thomas said that the Supreme Court should reconsider other landmark cases, such as Obergefell.
Ohio Equal Rights is trying to get two amendments on next year’s ballot — including one that would eliminate the same-sex marriage ban in the Ohio Constitution. 
The other amendment would add language to the state’s constitution protecting citizens from discrimination based on race, color, creed or religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression regardless of sex assigned at birth, pregnancy status, genetic information, disease status, age, disability, recovery status, familial status, ancestry, national origin, or military and veteran status.  
Follow Ohio Capital Journal Reporter Megan Henry on X or on Bluesky.
