title: Michigan’s next governor will face major challenges at the Department of Corrections
description: No matter who becomes governor in January, Michigan’s next administration will face a major corrections problem. Prison advocates and corrections union leadership might generally have very different perspectives on what changes are needed within the state’s prisons. But in conversations with the Michigan Advance, they agreed on one overarching sentiment — so[...]
text:
Michigan Department of Corrections office in Lansing. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)No matter who becomes governor in January, Michigan’s next administration will face a major corrections problem. Prison advocates and corrections union leadership might generally have very different perspectives on what changes are needed within the state’s prisons. But in conversations with the Michigan Advance, they agreed on one overarching sentiment — something has to change at the top of the Michigan Department of Corrections.
The Michigan Department of Corrections has come under bipartisan criticism from advocates and state legislators, especially in recent months — during which time five women incarcerated at Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Center, the state’s only prison for female inmates, died in a matter of months, and the Michigan Corrections Organization, an SEIU local representing Michigan’s corrections officers, noted a “significant escalation in violence, large‑scale disturbances” throughout July and August.
“The new governor and the new Department of Corrections director are going to have to have a different approach,” Hakim Crampton, the legislative liaison at Michigan Citizens for Prison Reform, said.
Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility in Saline Township, Michigan. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance
Heidi Washington has served as director of the department for over 11 years, first appointed by Republican Gov. Rick Snyder and then kept in the position by Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.
“We don’t know who’s going to be the next governor, but whether it’s Benson or James, doesn’t really matter to us,” said Byron Osborn, the president of the Michigan Corrections Organization. “We just hope whoever wins sees us over here and throws us a damn life ring because we’re going under.”
Gubernatorial candidates for both major parties — Democrat Jocelyn Benson, the current Michigan secretary of state, and Republican John James, the U.S. House representative for Michigan’s 10th Congressional District — were asked to participate in a one-on-one interview with Michigan Advance to discuss the concerns with the Department of Corrections and their plans for the department if elected in November.
Both campaigns declined to make their respective candidate available for an interview. James’ team initially scheduled an interview with the Advance, but canceled due to schedule changes and did not reschedule.
After declining to interview for this story, both candidates were sent seven written questions about their plans to address specific concerns within the Department of Corrections. The James campaign did not respond to those questions or provide any other written comment on the issue. 



Quotation







There’s no one person who is responsible for where the department is right now. So I think that a change in the director is important, but I also don’t think that just going down the current rank and file is where the next person would need to come from.


– State Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia) on the need for new leadership at MDOC


Benson shared a written statement in response, in which she said that, having visited the Women’s Huron Valley prison, “it’s clear that the Michigan Department of Corrections needs new leadership.”
“The repeated tragedies, threats to staffs’ lives, and unsafe workplace and living conditions are unacceptable. Corrections officers and incarcerated people alike deserve to work and live free from the constant threat of violence,” Benson said in an email. “As governor, I will appoint new MDOC leadership, hold them to strict accountability standards, and sit down with officers, their union, and families to hear directly what they’re facing. I will also support legislation to improve pay, pensions, and benefits so we can recruit and keep officers. My north star as governor is costs down, wages up, and rights protected, and that includes everyone involved in our corrections system.”
“It’s sad. It’s very unfortunate,” Crampton said in response to both candidates’ declining to schedule interviews on corrections issues. “Once they appoint someone, hopefully they’ll be open to some real change.”
Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia), who has been outspoken on issues especially around the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Center, said that she hopes the next administration will be “a bit more collaborative” on issues around the Department of Corrections.
She said the current administration “just does not have a willingness to address” those issues with the Legislature.
“Overall conditions need to be addressed, and I mean that in terms of the people who are incarcerated there and also staffing,” she continued, noting a bipartisan appetite in the Legislature for real reform in the department. “There’s absolutely a bipartisan consensus that things do need to change, and there’s also an awareness that there is no one single policy that is going to fix everything. This is going to be something that is going to take time. It’s going to take multiple different policies going into effect.”
State Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia) testifies to the House Oversight Committee on health and sanitation concerns at the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility. Feb. 24, 2026. | Screenshot.
Staffing shortages drive problems across MDOC
Many of the concerns raised about conditions in Department of Corrections facilities, for both those incarcerated there and the corrections officers employed there, can be traced back in some way to understaffing at MDOC facilities. 
Nearly all of the state’s correctional facilities have at least some vacancies, and some have over a quarter of their positions vacant, according to department data through May 2026.  


Osborn said that the staffing vacancy issue exacerbates all of the other problems that he has with the department.
“When you’re running a prison setting with facilities that have anywhere from 15 to 35 percent vacancy rates, you can imagine what that does to the remaining workforce that is there. They’re subject to mandatory overtime on a daily basis. Many of our officers are working 16-hour days, consecutive days in a row,” he said. “This is just not the type of work setting where you should be having exhausted, mentally fatigued, and physically fatigued staff running a prison. But that’s exactly what we’ve had for these past few years.”
That, combined with the risk of working in a potentially violent environment and a lack of substantial retirement benefits, has pushed officers out of the department and failed to attract new talent, Osborn, who has worked for the department for more than three decades, said.


Pension changes could help recruit, retain officers
A set of bills to improve the pension plan that corrections officers have access to was among the nine bills vetoed by Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in July. Although those bills have been reintroduced and passed by the state Senate, their future remains uncertain, even as the corrections union emphasizes their importance. 
“The next governor, we hope, is going to advocate for bipartisan cooperation to get something done to make it appealing to come work for the Michigan Department of Corrections again,” Osborn said, highlighting pension reform as part of that.
Benson said in a press release following Whitmer’s veto that she would sign the bills into law if elected.
“I think that that’s something that we can expect to see reintroduced early on and I would like to see that taken care of and squared away,” Pohutsky noted as a policy she would like to see the next governor prioritize early on in their administration. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Crampton added that staffing shortages also have distinct negative effects on incarcerated individuals as well, including limiting access to programs, outside exercise or even eating meals in the cafeteria as opposed to having to eat them still in a cell.
“It affects the overall operation of everything, and especially, you’ve got to be thinking about this, there are people who are incarcerated who are working their way toward their freedom, who are in necessary, essential programming,” he said. “When the institutional flow ceases to have that same speed and consistency, then it slows down their integration with the programming … their opportunity to be released.”
“The prison population is getting screwed over,” Osborn agreed. “There are things that they are required to have. They’re supposed to be able to get out to the yard and go to the rec yard. They’re supposed to be able to get on the phone and call their families. You know, they’re supposed to have day room time.”


Crampton, who has had family members working as correctional officers in MDOC facilities and other family members incarcerated in MDOC facilities, also said that the mindset within the department, of continuing the same cycles of the carceral system that have existed for decades, must change. 
“They are the ones that are responsible for the lives and safety and health of people in their system, and people in there stabbing each other, assaulting staff, killing each other, and they are not taking accountability, responsibility,” he said of the department’s leadership. “They seem to think that the design of the Department of Corrections, the way it’s been, is the way it’s going to be, and the way it has to be. And it’s not conducive to either correction staff or people returning home back to our community. We want to see advanced programming, education, vocation, treatment services. Everyone in there should be out of their cell each day involved in programming, participation, and treatment services.”
Competing views on security and violence
Osborn also said that he believes the addition of more high-security beds — the department did announce in September plans for 870 new high-security prison beds across four correctional facilities — will help in reducing violence between prisoners. 
“We’ve got all of these prisoners who normally, if the prison system was operating correctly, would be housed in a higher security level due to their misconduct reports and their bad behavior,” he said. “That’s why you see, when we report on a lot of these staff assaults and even some of the prisoner assaults, we’re saying some of these assaults, in most cases, most of them would not be occurring if the department didn’t have a security classification problem. These guys would be in single man cells at Level V, where they can’t assault anybody.”


Crampton had a different perspective on the issue, especially around solitary confinement, and a press release from Citizens for Prison Reform referenced research linking solitary confinement to worsening mental health and self-harm, without consistent evidence that it reduces prison violence.
“If they’re going to continue cycling in and out of our system, and we’re not going to solve the problem of crime in our community, then that system that is holding people is going to have to be accountable to how it operates,” Crampton said. “Because it’s returning people back to our society, who are scorned, torn, traumatized, broken, and unable to pick their lives back up, and help being contributed to our society. They are having an impact on families, on children, and the correction guards, likewise, who work and operate.”
Neither candidate has indicated who they might tap to lead the department if elected. Pohutsky, however, emphasized that a need for a change in leadership might require pulling in a director who is not currently a part of the department. 
“I’ve been pretty vocal about the need for a change in leadership. That obviously includes the director, but is not necessarily limited to the director,” she said. “There’s no one person who is responsible for where the department is right now. So I think that a change in the director is important, but I also don’t think that just going down the current rank and file is where the next person would need to come from.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: The Great Plains face a surprising threat: Too many trees
description: This story was produced by Grist and co-published with the Nebraska Examiner. To really understand what’s going on in the Nebraska Sandhills, Shelly Kelly told me, it’s helpful to see it from the air. From the window of her father’s Bonanza A36, we looked out over the heart of one of the most rural landscapes […]
text:
A red cedar grows near Wauneta, Nebraska. (Getty Images via Grist)This story was produced by Grist and co-published with the Nebraska Examiner.
To really understand what’s going on in the Nebraska Sandhills, Shelly Kelly told me, it’s helpful to see it from the air. From the window of her father’s Bonanza A36, we looked out over the heart of one of the most rural landscapes in the United States. The Sandhills are a 19,500 square-mile swath of grassy dunes embellished with grazing cattle, serpentine rivers and sunflowers. 
Kelly has spent her life on the prairies of the High Plains. As a child, she made bouquets of flowering grasses and hunted for mudpuppies in the interdunal buffalo wallows on her parents’ ranch. Now a rancher herself, she’s trying to preserve the landscape she loves against the usual suspects — overgrazing and overharvesting — and one surprising new threat: trees. 
She pointed out my window to the prairie below. “You can see it there,” she said, pointing to a neat grove of Juniperus virginiana, eastern red cedar, deliberately planted by ranchers to protect calving heifers from the wind. These windbreaks are standard features on the Plains. But to the south of their orderly rows, a dozen cedars have popped up in the middle of the grass, scattering across the nearby range like race-runners breaking free of the pack. 
Trees grow along the Spring Creek Prairie Audubon Center on March 18, 2024 near Lincoln, Nebraska. The Center works to conserve the tallgrass prairie ecosystem and associated wildlife. (David Madison / Getty Images via Grist)
This spreading of trees is known as woody encroachment — or the “green glacier,” as some call it, evoking the slow creep of tree species over grasslands — and it’s got ecologists and ranchers of the Plains on high alert. 
“We’re losing our biodiversity,” Kelly said. “We’re losing our resiliency.”
For ranchers, a woody takeover of their rangeland creates an obvious problem: less land to graze. The Texas A&M Agrilife extension estimates that woody encroachment over the 10 Great Plains states represents $4 billion in lost range production. Ecologists predict biodiversity losses would affect the insects, birds and small mammals that populate the country’s remaining prairies. Everybody worries about what those thirsty trees will do to the already stressed water supply as the green glacier expands from the wetter climate in the eastern prairie states to the arid western regions. 
Prairies — on the High Plains and around the world — thrive in cycles of stability and disruption. Fire, grazing, dry seasons, and the area’s particular mix of vegetation all play a role in preserving the healthy root systems that allow a diverse mix of grasses to continue growing year after year. Some heartier grasses with root systems 20 feet deep can keep the prairie green in a drought, while healthy soil can hold dormant seeds until the conditions are right. 
Fire — both naturally occurring and prescribed burns — has long been a feature of the prairie landscape. Suppressing it is part of what has allowed woody plants to seed, spread and develop the thick bark that makes them more likely to then withstand future fires. Meanwhile, overgrazing reduces trees’ and shrubs’ grassy competition, allowing them to grow faster. Cattle and bison don’t eat the woody plants. Goats, sheep, elk and other “browsing” species don’t eat enough of them to control the spread, though some are experimenting with browsers as a component of a larger management plan. 
The Flint Hills of Kansas and Osage Hills of Oklahoma are home to two-thirds of the nation’s remaining tallgrass prairie, said Brian Obermeyer, The Nature Conservancy’s Great Plains grasslands strategy director. The persistence of the prairie in this region is largely because of the longstanding culture of prescribed burns, dating back to when Chisholm Trail cattle drives would divert their skinnier livestock to fatten up on the highly nutritious, tender, juicy grasses that grow back after a burn. Obermeyer even found a lease contract dating back to 1915 requiring the land to be burned regularly so that cattle would have access to the new growth. But in regions where that practice is not common, Obermeyer said, “Getting people comfortable with the culture of prescribed fire takes time.” 
The Sandhills in Nebraska don’t have the fire culture, though Kelly and others are trying to change that. What they do have, Kelly said, is a culture of tree-planting. 
The sun rises over the Joseph H. Williams Tallgrass Prairie Preserve in Osage County on June 03, 2026 in Pawhuska, Oklahoma. (Heather Diehl / Getty Images via Grist)
“Most of the people that settled Nebraska came from areas that were full of trees,” she said. In fact, before it was known as the “Cornhusker State” Nebraska’s official nickname was the “Tree Planter State.” It dates back to the Homestead Act of 1862, which required settlers to cultivate their land with crops or trees to establish ownership, and Nebraska’s Kinkaid Act of 1904, which offered free trees to help settlers cultivate 640-acre tracts in the state. The tradition has gone on for centuries now, and thanks to advances in horticulture, ranchers buy heartier and heartier red cedar saplings for their windbreaks, which then spread their juggernaut offspring across the plains. 
As executive director of the Sandhills Task Force, a nonprofit established 33 years ago to promote conservation and sustainable land management in the ranching industry, Kelly knows that half the battle is changing the culture. “We’re not talking about trees being bad everywhere,” she said. “But trees are not good on a prairie, especially invasive trees.” On her water bottle I spotted a sticker: Be A Leader, Cut a Cedar. 
Another cultural shift might be necessary as well, particularly for the broader conservation community. The prevailing climate wisdom has been pretty clear: Trees are good, and planting them is virtuous — the more the better. But actually, Obermeyer said, grasslands can be a more secure carbon sink than forests. A big reason for that goes back to the cycle of fire on the landscape, and the worsening threat of out-of-control wildfires that are often the result of too much fire suppression. Woody plants store most of their carbon above ground in their trunks and leaves. When they burn, all of that carbon is released, and the charred remains continue to release carbon after the initial burn. It can take years for the forest to return to its storage capacity. Grasslands store the vast majority of carbon safely underground in their deep root systems, and after a fire their stems and blades quickly rebound. 
There is evidence that the increased atmospheric carbon may be giving another advantage to woody plants, which utilize a different carbon pathway than grasses in photosynthesis, making them more efficient photosynthesizers in carbon-soaked, warm, dry air. While this means that trees may, in the short term, capture carbon more quickly, the loss of an entire ecosystem, especially one that stores carbon more securely, isn’t a good tradeoff in the long term, said Chris Helzer, Nebraska director of science and stewardship for The Nature Conservancy. 
Climate change is one of many reasons that a nonintervention strategy — letting nature take its course — won’t work on the High Plains. There are too many things in motion to simply go “hands-off.” But, really, Helzer said, grasslands as we know them have never been free of human intervention. From the time that Indigenous peoples hunted free-ranging bison, grasslands have evolved in tandem with humans, explained Helzer. The Nature Conservancy has also worked with the InterTribal Buffalo Council and Tanka Fund, to support the return of bison to the Plains along with other tribal-led efforts to restore damaged ecosystems and build management capacity. 
Over 2,000 bison, also known as American buffalo, roam in the Joseph H. Williams Tallgrass Prairie Preserve in Osage County on June 3, 2026, in Pawhuska, Oklahoma. Heather Diehl/ Getty Images via Grist
Ranchers also have a critical role to play, Helzer said. And many are playing it with gusto. Kelly’s dad, John Taylor, has had a front-row seat to his daughter’s crusade and benefited from her growing expertise. On his ranch the cedar is under control, but near the fenceline, a few of the evergreen treetops peeked over a neighboring dune, like Birnam Wood advancing on MacBeth’s Dunsinane Hill. These trees are prolific, spreading their seeds across a 200-foot radius. Seedlings grow at about a rate of 1 to 2 feet per year, and once they reach 5 feet tall, they start spreading seed in their own 200-foot radius. That said, the Sandhills are mostly lucky, Kelly said. Eastern red cedar is easy to kill. Cut it down to the root and it mostly doesn’t grow back.
Kelly has even helped Nebraskans connect to funding opportunities to clear the cedars. Through grants and fundraising, the Sandhills Task Force can help ranchers pay for up to 75% of cedar removal. The funds are stimulating a growing cedar removal industry in the region. State and federal programs will also help fund the removal — but, ironically, the same departments still subsidize tree-planting for windbreaks, Kelly said, though they are increasingly discouraging red cedars. 
The Nature Conservancy is using its preserves to test grazing patterns, new mixes of plant species and other mitigation techniques that can help private landowners across the High Plains find the right balance of grazing, burning and rewilding to keep their grasslands healthy. “To some extent, you can have a prairie that has trees,” Helzer said. “But there’s a line — when you cross that line, you have a woodland with clearings, not a grassland with trees.” 
Grassland prairies — short, mixed, tall and other types — used to stretch from Texas to the Dakotas, into Kentucky and up to the foothills of the Rockies. Only 4% of tallgrass prairies are left, making it, Obermeyer said, “the most altered landscape in North America in terms of acres lost.” At the same time, he said, places like the Flint Hills and Sandhills give him hope. More people are recognizing the subtle beauty and ecological power of the plains. 
“We can’t lose sight of the fact that we have a tremendous amount that we have the chance to preserve,” Obermeyer said. “We have a lot of opportunities to get this right.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: The promise of a free education is fundamental to our democracy
description: This commentary was originally published in the West Virginia Watch. The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia announced a lawsuit last week over the unconstitutional underfunding of public schools. I’m not exaggerating when I say this may be the most important case we have filed in my 10 years with this organization. The promise […]
text:
A boy plays with a wooden numbers puzzle. (Getty Images)This commentary was originally published in the West Virginia Watch.
The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia announced a lawsuit last week over the unconstitutional underfunding of public schools. I’m not exaggerating when I say this may be the most important case we have filed in my 10 years with this organization.
The promise of a free education is fundamental to our democracy itself. It’s so vital that it was enshrined as a right in our 1863 state Constitution, and courts have interpreted that right to mean that schools must not only be adequately funded, but also fairly funded from county to county.
And yet, West Virginia sits at or near the bottom of most national rankings. Politicians have blamed schools, teachers and parents for poor educational outcomes, when the true cause is in black and white on the balance sheets.
During the 2022-23 school year, West Virginia’s average per-pupil expenditure was $14,909 — a total that includes state, local and federal money.  While $14,909 was the reported average, the actual amount per student spent by counties ranged from a low of $12,158 in Barbour County to a high of $22,500 in Doddridge.
That gap gets even wider when you look at only the funding within the state’s control. Combined state and local education funding per pupil ranged from $10,542 in Barbour County to $24,924 in Tyler. In a system that requires that education funding be allocated fairly, some counties receive double the funding of others — not only presenting constitutional concerns, but driving averages up in a way that hides how significantly underfunded many West Virginia counties are.
Across the country, states spend more on education in counties with high rates of students with disabilities and students experiencing poverty because providing quality education to those students is often more expensive. In West Virginia, we do just the opposite: we spend less in counties with the greatest need, and more in counties with higher property wealth.
Chief among the many flaws in West Virginia’s school funding system is the failure to account for special education services. West Virginia’s special education funding is worse than it was decades ago. Because these services are required by law, failure to provide sufficient funding means that school districts need to dip into funding that would otherwise be used for general education services, or to cover the costs of keeping schools operational.
Looking beyond the funding formula, and including all state grants and special education funding, West Virginia provided an average of $8,057 per student. When the state doesn’t pay enough, counties are left to foot the bill. And a county like Lincoln will never be able to generate enough local wealth to operate the school system that students deserve. Counties generate local revenue for schools primarily through the general school levy, with statewide rates established by the Legislature, and optional excess levies meant to supplement basic school spending. Because these funding sources are tied to property tax, the amount of revenue available to counties — and the amount that gets spent on students — varies not based on need, but on whether students are being educated in counties with high property wealth.
The last time the courts took up this issue the case became so influential it still bears the name of the judge who decided it: the Recht Decision set the standard for school funding in West Virginia and changed the nationwide conversation about it. Despite these clear legal requirements set by our courts, the current funding system leads to outcomes that are worse than what was declared unconstitutional almost 50 years ago.
The current staffing formula provides Lincoln County with fewer staff than the formula at the time the system was declared unconstitutional. The gap between what counties receive, and what they spend, has widened instead of narrowed. School closures are increasing rapidly, as schools struggle to stay afloat with the meager funding provided by the state.
The law believes — as do I — that every West Virginia child is capable of great things that make our communities stronger, healthier and happier. A thorough and efficient system of free schools is what permits those futures to come to fruition.
After years of neglect by the Legislature, it has become clear that children’s constitutional right to education will be left to erode if the courts don’t demand action and declare that the current system isn’t just immoral — it’s also unconstitutional.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Woman accusing Sherrod Brown of forcing trans surgeries not Ohioan, didn’t have procedure as minor
description: In an attack ad against U.S. Senate candidate Sherrod Brown, a woman accuses the Democrat of pushing transgender surgeries on minors “like her.” As it turns out, she isn’t from Ohio and didn’t have surgery until she was an adult. The Senate Leadership Fund, one of the main groups supporting Republicans, has created multiple ads […]
text:
Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026. (Getty images)In an attack ad against U.S. Senate candidate Sherrod Brown, a woman accuses the Democrat of pushing transgender surgeries on minors “like her.” As it turns out, she isn’t from Ohio and didn’t have surgery until she was an adult.
The Senate Leadership Fund, one of the main groups supporting Republicans, has created multiple ads about former Sen. Sherrod Brown. In them, the political action committee accuses him of “forcing childhood sex change surgery.”
Two of their most recent ads feature a woman and social media influencer Soren Aldaco.
“Sherrod Brown supports sex changes for minors, irreversible surgery on kids like me,” Aldaco says.
Another ad featuring Aldaco explains that she was misled.
“After a 20-minute meeting, doctors told my parents I was transgender,” she states. “That led to hormone shots, a botched double mastectomy, and years of trauma.”


Aldaco starts another ad by saying that at 11, she was groomed online, but at 15 she was told she was transgender.
“Surgery without my parents’ consent,” Aldaco said. “I was a kid.”
Well, as it turns out, Aldaco received surgery without parental consent because she was 19. Records show she lived and received her treatments in Texas, not Ohio.
Detailed in a public Texas Supreme Court battle, her attorneys share that she had her double mastectomy once she was an adult.
Columbus-area Democrat and OB-GYN Dr. Anita Somani explained it is illegal in Ohio to perform gender-affirming care procedures on minors.
“Under 18, there is not a single surgery that’s been done here in the state, so I think the ads are misleading,” Somani said. “They are lies.”
The ad stems from when Brown said in 2023 that he believes medical decisions should be made between families and their doctors, not politicians.
Brown has a new ad addressing it.
“Here they go again, those same attacks against Sherrod Brown. With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about. In Ohio, it’s against the law to perform transgender surgeries on kids. That’s right, it’s illegal,” multiple individuals in the ad say.
When Ohio was debating its law to get rid of transgender medical procedures for minors, Somani noted that the de-transitioners, like Aldaco, were from out-of-state.
“To say that you had surgery or you were forced into surgery as a minor is clearly inaccurate… Did not live in Ohio, had no connections to Ohio,” the lawmaker said.
Republican strategist Bob Clegg said it doesn’t matter where Aldaco lives.
“That person is talking about how she should have never been allowed to have that kind of medical intervention,” Clegg said. “She doesn’t like the fact that there are politicians out there that think that that’s perfectly okay to do so.”
When it was pointed out that Aldaco was a legal adult when she got surgery, Clegg asked, “how many mature 19-year-olds have you met?”
The GOP-controlled state supreme court is reviewing the gender-affirming care ban, so Clegg said it isn’t completely settled law. This is why voters need to know that Brown doesn’t support the law, he added.
“We’re only under a temporary prohibition,” he said.
Somani said it’s telling that Republicans are focusing on culture war topics instead of affordability concerns.
“It’s a way to create an issue that’s a non-issue,” she added.


Follow WEWS Statehouse reporter Morgan Trau on X and Facebook.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Access to abortion care is improving in Ohio, but abortion opponents continue efforts against it
description: As studies show improvements in access to abortion care in Ohio, abortion opponents both in and outside of the state legislature are attempting to bring more regulations against it. An multiyear assessment called the Reproductive Health Experiences and Access Study found that access to abortion care has improved in Ohio, based on interviews with policymakers[...]
text:
People gather for the Ohioans for Reproductive Freedom Bans OFF Columbus rally for Issue 1, October 8, 2023, outside the Statehouse in Columbus, Ohio. Issue 1, a constitutional amendment to establish reproductive rights, passed with 57% of the vote in November 2023.(Photo by Graham Stokes for Ohio Capital Journal. Republish photo only with original article.)As studies show improvements in access to abortion care in Ohio, abortion opponents both in and outside of the state legislature are attempting to bring more regulations against it.
An multiyear assessment called the Reproductive Health Experiences and Access Study found that access to abortion care has improved in Ohio, based on interviews with policymakers, healthcare providers, advocates, and focus groups of women ages 18 to 49.
“Interviewees perceived Ohio’s reproductive rights amendment has meaningfully reduced barriers to care, but said access remains uneven, politically contested, and shaped by institutional, financial, and geographic constraints,”according to the study.
The study was conducted in a collaboration with the Urban Institute, the Reproductive Equity Action Lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and SisterSong Women of Color Reproductive Justice Collective.
Those interviewed said the removal of a 24-hour waiting period for abortion care and other requirements were positives for them, and expansion of medication abortion was described as “especially impactful for rural and Appalachian communities, where access to procedural (surgical) abortions remains limited.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Ohio’s constitutional amendment protecting reproductive rights was passed in 2023 by 57% of Ohio voters. Some included in the access study noted that the amendment “has not ended political efforts to restrict abortion access in Ohio.”
Republican state lawmakers have made several attempts to undermine the amendment with regulatory tweaks and measures to bar funding from going to facilities that provide abortion care.
“Consistently, bills keep popping up to undo what we already voted on,” one focus group participant said in the study. “To me, that’s very scary. If whoever can decide, ‘I don’t like that vote, and I don’t care that over half the state voted on it,’ they’re going to keep trying. They don’t care (whether) we have a say.”
According to the Pew Research Center, most adults in America support legal abortion, with 60% of those surveyed in January of this year saying it should be legal in all or most cases.
Even among religious individuals, support for abortion is high, except among white evangelical Protestants.
Pew’s survey found only 24% of those identifying as white evangelicals support abortion, while 68% of Black Protestants, 63% of White nonevangelical Protestants, and 57% of Catholics polled said abortion should be legal.
Movements against abortion care are still active in the country and in Ohio.
Ohio Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted participated in a congressional hearing on the alleged “dangers” of the abortion drug mifepristone, which has been approved as safe and effective by the FDA since 2000.
The president of the Ohio religious lobby group Center for Christian Virtue signed on to a statement with organizations across the country like the National Association of Christian Lawmakers, the U.S. Pastors Council and anti-abortion rights group Live Action, calling on the nominee for FDA commissioner, Dr. Heidi Overton, to “reverse Biden-era mifepristone policies while the FDA completes its ongoing review.”
In the letter, the groups express skepticism about a re-review of FDA regulations that have controlled distribution of the abortion drug since it was approved more than two decades ago, and arguing that mail-order abortion is “undermining state laws enacted to protect unborn life and women.”
The letter also provides guidance for a congressional hearing to decide whether Overton will be confirmed as FDA director.
Decades of scientific studies have shown that abortion medication is safe to use, and serious complications are rare. Anti-abortion rights groups have used one study in particular to show that “adverse effects” are occurring more frequently than other studies have shown.
Overton has already taken a stance against medication abortion, co-authoring a 2023 piece for the America First Policy Institute saying the institute’s policies should focus on “immediately halting the effort to normalize abortion-on-demand.”
Meanwhile, clinics backed by religious groups and those who don’t provide abortion as an option are receiving funding from national and state sources, according to Reproductive Health and Freedom Watch.
The group conducted a national analysis of legislation for and against “unregulated pregnancy clinics,” also called crisis pregnancy centers and pregnancy resource centers, depending on whether the reference is in support of or in opposition to the facilities.
Overall, the research estimated 2,600 clinics operating in the United States, projecting an annual national revenue of $2.6 billion in 2026. The organization also found more than 100 pieces of legislation related to the pregnancy clinics in 32 states.
Ohio was particularly noted for Ohio Senate Bill 9, a measure that created a tax credit for those donating to the clinics.
The bill was a comprehensive measure to revise tax laws, but one provision specifies that Ohioans can deduct up to $750 in “contributions the taxpayer makes to a pregnancy resource center.”
S.B. 9 was passed unanimously by the Ohio Senate, and 87-6 in the House earlier this year.
“By reducing the total an individual owes in state taxes based on the amount that person donated to a UPC, states effectively route millions in taxpayer funding to UPCs,” researchers from Reproductive Health and Freedom Watch stated.
As the 2026 general election approaches, reproductive rights are likely to come up as part of voters decisions, with a new governor and any changes in the legislature certain to have an effect on abortion and anti-abortion rights measures.
Republican governor candidate Vivek Ramaswamy has taken to social media to call himself “unapologetically pro-life,” while Democratic nominee Dr. Amy Acton has said she supports maintaining and broadening reproductive care including abortions and contraception, though solid plans have not been made clear.

title: Enbridge breaches aquifer along Line 5 reroute path
description: An aquifer breach has occurred in northern Wisconsin, along the reroute path of the Enbridge Line 5 oil and gas pipeline. In a statement, Enbridge spokesperson Juli Kellner said that “a flow of water was observed following the direct installation of pipe beneath the Marengo River.” Kellner said that Enbridge is working with the Department […]
text:
Laina G. StebbinsAn aquifer breach has occurred in northern Wisconsin, along the reroute path of the Enbridge Line 5 oil and gas pipeline. In a statement, Enbridge spokesperson Juli Kellner said that “a flow of water was observed following the direct installation of pipe beneath the Marengo River.”
Kellner said that Enbridge is working with the Department of Natural Resources “and other engineering and environmental specialists to determine next steps.” The breach was first reported by Northern News Now.
It’s unclear how much water was released due to the breach. The DNR didn’t respond to requests for comment. 
In August, a section of Line 5 released more than 1.3 million gallons of natural gas liquid after an unoccupied truck rolled and damaged the pipeline. WPR reported that the leak was the largest of its kind for both Enbridge and the state of Wisconsin. 
Enbridge previously  breached an aquifer while building the Line 3 pipeline in Minnesota. The breach led to an uncontrolled release of hundreds of millions of gallons of groundwater. Minnesota’s attorney general filed charges against the company in that case. 
Line 5 is a decades-old pipeline that carries up to 23 million gallons of crude oil and natural gas liquids daily from Ontario to the southern Unites States. In 2019, the Bad River Band of Lake Superior Chippewa sued Enbridge to shut the pipeline down and to expel the Canadian-owned company from tribal lands. 
Enbridge has since begun work on rerouting Line 5 around the reservation, a move that has been contested by tribal communities and environmental groups as endangering ecosystems and natural resources. Legal battles over the pipeline’s future continue in federal court. Advocates have called on the Wisconsin DNR to revoke the permits granted to Enbridge to carry out the reroute.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania’s public defense crisis is a constitutional crisis
description: The constitutional right to counsel is one of the cornerstones of American democracy. But a constitutional right without adequate funding is merely a promise on paper.
text:
A judge's gavel in a courtroom. ((Stock photo by Greenleaf123/Getty Images)The constitutional right to counsel is one of the cornerstones of American democracy. But a constitutional right without adequate funding is merely a promise on paper. 
After years of chronic underfunding, the Defender Association of Philadelphia has been forced to make painful staffing reductions and reduce services that thousands of Pennsylvanians rely upon every year. 
The recent service reductions in Philadelphia should serve as a warning to the commonwealth: if the largest public defender office in Pennsylvania is reducing staffing to critical court programs — despite years of operational improvements, grant funding, and careful financial stewardship — the problem is structural underinvestment. 
These cuts are the predictable consequence of a system that has failed to invest in one of its most basic constitutional obligations. 
This is not simply Philadelphia’s problem. 
It is Pennsylvania’s.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While public attention mainly focuses on police, prosecutors, and prisons, public defenders are equally essential to a functioning justice system. An effective public defense system strengthens public safety. 
Defenders help identify people who need treatment rather than incarceration, reduce unnecessary pretrial detention, negotiate resolutions that hold people accountable while promoting rehabilitation, and ensure court proceedings move efficiently. 
Every part of the justice system functions better when public defenders have the resources to do their jobs well.
Pennsylvania remains an outlier nationally when it comes to funding public defense. For decades, it was one of the only states that did not provide recurring indigent defense funding, forcing counties to shoulder nearly the entire cost of this constitutional mandate. 
Although the commonwealth has finally begun investing in public defense, the current statewide appropriation of just $7.5 million is nowhere near enough to meet the need.
While local governments in New York and New Jersey still carry significant fiscal responsibilities for public defense, they still invest more than Pennsylvania. Neighboring states like  Delaware, Maryland and Massachusetts assume primary responsibility for funding statewide public defense systems. 
These states invest tens or hundreds of millions of dollars annually to ensure constitutional representation, regardless of where someone lives. 
Pennsylvania’s fractional investment creates a patchwork system, where justice depends largely on local resources instead of constitutional guarantees. In our Commonwealth, the quality of representation — and ultimately, access to justice — can vary dramatically depending on zip code.
A hallway in the Schuylkill County Courthouse in Pottsville on March 12, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
That is not what the Constitution promises.
Pennsylvania has already acknowledged that indigent defense is a statewide responsibility by appropriating state funds for the first time. 
Gov. Josh Shapiro and the General Assembly should move the state toward a funding model that reflects making an investment in public defense a priority. 
The commonwealth should move toward a funding model that reflects the true cost of providing effective representation in all 67 counties — not one that leaves local governments to shoulder nearly the entire burden.
Public defense is not a discretionary government program. It is a constitutional mandate. 
We would never expect police departments, prosecutors’ offices, or the courts to fulfill their responsibilities without adequate funding. We should not expect public defenders to do so either.
The Defender Association of Philadelphia’s decision to reduce some services is more than a local budget story. It is a warning that Pennsylvania’s constitutional promise is becoming increasingly difficult to keep. 
The question is not whether we can afford to invest in public defense. The question is whether we can afford not to.
A justice system is measured not only by how it prosecutes crime, but by how faithfully it protects the rights guaranteed to every person. 
Pennsylvania has an opportunity to demonstrate that those rights are more than words on paper.
 
Keisha Hudson is the Chief Defender at the Defender Association of Philadelphia, which represents about 75% of the youth and adults charged with crimes in the city. She has more than 20 years of experience providing legal counsel to Pennsylvania’s most economically vulnerable citizens.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A self-defense instructor’s thoughts on the Cornell sexual assault case
description:
I teach sexual assault prevention. And I'm going to tell you something most instructors won't say out loud. 
There is no technique for this.
text:
I’ve been teaching self-defense for 25 years. I teach people to strike, to escape, to fight when they have to. I teach sexual assault prevention. And I’m going to tell you something most instructors won’t say out loud.
There is no technique for this.
Look at what is unfolding at Cornell right now.
A former Cornell student says that in 2024 she was pressured to drink and take ketamine at the Chi Phi fraternity house until she could no longer function. Then, according to her lawsuit, seven men raped her over a period of hours. One of them allegedly advertised her in a fraternity group chat and invited his brothers to join in.
No one was arrested. No one was charged.
The only reason this story is in front of you now is that she filed a civil lawsuit this month. The public saw it. The public got angry. And only then did the district attorney reopen the case and announce he would take it to a grand jury.
Read that again. The system moved because of public outrage. Not because of what happened to her.
Cornell says it ran a months-long Title IX process. Her attorney says two of the seven were expelled. The rest got suspensions, workshops, and written assignments. The lawsuit alleges they were allowed to write essays to soften their punishment. Cornell denies that. But even by Cornell’s own account, most of the seven men accused of a gang rape were not expelled.
And the men in that group chat? The ones who watched the invitation come in and did nothing? I haven’t heard a word about consequences for them.
Online, the pile-on has already started. Not on the men. On her. She wanted it. She put herself there. She should have known better.
That’s rape culture. Not a slogan. A pattern.
Now let me speak as an instructor.
Here’s the hard truth from the mat. I can teach a woman to fight off an attacker. I cannot teach a woman to fight off an attacker when her brain has been chemically switched off.
Alcohol and ketamine don’t just slow your reflexes. They take away your judgment. Your awareness. Your ability to recognize you’re in danger at all.
Every defense starts in the mind. When the mind is compromised, the defense is gone.
The only tool left is the one that works before you lose it: presence of mind. The ability to notice that something is wrong with you and leave while you still can. I know how close this can come to home. Two stories stay with me.
My daughter was a student at NYU. She was in a friend’s dorm room. Two male students were there. She took a drink. Within minutes she felt herself changing. Something had been slipped into it.
She recognized what was happening. She said she was going to the bathroom. She walked out quietly, called an Uber, and went back to her own dorm.
She did everything right. And I think about that night all the time. If she had waited ten more minutes, if the drug had hit harder or faster, she wouldn’t have had a choice to make. It could have ended very differently. And the people asking questions afterward would have been asking about her drinking.
I know that because of the second story.
One of my students has a daughter at a well-known university in the Southeast. Her daughter’s roommate was raped. When the university investigated, they interviewed my student’s daughter. Every question pointed in one direction. Was her roommate promiscuous? Was she the kind of girl who invited attention?
They weren’t investigating a rape. They were building a case against the victim.
Why would a university do that? Because institutions protect themselves first.
Universities live and die by reputation. Sexual assault numbers hurt enrollment. Headlines hurt donations. So, there is pressure, spoken or not, to shrink the story. Reframe it. Find a reason it wasn’t really what it looked like.
Essays. Workshops. Quiet suspensions. A victim who leaves school while the accused move on. That isn’t justice. That’s damage control.
The law isn’t much better.
New York has what’s become known as the “voluntary intoxication loophole.” Rape charges generally require force or a clear refusal, unless the victim was unconscious or drugged without her consent. If she drank on her own, even to the point where she could no longer say yes or no, prosecutors face a steep climb. The Tompkins County DA pointed to that very law when he explained why no charges were filed the first time.
Think about what that means. The moment a woman takes a drink, the law hands her a share of the blame for whatever is done to her after she can no longer resist. The man who chooses to exploit her incapacity is protected by her choice to have a beer.
That thinking runs deep, and it doesn’t stop at the dorm room door. It reaches into marriage. In 2015, a lawyer for Donald Trump insisted that you cannot rape your spouse. Years earlier, a Virginia lawmaker argued that a husband-wife rape conviction was nearly impossible when a couple shared a bed. These weren’t fringe voices. They were people with power, saying out loud that a woman’s consent can be assumed.
And the imbalance doesn’t stop there. In a number of states, a woman who becomes pregnant from rape has no legal way to end that pregnancy, because the abortion ban makes no exception for rape. In some of those states, the doctor who helps her faces a harsher maximum sentence than many convicted rapists. She carries the consequences. He may never be charged at all.
So where does that leave someone like me?
I’m frustrated. I’ll say it plainly. I’ve spent my career building women’s confidence and capability. I believe in that work, and I’ll keep doing it. But if we measure sexual assault prevention by whether a woman can physically fight off her attacker, we are measuring the wrong thing.
The defense has to start earlier. Before the drink gets spiked. Before the group chat lights up. Before anyone decides a woman’s body is there for the taking.
It starts with men.
“Boys will be boys” is not an excuse. “Locker room talk” is not harmless. Words become thoughts. Thoughts become actions. A culture that shrugs at the words will eventually shrug at the actions. We just watched it happen in a group chat, where one message offered a woman up and nobody stopped it.
So, here’s what I’m asking for.
From the law: close the loophole. Incapacity is incapacity, no matter how it happened.
From universities: stop managing your reputation and start delivering consequences. Expulsion, not essays.
From men: speak up. In the chat. In the locker room. At the party. The bystander who stays silent is part of the system that lets this happen.
I’ll keep teaching women to protect themselves. But I’m done pretending that’s where the defense begins.
It begins with the people who choose to cause harm, and the people who let them.
Gus Bottazzi is Chief Instructor at Krav Maga Personal Safety and author of The Krav Maga Essentials Handbook: A Practical Safety System for College Students; How to Avoid, De-escalate, and Escape Real-World Threats

name: Maryland Matters
title: Poll: Moore sits with a comfortable 2-1 margin over Republican challenger Cox
description: The results are part of a new poll released Tuesday by the Institute of Politics at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County. That poll finds that Moore would pick up 51% of the vote while another 24% said they favor Republican Dan Cox.
text:
Republican gubernatorial nominee Dan Cox, right, and Gov. Wes Moore (D) will share a stage for their only debate of the election on Oct. 6 on Maryland Public Television. A new poll released Tuesday by the University of Maryland, Baltimore County finds Moore with a comfortable double-digit lead over the Cox. (File photos by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) would cruise to a second term in office if the election were held today, according to a new poll from the Institute of Politics at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County.
The poll, released Tuesday, finds that Moore would pick up 51% of likely voters while Republican Dan Cox was favored by 24%. Another 14% didn’t know, while 11% was divided between other candidates.
“If anything, what’s notable is that sometimes incumbents will pick up an anti-incumbency bias — people who are just sort of frustrated with incumbents in general,” said Mileah Kromer, director of the UMBC Poll. “You’re really not seeing a lot of that here. The numbers very much look like you would expect, given the demographic characteristics of the state and the disproportionate fundraising numbers between the two candidates.”
The poll comes with four weeks left in the campaign season. Nearly 600,000 voters have already received mail-in ballots. Early voting begins Oct. 22 and ends on Oct. 29.
The survey is based on interviews with 776 Marylanders who said they were likely to vote. It was conducted from Sept. 22-27 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5%.
The roughly 2-1 margin is reminiscent of the 2022 race between Moore and Cox. Four years ago, Moore, who had never held public office, trounced Cox by 32 percentage points to become Maryland’s first Black governor.
Third-party candidates decry exclusion from only debate of the governor’s race

Moore and Cox are scheduled to square off Tuesday afternoon in what is expected to be the only head-to-head debate of their rematch. But Todd Eberly, a political science professor at St. Mary’s College of Maryland, said the UMBC poll casts doubt on how much the debate will matter to voters.
“It would be hard for me to imagine anything that could happen in that debate that would alter the trajectory of this race,” Eberly said. “Even if Cox had a fantastic debate performance, I don’t see how he closes that gap, or in any way really improves the clear problem he has winning over Democratic voters.”
Two third-party candidates on the ballot are not included in the Maryland Public Television debate. Green Party nominee Andy Ellis and Working Class Party nominee Cathy White each got 3% in the UMBC survey, below the 10% threshold set by MPT to qualify for the debate.
Moore does best among Democratic voters, 72% of whom said they support the incumbent. Cox picked up three out of every four Republican voters in the UMBC survey, along with 4% of Democratic voters and 14% of the unaffiliated voters.
In Maryland, where Republicans are heavily outnumbered, a GOP candidate running statewide needs to pick up about 90% of the voters in their party, along with roughly three in 10 Democratic voters and more than 55% of unaffiliated voters. It’s a formula that has cracked the door for some successful statewide Republican candidates over the last 20 years.
“Our poll suggests that Dan Cox is not rebuilding the Larry Hogan coalition,” Kromer said, of the Republican governor who served from 2014-2022. “It’s very clear. He’s getting most, almost all the support from Republicans that are his party base. Unaffiliated voters are the required pathway to victory for a Republican statewide candidate.”
Republicans are “running against an incumbent who is polling at 51% in this poll in a Democratic state — an incumbent that, at least according to this, is currently only winning over about three quarters of Democrats,” Eberly said. “That would normally be the recipe for the potential for a Republican to be competitive, and yet they are not competitive at all.”
“Look, Moore is not in danger of losing, but he’s an incumbent Democrat polling at 51%, and the cross tabs show that he’s got 72% of Democrats,” Eberly said. “This is the kind of environment where Larry Hogan showed us Republicans could be competitive in Maryland, and they’re not. I really do wonder, will they get the message, or will they continue to move away from a Larry Hogan-type or even a Bob Ehrlich-type nominee.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Voter perceptions of Cox and his party appear to be factors.
Cox spent four years in the House of Delegates as a conservative firebrand. He once brought articles of impeachment against Hogan for the governor’s handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. Cox also opposed closures and restrictions on restaurants and other businesses and filed lawsuits on their behalf.
He also closely aligned himself with President Donald Trump, organizing a bus trip to Washington on Jan. 6, the day that turned into a violent political protest at the U.S Capitol.
Efforts by Cox to separate his history from his current political incarnation have not been successful, according to the UMBC poll. Three voters in five identified Cox as conservative or very conservative. Just 11% identified him as a moderate candidate.
In 2018, 47% of those surveyed in another poll conducted by Kromer identified Hogan, in his bid for a second term, as a moderate.
“He’s just not perceived as the type of Republican that Maryland Democrats and frankly a lot of unaffiliated voters are willing to cast the ballot for,” Kromer said. “He doesn’t have the campaign funding to try to make the case that he is a moderate. That’s the path to victory. He doesn’t have the money to do that statewide, or frankly the record to claim political moderation.”
Eberly added that there’s reasons for Democrats to be cautious in the days after the Nov. 3 election.
“Let’s assume Democrats win big,” he said. “The worst thing Democrats could do is interpret a big win as some big endorsement for the Democratic Party. What they should do is realize this is a rejection of the Republican Party, and Democrats were the only other choice on the ballot.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A move to gut Head Start standards
description: Speak up to oppose federal cuts on Head Start rules that will gut its standard of care.
text:
In 2004, as a social worker serving families in deep poverty, I started a diaper bank because many of my clients were unable to afford enough diapers to keep their babies dry and healthy. It was a no-brainer. Head Start already required programs to provide diapers for enrolled children.

Joanne Samuel Goldblum

This gold-standard early childhood program’s regulations included many small but essential items to be in stock for children. This is because long before President Lyndon Johnson established Head Start, he was a young teacher in a Texas border town where families could not afford basic necessities. He wrote his mother heartfelt letters asking her to send toothpaste and toothbrushes for his students.
A proposed federal rule would reduce Head Start’s requirements from 133 pages to about a dozen. That’s not a move to trim red tape but to slash basic standards. No diapers, no formula, no toothbrushes, no class size or staffing ratio requirements.
This follows earlier Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) cuts that have led to closure of some regional offices. Head Start was one of Johnson’s “Great Society” programs, along with Medicare, Medicaid and what we now know as SNAP (Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program).
When I was growing up in the 1960s and 70s, a bipartisan majority in our government believed that all Americans benefitted from a strong social fabric. This was woven of help for seniors who could not afford their doctor bills or workers who had trouble putting food on the table after a factory closure. Nobody wanted to live in a society plagued by anxiety, where one piece of bad luck could cause a downward spiral. We wanted to be able to raise our families in vibrant communities, with parks and libraries, and send them to college, obtainable to working families through student loans.
There was no shortage of exclusion, injustice or want in these years, but there was some recognition that we needed to conquer these evils because Americans shared a common destiny. If some other family’s children were denied the opportunity to thrive, it threatened our common prosperity.
Today all the programs I grew up with that wove a strong social fabric are under attack. The National Diaper Bank Network (NDBN), more than 300 nonprofit basic needs banks across the country, is seeing requests for help reach an all-time high, even exceeding what we faced during Covid.
When Covid-19 was rampant, I was so proud of how NDBN members rose to the moment by organizing drive-through pick-ups for families and expanding to serve people who had never needed to ask for help before. A pandemic, this country can survive. But we will not survive the loss of community, the denial that we all have an interest in making sure that everyone in our society can thrive.
Let me tell you about “Sophia,” the client who convinced me to start a diaper bank in New Haven. I saw her dump the solids out of a diaper and put it back on her baby. I tried not to show my shock and calmly explained that a baby needed a fresh diaper with every change to stay healthy. Sophia told me should could not afford a new diaper every time.
I assumed that there was some government program to pay for diapers, but then, as now, that was not the case. She couldn’t use cloth because she had no washing machine, and the coin laundry would not let her wash diapers. To make matters worse, Sophia’s cash assistance relied on her going to job training. She got a voucher for free child care to facilitate this, but the provider required parents to buy diapers for use while the babies were in care. Sophia couldn’t. She was falling through a gaping hole in the social fabric and at risk of losing the few dollars she got to pay her rent.
Her story, sadly, is far from unique. NDBN research shows that nearly half of young U.S. families struggle to afford the diapers that their children need. Most of the families that NDBN diaper banks serve include working adults, but average pay has not kept pace with expenses. It’s a rigged system that profits those at the top, creates misery at the bottom, and hurts the vast majority of Americans.
 Research shows that when children receive diapers they have fewer pediatric sick visits, creating savings for Medicaid. Giving families diapers protects their access to child care, allowing parents to work more hours and attend school more consistently. Family income rises and so does the amount that the household contributes through taxes. Diapers are also a low-cost intervention to address the maternal mental health crisis. Moms report that diaper insecurity is more stressful to them than food insecurity.
I could go on at length about the social good that arises from the simple act of helping families out with diapers. I encourage people to comment on the disastrous rule proposal to gut Head Start, which we can do through October 6.
More basically, I urge you to speak up about the kind of society you want to live in. In a truly great society, every child has the opportunity to thrive.
Joanne Samuel Goldblum is the CEO at The National Diaper Bank Network in New Haven.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Baltimore can show how to prevent youth homelessness before it begins
description: Any number of problems -- an unexpected expense, loss of transportation, a family fight -- can tip a young person over into homelessness, write Larry Cohen and Tom Coale, but minimal assistance they go into a shelter can help them avoid homelessness.
text:
A homeless encampment is seen in Paterson, New Jersey. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Until very recently, Maryland’s response to youth homelessness kicked into gear only after a young person had already lost a place to live, at the most difficult and expensive point in a housing crisis. But Baltimore is bringing a logical, practical and scalable approach to addressing housing insecurity among young people with a simple proposition: Identifying what would keep a young person housed and providing it before a temporary crisis becomes lasting homelessness.
For many young people, homelessness begins with a specific financial emergency. A family conflict leaves someone without a place to stay. An unexpected expense consumes the money needed for rent. A young parent needs a security deposit. A student loses campus housing or lacks transportation to keep a job.
The amount required to stabilize the situation may be modest compared with the cost and disruption that follow. Yet available assistance is frequently too small, arrives too late or can be used only for an expense that does not match the actual problem.
Point Source Youth’s Targeted Housing Assistance Program was designed around that mismatch. A young person facing an imminent housing crisis works with a trained community provider to develop an individualized housing action plan. The program then supplies a one-time, flexible payment large enough to carry out that plan, whether the need involves rent, utilities, transportation, moving expenses or another immediate barrier to stable housing.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




The model has now produced encouraging evidence. In a seven-state pilot evaluated by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, 345 young people ages 16 to 27 received an average of approximately $3,700, generally within 48 hours, and those funds ended their crisis and slide into homelessness. Including dependents and other household members, the program affected 623 people. Administrative homelessness system records showed that 92.8% of participants had not accessed homelessness services six months after receiving assistance.
Those findings show that rapid, adequately funded assistance delivered before shelter entry merits expansion, and merits investment.
That next phase is underway in Baltimore through Point Source Youth’s partnership with Thread, a local organization with the relationships and community knowledge needed to reach young people before a housing crisis becomes visible to the formal homelessness system. The results in Baltimore will help determine whether the national pilot’s results can be reproduced locally, and what infrastructure is required to sustain the model.
Private funding has made that work possible, but it cannot be the endpoint.
Baltimore City and the state of Maryland should help finance future cohorts and the local capacity required to serve them. That means supporting the payments themselves, along with the outreach, staffing, housing planning and follow-up that make the intervention work. Public partners can also help establish efficient disbursement procedures, strengthen responsible data sharing and support independent evaluation of Baltimore’s results.
Such an investment would be disciplined rather than open-ended. Public officials could examine who the program reaches, how assistance is used, whether participants remain outside the homelessness system and which elements must be preserved as the model grows. Local evidence would then determine the appropriate scale and funding structure.
Maryland is particularly well positioned to do this work. Baltimore has experienced community organizations capable of delivering the program, Johns Hopkins researchers who can continue evaluating it and public leaders who understand that housing instability affects education, employment, health and family stability. This October, Point Source Youth’s national symposium in Baltimore can bring those groups together around a concrete question: What would it take to make prevention a durable part of Maryland’s homelessness response?
The national implications are significant. Communities across the country are searching for ways to reduce homelessness while controlling the cost of crisis systems. A successful Baltimore implementation, backed by credible local evidence and a serious public-sector partnership, could give other jurisdictions a model they can adapt.
Maryland does not need to wait until every question has been resolved. It should invest enough to learn what works while young people still have housing within reach.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland Supreme Court removes Anne Arundel Orphans Court judge from bench
description: The Maryland Supreme Court ordered the immediate removal Monday of Anne Arundel County Orphans' Court Chief Judge Vickie Gipson for what it called "egregious ... misconduct" in office, just months after removing another judge on the same court.
text:
Anne Arundel County Circuit Court in Annapolis. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)The Supreme Court of Maryland ordered the immediate removal Monday of Anne Arundel County Orphans’ Court Chief Judge Vickie Gipson for what it called “egregious … misconduct” in office.
The four-page order came just hours after Gipson pleaded her case to the court Monday, asking it to reject the Maryland Commission on Judicial Disabilities’ recommendation that she be removed from the bench and instead let her serve out the remaining few months of her term and retire.
It’s the latest chapter in an ongoing dispute between Gipson and former Orphans Court Judge Marc Knapp, who was ordered removed from the bench in June for conduct “fundamentally incompatible with judicial office” — conduct that stemmed from a series of run-ins with Gipson. As with Gipson on Monday, the court in July cited egregious misconduct as the reason for Knapp’s removal.
In her comments to the court Monday, Gipson, the first Black chief judge of the county orphans court, touted the improvements to the court during her tenure despite “a concerted effort by some to undermine the process.”
“I understand the seriousness of the court’s review, and ask the court to consider the full record including my conduct, the circumstances under which I served, the steps I took to seek help with resolution and the work that I accomplished on the Orphans’ Court,” Gipson told the justices.
Anne Arundel County Orphans’ Court Chief Judge Vickie Gipson. (Photo courtesy Maryland State Archives)
“I apologize for the strain this matter has placed on the court, the judiciary and public confidence,” she said. “I regret the moments when I could have communicated with greater restraint, or responded to conflict in a more measured way.”
She said she accepted responsibility for her choices, but was “respectfully maintaining my objections to findings I believe are not supported on the record.”
The commission had recommended that Gipson be removed from the bench for a “persistent course of unprofessional action unbecoming of a judicial officer.” The court apparently agreed in Monday afternoon’s order. It said a full opinion would follow at a later date.
The commission said Gipson, who was first elected in 2018, and Knapp, elected in 2022, initially had a cordial working relationship on the three-judge court, but that it quickly turned acrimonious.
The two “engaged in repeated verbal altercations” that were at times “mutual, with both … exhibiting unprofessional behavior to varying degrees and would inhibit the court’s deliberations and cause staff present in or near chambers to be uncomfortable.” These altercations could be heard by court personnel and, occasionally, by the public, the commission said.
Because of her disputes with Knapp, the commission said Gipson tried to refuse to let him submit dissenting opinions and would attempt to bar the court “from issuing orders which had been signed by” Knapp. When he refused to leave the courtroom after one such dispute, she called police to remove him.
The commission said Gipson inappropriately invoked her title as chief judge “in legal proceedings and public statements to advance her personal interests.” It also said she violated court confidentiality in comments to reporters about Knapp, the court and complaints she filed with the commission against other judges, which are confidential.
While she was feuding with Knapp, the commission said Gipson was making accommodations for the third judge on the court, Judge David Duba. Orphans’ court is required to meet at least twice a week, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., but when Duba could not get to court until 11 or later, Gipson allowed for cases to be rearranged around his schedule, inconveniencing the public and workers in the Orphans’ Court and the Register of Wills office who had to work extra hours to accommodate the change.
State Supreme Court removed Anne Arundel Orphans’ Court judge for ‘egregious misconduct’

When pressed by the justices, Gipson said she believed she had the authority as chief judge to rearrange the court schedule and to deny dissenting opinions on the court’s orders. She conceded that she sometimes lost her temper with Knapp, who she felt was threatening, and that she could have sought advice from the commission sooner. But in other areas, like seeking a peace order against Knapp, she said she was just following recommendations from the commission and from police when she expressed concerns about her safety and the safety of others in the office.
“I hope to leave the court with my head held high, not because I believe I am flawless, but because I served with commitment, I learned from this experience and I made a meaningful contribution to the court and the people it served,” she told the justices.
But Kendra Jolivet, the attorney for the commission, said that Gipson’s actions merited removal from the bench because they violated court rules and “impaired court functionality, public access and the administration of justice.”
“The respondent [Gipson] devotes large portions of her exceptions to alleging institutional hostility, bias, racial tension or past disagreements with colleagues,” Jolivet told the justices. “Even if accepted as true, none of these allegations justify altering court operations without consensus, they don’t excuse inappropriate conduct toward colleagues and staff or negate the cumulative seriousness of the misconduct found.”
The commission found that while Knapp was the “primary aggressor in the underlying interpersonal conflict,” that does not outweigh the “gravity and breadth of respondent’s sanctionable conduct.”
In its unsigned order, the Supreme Court said it found that Gipson “committed one or more of the violations” charged by the commission and that “based on the egregious nature of the misconduct in this case, removal … is the appropriate disposition,” to take effect immediately.
Gipson did not run for reelection this year, in deference, she said, to the court and the charges against her. With her removal Monday, none of the three judges elected to the orphans’ court in 2022 remain on the bench. In addition to Knapp being removed this summer, Duba resigned in November 2024.
