name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Michele Tafoya hopes national Republicans put money behind their praise
description: LE SUEUR — Michele Tafoya has TV skills and an opponent saddled with the state’s fraud scandal. What she needs now is money. Polls show Tafoya is in a dead heat with Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, even with significant national political headwinds forcing Republicans to spend heavily in traditionally red strongholds such as Iowa, […]
text:
Republican Senate candidate Michele Tafoya appears at a campaign event with Senate Majority Leader John Thune in Le Sueur, Minn. on Oct. 5, 2026. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)LE SUEUR — Michele Tafoya has TV skills and an opponent saddled with the state’s fraud scandal. What she needs now is money.
Polls show Tafoya is in a dead heat with Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, even with significant national political headwinds forcing Republicans to spend heavily in traditionally red strongholds such as Iowa, Alaska and Kansas.
At a campaign stop with farmers on Monday in Le Sueur, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., boasted that Tafoya is a strong candidate with a convincing message to give Republicans hope for winning in a state they’ve mostly surrendered.
But he was noncommittal on deploying some of Senate Republicans’ vast war chest to boost Tafoya’s campaign before the Nov. 3 election. Fox News reported in August that the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Thune, and allied groups had raised more than $500 million for the midterms thus far.
“We’ve got a big map this year. It’s a very competitive environment,” said Thune, who’s touring battleground states. “But Minnesota is unique in a lot of ways.”
Tafoya has a strong pitch to make that she can be the first Republican to win a Senate seat in Minnesota since 2002. She has high name recognition from her successful career as a sports reporter on virtually every major television network. She isn’t bogged down with any major personal scandals besides frequently bashing Minnesota and threatening to decamp to Florida. And her opponent is an easy target to hammer on the fleecing of the state’s generous safety-net programs, which unfolded during her two terms as No. 2 in state government.
“I think we can make a very strong case out of all these Senate races … This is one worth investing in,” Tafoya said. “We’re going to talk. We haven’t had that conversation yet.”
Money isn’t everything, as Flanagan showed when she trounced U.S. Rep. Angie Craig in the Democratic primary despite being far outspent.
Monday’s stop at the Pfarr family’s farm — 4,000 acres of corn, soybeans, alfalfa, peas and hogs about an hour southwest of Minneapolis — was Tafoya’s first open press event since the August primary.
After a private roundtable with farmers organized by the Minnesota Farm Bureau, Thune and Tafoya briefly addressed the press to promote Republicans’ work on a farm bill and reaffirm their commitment to passing year-round E15 fuel, which would be a boon for corn growers whose crops become ethanol.
GOP Senate candidate Michele Tafoya reports assets totaling $10.7M to $37.9M

Farmers have been whipsawed by President Donald Trump’s trade war, which hurt grain exports, and war with Iran, which drove up fuel costs.
Nevertheless, many farmers are sticking with him, and the Minnesota Farm Bureau endorsed Tafoya for Senate.
Flanagan held an event at a gas station in Brooklyn Park on Monday with Minnesota Farmers Union President Gary Wertish to draw attention to high fuel prices, though it hardly needed pointing out. Gas station signs are serving as a kind of campaign ad for Democrats across the country.
Matthew Pfarr, whose family hosted Tafoya, approached the current state of affairs with equanimity. He said farmers face ups and downs no matter which party controls the government.
“So, farmers have gotten quite good at weathering those,” Pfarr said.
Asked whether he was backing Tafoya, Pfarr demurred.
“We will host anyone who wants to come to the farm,” Pfarr said. “I prefer not to discuss my politics, personally.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Grand Island-area lawmaker reflects on Trump’s visit to central Nebraska
description: GRAND ISLAND, Neb. — One of two state lawmakers representing Grand Island in Nebraska’s one-house Legislature praised President Donald Trump for visiting the area Monday. Trump’s rally was at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds in Legislative District 35, represented by state Sen. Dan Quick of Grand Island. The fairgrounds are one block away from Legislative Dist[...]
text:
Merchandise for sale on the Nebraska State Fairgrounds in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, ahead of a campaign rally featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)GRAND ISLAND, Neb. — One of two state lawmakers representing Grand Island in Nebraska’s one-house Legislature praised President Donald Trump for visiting the area Monday.
Trump’s rally was at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds in Legislative District 35, represented by state Sen. Dan Quick of Grand Island. The fairgrounds are one block away from Legislative District 34, represented by state Sen. Loren Lippincott of Central City. Quick is a Democrat; Lippincott is a Republican. The Legislature is officially nonpartisan, meaning lawmakers do not officially organize by political party and lawmakers’ party affiliation doesn’t appear on the ballot.
State Sen. Loren Lippincott of Central City holds up a sign reading “I’m Billy Bob!” referring to comments made by registered nonpartisan Senate candidate Dan Osborn in reference to Red Cloud, Nebraska residents, in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds ahead of a midterms rally featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Lippincott told the Nebraska Examiner inside the Pinnacle Bank Expo Center that Nebraska is “very honored” to host Trump. Lippincott stretched his arms to thousands gathered Monday as proof “Nebraskans are absolutely thrilled” for the president of the United States to come.
“We’re very excited here in Grand Island,” Lippincott said. “Not only do we have the State Fair, but then to be selected for a Trump rally is just absolutely spectacular. We are totally thrilled about it.”
In 2025, Lippincott led the effort to restore Nebraska’s “winner-take-all” Electoral College model. Nebraska currently awards two Electoral College votes to the statewide winner and one vote for each of Nebraska’s three congressional districts. Two Republicans buckled. Had all of the Legislature’s 33 Republicans unified, the measure could have passed the 49-member body.
But on Monday, Republicans sought a different message behind Trump as thousands came dressed in red, some in sequins and others in clothing they’d made to honor Trump. Trump won Hall County, which includes Grand Island, with 65% of the vote in 2016, 66% in 2020 and 68% in 2024.
“We know that this part of the state is red already, so it’s not like he’s coming here just to pick up a lot of votes, but instead, it’s to honor the individuals that do support his agenda and do support the work that he has done, which has been substantial,” Lippincott said. He said some of the biggest accomplishments for Trump are around public safety, in crime rates and immigration.
State Sens. Bob Hallstrom of Syracuse, left, and Dan Quick of Grand Island. Jan. 7, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Quick, a Democrat, has twice outperformed Trump in the three times both have been on the ballot in the district. In 2016, Quick won with 50.3% of the vote.
But in 2020, Quick handily lost reelection — 53.6%-46.4% — to former state Sen. Ray Aguilar of Grand Island. Aguilar had previously served from 1999-2009. Quick staged a rematch in 2024 and won with 50.3% of the vote again. That race was the most expensive in direct spending for legislative races in 2024, with nearly $670,000 between Quick and Aguilar. Quick outspent Aguilar by $84,000.
Quick, one of the more moderate Democrats in the Legislature, said in a text that he had meetings in Lincoln on Monday. He declined to comment on Trump’s visit.
Some Nebraska Democrats, such as Nebraska Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb of Hastings, have said Trump’s 2026 midterms tour is a sign of weakness. Kleeb encouraged an “unwelcoming committee” for Trump on Monday and said on social media that Trump’s visit “tells you one basic fact: Republicans are in trouble, even in Nebraska.”
Trump asks Nebraska to ‘pretend’ he’s on the midterm ballot

Other Trump critics have scrutinized possible local costs for security and law enforcement overtime. Lippincott hailed Falls City agribusinessman Charles Herbster, who announced he would pay those costs.
Furthermore, Lippincott said he expected the rally to boost Grand Island’s economy by increasing sales and lodging tax revenue.
On Republican vulnerability, Lippincott offered a different view from critics such as Kleeb. He said Trump has a “forehead of flint, and whenever he finds any kind of resistance, he runs headlong into it.”
“In my opinion … these kinds of rallies are like what the sunshine is to Superman,” Lippincott said. “It restores his strength. He loves this type of arena, this type of environment, and this recharges him.”

title: Supporters of Barrett, Lawrence clash at dueling protests ahead of debate

text:
Members of “Spartans for Will” Lawrence and supporters of U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) clashed in a war of words and protest signs in downtown Lansing on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, during a pair of demonstrations calling out Lawrence and Barrett over their respective campaign planks — and in the case of Barrett, his congressional record — with just 31 days left in the 2026 general election cycle. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Members of “Spartans for Will,” who back Democrat Will Lawrence, and supporters of Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) clashed in a war of words and protest signs in downtown Lansing on Monday evening during a pair of demonstrations calling out Lawrence and Barrett over their respective campaign planks — and in the case of Barrett, his congressional record — with just 31 days left in the 2026 general election cycle.
Lawrence, the Democratic nominee for the 7th Congressional District, and Barrett, the seat’s incumbent, are set to square off Tuesday in a debate hosted by WKAR-TV in Lansing.
Organizers of the pro-Lawrence demonstration, which was held outside of Barrett’s office in Lansing, called attention to the congressman’s record on artificial intelligence, the data centers that power its proliferation, healthcare and other issues that progressives have noted in their calls to elect Lawrence in the fall.
Camden Kimmel, a Michigan State University student and a member of “Spartans for Will,” gave remarks at the protest, highlighting the group’s issues with Barrett. Cynthia Burton, with Bee Accepting, also aired grievances with Barrett’s time in office.

“We must act now. Status quo systems, policies, and politicians are never going to fix the damaging mistakes of the past two, 12, 20, 189 and 250 years. The opportunity to unite people towards a better future is here, and we will not let it pass us by,” Kimmel said. “I very much consider Tom Barrett a status quo politician. Taking corporate PAC money, bowing down to Trump and voting for the ‘Big Beautiful Bill,’ supporting the war in Iran, and entrenching our energy grid’s dependence on the fossil fuel industry. He has expressed no desire to stand up to AI startups and data center builders, instead preferring to pass that responsibility over to the local townships.”
Lawrence spokesperson Mya Legel told Michigan Advance following the event that “Michiganders have paid the price of Tom Barrett’s cost- raising record in Congress.”
“One night on a debate stage is too little, too late to make up for two years of absence, billionaire tax breaks, and rubber-stamping Donald Trump’s agenda,” Legal added.
Barrett’s supporters counter-programmed the protest by holding one of their own, calling out Lawrence’s associations with the democratic socialist movement, his arrest record from days of protesting oil pipelines, and other grievances with Lawrence’s campaign.
Several members of the pro-Barrett demonstration were asked if they would like to be interviewed by the Advance, but declined. Those present and representing Barrett at the counter-demonstration included members of the the Michigan Republican Party, from GOP legislative aides to members of regional and county GOP offices.
A message seeking comment from Barrett’s campaign was not returned at the time of publication. This story will be updated when a response is received.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Trump asks Nebraska to ‘pretend’ he’s on the midterm ballot
description: Trump vist to Nebraska was just one stop for the president on a midterm campaign blitz to shore up red states.
text:
President Donald Trump headlines a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)GRAND ISLAND — President Donald Trump told the crowd in Grand Island Monday to pretend that he is on the ballot this November. 
Trump, during his rally speech at Pinnacle Bank Expo Center, announced an executive order that allows anyone to use red-dyed diesel, waiving the off-road requirement and allowing anyone to purchase it for any reason.
Trump said the order should “assure” Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts and Gov. Jim Pillen of reelection. 
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen announces he has inducted President Donald Trump as the newest “admiral” of the largely honorific Nebraska Navy in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds for a midterms rally featuring the president. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
It’s been roughly 20 years since the last presidential visit to Grand Island. Then-President George W. Bush visited in 2006, during the tail end of that year’s midterm election campaign. Former Gov. Ben Nelson won another term in the U.S. Senate against Ricketts that year. 
Ricketts, now a U.S. senator, is in a bitter race against nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn. The Ricketts campaign was handing out signs saying “I’m Billy Bob!” and “I’m Mary Jane!” — referring to Osborn’s comments about hypothetical Red Cloud Trump supporters.
The Trump visit comes as the political environment for Republicans has worsened. Nebraska was just one stop for the president on a midterm campaign blitz to shore up red states.  Before Trump went on stage, Ricketts hit his campaign-trail classics when talking about his opponent, calling Osborn a Democrat and mentioning audio leaks and Osborn paying his family for campaign work. 
Ricketts, in a joke he often tells on the campaign trail, asked the audience to vote 10 times but not the “Democrat way,” meaning he wants them to bring along people they know to vote. 
“We will keep Nebraska red,” Ricketts told the crowd.

Trump jokingly said both Ricketts and Pillen are always asking for money for the state. Trump followed Ricketts’ lead, calling Osborn a “fake independent,” adding that Ricketts is a true warrior. Trump also mentioned Democratic gubernatorial challenger Lynn Walz, saying she is related to Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, whom he called probably the worst governor ever. 
Lynn is related to Tim Walz through her husband, who is a distant cousin. 
U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., greets thousands of Nebraskans gathered in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds for a midterms rally featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The president highlighted his record — blaming “fake news” for people not knowing about his successes — and touted the tax cuts from his “big beautiful bill,” a secured border and the economy. 
“We were a dead country a few years ago. … Now we’re the hottest country ever on that,” Trump told the crowd. 
Trump went on to say that the U.S. is kicking “Iran’s ass.” The president added that higher gas prices are just a small price to pay. 
“[Iran] can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles or San Diego. This is a very small price to pay. It’s essentially almost over with,” Trump said.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilger, 3rd District Rep. Adrian Smith, Pillen and Ricketts spoke before Trump took the stage.  
The Osborn campaign released a statement thanking Trump for announcing his support for “right to repair” laws and for expanding access to red-dyed diesel.
Walz, in a campaign statement, said, “Political attacks won’t lower anyone’s property taxes or reopen a single market for our farmers. Nebraskans deserve a governor whose word actually means something. I’m ready to show up for you.”
The Nebraska Democratic Party held a protest near the venue. The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting has already started.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Roger Marshall’s attack ad against Adam Hamilton contains unauthorized image of children
description: U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall's commercial critical of Democrat Adam Hamilton features unauthorized use of a picture taken of youth sitting in a Kansas chapel.
text:
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall's latest reelection campaign ad critical of Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton makes unauthorized use of an image of children sitting in a chapel at a Linwood camp. The camp's leaders insist Marshall remove the photo from the ad that opens with a picture of Marshall leaning on a fence. (Kansas Reflector screen capture of Marshall's campaign commercial)TOPEKA — The Tall Oaks Camp and Conference Center demanded Monday that U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall suspend a campaign commercial attacking Democrat Adam Hamilton that made unauthorized use of a photograph of children at Tall Oaks’ chapel in Linwood.
A senior advisor to the Marshall campaign said the ad was “corrected,” but hours after that statement was issued, a version of the commercial available on social media still included an image of the Tall Oaks’ distinctive chapel and about two dozen people sitting on pews.
Lea Ann Combs, president of the board of directors at Tall Oaks, a nonprofit summer camp and retreat center, said Tall Oaks wasn’t consulted by the Marshall campaign and didn’t approve inclusion of the photograph in the commercial. The ad denounced Hamilton in relation to allegations of sexual abuse perpetrated by a volunteer at Church of the Resurrection, the prominent Johnson County-based church founded and led by Hamilton.
“Our concern is straightforward,” Combs said. “This advertisement creates a misleading association between Tall Oaks, the young people pictured and events that did not happen here. Protecting the dignity of these young people and accurately representing our organization should be a shared priority.”
She said Marshall’s campaign should stop broadcasting the 30-second commercial until confirming the Tall Oaks photograph had been deleted.
The commercial began airing in conjunction with reports on a decision by the Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican super PAC, to pull $8 million from a North Carolina campaign and redirect it to help Marshall’s reelection bid in Kansas. The latest New York Times/Siena College Poll shows Hamilton and Marshall tied at 45% support each, based on a survey of likely voters.
In the ad paid for by Marshall’s campaign, a photograph of the senator appeared in the opening sequence while a recording of his voice said he approved content of the commercial. The senator’s ad claimed Hamilton didn’t respond promptly to a report suggesting a church volunteer may have touched or attempted to touch boys attending a 2005 program hosted by Church of the Resurrection.
“Parents were ignored and Hamilton never called police,” Marshall’s attack ad says. “He should never be our senator.”
The commercial included still photos of Marshall and Hamilton, cottages, dormitory-style rooms, hiking trail, rural property and a group of people sitting in rows, most with their back turned, in the chapel at Tall Oaks.
Combs said permission had been granted to photograph young people at Tall Oaks for the purpose of promoting the camp and its programs. She said that approval didn’t extend to inclusion of photographs in political campaign advertising, particularly commercials delving into claims of sexual abuse. Tall Oaks works to provide a safe environment for children, families, faith communities and other organizations using its facilities, the statement said.
The statement said Tall Oaks encouraged Marshall to remove the photograph from all platforms tied to the campaign. The objective was to make certain no one viewing the ad would mistakenly believe Tall Oaks or the children appearing in the ad were connected to allegations of abuse, the statement said.
The request shouldn’t be interpreted as an endorsement or rejection of any candidate or a comment on the merit of allegations raised in the commercial, the statement said.
Brent Robertson, Marshall’s chief of staff, said the photograph from Tall Oaks was thought to have been a “stock image” available for general use. The Tall Oaks picture wasn’t taken at the site of Hamilton’s “child molestation cover-up,” Robertson said.
“The image has already been corrected and, luckily, Kansas families care far more about Hamilton’s failure to protect kids from a child sex predator than what cabin picture was used,” Robertson said.
Tyson Brody, a campaign spokesperson for Hamilton, said the ad wasn’t in line with Marshall’s vote in September 2025 to block a U.S. Senate measure directing the U.S. Department of Justice to release unclassified records about Jeffrey Epstein. The wealthy financier, child sex offender and acquaintance of President Donald Trump committed suicide in 2019 while awaiting trial on charges of sex trafficking of minors.
“Marshall lies and uses children as political pawns to distract from the fact he had pregnant mothers arrested and jailed over small medical debts, and voted to protect the predators named in the Epstein files. Roger Marshall is desperate to hide from his record of protecting predators, and preying on low-income families in Kansas,” Brody said.
In a Kansas Reflector report published in July on abuse allegations involving Church of the Resurrection, Hamilton said two church employees conducted an internal investigation into claims that surfaced in 2005. The inquiry was inconclusive, Hamilton said, because the children couldn’t identify the perpetrator.
Hamilton said he should have forwarded information to law enforcement rather than depend on church staff. When new allegations surfaced against volunteer Scott Moore in 2006, the church informed police of allegations associated with camp retreats in 2005 and 2006.
Moore was accused of sex crimes in the Kansas City area and Massachusetts. He was convicted in 2013 in Kansas of a misdemeanor count of sexual battery. In 2015, Moore was found unconscious after he fled police when caught half-naked in a car with a teenage boy. He died at a hospital.
Tall Oaks is a nonprofit camp, retreat and conference facility on 236 acres near Linwood.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Feds approve $150 million for second power link between Interior and Southcentral Alaska
description: The U.S. Department of Energy said on Monday that it has approved $150 million to partially fund a second electrical intertie between Southcentral Alaska and the Interior. When built, the Beluga-Healy Transmission Project would result in a redundant power link between Fairbanks and Anchorage, increasing the ability of power companies to use the cheapest elec[...]
text:
A high-voltage power line is seen on Sept. 4, 2018, in Alaska. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)The U.S. Department of Energy said on Monday that it has approved $150 million to partially fund a second electrical intertie between Southcentral Alaska and the Interior.
When built, the Beluga-Healy Transmission Project would result in a redundant power link between Fairbanks and Anchorage, increasing the ability of power companies to use the cheapest electricity possible, even if it’s coming from the opposite end of the railbelt.
Construction isn’t expected until after 2030.
The project is expected to cost $418 million altogether, with the new federal money likely going toward engineering, planning and permitting, said Curtis Thayer, executive director of the Alaska Energy Authority.
The remaining $268 million could come from other federal grants, the state, or even AEA itself, through loans. 
AEA has been planning the second intertie for almost five years as part of a broader campaign of electrical upgrades across the state but didn’t intend to go ahead until other parts of that campaign — including high-voltage links to support a newly renovated Bradley Lake hydroelectric project — came online.
On Monday, Thayer said the announcement came as a surprise. He had heard last week that the state was in the running for a large grant through a Department of Energy program intended to benefit defense readiness, but he didn’t know until Monday that AEA had won.
Alaska’s existing intertie was built in the 1980s and is used primarily for shipping lower-cost hydropower and natural gas power north to Fairbanks. In recent years, it has also been used to ship coal-fired power south to Anchorage amid natural gas shortages.
Adding a second intertie increases the amount of power that can flow north or south, something that could encourage the development of wind or solar power plants that could provide cheaper power, albeit intermittently.
A second link also means that when the first intertie is upgraded and replaced — something intended in a separate project — power will continue to flow across the railbelt. 
Monday’s grant comes from the Defense Production Act and $1 billion approved by Congress and President Donald Trump for energy-related projects deemed critical to national security.
Most of Alaska’s military bases use energy that flows through the intertie, and the state’s Congressional delegation emphasized that fact as it lobbied for federal funding.
On Monday, the three members of the delegation — Rep. Nick Begich III and Sens. Lisa Murkowski and Dan Sullivan, all Republicans — issued statements in support of the new grant.
Sullivan and Begich are running for re-election this year, and on Monday, Vice President J.D. Vance was scheduled to travel to Fairbanks in order to campaign for both men, as well as other Republicans seeking office in November’s general election. According to Reuters, Vance was expected to speak about the grant during a rally at Fairbanks International Airport.

name: Daily Montanan
title: District Court judge rules birthdate voter law unconstitutional
description: A Lewis and Clark County District Court judge has ruled a law requiring voters to put their birth year on absentee ballots violated the state’s constitution, and has ruled in favor of Disability Rights Montana and Big Sky 55+, which challenged the legislation. Ballots for the Nov. 5 general election have already been sent overseas, […]
text:
Lewis and Clark Courthouse is pictured on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026, in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)A Lewis and Clark County District Court judge has ruled a law requiring voters to put their birth year on absentee ballots violated the state’s constitution, and has ruled in favor of Disability Rights Montana and Big Sky 55+, which challenged the legislation.
Ballots for the Nov. 5 general election have already been sent overseas, with voter packets headed to Montanans by the end of the week. Some overseas ballots have been sent and returned. 
In a statement, the Secretary of State’s Office said county election officials have been notified that the courts have blocked House Bill 719 and expressed frustration with the ruling.
“This type of mass confusion is why courts shouldn’t get involved when the election is underway,” Secretary of State’s Office spokesperson Richie Melby wrote in an email.
The Montana Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment or say if it planned to appeal the decision. 
The court’s decision also invalidates the law, meaning a ballot couldn’t be thrown out simply for not having a voter’s birth date on the ballot. When asked if any ballots would be reprinted, the Secretary of State’s Office said it takes counties “weeks” to contract with printing companies and get the ballots ready for mailing.
“The law requires that absentee ballot materials were available to voters for in-person absentee voting beginning today,” Melby said Monday. “The election is well underway.”
Three elections have been held under the new law, with data submitted to the court showing more ballots have not been counted since the new law has been in effect. The court compared voter data from the November 2024 election, which was before the new birth date law, with an all-mail May 5, 2026, election that was held in 30 counties after it was signed into law.
Lewis and Clark County’s ballot rejection rate was 0.29% in 2024 and 0.8% in the May 2026 election. In Gallatin County it rose from 0.47% in 2024  to 2.75% in 2026, court documents state.
The state argued adding the birth year helped prevent voter fraud, with attorneys pointing to a case where another person voting in Montana impersonated his ex-wife in 2011. 
“Balanced against the state’s lack of evidence of election fraud and its inability to explain how public confidence in elections is elevated by requiring a birth year on absentee ballots, the state has failed to meet its burden of proving HB 719 is reasonable and serves a legitimate state interest or that its asserted interests are more important than the burden on the right to vote,” Judge Mike Menahan wrote in his decision.
In a press release, Big Sky 55+ praised the decision.
“The court’s decision means that no Montanan will have their ballot thrown out for arbitrary reasons under HB719,” Terry Minow, chairperson of Big Sky 55+, said in a press release. “When more people vote and have their votes counted, our democracy is healthier. We encourage everyone to vote in every election.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Bank of North Dakota announces stablecoin pilot program with local partners
description: MEDORA, N.D. – The Bank of North Dakota announced Monday it has launched a pilot program for its Roughrider Coin.  Four local banks and credit unions are using the state’s unique banking model, led by the Bank of North Dakota, to learn about possible benefits and pitfalls of the stablecoin financial technology.  “The way money […]
text:
Don Morgan, center-right, CEO of the Bank of North Dakota, announces the launch of a stablecoin pilot program with four local partners during a banking forum at the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in Medora on Oct. 5, 2026. The chair of the state-owned bank's advisory board, Karl Bollingberg, center-left, joined Morgan on stage alongside nearly two dozen people who have been involved in the Roughrider Coin's development.  (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)MEDORA, N.D. – The Bank of North Dakota announced Monday it has launched a pilot program for its Roughrider Coin. 
Four local banks and credit unions are using the state’s unique banking model, led by the Bank of North Dakota, to learn about possible benefits and pitfalls of the stablecoin financial technology. 
“The way money moves is drastically changing, and we are utilizing our incredibly powerful financial tool to be on the forefront of that change,” said Don Morgan, CEO of the Bank of North Dakota. “We believe it will benefit the state over the next decade in huge ways.”
Bank of North Dakota to launch state’s first stablecoin known as Roughrider coin

The state-owned bank will partner with Gate City Bank, First International Bank, Capital Credit Union and North Star Community Credit Union on the pilot program to test stablecoin in a controlled environment. Fiserv, a Fortune 500 technology company that already provides services for the Bank of North Dakota, is also part of the partnership. 
Roughrider Coin is North Dakota’s branded stablecoin. Stablecoin is a form of cryptocurrency because it uses blockchain technology to complete transactions. But it doesn’t experience the same value fluctuations of cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin because stablecoins are tied to the value of the U.S. dollar.
“Stablecoin at its very foundation is pegged to the dollar, and $1 of stablecoin is going to be worth $1. It won’t be worth $1.10 the next day,” said Bob Herrington, CEO of North Star, a credit union that started in Benson County and now has 13 locations. “Its use, because of that, is not one of investment and appreciation but it’s a transactional use and it is more secure because of the blockchain technology.”
Herrington said North Star wanted to be part of the pilot program because the credit union wants to be prepared down the road if stablecoin becomes an essential tool in the world of financial technology.
“Right now, the impact to everyday member or customer base transactions is very, very far down the time horizon,” Herrington said. “If you don’t start here, you’re not going to be prepared for the next phases of stablecoin.”
Ryan Goellner, executive vice president of Gate City Bank, said he hopes the Roughrider Coin will create efficiencies in how the bank operates. But he and bank leaders are still evaluating its potential uses and view the pilot program as a learning opportunity.
“Participating in the Rough Rider Coin pilot really gives us an opportunity to learn firsthand in that controlled environment, rather than kind of just waiting on the sidelines,” Goellner said. “The focus right now is just really for us to get that understanding of the stablecoin and then how we can actually utilize it internally.”
North Dakota bankers cautiously optimistic about stablecoin announcement, though future risks exist

The pilot program’s announcement was made at the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in Medora during a three-day forum the Bank of North Dakota is hosting for the state’s banking leaders to learn more about financial technologies like stablecoin. 
Morgan said the bank has completed its first live transactions outside of a test environment by using the stablecoin to move a penny almost instantly between two partners. He said the occasion is the start of a foundational change in the banking world, similar to the moment when an automobile first replaced a horse-drawn carriage. 
“That’s the importance of today because North Dakota is on the forefront of that,” Morgan said.  
Karl Bollingberg, chair of the Bank of North Dakota’s advisory board, said he believes stablecoin could have ramifications on a similar scale to the advent of internet banking. 
Bollingberg said he remembers how complex it was when the bank’s leaders first approached him about what would become Roughrider Coin. 
“It was a bit like listening to someone speak underwater. You knew that they were saying something. Just had no idea what,” Bollingberg said, adding he’s grateful the Bank of North Dakota is providing education for banking leaders. 
North Dakota moves forward with stablecoin as local banks express interest in pilot project

The Roughrider Coin is not available for use by the general public or merchants. The pilot program is designed to test bank-to-bank transactions behind the scenes. Morgan said the Bank of North Dakota chose to limit the scope of the pilot program to minimize the potential risk of the new financial technology early on. The bank’s internal and external risk assessments concluded the initial Roughrider Coin program would be considered low risk.  
Banks typically use existing systems like ACH or wire transfers to move money from one bank to another. But these systems take time to complete a transaction, especially when crossing international borders. The systems also have daily deadlines that can create difficulties and cost money. 
“If we miss the cutoff by even a few minutes, it’s going to have to go out the next morning. Whereas if I used Roughrider Coin to do that same transaction, they’re gonna get it while I’m on the phone with them, telling them it’s coming,” Herrington said.
The Bank of North Dakota hopes the Roughrider Coin will become a faster and cheaper alternative to traditional payment methods. But to what extent it will complement or replace those existing payment methods depends on a lot of factors. It’s something the bank hopes to learn more about during the pilot program. 
“I’d be shocked if this doesn’t have a high rate of adoption and a high rate of transactions fulfilled within it,” Morgan said. “But there are a lot of unknowns still.”
North Dakota banking customers should not see any immediate changes or impacts even if their financial institution is involved in the pilot program. Long term, Morgan said one of the first benefits customers could potentially see is pushing daily transaction deadlines later in the day.
“There could potentially be quicker transaction times when that gets rolled out to the client level,” Morgan said. “You could see that as one of the first kind of benefits to occur.”
Ag commissioner lukewarm on Bank of North Dakota’s foray into stablecoin

Morgan said the Bank of North Dakota plans to add more banks and credit unions in the state to the program over time. There is no set deadline for the pilot program. 
“We’re not getting in any hurry. We have no rush to market. We’re not trying to meet shareholder return expectations. We’re trying to build this very safely, thoughtfully,” Morgan said. “If this pilot went on for a whole ’nother year of simply just testing and working out kinks and bugs, I would be OK with that.”
The Bank of North Dakota will provide regular updates to the North Dakota Industrial Commission, a three-person board chaired by Gov. Kelly Armstrong, which oversees the bank. One member of the commission, Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring, has urged the bank to proceed with caution.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Is Utah’s new 3-judge panel unconstitutional? Utah Supreme Court hears arguments
description: The Utah Supreme Court heard three back-to-back cases on Monday asking the high court to block a transfer of the cases to the Utah Legislature’s newly created, randomly selected three-judge panel specifically meant to hear challenges to Utah laws.  Attorneys in the three lawsuits — Planned Parenthood’s challenge to the state’s near-total abortion ban, the […[...]
text:
The newly expanded seven-member Utah Supreme Court hears arguments over whether a lawsuit over fossil fuel development should be transferred to a new three-judge panel in a hearing at the Utah Supreme Court's chambers in Salt Lake City on Oct. 5, 2026. (Pool photo by Julian Conrads/FOX 13 News)The Utah Supreme Court heard three back-to-back cases on Monday asking the high court to block a transfer of the cases to the Utah Legislature’s newly created, randomly selected three-judge panel specifically meant to hear challenges to Utah laws. 
Attorneys in the three lawsuits — Planned Parenthood’s challenge to the state’s near-total abortion ban, the League of Women Voters’ of Utah’s anti-gerrymandering case, and young Utahns suing the state over harms caused by fossil fuel permits — argued the Republican-controlled Utah Legislature overstepped its constitutional authority when it created the three-judge panel earlier this year. 
Faced with more lawsuits, Utah lawmakers move to change their new ‘constitutional court’

Proponents of the new panel made up of three district court judges have argued it’s meant to prevent “forum shopping” — or filing lawsuits in specific courts in order to receive a favorable outcome — and increasing the number of judges that would consider high-stakes cases that challenge the constitutionality of state laws. 
However, critics have alleged that the three-judge panel is unconstitutional, arguing the Utah Constitution doesn’t grant the Legislature the authority to create a district court structure that’s made up of more than one judge — and that it violates separation of powers between the courts and the Legislature. 
The plaintiffs in the three cases also argue the new court structure has delayed ongoing district court proceedings in each of their cases while allowing state officials to move cases away from judges that haven’t given them favorable outcomes. 
The trio of hearings marked the first high-profile cases to come before the newly expanded seven-member Utah Supreme Court, and they are among the first to spotlight how the court’s four newly appointed justices operate from the bench. 
Utah Supreme Court justice recused from 2 cases challenging constitutionality of new 3-judge panel

Two of them — Justices Jay Jorgensen and Stephen Dent, who have not held judicial positions prior to their appointments — jumped right into the fray, quick to start grilling attorneys. 
Justice John Nielsen recused himself from two of the hearings (the abortion and redistricting cases) due to past work he did as a private attorney for Pro-Life Utah in 2022 and the Utah Republican Party in a prior appeal to the underlying anti-gerrymandering lawsuit. 
For the Planned Parenthood and redistricting case hearings, 2nd District Judge Joseph Bean was appointed to fill in for Nielsen, though Nielsen sat on the bench for the case over fossil fuel development. 
Monday’s hearings stretched hours, well into the afternoon, with no decisions made. The court took the matter under advisement and is scheduled to recess until November. The justices gave no indication of when they might issue a decision in any of the cases. 
Planned Parenthood
Planned Parenthood Association of Utah’s attorney, Camila Vega, started her opening argument by saying the Legislature’s creation of the three-judge court came as the lawsuit over Utah’s near-total abortion ban neared its finish line, changing the rules of the game at the eleventh hour. 
“After four years of litigation and sitting inches from the finish line, PPAU’s case has been disrupted by legislation threatening to overhaul the structure of Utah’s judiciary,” Vega said. 
Planned Parenthood Association of Utah’s attorney, Camila Vega, argues against transferring Planned Parenthood’s lawsuit over the state’s near-total abortion ban to a new three-judge panel during a hearing at the Utah Supreme Court’s chambers in Salt Lake City on Oct. 5, 2026. (Pool photo by Julian Conrads/FOX 13 News)
Currently an injunction continues to block Utah’s near-total ban, upheld by the Utah Supreme Court in 2024 — one of the rulings that year that infuriated Utah’s GOP lawmakers. Today, abortion remains legal in Utah up to 18 weeks gestation. 
Frustrated with that case and how long it has taken to wind its way through the courts, the abortion lawsuit was one of the first state officials moved to transfer to the three-judge panel soon after the Legislature created it earlier this year. 
“This case and the two others this morning raise important questions,” Vega said. “Can the Legislature create a new type of district court without the express, constitutional authority to do so? Can it make this court available only at a party’s election and only for certain cases, including those against state defendants, like the Legislature itself? And can it do all of this in the name of solving problems that simply do not exist?” 
Utah governor swiftly signs bill to create 3-judge ‘constitutional court’ to hear challenges to laws

It was that moment — less than a minute into Vega’s opening argument — that Jorgensen started grilling her. 
“Who are we to tell the Legislature what problems exist in society?” Jorgensen interjected. 
Vega answered by saying lawmakers, in making recent changes to the judiciary, have pointed to “problems like solving judicial trust, efficiency … these are serious accusations, and there is really no evidence of any existence of these problems.” 
“There’s no evidence with us,” Jorgensen said. “But that’s why courts on all topics really defer to the Legislature. They talk to people out in the community … they get stopped in the grocery store. We talk to nobody. Somebody stops me in the grocery store, I won’t talk to them because we can only consider what’s in the record.” 
Vega argued that what the “record reflects, your Honor, is not that there is distrust in the judiciary but there is disagreement with certain judicial decisions.” She argued the creation of the three-judge panel is an “improper legislative purpose.” 
Dent also pressed Vega on her assertion that the Legislature doesn’t have the “express” constitutional power to create a three-judge district court panel. 
“One of our core principals is that the state constitution is not a grant of power, but a limitation of power,” Dent said. “So why should we be looking for express grants of power, and how does your position square with that fundamental principle?”
Newly appointed Justice Jay Jorgensen listens to arguments over whether a new three-judge district court panel is constitutional during a hearing at the Utah Supreme Court’s chambers in Salt Lake City on Oct. 5, 2026. (Pool photo by Julian Conrads/FOX 13 News)
Vega argued that Article VIII of the Utah Constitution, which outlines the state’s judicial department, “lays out a very careful balance” and “contains numerous express provisions of authority to the Legislature for the ways that it can shape the judiciary” through lawmaking. Those provisions set parameters, she argued, and don’t grant the Legislature “plenary authority over the judiciary.” 
Justice Paige Petersen also raised questions, while pointing out the law and resolutions that created the three-judge panel are “unusual” in the sense that, when invoked, they immediately take cases away from the original district court judge without allowing that district court to rule on whether transfer is proper. 
“So there’s no way for a plaintiff to challenge the transfer or to avoid the transfer happening,” Petersen said, questioning whether that creates a separation of powers issue. 
Petersen also noted she’s heard complaints about the abortion case and that it’s “taking too much time,” but she pointed out Planned Parenthood of Utah and the state’s attorneys agreed on a schedule more than a year ago, and they would have been back in court earlier this year, in April. 
But then the Legislature created the three-judge panel, which delayed the case further. 
Cox appoints 2 more justices in year of major changes to Utah’s Supreme Court

“I am concerned about the delay caused,” Petersen said. “I mean, you had arguments scheduled … and the filing of this notice to transfer threw a wrench into the whole case.” 
Erin Middleton, assistant solicitor general with the Utah Attorney General’s Office, defended the law creating the three-judge panel, arguing lawmakers were within their constitutional authority to make the “procedural” rule change and create the new district court structure. 
“This law does not do anything to interfere with that constitutionally guaranteed structure. There is still a district court of general jurisdiction,” Middleton said. “Much like the Legislature can legislate things like how many judges, the number of judicial districts, make changes to jurisdiction, it can determine in certain cases that three judges ought to sit instead of one.” 
In writing the constitution, Middleton argued “they didn’t set up the Constitution to expressly permit everything that might happen. They put in limitations. The limitation is just not in the constitution.” 
The questioning in the Planned Parenthood case spanned more than an hour. At the end, the court took the matter under advisement with no indication of when a ruling might come.

Notably, if a court finds the three-judge panel to be unconstitutional, Utah lawmakers included a trigger provision in another law, HB366, that creates a whole new court structure, a “Constitutional Court” that would have “exclusive jurisdiction” over lawsuits challenging the constitutionality of state laws, with judges chosen by a seven-member Constitutional Court Nominating Commission, each appointed by the governor for a four-year term. 
Associate Chief Justice Jill Pohlman wrestled with that issue while questioning Vega. 
“What would happen if we were to declare HB366 unconstitutional based on how it’s been invoked at this point in time?” she said, pointing to the trigger provision. “So if we were to agree with you that (HB366) is unconstitutional, what happens with that trigger part? Is that something that we decide now? Is that something that comes up later? I’m just not sure what happens with that.” 
Redistricting
Mark Gaber with the Campaign Legal Center represented the League of Women Voters of Utah and the other plaintiffs in the anti-gerrymandering case, which state officials have also moved to transfer away from 3rd District Judge Dianna Gibson to a three-judge panel.
Gaber argued that their case suffers from the transfer to the new panel at the late stage in the lawsuit. 
“For our case, we have had an evidentiary hearing. … All of the party’s expert witnesses came and testified,” Gaber said. “But we now have three new judges who did not sit and hear any of that evidence, who did not see those witnesses testify, and so lack the benefit in knowing the record in the case.” 
Mark Gaber, with the Campaign Legal Center, speaks on behalf of the League of Women Voters of Utah and other plaintiffs in Utah’s redistricting lawsuit, arguing against transferring the case to a new three-judge panel during a hearing at the Utah Supreme Court’s chambers in Salt Lake City on Oct. 5, 2026. (Pool photo by Julian Conrads/FOX 13 News)
The question at the center of the yearslong redistricting lawsuit is whether the Utah Legislature overstepped its constitutional authority when it repealed and replaced a voter-approved ballot initiative known as Proposition 4, which created an independent redistricting process and banned partisan gerrymandering. 
A preliminary injunction has blocked the Legislature’s 2021 congressional maps as the result of an “unconstitutional process” — which led to a court-ordered map for this year’s elections — but the larger case, including discovery, a trial and final determination, has yet to play out. 
Tyler Green, representing the state, argued the Legislature is supported by a “longstanding history” that allows them to have a say over court structures.
In Utah redistricting fight, plaintiffs ask judge to block Legislature’s new ‘constitutional court’

“We’re going to say for certain types of disputes, that have a statewide impact and are of sufficient importance, we’re going to use this particular process,” Green said, while arguing that there are benefits of “having more than one set of judicial eyes on them.” 
Green argued there’s “no express prohibition” in the constitution that prevents the Legislature from creating a three-judge district court panel. 
“There’s no basis for the argument that the Legislature must have pointed to a specific grant of power in Article VIII to be able to justify” all of its changes to court rules that already exist, Green said. 
Bean, the judge sitting in on the case in place of Nielsen, also raised a question of “fairness” and whether the new three-judge panel actually speeds up the court process — or bogs it down. 
“If it’s supposed to be a faster process and it turns out it’s not, does that then implicate that this is not fair — fair under the constitution?” he questioned. “If it slows it down so much that it’s not as good as one (district court) judge?”
Fossil fuel development
Attorney Joanna Zeigler, with Our Children’s Trust, argued on behalf of the 10 young Utahns suing over the state’s issuance of oil and gas permits, which they allege violates their rights to life, health and safety under the Utah Constitution. 
She urged the Utah Supreme Court to grant their request to stop the transfer of their case away from 3rd District Judge Laura Scott to the three-judge panel. 
Utah Supreme Court hears arguments from teens that fossil fuel policies violate their rights

Nielsen asked whether plaintiffs “engage in forum shopping” all the time by choosing which district to file their cases in, even if they have statewide impact. 
“I mean, this isn’t the kind of case that had to be filed in Salt Lake County because the stuff is just happening here,” he said. “Hypothetically, this could have happened anywhere in the state. So couldn’t the Legislature see this as a remedy to the plaintiffs’ forum shopping?”
Zeigler said the majority of the plaintiffs in the case live in Salt Lake City, so it was a convenient venue because of its proximity. “The 3rd District was not necessarily forum shopping, but it was a convenient venue for all parties,” she said. “And the venue was never challenged.”
Much of the justices’ lines of questioning challenged attorneys on both sides of the issue. 
While Jorgensen, Dent and Nielsen in particular raised questions that indicated positions that could align with the Legislature’s arguments, it’s premature to assume they’ll side one way or another.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Six years ago, Maryland changed how some electric rates are set. It went poorly, officials say.
description: Maryland regulators are concerned about a rate-setting practice that let electric utilities project future spending and ask that customers' rates be set accordingly.  But while they said the pilot program had failed, they aren’t ready to abandon it altogether.
text:
Commissioners on the Maryland Public Service Commission hear a case involving a rate increase request from Baltimore Gas & Electric on Aug. 11, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)Maryland regulators say they’re concerned about a rate-setting practice that electric utilities have been using in the state since 2020. But they aren’t ready to abandon it altogether.
The Maryland Public Service Commission ended a pilot program Thursday that had allowed utilities in the state to file “Multi-Year Rate Plans,” during which the companies could project their future spending on the electric system and ask that customers’ rates be increased accordingly.
The pilot program was a big change compared to traditional ratemaking, wherein utilities completed work on the electric system and then asked for regulators’ permission to charge those costs to customers.
The commission had hoped that the pilot program would lead to more transparency about utilities’ planned spending, make customer rates more predictable, spread rate increases out over several years and make rate proceedings less burdensome. But it found that those goals were “largely unachieved.”
Under the model, the utility companies were able to recover their costs more quickly, and they did provide more information about planned capital spending. But “the Commission did not find that those changes produced clear, measurable benefits for ratepayers,” according to a commission news release.
In its order, the commission wrote that it “generally agrees” with the idea that, “The current [MRP] process doesn’t need a little tinkering up or down, it needs a major rehaul or a complete elimination.”
Maryland officials say changes to electric grid governance aren’t enough

The commission ordered a working group to make recommendations for a possible “substantially reformed” multiyear rate plan procedure by June 30.
Maryland’s consumer advocate, People’s Counsel David Lapp, argued in a statement Thursday that the order from the commission “makes clear that MRPs have failed to deliver for customers.”
In a March analysis, Lapp’s office determined that customers’ rates increased at a more rapid clip under multiyear rate plans, compared to the six-year period prior.
His office has argued that utilities do not contain costs as much as they would have previously, because of the specter of possible rejection from the commission. Instead, the utilities submit long lists of construction projects that regulators and watchdogs must spend a considerable amount of time and effort vetting.
In his statement, Lapp lamented the fact that some form of multiyear ratemaking could continue in the future.
“Unfortunately, despite the PSC’s findings, new ratemaking practices based on utility forecasts are still possible in the future, which will require putting more resources into a fundamentally flawed approach,” Lapp said.
In a joint statement, Maryland’s three Exelon utilities, which used the multiyear ratemaking process, applauded the commission’s willingness to continue allowing forward-looking ratemaking.
“The Maryland Public Service Commission affirmed that forward-looking ratemaking does have a place in Maryland’s regulatory future. We support efforts to strengthen the process and place more focus on customer value,” wrote Nick Alexopulos, a spokesman for Baltimore Gas & Electric.
In its order, the five-member commission, whose members are appointed by the governor, admonished utilities for providing insufficient information up front about their planned projects, forcing watchdogs to make a high volume of requests for additional information.
“The Commission finds that, from their initial filing, utilities should have taken a proactive upfront approach to sharing detailed information with parties, similar to how a person applies for a grant,” the order said.
And while the commission wanted utilities to have some flexibility after their projects were approved, it noted that the utilities sometimes made significant changes to their work plans after the fact, diminishing the benefits of early review.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“There appears to have been significant variations in what projects were added or removed such that the benefit of a preliminary review afforded by an MRP is lessened,” reads the order.
Although the commission hoped that utilities recovering their construction costs more quickly would place them on stronger financial footing, which could provide benefits to the customers, the order said there’s no evidence customers saw any upside.
“It is unclear if or how that translated into a financial benefit to ratepayers as there was no indication of improved debt ratings, measurably lower financing costs, or that it was in the ratepayers’ interest to see their rates increase earlier than would have occurred under traditional ratemaking,” reads the order.
The commission also evaluated the pilot program on a few other grounds, and found that it did not demonstrably increase the utilities’ innovation, or advance Maryland’s energy policy goals.
The Maryland General Assembly has intervened repeatedly in the multiyear ratemaking debate — but has so far allowed the practice to continue.
In 2025, lawmakers added criteria that utilities must meet in order to have their multiyear plans approved. The legislature also prohibited utilities from coming back to the commission for “reconciliation,” after cost or revenue variances.
Earlier this year, the legislature modified the law again, noting that utilities could return money to customers if they under-spend, but could not request more money from consumers if they overspend, relative to their projections.
Even with sweeping utility reform legislation in place, regulators fight rising rate requests

In the same bill, lawmakers temporarily prohibited “forecast test years,” a general term that includes multiyear rate plans. The legislature commissioned a study from the commission comparing forecasting with traditional ratemaking, or a potential hybrid model.
The commission has asked its working group to deliver that study by Feb. 1, so it can be sent to the legislature by the April 1 deadline.
House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Anne Arundel and Prince George’s) supported ending forecasted ratemaking altogether, and that provision passed the House of Delegates this year. But it faced opposition in the Senate, and she ultimately reached a compromise with Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore) establishing the pause on forecasted ratemaking.
In a statement, Peña-Melnyk said she appreciates the commission’s “willingness to acknowledge where the model fell short.”
“The Public Service Commission’s findings reinforce why the General Assembly required a closer examination of how utility rates are set in Maryland,” Peña-Melnyk wrote. “If a ratemaking model asks families to pay today based on what a utility projects it will spend tomorrow, we need strong evidence that those investments are necessary, that the projections are accurate, and that customers are actually receiving the promised benefits.”
Consumer group Maryland PIRG wrote that the commission’s findings about the multiyear rate process “align with what consumer groups have been arguing for years: forecasted ratemaking means Marylanders are paying more and getting less.”
“Until our state leaders permanently end forecast ratemaking and other profit guarantees, ratepayers will continue to be at risk. Experimenting with anti-consumer ratemaking pilots once is a mistake. Twice is a choice.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota man pleads guilty in cattle Ponzi scheme; state license revoked
description: A North Dakota cattle broker has pleaded guilty to a charge stemming from an investigation that found a beef marketing company operated as a Ponzi scheme.  Taylor Bang of Killdeer pleaded guilty Sept. 9 to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud in U.S. District Court in Texas, according to court records.  Sentencing has […]
text:
A box used by Agridime, now known as American Grazed Beef, to ship frozen meat products to consumers. (Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor) A North Dakota cattle broker has pleaded guilty to a charge stemming from an investigation that found a beef marketing company operated as a Ponzi scheme. 
Taylor Bang of Killdeer pleaded guilty Sept. 9 to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud in U.S. District Court in Texas, according to court records. 
Sentencing has been set for Jan. 7. The maximum sentence could include up to five years in prison, a fine and restitution payments.
The North Dakota Department of Agriculture on Monday ordered Taylor Bang Cattle Sales to cease any livestock related sales. Bang’s guilty plea triggered the cease and desist order and the revocation of Bang’s livestock dealer license.
Bang was among five people charged earlier this year in the Agridime investigation. The charges were filed in Texas, where Agridime was based. 
North Dakota man among 5 charged in Agridime cattle fraud case

A judge in August 2024 determined that Agridime had operated as a Ponzi scheme, paying off early investors with money raised from new investors, instead of paying investors with profits from the company. 
The company bought cattle and sold frozen beef from its website to consumers. But payments to investors and cattle producers dried up, with the company owing investors $220 million, court records alleged. 
Many of those owed money were in western North Dakota, where Bang bought cattle for Agridime. The North Dakota Securities Commission has said North Dakota investors were owed about $40 million when federal authorities took over the business late in 2023.
The North Dakota Securities Department has said Bang earned $6 million in commissions from Agridime. Bang told the North Dakota Monitor in December 2023 that the figure was “way high.”  
A voicemail message and text message sent to Bang on Monday was not returned. His attorney in Texas, Dan Cogdell, was not available for comment Monday, according to office staff. 
Bang in February was charged with eight counts of wire fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and one count of money laundering. 
A court filing by Bang’s attorney in March contended Bang did not engage in fraud or knowingly take part in a Ponzi scheme. 
The indictment said someone sent $240,000 to an account controlled by Bang rather than to an account controlled by Agridime in order to conceal the transaction. The indictment also said Bang falsified dates on records and gave investors false information about identification tags for cattle.

title: US Transportation chief urges creative solutions for infrastructure funding
description: U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy urged Arkansas business leaders to consider creative solutions to funding infrastructure projects during a visit to the state’s 3rd Congressional District Monday.  There’s not enough federal funding to support all of the country’s needed projects, but partnerships can help address this challenge, Duffy said.  “We n[...]
text:
U.S. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy speaks with business leaders during a working lunch at Northwest Arkansas National Airport on Oct. 5, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy urged Arkansas business leaders to consider creative solutions to funding infrastructure projects during a visit to the state’s 3rd Congressional District Monday. 
There’s not enough federal funding to support all of the country’s needed projects, but partnerships can help address this challenge, Duffy said. 
“We need to figure out better how these projects can work together with community, states, private capital and with us all coming together to make them feasible for the communities that use them,” he said.
Northwest Arkansas airport officials seek federal loan to support terminal expansion

Duffy said he wants to invest in projects that move the most people and goods during a working luncheon with transportation and business leaders at Northwest Arkansas National Airport Monday. 
The region’s officials have invested in various infrastructure projects in recent years to serve a growing population. Companies like Walmart, Tyson Foods and J.B. Hunt also have their headquarters in Benton and Washington counties and rely on local infrastructure to provide services to the rest of the country.
Republican U.S. Representative Steve Womack invited Duffy to Arkansas to view some of the region’s infrastructure projects, including a 14-mile segment of Interstate 49 between Alma and Barling. 
Locally, construction of the Arkansas River Bridge Crossing will provide congestion relief for Fort Smith and Van Buren, according to a press release from Womack’s office. 
Nationally, it’s helping close a 155-mile gap in I-49, which will provide a north-to-south interstate connection from Canada to Louisiana once it’s completed. 
Womack chairs the House Appropriations Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, and Related Agencies Subcommittee, and helped secure $21 million for the project’s construction through the appropriations process. The Arkansas Department of Transportation also received a $25 million federal grant for the project. 
Duffy was the third federal official to visit Northwest Arkansas National Airport at the invitation of Womack this year. Federal Aviation Administration Bryan Bedford attended a celebration in March for the airport’s new traffic control tower, which was supported by state and federal grants.
FAA leader highlights importance of airspace modernization in Arkansas visit 

Morteza Farajian, executive director of the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Build America Bureau, discussed in August the airport’s application for a federal low-interest loan to support construction of a new terminal. 
The $1.2 trillion infrastructure bill that then-President Joe Biden signed in 2021 has funded several projects in Arkansas. All six members of the state’s Republican congressional delegation, including Womack, voted against the law.
Airport CEO Aaron Burkes said he’s optimistic the application will be approved, but Congress’ approval of a continuing resolution that funds the budget through Dec. 11 has presented some complications. 
Congress is in recess until after the midterm elections, at which point Womack said lawmakers have work to do to finish approving fiscal year 2027 appropriation bills. Womack, who has long criticized Congress’ process for funding the federal government, said he’s set aside a lot of money legislatively for community projects across the country, including in Arkansas.
“So if you don’t get the bill signed into law, those projects go away,” he said. “And in the case of the 3rd District of Arkansas, that would cost us over $100 million.”

description: A child died last month from complications of the invasive Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) infection, the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services reported Monday. H. Influenzae is a bacterium that can cause mild ear infections and also severe infections, including ones in the bloodstream, pneumonia and meningitis, the health department sai[...]
text:
CDC data on H. influenzae disease cases. A vaccine exists for Hib, or type b. (Screenshot of CDC site on Hib)A child died last month from complications of the invasive Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) infection, the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services reported Monday.
H. Influenzae is a bacterium that can cause mild ear infections and also severe infections, including ones in the bloodstream, pneumonia and meningitis, the health department said.
It spreads through coughing or sneezing, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The CDC said Hib vaccination began for children in 1987 and for infants in 1990, and since then, type b cases in children decreased by 99%.
In a statement from the health department, Douglas Harrington, state medical officer, said the tragedy in Montana is a reminder the disease still exists “and can have devastating consequences.”
“I encourage Montana parents to consult with their medical provider to keep their child up to date on all recommended vaccines, including the Hib vaccine,” Harrington said.
The health department is not releasing the age, gender or county where the child lived.
“Vaccination protects against one type of H. influenzae, commonly called Hib,” the news release said. “This patient had not received the Hib vaccine. Hib vaccination recommendations vary based on age, vaccination history, and certain medical conditions.”
A news release said Montana has recorded four other pediatric deaths since 2012 due to the invasive H. influenzae, but none of those were identified as type b. It said vaccines are not available for other strains.
The CDC recommends Hib vaccination for all children younger than 5 years old. The news release said older children and adults usually don’t need the Hib vaccine unless they have certain medical conditions.
“Hib and other recommended childhood vaccines are available at no cost for eligible Montana children through Vaccines for Children providers statewide,” the news release said.
To find a Vaccines for Children provider, contact the Montana Immunization Program at (406) 444-5580.

title: Crop condition dips slightly as Iowa farmers face another wet week
description: After one of the wettest Septembers on record, corn and soybean conditions are dipping slightly as farmers have had scarce opportunities to harvest, according to the latest crop progress and condition report.  Corn condition rated 72% good to excellent for the Sept. 28 through Oct. 4 reporting period, a 3 percentage point decline from the […]
text:
Mature corn on the edge of a partially harvested field in western Iowa in October 2025. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) After one of the wettest Septembers on record, corn and soybean conditions are dipping slightly as farmers have had scarce opportunities to harvest, according to the latest crop progress and condition report. 
Corn condition rated 72% good to excellent for the Sept. 28 through Oct. 4 reporting period, a 3 percentage point decline from the previous reporting period. Soybeans rated 70% good to excellent for the period, marking a 4 percentage point decline from the week prior. 
Iowa has had above-average precipitation levels for the past three reporting periods, two of which had fewer than two days suitable for field work. The latest report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture showed 1.2 days suitable for field work, meaning farmers have not been able to get out into the field to harvest even though 85% of corn acres had reached maturity during the reporting period and 81% of soybean acres were dropping leaves. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As of the latest reporting period, 7% of Iowa corn acres had been harvested, which is just a 2 percentage point increase from the week prior and is 13 percentage points behind the five-year average. Due to the government shutdown last October, crop data from 2025 is not available. 
Soybean harvest, as of the reporting period, was 5% compared to a five-year average of 38%. 
With the wet conditions, there is a concern for mold or fungus growth on corn and soybeans, according to Iowa State University Extension and Outreach professionals.
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig said farmers should be able to “make some progress in the field” this week as warmer, drier conditions are forecast. 
“After a historically wet September, we finally got a stretch of dry weather,” Naig said in a news release. “The warmer temperatures and sunshine are helping fields dry down, though some of the wetter areas are going to need several more days before equipment can roll.” 
According to the report, 45% of topsoil and 34% of subsoil had surplus moisture conditions.
State Climatologist Justin Glisan reported a statewide average temperature for the reporting period of 61.8 degrees, which was 4 degrees above the climatological average. 
While the end of the reporting period had drier conditions, according to Glisan, the statewide precipitation average for the week was just under 2 inches and about 1.2 inches above the normal. Most of the state received 1.5 inches of precipitation or more, with Portsmouth in Shelby County logging the greatest precipitation for the week at 6.49 inches.
