title: Montana health officials warn of severe risks as Fergus County confirms measles case
description: Some health experts say Montanans are at risk of measles with declining vaccination rates, and Fergus County confirmed this month a case of measles. Measles is a highly contagious disease, but two vaccination doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are 97% effective, according to the Fergus County Health Department and other health officials. […]
text:
(Photo by George Frey/Getty Images)Some health experts say Montanans are at risk of measles with declining vaccination rates, and Fergus County confirmed this month a case of measles.
Measles is a highly contagious disease, but two vaccination doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are 97% effective, according to the Fergus County Health Department and other health officials.
Montana has counted six measles cases this year, according to a dashboard of the state Department of Public Health and Human Services.
In March, Lewis and Clark County had five cases, according to the dashboard. Flathead County issued a warning last month of a possible exposure, but it had no cases, the county confirmed Monday.
Friday, a news release from Fergus County said the local health department confirmed a case that had potential exposures.
The possible exposures were at the Amtrak station in Malta at 2:20 p.m. Sept. 24, and at Evergreen Wood Products in Moore on Sept. 25.
Measles spreads mainly through the air. The news release from Fergus County says droplets with the virus that are released in coughs, sneezes or talking can remain in the air for as long as two hours.
“This means someone can get measles even without direct contact with the infected person,” Fergus County said in the news release.
When more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated, most residents are shielded from measles, but vaccine rates are dropping, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services spokesperson Jon Ebelt did not respond to a request Monday for the estimated portion of Montanans who are immunized against measles.
Providence, a health care organization that operates major hospitals in Montana and beyond, said in a news update this year that declining measles vaccination rates are putting Montanans at risk.
The update from Providence didn’t quantify the decline in Montana, but a CDC survey of 347 2-year-olds in Montana from 2021-2023 shows the rate was 86.3%.
The CDC said the vaccination rate among kindergartners nationally has dropped from 95.2% in the 2019-2020 school year to 92.4% in 2025-2026.
In Idaho, an estimated 75.2% of kindergartners were fully vaccinated for measles last school year; in Wyoming, it was 92.6%; in North Dakota, 88.5%; and in South Dakota, 89.3%, according to the CDC.
In 2021, Republican Gov. Greg Gianforte signed House Bill 334, which removed local and state health department access to student immunization records and deemed them private, among other provisions.
A spokesperson for the Governor’s Office could not be reached Monday afternoon by email about whether the governor would support a reinstatement of the health department’s access to those records given the threat of measles.

name: VTDigger
title: Brattleboro fire chief deploys for 13 months
description:
Chief Jay Symonds serves with the New York Army National Guard. The planning for a handoff to an interim chief began several months ago.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Brattleboro fire chief deploys for 13 months.
text:
First responders and town officials gathered at Centra Fire Station in Brattleboro to say goodbye to Fire Chief Jay Symonds before he leaves for approximately 13 months of military service with the New York Army National Guard on Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. Photo by Kristopher Radder/Brattleboro Reformer

This story by Kristopher Radder was first published in the Brattleboro Reformer Oct. 4, 2026.
BRATTLEBORO — The meeting room at Central Fire Station was filled with firefighters, first responders and town officials Friday morning as Brattleboro Fire Chief Jay Symonds prepared to leave for 13 months of military service.
Symonds, who has served as Brattleboro’s fire chief and emergency management director, was scheduled to depart in early October for an approximately 13-month deployment with the New York Army National Guard.
Assistant Fire Chief Charles Keir addressed Symonds during the gathering, thanking him for his service to both the community and the country.
“Stay sharp. Look after your troops, and know that we are proud of you today, tomorrow and every day that you’re away,” Keir said. “May you go with courage and serve with honor and return safely.”
“Thank you for your service, Chief,” Keir said. “Thank you for your service to the community and to our country.”
Symonds said the support he has received from people around town has made an impression on him and his family.
“Walking down the street, people saying, ‘Hey, good luck on your deployment,’” Symonds said. “It’s really impactful to me and to my family, and we all really appreciate it.”
While he will be away, Symonds said, the Brattleboro Fire Department and the people he serves will remain on his mind.
“Know that while I’m deployed, you will all be in my thoughts as well,” he said. “I appreciate your thoughts and support, but I will be thinking of you every day.”
Symonds said he will miss being part of the department and the daily interactions that come with his job. He also joked that he would be keeping an eye on things from afar.
“I will be hovering a little bit,” Symonds said. “I’ll be keeping an eye on you.”
The transition to interim leadership has been in the works for months.
Symonds said he, Town Manager John Potter and Peter Lynch began planning the handoff several months ago, working to document projects, responsibilities and other information that had largely been kept in Symonds’ head.
“There’s a lot of things that are in my head that are written down on paper, and trying to get all those things down on paper and sharing those with Pete so that there’s that continuity between the two of us,” Symonds said. “It’s like I never left.”
Lynch, a longtime member of the Brattleboro Fire Department and former assistant fire chief, will serve as interim fire chief and emergency management director during Symonds’ absence.
Symonds said the transition has been stressful, in part because he is simultaneously preparing for his military service, handling responsibilities at home, and making sure the department is prepared for his absence.
“I want to keep an awareness of what’s happening while I’m gone, so that when I come back, it’s like I never left,” he said.
Symonds said he also plans to remain involved in some town business when his military duties allow.
That includes participating in the development of the town’s fiscal year 2028 and fiscal year 2029 budgets. He has also offered to help with projects that require research if he has the time to do so while deployed.
He serves with the New York Army National Guard and is a command sergeant major with the 204th Engineer Battalion. This marks his 29th year of military service.
Symonds originally served as a heavy equipment operator, working with bulldozers and excavators, before his military career evolved into project management.
The deployment means leaving behind a job and community that Symonds said he cares deeply about.
“I’ll miss the people,” he said. “I’ll miss all the fire department personnel that I work with. I look forward to seeing them every single day.”
He said he will also miss interacting with other town department heads, residents, other fire departments and fire chiefs.
“I have a passion for fire service and emergency services,” Symonds said. “Being able to get out there and take care of people and be a part of the solution is something I really enjoy.”
“Going a year without that is, you know, I’m going to miss those things,” he said.
Despite the time away, Symonds said he is already looking forward to returning to Brattleboro.
“I truly look forward to getting back here and getting back into the position and back to the work that we started,” he told those gathered at Central Station.
After thanking the first responders and town officials who came to see him off, Symonds kept his final message simple.
“I look forward to coming back,” he said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: After Democrats boost JKT, national Republicans send $1.6 million to Alaska for governor’s race
description: A national Republican organization has put $1.6 million into the Alaska governor’s race — going toe-to-toe with Democratic money that’s also flooded into the state in recent days.
text:
Republican Bernadette Wilson placed third in the August gubernatorial primary election and has called on her two GOP opponents in the general election to suspend their campaigns. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)A national Republican organization has put $1.6 million into the Alaska governor’s race — going toe-to-toe with Democratic money that’s also flooded into the state in recent days.
The Republican Governors Association made the transfer Wednesday to Kodiak PAC, an Alaska group that’s working in support of GOP gubernatorial candidates, according to campaign finance disclosures.
A separate donation last week from an arm of the Democratic Governors Association brought its total contribution to a competing group, Forward Frontier, to $1.25 million.
A separate, organized labor-affiliated group, Putting Alaskans First, also reported spending $175,000 this week on radio ads intended to benefit Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the former state House member who’s the only Democrat in the four-candidate gubernatorial field.
While Kreiss-Tomkins won the primary and remains the heavy favorite among political insiders — and prediction markets — the contribution from the RGA indicates that national Republicans think Alaska is still in play. The group did not respond to a request for comment Thursday.
“I’m sort of surprised they’re even bothering at this point,” said Jim Lottsfeldt, a centrist political consultant who’s working with groups supporting Kreiss-Tomkins’ campaign. “It’s hard to imagine any of the Republicans prevailing. But I guess they have plenty of money.”
One unanswered question about the Republicans’ participation in the race is what message they will broadcast — and whether they’ll try to boost one of the GOP candidates over the others.
GOP activist Bernadette Wilson was the top-ranked Republican in the August primary, ahead of former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor .
Numerous conservatives, including Bronson and Taylor, have warned that GOP infighting could cost Republicans the governor’s race — if negative campaigning causes voters to choose just one or two of the three GOP candidates in Alaska’s ranked choice voting system.
But Wilson hasn’t played along, labeling both Bronson and Taylor as “spoilers” and asking them to suspend their campaigns.
Independent groups like Kodiak PAC are barred by law from working directly with candidates. Reached by phone Thursday, officials with both the campaigns of Republicans Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor said they hadn’t heard about the $1.6 million contribution.
“We hope this money goes to something that benefits the Republican Party in a ranked choice voting scenario,” said a spokesperson for Bronson. “It’s news to us.”
April Gettys, Taylor’s campaign manager, also denied any knowledge of the RGA’s donation or Kodiak PAC’s plans.
“As of right now, the campaign doesn’t know anything about the PAC,” she said.
Wilson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
A spokesperson for Kreiss-Tomkins also didn’t respond to a request for comment. His campaign sent a fundraising email earlier Thursday criticizing a new ad from Wilson that attacks him for raising campaign funds from employees of artificial intelligence companies and labeling him as “Chat JKT.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Bill to regulate kratom sales and ban synthetic compounds passes Pa. House
description: Kratom is an intoxicating substance that can be purchased at gas stations, smoke shops and corner stores across Pennsylvania and much of the country. In recent years, its popularity in America has exploded, as has the number of states that regulate its sale.
text:
7-OH products, a concentrated synthetic kratom derivative, are displayed at a retail store in Bismarck on Aug. 5, 2026, hours before a state ban took effect. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor) 

 
Members of the Pennsylvania state House voted unanimously Monday to pass a bill that would regulate natural leaf kratom products and ban the sale of synthetic compounds derived from the substance.
“This legislation is not about pretending that kratom is risk-free,” said the bill’s sponsor, Rep. Bridget Kosierowski (D-Lackawanna). “It is about acknowledging the reality that kratom is already here, and establishing rules that make the marketplace more transparent and accountable. We should not have to choose between doing nothing and criminalizing use. There is a responsible middle ground we can establish.”
Kratom is an intoxicating substance that can be purchased at gas stations, smoke shops and corner stores across Pennsylvania and much of the country. In recent years, its popularity in America has exploded, as has the number of states that regulate its sale.
It’s made from the leaves of a tree native to southeast Asia, where its been used for medicinal, ceremonial and recreational purposes for centuries. Its primary active ingredient, mitragynine, acts on the brain’s mu-opioid receptors, much like painkillers and other narcotic opioids.
Health experts, lawmakers push for Pa. kratom regulation; proponents warn they’ll fight a ban

Kratom leaves also contain trace amounts of a more powerful psychoactive compound called 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH, which also produces opioid-like effects.
In small doses, kratom acts as a stimulant, but in large doses more as a sedative. Public health experts and addiction treatment specialists warn that, while it appears to be far less likely to cause overdoses than more regulated opioids like heroin, it can still be addictive. And little research is available on the long-term health impacts of ingesting kratom or its interactions with other drugs.
In recent years, the number of kratom-related calls to poison control centers and overdoses involving the substance, whether taken alone or in combination with other drugs, have grown.
That’s in part because of the increasing availability of products containing synthetic compounds derived from kratom that are designed to be far more potent than the leaf itself. Products containing high levels of 7-OH, made by extracting it from kratom leaves, have also grown in popularity and availability.
But experts warn even in natural leaf form, kratom can still be addictive. Treatment specialists say it is becoming more common to receive patients seeking help with kratom addiction, even experiencing withdrawal symptoms that resemble other opioid users. It is not clear how many of those patients are using natural leaf kratom or more powerful, synthetic compounds.
Some kratom advocates, however, say the product has been beneficial for people seeking to wean themselves off more dangerous opioids. But doctors warn there is little data on its efficacy compared to other treatments that can be prescribed by doctors like suboxone or buprenorphine. Compared to those medications, kratom’s halflife is far shorter, meaning users may begin to experience withdrawal every three to six hours after ingesting it.
What would the regulations do?
The legislation passed by the house would continue to allow only the sale of products made from natural kratom leaf in powdered or capsule form by vendors who register with the state. It would also ban the sale of the kratom to anyone under 21 years old.
The bill also contains strict packaging requirements. 
Packages would have to include the manufacturer’s name and address, a warning that the products have not been evaluated by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and not contain any medical claims. They would also have to be child resistant and not designed to appeal to minors.
As it stands, a lack of labeling standards means it’s not always clear what users are receiving when they purchase products labeled as kratom.
Kratom products would be taxed at 12%, and the revenue would be directed into funds to ensure the legislation’s enforcement.
The measure would establish criminal penalties for would-be sellers who violate the new rules, as opposed to individual users.
The bill would still have to work its way through the state Senate before the end of the legislative session and receive the governor’s signature to become law.
Spokespeople for Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman (R-Indiana) and Senate President Pro Tempore Kim Ward (R-Westmoreland) did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The state Senate has only seven days scheduled for the rest of the legislative session.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Uthmeier announces arrests in alleged massive sea life poaching ring
description: State officials announced criminal charges Monday against 10 individuals in an alleged poaching conspiracy involving overfishing of reef fish including grouper, redfish, and snapper, plus protected sea turtles, including hatchlings. The arrests followed an investigation that began in 2022, when a party to the alleged scheme approached an undercover officer,[...]
text:
Charges announced Monday included poaching of protected sea turtles. (Via Sea Turtle Conservancy)State officials announced criminal charges Monday against 10 individuals in an alleged poaching conspiracy involving overfishing of reef fish including grouper, redfish, and snapper, plus protected sea turtles, including hatchlings.
The arrests followed an investigation that began in 2022, when a party to the alleged scheme approached an undercover officer, Attorney General James Uthmeier said during a news conference in Carrabelle.
Participating agencies included the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, the Office of Statewide Prosecutor, and local law enforcement.
The suspects are from an area stretching from Florida’s Big Bend region to Tampa Bay, according to authorities. The haul allegedly ran to approximately 23,000 pounds of fish and sales totaled more than $150,000 worth of fish, shrimp, and turtles. That harmed legitimate commercial and recreational fishermen, law enforcement said.
The more serious charges include racketeering, conspiracy to commit racketeering, and unlawful possession or sale of marine turtles. Potential sentences on these charges range between 65 and 75 years, Uthmeier’s office said.
Still, Uthmeier said he plans to ask the Legislature to boost penalties for poaching.
“A lot of the poaching laws on the books today are just misdemeanors. Yes, people trespassing, having firearms on private land, there’s going to be other crimes involved,” he said.
“But if you’re bringing a rifle out and you’re shooting near a dwelling where families are living, illegally poaching at night, you need to be charged with a third-degree felony. If you’re in close proximity to people, you need to be looking at more than five years behind bars, for sure.”
The matter “started as something that seemed like a much more minor offense — just some small-scale poaching of some reef fish. And then, all of a sudden, you realize it’s more than just a couple of actors here — you’ve got over a dozen people engaged in a statewide network to sell the harvest illegally, violating multiple state laws up and down much of North Florida,” Uthmeier said.
Appointed to his office by Gov. Ron DeSantis in 2025, Uthmeier is seeking election in his own right against Democratic former state Sen. José JavÍer Rodriguez.

name: VTDigger
title: Attorney for man charged in a deadly police chase seeks to quiz potential jurors before seeking change of venue
description:
The lawyer called it an “efficient way to address the enormous amount of publicity this case has generated, and the strong feelings that appear to exist in a large number of people in Rutland County.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Attorney for man charged in a deadly police chase seeks to quiz potential jurors before seeking change of venue.
text:
Tate Rheaume appears in Rutland County Superior criminal court in April 2024. Rheaume is charged in the crash that killed Rutland City police officer Jessica Ebbighausen in 2023. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The attorney for the man accused of driving into and killing a Rutland officer during a chase wants to question prospective jurors about what they may know and feel about the case before moving forward with a request to move the case to another county.
David Sleigh, the lawyer for Tate Rheaume, told Judge Susan McManus during a hearing Monday in Rutland Superior criminal court that extensive media coverage of the case has raised concerns about selecting an impartial jury.
Rheaume, 23, of Salisbury, has pleaded not guilty to several offenses, including aggravated murder, in the July 7, 2023 pursuit that led to the death of 19-year-old Jessica Ebbighausen, a Rutland City police trainee.
The chase ended on Woodstock Avenue in Rutland when Rheaume drove his pickup nearly head-on into a cruiser driven by Ebbighausen as another officer had been pursuing Rheaume.
Sleigh suggested Monday to the judge that prospective jurors be sent an “initial” questionnaire asking two or three questions, such as:

Are you aware of this case?
Have you formed a judgement about Rheaume’s guilt or innocence?

That, Sleigh said, would likely “weed out quite a few potential jurors” and those that remained in the jury pool could then be sent a “more elaborate questionnaire” in the process of selecting a jury and determining whether a fair and impartial jury could be seated.
“I think it’s an efficient way to address the enormous amount of publicity this case has generated, and the strong feelings that appear to exist in a large number of people in Rutland County,” Sleigh told the judge.  
Rutland County Deputy State’s Attorney Daron Raleigh, the prosecutor, said during the hearing that Monday was the first time she had heard about Sleigh’s proposal and she was not prepared to sign off on it. 
McManus, the judge, didn’t issue any decision and scheduled another hearing in the matter in two weeks.
“If there’s no agreement between the parties, Attorney Sleigh, regarding your proposal, do you anticipate going forward on the motion to change venue?” the judge asked. 
“I don’t know, your honor,” Sleigh replied. “But I’ll certainly have an answer for that the next time we speak.”
Sleigh submitted a motion earlier this year to move the trial in the case out of Rutland County, citing, in part, the amount of media attention it has received. The prosecution filed a motion opposing such a move. 
No trial date has been set in the case. 
The case has been delayed as a separate issue raised by the defense worked its way through the legal system. 
Sleigh had sought authority from the judge to introduce during the trial details from a blistering internal affairs report that found officer misconduct by other officers in the pursuit. A Rutland judge denied that request and the Vermont Supreme Court later upheld that ruling in August.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Nonprofits to erase $34 million in medical debt for 21,000 Kansans
description: TOPEKA — More than 21,000 Kansans are set to receive a letter this month notifying them that their medical debt has disappeared. A pair of nonprofit organizations announced they will abolish nearly $34 million in medical debt for 21,490 Kansans who meet certain criteria in a large-scale, one-time economic relief initiative. “This isn’t actually about […]
text:
A pair of nonprofits announce sweeping medical debt relief for nearly 21,500 Kansans. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)TOPEKA — More than 21,000 Kansans are set to receive a letter this month notifying them that their medical debt has disappeared.
A pair of nonprofit organizations announced they will abolish nearly $34 million in medical debt for 21,490 Kansans who meet certain criteria in a large-scale, one-time economic relief initiative.
“This isn’t actually about medical debt,” said Melissa Morales, founder of Somos Votantes and a native Kansan. “This is about a broken healthcare system that people can’t afford.”
The mechanics of erasing $33.9 million in medical debt in Kansas began with a partnership between the national nonprofit Undue Medical Debt, which acquires medical debts in bulk from providers and collection agencies for pennies on the dollar, and Somos Votantes Education Fund, a nonpartisan civic engagement organization that donates to abolish the debt. On average, one dollar donated erases $100 in medical debt, according to an announcement from the two organizations.
Kansas is the first in the partnership’s history to receive statewide medical debt relief for low-income Kansans. The two organizations abolished $133 million in medical debt for more than 128,000 people in select counties in Nevada in 2025 and this year are expected to eliminate $240,000 in utility debt in Michigan. Each effort is part of the education fund’s Seeds of Relief program.
Eligible people in Kansas include those with medical debts that are 5% or more of their annual income or people who earn less than four times the federal poverty level, which totals about $100,000 for a family of three.
They will receive letters branded with Undue Medical Debt’s information beginning the week of Oct. 19 that will indicate which debts have been forgiven. No action has to be taken.
“Nobody chooses to have medical debt,” Morales said. “Nobody chooses to get sick.”
She said she hopes the debt relief brings “a little bit of breathing room” for Kansans. Morales, who is from Liberal, founded Somos Votantes, a Latino voter outreach organization. The medical debt initiatives from the organization’s philanthropic arm, Somos Votantes Education Fund, is nonpartisan, Morales said, helping families regardless of party or affiliation.
“At Somos, we believe a medical bill shouldn’t be the reason someone can’t pay rent or put food on the table, but that’s the reality for too many hardworking Kansans right now,” Morales said in an announcement. “Somos will step in for working families when no one else will.”
She said additional relief in other states is planned for next year.
As of 2024, 36% of U.S. households had medical debt, according to research published in the University of Oxford Press. Healthcare costs have remained in 2026 near the top of people’s list of financial worries, according to polling by KFF, a health policy research and news organization. Six in ten people told the organization they are “very” or “somewhat worried” about affording healthcare for themselves and their families, which included  insurance and out-of-pocket costs.
In Kansas, medical debt has become a political hot topic after the New York Times reported in September that U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, a Republican running for reelection in November and a former OB-GYN in Great Bend, sued hundreds of patients for medical debt and had dozens arrested for failing to respond to their collections cases in court. Kansas Reflector reported in July about aggressive collections actions by a Topeka hospital against people who qualified for free care.
Allison Sesso, president and CEO of Undue Medical Debt, said families are increasingly squeezed between bills, groceries and rising costs.
“Medical debt, or fear of accruing it, shouldn’t prevent anyone from seeking the care they need,” Sesso said, “and I’m hopeful that removing these burdens in Kansas empowers families to re-engage with the healthcare system and put their health first.”

title: Trump to stump in Montana
description: U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to make a stop in Montana as part of a 10-state tour through competitive states and districts in the final month before November’s election.  Politico reported on Friday that the president would pass through the Treasure State as well as Pennsylvania — states with competitive U.S. House races — […]
text:
Then-former President Donald Trump speaks at a rally in Bozeman on Aug. 9, 2024. (Photo by Blair Miller, Daily Montanan)U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to make a stop in Montana as part of a 10-state tour through competitive states and districts in the final month before November’s election. 
Politico reported on Friday that the president would pass through the Treasure State as well as Pennsylvania — states with competitive U.S. House races — and eight states with tight U.S. Senate races. 
It is unknown what city Trump will visit, but it will likely be in the western district, the state’s most competitive federal election. 
The White House did not immediately respond to requests for confirmation about Trump’s travel plans. 
Trump immediately endorsed Republican Aaron Flint to replace retiring U.S. Rep. Ryan Zinke when Flint, a veteran and radio host, announced his campaign this spring. 
Flint’s campaign was not able to confirm dates or locations of the expected visit. 
Recent polls have shown Flint in a close matchup against Democrat Sam Forstag, a union leader and smokejumper. 
The visit comes as Trump’s approval ratings continue to decline, with just 35% approval among Americans.
When Trump visited the Treasure State in 2018, his approval rating was 50% or higher among Montanans, according to Gallup. A recent Montana Free Press-Rutgers Eagleton Poll put his approval at 42% in the state.
In 2024, Trump headlined a rally in Bozeman in support of now-U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy during his campaign to unseat Democratic Sen. Jon Tester, drawing around 8,000 people to Montana State University. 
The president also visited Montana during the 2018 midterms to stump for Republican Matt Rosendale’s unsuccessful attempt to unseat Tester. He stopped in Great Falls, Billings, Missoula and Gallatin County. 
A spokesperson for Forstag’s campaign told the Daily Montanan that Forstag would be “happy to take some time to sit down with [Trump] and share some stories about the pain this administration’s policies are causing people across this state — whether it’s the farmers and ranchers facing the cost of tariffs and $6 diesel or the folks being priced out of house, home and healthcare because of the policies my opponent cheered on.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Baldwin attacks Trump administration cuts for rural housing loans
description: The Trump administration has cut funding for a federal rural housing program in half nationwide and by 85% in Wisconsin, ignoring the $1 billion congressional appropriation for the program, Sen. Tammy Baldwin said Monday. “The Trump administration has the money, but they are making an active choice not to use it and not to invest […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin, shown here speaking at the Wisconsin Democratic Party convention in June, criticized the Trump administration Monday for spending half of what Congress has appropriated to help low-income rural residents afford housing. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)The Trump administration has cut funding for a federal rural housing program in half nationwide and by 85% in Wisconsin, ignoring the $1 billion congressional appropriation for the program, Sen. Tammy Baldwin said Monday.
“The Trump administration has the money, but they are making an active choice not to use it and not to invest in rural America,” Baldwin said in a statement issued by her office.
At issue is funding for the U.S. Department of Agriculture Single Family Housing Direct Home Loans program. The program has typically provided financing for about 5,500 mortgages per year for low- and very-low-income residents in rural areas.
Congress rejected a Trump administration proposal to eliminate the program in 2026, according to Senate Appropriations Committee Democrats, and instead approved $1 billion for the program.
By the end of the 2026 fiscal year Sept. 30, however, the administration had spent $518 million. Of the remaining funds, $230 million expired with the end of the fiscal year, unable to be lent.  Another $250 million of the appropriation can still be used in the new fiscal year.
Senate Democrats also stated that the Trump administration has added “harmful red tape” making loan applications harder.
A chart distributed by Baldwin’s office showed that while in past years Wisconsin accounted for an average of more than $13 million in loans annually, that plummeted to $1.98 million in 2026. Both Wisconsin and Connecticut had the steepest drop in loans compared with their past year averages — 85%.
“The price of housing is crushing families and is putting the dream of homeownership further and further out of reach,” Baldwin said. “Instead of helping these folks afford the roof over their heads, the Trump Administration is making matters worse by slashing resources that help working families in our rural communities afford a home.”
A USDA representative did not respond to a request for comment Monday afternoon about the funding cuts for the program.

name: VTDigger
title: New report finds low reconviction rates for teens in first years of Vermont’s ‘Raise the Age’ law
description:
“My hope is that this will encourage our lawmakers and policymakers and the administration to hold the course with ‘Raise the Age,’” said the chair of Vermont’s Council for Equitable Youth Justice.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  New report finds low reconviction rates for teens in first years of Vermont’s ‘Raise the Age’ law.
text:
The McCaffrey Courthouse in Rutland on Thursday, September 10, 2026. The building houses Vermont Superior Court. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
As Vermont considers the future of its “Raise the Age” law, a new report has found relatively low rates of reconviction among the teenagers whose cases have been affected by the reform — though the data come with important caveats.
The landmark law, which sought to route young adults charged with most offenses through juvenile delinquency proceedings rather than adult criminal court, began to take effect in 2020. And though it currently extends only to 18-year-olds, the reform is set to include 19-year-olds starting next year. 
The matter has seen increasing debate in recent years as Republican Gov. Phil Scott and his administration have indicated opposition to the law’s continued rollout and cited public safety concerns. The law’s supporters say the change directs young people charged with lesser infractions to a more developmentally appropriate venue for addressing their behavior and providing them the right services.
The Vermont-based nonprofit Crime Research Group released a new report last Thursday detailing outcomes for 377 18-year-olds whose cases were processed via Family Division courts rather than adult criminal proceedings since 2020. 
The report, which was commissioned through the Vermont Department for Children and Families and the state Council for Equitable Youth Justice, found that the reconviction rate among the observed teenagers was 6.9% after one year, and 18.7% after three years among the 160 cases where longer observation was possible.
The reconviction rates in Thursday’s report were much lower than those in a 2022 baseline report from the Crime Research Group, which found that 24% of 18- and 19-year-olds processed through adult criminal court were reconvicted within one year, and 46% were within three. But the comparison comes with important limitations: The two groups were studied over distinct periods and selected for observation using somewhat different criteria, according to Monica Weeber, the research organization’s executive director. 
While some officials remain skeptical, a number of advocates and juvenile justice experts say the data indicate promising progress since the reform’s passage.
The low three-year recidivism rate from Thursday’s study is an excellent new benchmark for Vermont, according to Marshall Pahl, the state’s top juvenile defender. 
“That’s pretty incredible work by our court system, our defense attorneys, our prosecutors and our (Department for Children and Families),” he said in an interview Friday. “This is showing that every component of the system is working.”
Matthew Bernstein, the state’s child, youth, and family advocate, was similarly enthusiastic.
“We already know that ‘Raise the Age’ is working, and this completely echoes that,” he said. 
While these data are limited, the results line up with existing research on this type of law and offer an opportunity to fine-tune the state’s youth justice system, he said.
The report also comes as the state has seen overall juvenile delinquency cases trend downward over the last nine years, Bernstein added. That’s part of why he believes the state’s youth justice system has “ample capacity” to proceed as planned with “Raise the Age.”
Some officials remain unconvinced.
Routing 19-year-olds through the Family Division could protect offenders at the expense of victims, according to Timothy Lueders-Dumont, executive director of the Vermont Department of State’s Attorneys and Sheriffs. 
The state’s court system is already sensitive to defendants’ ages through options like “Youthful Offender” status, which moves certain cases from criminal court to the Family Division at the discretion of prosecutors and judges, he added. Under “Raise the Age,” young people accused of more serious crimes like murder, kidnapping and sexual assault are still tried as adults in criminal court.
“The Department remains focused on elevating the voices of victims and survivors of crime,” who are often left feeling unheard despite being most impacted, Lueders-Dumont said in an email.
Aryka Radke, who leads the Family Services Division at the Vermont Department for Children and Families, agreed that the recidivism rates in Thursday’s report were low. But because 18-year-olds tend to have access to some supports that older youth don’t, like school, 19-year-olds wouldn’t necessarily respond in the same manner to such reforms, she said.
Bernstein also underlined the high rate of cases — nearly half — that ended in diversion, a path that requires an admission of responsibility followed by a restorative justice process. It’s a judicial tool that helps young people connect with the support they need to refrain from breaking the law in the future, he said.
Pahl, the juvenile defender, agreed. 
Diversion “matches perfectly with this population of kids,” he said. “It’s much more personalized, and it focuses not on punishing someone for what they’ve done wrong but on having that person repair the harm that they’ve done.”
It’s a practice that’s considerably less common in adult court than in juvenile delinquency proceedings. In 2024, nearly twice the share of juvenile cases ended in diversion compared with adult criminal proceedings, according to data from the Vermont Attorney General’s office.
Scott has signaled a desire to stop the law’s full rollout on a number of occasions. The Department for Children and Families also recently indicated that it intended to include neither 18- nor 19-year-olds in designs for a new locked juvenile facility slated to open in the coming years.
But for the reform’s supporters, Thursday’s report is a clear indication that the state should proceed with its plan to extend the juvenile court process to 19-year-olds.
“My hope is that this will encourage our lawmakers and policymakers and the administration to hold the course with ‘Raise the Age,’” said Karen Vastine, who chairs the Vermont Council for Equitable Youth Justice, an advisory body to both lawmakers and the governor.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Byron Donalds unveils proposal to protect Florida waterways
description: INDIAN SHORES — While the environment has not taken much prominence in the race for governor, public opinion surveys have consistently shown Floridians place high value on issues like marine protected areas and clean waterways. Declaring that the issue is important to him, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds unveiled a “Florida’s Coastal Corrido[...]
text:
Florida GOP gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds speaking at Caddy's in Indian Shores on Oct. 5, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)INDIAN SHORES — While the environment has not taken much prominence in the race for governor, public opinion surveys have consistently shown Floridians place high value on issues like marine protected areas and clean waterways.
Declaring that the issue is important to him, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds unveiled a “Florida’s Coastal Corridor” proposal Monday that he promised to enact if he gets elected next month. He calls it the marine equivalent of Florida’s Wildlife Corridor, which state lawmakers passed in 2021 to preserve migration paths for animals like the Florida panther.
“Where the Wildlife Corridor connects inland habitats from the north to the south, the Coastal Corridor links and protects our coastal waterways along the Gulf of America and the Atlantic Ocean. It connects them to inland watersheds that feed them,” Donalds announced at Caddy’s in Indian Shores, a waterfront bar and restaurant with clear views on the Intracoastal Waterway in Pinellas County.
The “Gulf of America” is Donald Trump’s preferred name for the Gulf of Mexico.
Donalds said the proposal doesn’t add layers of bureaucracy or regulations and won’t restrict fishing on public access. “Instead, it brings our existing agencies and existing programs and existing authorities under one coordinated, operational plan,” he said.
As announced on Monday, the proposal would:

Using Florida’s Seafloor Mapping Initiative and state habitat monitors, “target every taxpayer dollar where it delivers the highest ecological and economic return.”
Execute scientifically sound habitat investments, deploying artificial reefs, rebuilding oyster bars, replanting seagrass beds, restoring living shorelines, and propagating coral. “These projects restore fish habitat while building natural storm protection for our coastal communities,” he said.
Future land conservation to protect coastal headwaters would be 100% voluntary, “working through willing sellers to sell the easements under proven tools like Florida Forever.”

Florida Forever has been considered the state’s biggest conservation and recreational lands acquisition program, established by the Florida Forever Act of 1999. Since it began in 2000, it has allowed the state to purchase more than 1 million acres of land.
However, the Legislature declined to provide any funding for the program this year. Instead, lawmakers redirected millions of dollars previously dedicated to land acquisition in the Florida Wildlife Corridor towards other projects, including $425 million for the Rural and Family Lands Protection Program, which allows agriculture landowners to permanently preserve their land from development but doesn’t require public access.
Citizens’ initiative blocked 
Concerns about the state’s waterways is what has led a group of environmental advocates to push for a proposed “Right to Clean and Healthy Waters” constitutional amendment. Efforts to get that proposal on the 2026 ballot were scuttled in 2025 following passage of legislation (HB 1205). That law created major barriers to citizen-led initiatives gathering the required signatures, the result being that no citizen-led constitutional amendments made it to the November 2026 statewide ballot.
The campaign behind the Right to Clean and Healthy Waters says participants hope to regroup to restart a similar campaign for the 2028 fall election.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly has spelled out some of his plans for those who live in coastal communities and Florida’s water quality crisis on his campaign website. It says his plan “ties water quality to broader environmental investment.”
“Blue-green algae crises are addressed by reducing discharges of nutrient pollution to our coastal waters, and springs degradation is addressed through septic to sewer conversations, agriculture runoff rules, and groundwater protection. Protecting Florida’s coast requires changing what flows into it.”
A number of mostly Pinellas-based state and federal lawmakers joined Donalds at his press conference, including U.S. Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, state Sen. Nick DiCeglie, and state House members Berny Jacques and Toby Overdorf.
