name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Here’s what could happen if NC lawmakers pause the gas tax in a special session
description: Suspending state gas taxes in North Carolina could lead to delays in roadwork, according to a leading economist.  House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell and Senate Leader Phil Berger, R-Rockingham, announced over the weekend they plan to call lawmakers back to Raleigh for a special session on reducing gas prices. They did not offer further details […]
text:
Voters say they are struggling economically as the price of gas rises above $4 a gallon. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) Suspending state gas taxes in North Carolina could lead to delays in roadwork, according to a leading economist. 
House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell and Senate Leader Phil Berger, R-Rockingham, announced over the weekend they plan to call lawmakers back to Raleigh for a special session on reducing gas prices. They did not offer further details on their plans.
At 41 cents per gallon, North Carolina has one of the highest gas taxes in the country. That revenue goes towards building, repairing, and maintaining roads. Lawmakers could suspend or repeal part or all of it.
NC State economist and professor emeritus Mike Walden said drivers can expect to see a “noticeable decline” in what they’re paying at the pump if lawmakers decide to suspend the tax. 
“But the state gas tax is a major source of funding for road repair, road expansion, and other road improvements,” Walden said. “Much of this work would stop during the tax suspension.”  
Some of these projects could include construction on the I-26 connector in Asheville and widening I-40 around the Triangle, according to the North Carolina Department of Transportation website. NCDOT did not immediately respond to NC Newsline’s request for comment. 
Walden thinks drivers would be willing to accept a temporary slowdown in roadwork for lower gas prices. 
“My expectation is the legislature would suspend the tax for a limited period of time, and then re-impose it so road spending can continue,” Walden said. 
Some Republican state lawmakers have suggested that they could offset the lost tax revenue with funding from state reserves. 
“We have some surplus revenue,” Rep. Grant Campbell, R-Cabarrus, said in a post on social media Monday. “This is going to give us the opportunity to temporarily suspend the gas tax.”
The action comes as North Carolina polls show declining approval numbers for President Donald Trump and Republicans down the ballot. National GOP groups are pulling spending from U.S. Senate Michael Whatley’s campaign, opting to focus on other states instead. 
NC legislative leaders call for special session on high gas, diesel prices

At a campaign stop in Nebraska on Monday, Trump is expected to announce an executive order aimed at lowering gas prices, according to Politico. 
Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp declared a state of emergency last week, suspending the state’s motor fuel excise tax for 30 days. On Wednesday, Ohio lawmakers approved a 90-day gas tax holiday, following urging by GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. And in Indiana, Gov. Mike Braun recently renewed the state’s gas suspension for another 30 days, set to expire right after the general election. 
Hall and Berger had not announced a date for the special session by mid-afternoon Monday, but Campbell and other lawmakers say they expect to meet this week. 
Democrats say it’s a political move.
“We’re glad to see legislative Republicans finally acknowledge that the Trump administration’s war of choice in Iran and tariffs have led to sky-high fuel prices for North Carolina families and farmers,” said a spokesperson for Gov. Josh Stein in a statement Monday. “If they’re serious about lowering costs long after the campaign ads stop, let’s also get to work on the Governor’s Working Families Tax Cut and heed his calls to protect our electricity bills from data centers’ massive energy consumption.”
Senate Democratic Leader Sydney Batch, D-Wake, criticized GOP leadership for calling a last-minute session rather than addressing affordability earlier. She pointed out that the House and Senate met just last week for an administrative session that was already on the schedule.
“This is the exact same pattern, from the same failed, weak leadership that took three years to produce one state budget,” Batch said in a statement. “Session after session, we’ve seen that when it comes to protecting their own power, Republicans will move with lightning speed. But when your family needs help, they’ll wait until it’s politically convenient for them.”


4:19 pmUpdated to add a statement from a spokesperson for Gov. Josh Stein.

title: Corporation Commission candidates differ on Oklahoma data center regulation, utility rates
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahomans will decide between two Oklahoma Corporation Commission candidates who differ in how they want to regulate data centers and utility rates.  Republican Brad Boles said he believes the Corporation Commission needs to enforce whatever data center regulations the Legislature enacts, while Democrat Rhonda Eastman said she thinks there s[...]
text:
Republican Brad Boles, left, and Democrat Rhonda Eastman, right, will compete in the general election for a spot on the Oklahoma Corporation Commission. (Photos provided)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahomans will decide between two Oklahoma Corporation Commission candidates who differ in how they want to regulate data centers and utility rates. 
Republican Brad Boles said he believes the Corporation Commission needs to enforce whatever data center regulations the Legislature enacts, while Democrat Rhonda Eastman said she thinks there should be a pause on new ones while they are studied further by the state. 
The two candidates are set face off on the Nov. 3 ballot for a six-year term to fill a seat currently held by Commissioner Todd Hiett. Hiett cannot run again due to term limits.
The Oklahoma Corporation Commission is a three-person elected body that regulates various state industries from public utilities to oil and gas. Commissioners earn an annual salary of $150,000. 
Boles, a state representative from Marlow, said his experience growing a small business in the private sector, his time as the House energy chair and his education in finance set him apart from his opponent. 
He authored a bill to require new data centers to pay for their own cost of construction and energy costs in an attempt to protect Oklahomans’ energy bills. 
The role of the Corporation Commission in regulating data centers is to enforce what the Legislature mandates, he said. 
“Every rate case is unique, and we don’t want the Legislature making a one-size-fits-all for everything,” Boles said. “So we want to create a basic framework that protects ratepayers, and let the commission do what they can. They have all the resources, the staffing, the experts to ensure that these laws go into effect …and if they want to go in addition to that, then that’s their prerogative.”
Eastman, of Spiro, also said regulation is up to lawmakers to define. But she said she wants to see data centers be “fully compliant” with whatever is enacted. 
She said she’d like additional studies on their impact, and she suggested potentially putting new construction of the centers, which house and maintain the physical equipment needed to process digital information, on pause. 
“My fear is this is going to become an extremely rapid pace and that certain jobs are going to be done away with,” Eastman said. “And when you do away with somebody’s livelihood and you haven’t built some kind of safety guards … it’s going to create a massive hardship on the economy of our state.”
Eastman worked for the state for 16 years at the Employment Security Commission before returning to the private sector. She is concerned about rising utility costs, abandoned oil and gas wells, and a lack of regulations for data centers.
Eastman said she stands out as a candidate because she is not a politician and has never held office before. She also said she is not accepting donations from the industries the Corporation Commission regulates. 
Regulating utility companies 
Boles said there needs to be a balance between affordability for ratepayers and having a reliable energy grid and infrastructure, especially as more large load consumers like data centers come to Oklahoma. 
“I think it’s important that we have that balance and we ensure that the residential ratepayers get the benefit of this extra volume going to the grid,” he said. 
The role of the Corporation Commission is to be an advocate for the ratepayer, not corporations, Eastman said. 
“Large corporations, they have an army and a fleet of attorneys that advocate for them,” she said. “But your commissioners, their role is to advocate for the people.”
Advocating for ratepayers also includes pushing back against legislation that could increase burdens on them, Eastman said. 
Agency oversight 
One issue that both candidates agree on is that the three corporation commissioners need the ability to provide greater oversight of the expenditure of public money.
The Oklahoma Corporation Commission entered into over $310,000 worth of severance agreements in the last 18 months, but only one was signed off on by the commissioners, according to records released to Oklahoma Voice through an open records request. 
Boles said there needs to be greater oversight. 
“I’m a business owner, and I understand sometimes you have to do compensation packages or whatever,” he said. “But I think it’s different with taxpayer money.”
The commissioners are the ones elected and accountable to the people, so they need the authority to sign off on every compensation package, Boles said. 
Eastman also said the commissioners should play a greater role and monitor agency executives.
“I definitely think that the Corporation Commission should do some oversight with all of the agencies that are under our umbrella and ensuring that the agencies are operating properly,” she said. 
If agency employees are acting in “bad faith,” there should be commissioner oversight, Eastman said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PODCAST: CT effort to support SNAP recipients stalls
description: Keith M. Phaneuf discusses the help CT lawmakers promised people who lost federal food assistance — and why it's been easier said than done.
text:
More than 60,000 Connecticut residents have lost federal food assistance since H.R.1, or the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” passed in July 2025. State lawmakers promised help — but it’s proven to be easier said than done.
WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s Keith Phaneuf to discuss his article, “Lamont’s plan to send gift cards to former SNAP recipients stalls,” as part of the collaborative podcast Long Story Short. Read the story here.
WSHU: Hello, Keith. This summer, Connecticut Governor Ned Lamont (D) announced that 25,000 former SNAP recipients would be receiving $300 grocery gift cards. Less than 1500 gift cards have been distributed. You’ve investigated this. What do state officials say is responsible?
KP: Well, Ebong, it looks like the Department of Social Services, which was working with nonprofit community action agencies, was particularly slow in getting the community action agencies the personal information on the card recipients. In other words, when an individual goes to the community action agency to pick up the cards, it would be nice to know if the community action agency would have a list of all the recipients and all their contact information, just so they could confirm it. The Lamont administration did not get that out the door in a timely fashion, so it basically tied the action agency’s hands.
WSHU: So basically, what’s the situation now? Is it going to speed up? Because these people have been waiting for quite a while, anticipating these $300 gift cards, and these are people who are having a hard time right now and have to go to food pantries.
KP: Keep in mind that the Department of Social Services is, I think, a very overworked agency, and I should have added in my initial response that they were trying to make sure they said that they were not going to run afoul of federal authorities in terms of whether they were giving out any private information about SNAP recipients. The problem is there’s not an easy answer. For your next question, which is what happens next, all we’re getting right now from the Lamont administration is we’re going to move as quickly as we can. But if you don’t have this data assembled, you might think it’s just nice and easy and quick to put together. That’s not always the case. I think we’re going to be watching them in the coming weeks. I think because the governor is in the midst of a re-election campaign, there’s going to be a lot of pressure on them to absolutely get this out the door before early November. But right now, we don’t have an estimate other than we’re going as fast as we can, which I don’t even think you can call that an estimate.
WSHU: Now, this is an election period here, so there’s GOP criticism. What are the Republicans saying?
KP: Well, the Republicans at this point are simply saying the administration’s not taking this seriously, and unfortunately, the governor is somewhat vulnerable in this area because of his track record. Governor Lamont’s a fiscal moderate. He has been very wary in the past about trying to use state dollars to backfill or mitigate cuts to federal human service programs. That’s not to say he hasn’t done it, but to say it runs opposite to some of his political beliefs, and it’s led to criticism from within his own party, and I’ll just give you a couple quick examples. Take us back in history. In 2022, there was a lot of pressure from rank-and-file lawmakers from both parties for us to use state dollars to increase winter heating assistance. We mostly distribute federal LIHEAP dollars. If you remember, 2022 is when the Russian invasion of Ukraine began. Home heating oil prices were skyrocketing. The governor at first did not want to do anything until he was starting to take heat from both sides of the aisle, saying it’s not the compassionate approach. So he agreed to put $30 million of state money on top of the federal. However, we never spent a single penny of it. People found out after the winter. Basically, we set the limits on the grants we gave to each household to basically make sure we would only spend federal money and not spend state. So that stuck in a lot of people’s memories.
Then, when we had a federal government shutdown and the SNAP program stalled in the fall of 2025, the governor took a lot of criticism from progressives in his party for only contributing money to food pantries, even though they said we can only solve about 1/7 of the problem, basically until the last minute, he waited and waited over a month while people were struggling in food pantries and couldn’t keep up. And then this most recent one, when he did announce that he was going to do the grocery store gift cards, he made the announcement in June, and then he was supposed to start the distribution in early August. That came only after again he’d been called out by people in his own party at the time he was in a battle for the Democratic nomination, facing a primary challenge from State Representative Josh Elliott, who basically put out a statement saying, “When the governor says maybe, he means no.” So when you look at the whole history, people are not ready to give the Lamont administration the benefit of the doubt anymore.
WSHU: In the meantime, advocates are quite upset that this program has not taken off the way they expected.
KP: I think that’s more than fair. Like I said, when you look at the totality of it, the feeling is that this simply has not been a priority for the Lamont administration, and that all too often a compromise is offered simply to take the political heat off the governor from the left. I should point out that the governor’s opponent, Senator Ryan Fazio, a Republican from Greenwich, does not favor using state funds to cover nutrition assistance that’s been cut by the federal government. But Fazio’s argument is, I’m upfront about that. I’m not trying to create the impression that I’m doing something, and that I’m not. The governor has taken some criticism from Republicans, but the bulk has come from his own party, who feel that given the massive surpluses, this shouldn’t be that difficult to do, quite frankly.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: B. Alan Sugg, longest serving University of Arkansas system president, dies at 88
description: B. Alan Sugg, who served more than two decades as president of the University of Arkansas system, has died. He was 88. Sugg died Saturday surrounded by his family in Houston, the university said in a news release over the weekend. The university did not give a cause of death. Sugg was the longest serving […]
text:
The University of Arkansas campus in Fayetteville (Photo courtesy of the University of Arkansas)B. Alan Sugg, who served more than two decades as president of the University of Arkansas system, has died. He was 88.
Sugg died Saturday surrounded by his family in Houston, the university said in a news release over the weekend. The university did not give a cause of death.
Sugg was the longest serving president of the UA system and oversaw its expansion from roughly 30,000 students on five campuses in 1990 to more than 70,000 students among 17 campuses when he retired in 2011.
B. Alan Sugg, former president of the University of Arkansas system. (Photo courtesy of the University of Arkansas system)
“While I wasn’t fortunate enough to meet Alan Sugg, I know of his lasting impact on the UA System,” UA System President Jay B. Silveria said in a statement. “We are only able to advance the work of the system today because of his outstanding leadership for those many years.”
Born in Helena in 1938, Sugg attended the University of Arkansas in Fayetteville on a track scholarship and graduated with a degree in finance. He was commissioned into the U.S. Army after graduation and stationed in Germany. He later received his master’s degree from UA and his doctorate in higher education from the University of Oklahoma.
Before joining the University of Arkansas system, Sugg worked in higher education in Texas for 22 years, including 13 years as president of Texas A&M University at Corpus Christi.
Sugg’s tenure at UA included several new additions to the system, including five community colleges and the founding of the Clinton School of Public Service on the grounds of the Clinton presidential library in Little Rock.
The UA Board of Trustees named Sugg president emeritus after his 2011 retirement and renamed the University of Arkansas System Administration Building in Little Rock for him.
“I’m proud of the work of our faculty, staff and administrators to help improve our state and the lives of its citizens through higher education,” Sugg said when he retired. “I’m thankful for having had the chance to work with many outstanding chancellors, and I’m grateful to our trustees and the citizens of Arkansas for giving me this opportunity.”

name: Delaware
title: Apple-Scrapple Festival returns to Bridgeville with food, fun and 100 years of RAPA
description: Bridgeville’s signature fall festival celebrates apples, scrapple and the agricultural traditions of western Sussex County as hometown producer RAPA marks its centennial. By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE BRIDGEVILLE — Apples, scrapple and a century of local food history will come together this week as Bridgeville welcomes thousands of visitors for the 34th[...]
text:
Bridgeville’s signature fall festival celebrates apples, scrapple and the agricultural traditions of western Sussex County as hometown producer RAPA marks its centennial.
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE
BRIDGEVILLE — Apples, scrapple and a century of local food history will come together this week as Bridgeville welcomes thousands of visitors for the 34th annual Apple-Scrapple Festival.
The festival officially opens Friday, Oct. 9, and continues Saturday, Oct. 10, filling downtown Bridgeville with food, carnival rides, music, hundreds of crafters and vendors, contests and some traditions that are difficult to find anywhere else — including a ladies’ skillet toss and an invitational scrapple sling.
This year also brings a milestone particularly appropriate for a festival with “scrapple” in its name: Bridgeville-based RAPA Scrapple is celebrating its 100th anniversary.
Ralph and Paul Adams started the company in Bridgeville in 1926, combining their first names to create RAPA. The company continues to operate from its Bridgeville production facility and says it is the leading-selling scrapple producer in the United States.
At 11 a.m. Saturday, RAPA will hold a special Scrapple Centennial Serving at its gate entrance on Cannon Street. The ticketed event is scheduled to include scrapple smash burgers, scrapple tacos, a scrapple breakfast bake and even scrapple cinnamon buns.
What exactly is scrapple?
For people who didn’t grow up in Delaware, Maryland or southeastern Pennsylvania, the festival’s second namesake may require some explanation.
Scrapple is traditionally made by cooking pork trimmings and other edible parts of the hog, grinding the meat and combining it with broth, cornmeal or buckwheat and seasonings. The mixture is formed into a loaf, chilled, sliced and fried — ideally, devotees will argue, until crisp on the outside while remaining soft inside.
The food’s roots go back much farther than Bridgeville.
Scrapple developed from German pork dishes brought to Pennsylvania by German-speaking settlers commonly known as the Pennsylvania Dutch. The German predecessor, called panhas or by similar names, dates to at least the 16th century. In America, ingredients such as cornmeal were incorporated into the recipe, creating the food that became known as scrapple by the early 1800s.
Like many traditional farm foods, scrapple was born from practicality. Families who butchered a hog wanted to use every edible part rather than waste food. Meat remaining after cuts such as ham, bacon and sausage were prepared could be combined with inexpensive grain to produce another food capable of feeding a family.
The tradition eventually became deeply associated with the Mid-Atlantic, particularly Pennsylvania, Delaware and Maryland.
Bridgeville makes a festival of it
The Apple-Scrapple Festival itself dates to 1992, when Bridgeville residents began looking for a way to promote their town and western Sussex County’s agricultural industry.
They found their theme almost literally in their backyard.
Apples were grown nearby at T.S. Smith and Sons, a Delaware Century Farm, while RAPA had been producing scrapple in Bridgeville since 1926.
Apples plus scrapple became Apple-Scrapple.
The first festival attracted about 2,500 visitors. Festival organizers say attendance has since grown to more than 20,000, turning the event into a major fundraiser for community organizations and one of western Sussex County’s largest annual celebrations. The festival remains organized largely by volunteers.
The food court reflects both the festival’s agricultural roots and the philosophy that a fall festival should not send anyone home hungry. Offerings include scrapple sandwiches, apple dumplings, pies, barbecue, cheesesteaks, funnel cakes and other festival foods. Organizers say apple dumplings served with ice cream remain among the most popular items.
Then there are the competitions.
Children can compete in the Kids Apple Toss Friday evening. On Saturday, competitors take over the Union Methodist Church lot for the Ladies Skillet Toss before the action returns to the bandstand for the Invitational Scrapple Sling.
Visitors who prefer eating rather than throwing their food can browse craft and vendor areas, visit the Bridgeville Historical Society Museum, attend the St. Mary’s luncheon and quilt display, see the car show or spend the day at the carnival.
Friday is a more limited festival night centered around the carnival, food court, entertainment, Little Miss Apple Scrapple Pageant and street dance. The full complement of crafters and vendors arrives Saturday.
And for anyone still debating the proper way to eat scrapple, there may never be agreement.
Some slice it thick. Others insist it should be thin. Some want it extremely crisp, while others prefer a softer center.
Then comes the most dangerous question of all: syrup, ketchup or apple butter?

name: Source New Mexico
title: Documentary on dangers of social media shown in New Mexico to highlight state’s fight against Meta
description: Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez and state Sen. Antonio Maestas (D-Albuquerque) held a panel after a screening of "Your Attention Please" — a new documentary about social media harm. The film follows Kristin Bride, who became a social media reform advocate after her son died from suicide after being cyberbullied. Bride celebrated New Mexico's recent lawsu[...]
text:
From left to right: Panel moderator Erin Muffoletto-Hernandez, Sen. Antonio Maestas (D-Albuquerque), Kristin Bride and New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez discuss social media reform efforts following an Oct. 2, 2026, screening of "Your Attention Please" in Albuquerque. The documentary follows Bride's efforts to press Congress to approve precautions for kids on social media. (Courtesy of Alysse Houliston)This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is contemplating suicide, please call or text the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988.
Kristin Bride describes her 16-year old son, Carson, as the comedian of her family, with an amazing smile and laugh. He was smart and loved acting. 
But a “huge hole remains in her heart” since Carson died by suicide in 2020 after being cyberbullied on Snapchat. 
“We didn’t know that Snapchat allowed an anonymous app to be integrated into the platform,” Bride said. “The last search on Carson’s phone before he ended his life was for hacks” to find the people harassing him with anonymous messages. 
Bride added that she blames the social media company for her son’s death.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Since Carson died, Bride’s advocacy for social media reform has taken her to Congress, where she testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee, and now to New Mexico, for a screening of “Your Attention Please.” The new documentary illustrates social media’s effects on mental health and youth safety, while highlighting social media reform advocates like Bride.
Bride attended the screening Friday at the National Hispanic Cultural Center in Albuquerque and spoke on a panel afterward with Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez and state Sen. Antonio Maestas (D-Albuquerque).
Showing the film in New Mexico was important because of recent courtroom showdowns between the state and social media behemoth Meta, said Jack LeMay, writer and editor of “Your Attention Please.”
“New Mexico is a small state with big state energy,” LeMay said. “New Mexico is leading the charge nationally in trying to hold these companies accountable. It’s a huge inspiration to bring our film here.”
On Sept. 25, a New Mexico jury found Facebook willfully engaged in unfair and deceptive trade practices regarding collection of user data, misinformation and hate speech on the platform. Attorneys representing the state requested a district court judge fine Facebook up to $40 billion in violation penalties. Attorneys representing Meta said the state is “trying to take advantage” of the jury’s ruling and “run up the score on penalties.”
In August, First Judicial District Judge Bryan Biedscheid ordered the company to pay $567 million for an abatement fund aimed at ameliorating harms done to the state’s youth. Meta said it intends to appeal.
And in March, a Santa Fe jury ordered Meta — Facebook’s parent company — to pay $375 million in damages to the state after it found the company misrepresented the risks to teen users’ mental health. 
The judgments are “definitely a victory,” Bride said during the panel. 
“I’m just so thankful to New Mexico and the other attorneys general that have gotten further than we’ve been able to get in D.C.,” Bride said. 
The film highlights Bride’s fight to pass the proposed Kids Online Safety Act, a 2024 federal bill that would impose stricter privacy rules and safeguards for children on the internet and social media. The bipartisan bill passed in the U.S. Senate in July 2024, but died in the House.
The federal proposal and the judgments against Meta in New Mexico, Torrez said, led to the creation of a proposed bill for the upcoming 2027 legislative session. Torrez announced plans to press for the Online Safety and Accountability Act Sept. 23 with state Rep. Linda Serrato (D-Santa Fe) and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland. It would require that developers make products with youth-specific features, including a chronological feed; a two-hour daily social media default limit; silenced notifications overnight and during school hours; and automatic blocks on profiles that exhibit sexual extortion or grooming behaviors. 
“The most important thing that we could do to help our kids is to bring about the change that we weren’t seeing in Washington,” Torrez said Friday during the panel. 
“Your Attention Please” also shows states which have passed legislation to ban phones during school hours. Maestas added that he and Sen. Crystal Brantley (R-Elephant Butte) intend to reintroduce Senate Bill 23, which died last legislative session, that would implement a bell-to-bell ban on cell phone usage in New Mexico schools. Maestas said he thinks the bill will pass in the next session with the “momentum and awareness that folks have.”
“Your Attention Please” director Sara Robin said the conversation around social media harm has changed since she first started the project in 2023 and New Mexico’s actions could inspire further change.
“For the longest time, we thought it may not be possible to take these companies to court,” Robin said. “We’re seeing that change now.”
“Your Attention Please” will be available to watch on Apple TV starting Tuesday.

title: US House Dems’ campaign chief predicts they'll gain majority control in midterms
text: WASHINGTON — Democrats expect they’ll gain a majority of seats in the U.S. House following November’s midterm elections, giving the party a platform to serve as a check on the president’s power. Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Suzan DelBene said during an interview Monday that curbing the war in Iran and working on legislation to address the costs of healthcare would be at the top of the party’s agenda if it is able to flip that chamber.  “And of course, act as an independent branch and do our job to hold the administration accountable,” she said. The Washington state Democrat said she views Republican super PACs spending millions of dollars in safe GOP districts as a sign that voters are moving toward Democratic candidates.“We've seen MAGA Inc. pour millions into House races and spending deep in red territory. Of the 38 districts that MAGA Inc. is spending in so far, 26 are on defense,” DelBene said, referring to the president’s super PAC. “And the speaker and the majority leader were campaigning recently in districts Trump won by double digits in 2024.”Additions to list of targeted racesThe DCCC announced earlier in the day that it had added six candidates to its “Red to Blue” program — Chris Jones in Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District, Dwayne Romero in Colorado's 3rd Congressional District, Eliott Rodriguez in Florida's 27th Congressional District, Teresa Benitez-Thompson in Nevada's 2nd Congressional District, Blake Gendebien in New York's 21st Congressional District and Justin J. Pearson in Tennessee's 9th Congressional District. The additions bring the DCCC’s targeted House races to a total of 46.DelBene said during the interview with States Newsroom and other journalists in the Regional Reporters Association that “while Republicans seem to have infinite amounts of money to throw at us, our momentum is simply too strong to stop.” “Republicans may have more money, but they have zero substance,” she said. “We know we don't need to spend more, but we do need to spend enough.”National Republican Congressional Campaign Chairman Richard Hudson, of North Carolina, wrote in a statement released Sunday that with less than a month to go until voting ends on Nov. 3, GOP candidates “are on offense.”“We’re competing in districts Democrats swore were safe. We’ve recruited candidates who served in uniform, built businesses, and put criminals behind bars,” he said. “And we’re running on results: lower taxes, a secure border, and an economy that works for working families.”Where analysts see the House races The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter categorizes 197 House districts as solid or likely Democratic and another 195 as solid or likely Republican. That leaves voters in 43 districts throughout the entire country to determine whether the House remains in Republican hands for another two years or shifts to Democratic control. Of those, 11 are rated as leaning Democratic, 10 are leaning toward a Republican candidate winning and 22 are true toss-up seats.The magic number for House control is 218, though every additional seat beyond that threshold makes governing much easier for party leadership. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has had to consistently balance the demands of moderate and far-right members to move legislation across the floor. The House majority currently sits at 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent who used to be a Republican and two vacancies. Erin Covey, editor for the House of Representatives at Cook, said on the “Stories from the States” podcast that during the last month or so “the overall political environment has really solidified to favor Democrats."“At this point, our estimation is that Democrats will likely end up with around 220 to 230 seats at the end of the day,” she said. “Of course, that would be a majority in all of those cases. But on the lower end that would be a pretty slim majority. Some of that is because the battleground of competitive districts is relatively small compared to previous cycles. And so the number of truly vulnerable seats that Democrats can pick up is capped in a way it wasn’t in 2018, for example. But the national political example is just as good as it was for Democrats in 2018.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Trump posts Sen. Tom Cotton’s phone number over dispute about daylight saving time bill
description: President Donald Trump posted on social media a cellphone number he claimed belonged to Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton in a Saturday tirade against the Arkansas lawmaker for opposing a bill that would make daylight saving time permanent. The Sunshine Protection Act passed the U.S. House of Representatives in July with bipartisan support but has […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton addresses supporters at Republican Party headquarters in downtown Little Rock on March 3, 2026 after being declared winner of his party’s primary. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)President Donald Trump posted on social media a cellphone number he claimed belonged to Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton in a Saturday tirade against the Arkansas lawmaker for opposing a bill that would make daylight saving time permanent.
The Sunshine Protection Act passed the U.S. House of Representatives in July with bipartisan support but has met bipartisan opposition in the Senate. Trump has been urging Republican senators for months to support the bill.
“For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill, and in the Senate, it’s very easy to do, it only takes one!” Trump wrote on TruthSocial, the social media platform he started after being banned from X, formerly Twitter.
Cotton’s policy stances and voting record typically align with Trump’s, but he reiterated his opposition to the bill in a Saturday Facebook post. 
Trump urges US Senate to pass bill making daylight saving time permanent

He wrote that  “no one likes changing the clock,” himself included, but noted that Congress has approved permanent daylight saving time more than once only to repeal it due to “absurdly late sunrises in the winter.”
“Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first,” Cotton wrote.
He did not address Trump’s apparent revelation of his personal phone number to the public. An attempt to call the number Monday revealed that the voicemail box was full.
Arkansas lawmakers have introduced bills to make daylight saving time permanent in the past four legislative sessions, but none have passed the chamber in which they were introduced.
Cotton is running for a third term and faces Democrat Hallie Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin in November. In a Saturday video on Facebook, Shoffner said she supports making daylight saving time permanent but considers it less important than making gasoline and groceries more affordable for Arkansans.
“Families are struggling, and changing the clocks isn’t going to change that,” Shoffner said.
Cotton’s stance was defended by colleagues from both parties. Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona wrote on X that a better approach would be “permanent standard time,” with more light in the morning and less light in the evening.
“Senator Cotton is right,” Kelly wrote. “Permanent Daylight Savings has been tried and Americans didn’t like it.”
Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana criticized Trump for giving out Cotton’s number and called Cotton a “rockstar senator.”
“I don’t think [Trump] should have given out Tom’s cell phone number,” Kennedy said on “Meet the Press” Sunday. “I don’t think that’s going to help convince Tom.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC colleges can apply to offer new Pell Grants aimed at in-demand trades. So far, none have.
description: So far, SC colleges and trade schools have yet to seek approval for training programs under a recently expanded Pell Grant program.
text:
Emergency medical technician students at the Beaufort-Jasper Academy for Career Excellence on their first day of clinicals March 24, 2025. (Photo provided by Beaufort-Jasper Academy for Career Excellence)COLUMBIA — Nursing and medical assistants, mechanics and commercial truck drivers, welders and construction equipment operators. These are among the South Carolina careers newly eligible for low-income, federal education grants.
But so far, colleges and trade schools in the Palmetto State have yet to seek approval for training programs under the recently expanded Pell Grant program.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The U.S. Department of Education has signed off on 21 programs in six states — Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Nebraska, North Carolina, Texas — since July, under new Workforce Pell grants.
While Pell Grants have existed for a long time, the Trump administration’s hallmark tax cut legislation — the “One, Big, Beautiful” law — opened up the financial aid to non-degree, certification programs as short as eight weeks long.
“Workforce Pell will help more South Carolinians gain the skills they need for good-paying, in-demand jobs without spending years in a traditional classroom,” Gov. Henry McMaster said in a statement in July. “This is a win for our state’s students, institutions of higher education, and employers that will benefit the economy and strengthen our state for years to come.”
Since passage of the bill in July 2025, states and federal education officials have been in a year-long sprint to rollout the effort.
The Congressional Budget Office estimates Congress will spend $1 billion on the program over the next decade and that by 2034, about 100,000 new recipients each year will receive grants of about $2,200 each.
“We have many citizens that don’t have the luxury of two years or four years to acquire the education that’s needed for certain occupations,” said Nina Staggers, executive director of workforce development at the state’s employment agency. “The Workforce Pell program is really targeting those short-term training programs that still lead to high-quality credentials.”
Home health workers, data scientists and cybersecurity projected to be SC’s fastest growing jobs

But colleges and training programs have yet to catch up with the fast-tracked implementation.
Final federal rules were not released until May 18. South Carolina’s employment agency opened up its first round of applications about a month and a half later.
“That gave states and colleges only a few weeks to understand the requirements and begin putting the program into place,” said Kelly Steinhilper, spokeswoman for the state technical college system.
So, the lack of applications at this stage is not unexpected, she added.
Whether that will change between now and Oct. 15, the deadline for the second round of applications, remains to be seen.
Colleges have a lot of hoops to jump through to qualify:

Eligible programs must prepare participants for one of two dozen career fields, selected by the state Department of Employment and Workforce, considered high-skill, high-wage or high demand. To be high wage, they must have a median annual wage of $44,760.
Programs must have existed for at least a year.
Classes may run for only eight to 14 weeks with between 150 and 599 hours of instruction.
They must also demonstrate past completion and job-placement rates of at least 70%.
And the data must show that graduates earn more after completing the program. Their wages must increase over and above the cost of the program.

“This is a new program with significant requirements, and colleges are being deliberate about making sure they are ready before submitting programs for approval,” Steinhilper said.
In some cases, colleges may have to retool their certificate programs just to make them fit.
Many technical colleges offer certified nursing and medical assistant certifications, for example, but they don’t meet the Workforce Pell guidelines as designed in terms of length and classroom hours, said Lara Hewitt, a senior vice president focused on workforce for the South Carolina Hospital Association.
“So, they’re having to figure out how do we change our curriculum? Should we change our curriculum so that this program is Pell eligible? There is considerable work on the part of educational providers to try to get their programs where they’re going to meet the requirements,” Hewitt said.
“While I would love for it to jump and take off, I do know it’s going to take a little bit longer,” she added.
Here’s how many are graduating from SC colleges with in-demand degrees. It’s not enough.

Hewitt said many hospitals in the state have previously offered to foot the bill for employees who want to advance their careers with these certificates. Several commercial driving schools, on their websites, also boast about employer-funded training, as well as existing federal programs that pay the full cost of licensing.
While Staggers said it’s true options are already available, Workforce Pell is another tool in the toolbox.
“What we find in in this line of work is that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution, and that we need to have a variety of pathways and mechanisms that individuals can use to access the education and training that they need,” she said.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania joins 20 states suing EPA to reinstate climate pollution rules for power plants
description: This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment.  More than 20 states, including North Carolina, New York, California and Pennsylvania, as well as several cities, are suing the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency over its repeal of most greenhouse gas emissi[...]
text:
The Homer City Generating Station towers over fields of corn in Indiana County, Pennsylvania. It's owners announced an agreement in principle to purchase $15 billion of Pennsylvania natural gas to support over 4 gigawatts of power generation at the former coal plant. (Photo by Audrey Carleton/Capital and Main)This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. 
More than 20 states, including North Carolina, New York, California and Pennsylvania, as well as several cities, are suing the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency over its repeal of most greenhouse gas emissions standards for coal- and natural gas-fired power plants. The agency’s proposal would also thwart future administrations from reinstating the rule.
The state attorneys general, all of them Democrats, filed the lawsuit Oct. 1 in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia. The plaintiffs are asking the court to review the proposed rescission.
In a press release, New York Attorney General Letitia James said the coalition is arguing that the administration’s actions are “clearing the way for millions of additional tons of greenhouse gas emissions that will worsen extreme heat, deadly storms, flooding, and wildfires.” The coalition includes Washington, D.C., Chicago, Denver and New York City.
The EPA told Inside Climate News it does not comment on pending litigation.
“We applaud Attorney General Jackson’s leadership in protecting our air quality and safeguarding public health,” said Jeffrey Robbins, executive director of the nonprofit CleanAIRE North Carolina, of North Carolina’s Attorney General Jeff Jackson. “Joining this lawsuit sends a clear message: North Carolina will not stand by while federal rollbacks force our families to pay higher costs at the pump for dirtier air. Our health should not be secondary to fossil fuel industry profits.”
Duke Energy operates five coal-fired power plants in North Carolina and 17 fueled by natural gas.
In announcing the proposed rule, the agency argued that it lacks the legal authority under the Clean Air Act to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, the largest stationary sources of the pollutants.
That’s not true, said John Broderick, an assistant attorney general in the New York Environmental Protection Bureau, during an Oct. 1 EPA public hearing on the proposed rule. The agency not only has the authority, Broderick said, it has a “statutory duty to regulate greenhouse gases from power plants.” He called the EPA’s move “a blatantly unlawful attempt to undermine the Clean Air Act.”
Greenhouse gas emissions drive climate change, which causes or worsens extreme weather, such as heat waves, droughts, floods and storms. This year’s Super El Niño is contributing to heat and strong hurricanes in the Pacific, but its effects are amplified by global warming.
August 2026 was the planet’s hottest August since recordkeeping began in 1850, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Western Europe endured five heat waves this summer, with temperatures at times exceeding 104 degrees Fahrenheit.
Amy Laura Cahn is a special assistant attorney general for the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, focused on energy and the environment.
During the public hearing, Cahn told the EPA the proposal is “wrong on the law, wrong on the science and wrongly ignores the harms it will cause and will be felt first and worst by our most marginalized communities.”
Massachusetts is a primary reason that greenhouse gas emissions regulations exist. In 2007, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in a landmark case against the EPA that the agency could legally regulate greenhouse gas emissions if it determines they endanger public health and welfare—which it did two years later.
Now the EPA says the scientific and legal foundation for these rules is flawed, an argument rebutted by major scientific organizations and legal experts.
“Carbon emissions contribute to climate change,” Cahn said. “Flawed and unsupported analysis can’t undermine reality.”
The EPA estimates that the repeal would save the power sector $95 billion to $160 billion in compliance costs over the next 20 years. The savings do not account for benefits such as ensuring electric grid reliability and other benefits that cannot be monetized, the EPA said.
Those estimates exclude the health and environmental costs of greenhouse gas emissions—and the financial benefits of reining in the pollutants. The Biden administration calculated the rules would save $370 billion in climate and public health costs through 2047.
“Erasing these standards doesn’t save money,” said Robbins of CleanAIRE NC in a prepared statement. “It simply transfers the financial burden from corporate polluters onto the backs of patients, families and ratepayers.”
This is the second instance in which the EPA has weakened rules governing greenhouse gas emissions. Earlier this year the agency revoked the endangerment finding for the pollutants related to motor vehicles.
“Federal rollbacks make state leadership more urgent than ever,” Robbins said. “We cannot rely on this administration to protect the air we breathe.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Former GOP lieutenant governor endorses Ballard in secretary of state race
description: Lincoln Party secretary of state candidate Greg Ballard picked up a notable endorsement Monday from former Lt. Gov. Sue Ellspermann. “I’ve always been about good governance, and that has to be the top priority, even above a party. It has to be about good people who will do the right thing for Hoosiers,” Ellspermann told […]
text:
Retired Ivy Tech Community College President Sue Ellspermann, a Republican, testifies during a House committee hearing on Dec. 2, 2025. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Lincoln Party secretary of state candidate Greg Ballard picked up a notable endorsement Monday from former Lt. Gov. Sue Ellspermann.
“I’ve always been about good governance, and that has to be the top priority, even above a party. It has to be about good people who will do the right thing for Hoosiers,” Ellspermann told the Capital Chronicle. “Greg is absolutely that candidate.”
The longtime Republican served from 2013 to 2016 under then-Gov. Mike Pence before resigning to become president of Ivy Tech Community College for about nine years. She now serves on multiple corporate boards and lives in southern Indiana.
Secretary of state candidate Greg Ballard speaks at the Indiana Statehouse on July 14, 2026. (Photo by Jack Forrest/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Ballard is representing the fledgling Lincoln Party and faces three other opponents — Republican Max Engling, Democrat Beau Bayh and Libertarian Lauri Shillings.
Ellspermann called Ballard a “proven leader, a proven high integrity public servant who made an incredible positive impact in Indianapolis as a two-term Republican mayor, who successfully worked across the aisle in a nonpartisan manner to get important, good things done for the citizens of Indianapolis.”
And she said she still considers herself a Republican.
“I believe that we should all, in our parties, be trying to support the elevation of great candidates. I think the Democrats have work to do in ensuring strong candidates who will serve all Hoosiers are elevated to these very important positions, and I didn’t see that happening in the Republican Party,” Ellspermann said. 
She acknowledged that she could have just quietly voted for Ballard but wanted to make her support public.
Ellspermann also broke with many top state Republicans last year when she spoke out last year against the proposed Indiana congressional redistricting plan pushed by President Donald Trump.
Ellspermann said she is confident Ballard will draw a strong following from central Indiana, where she believes he is well known and respected.
“However, there’s more of Indiana than central Indiana. I live in southern Indiana in a rural area. His name is not known across the state,” she said. 
“And so my hope is that if Hoosiers trust me, understand that I put a high premium on supporting high integrity, highly qualified, great public servants, then I’m hopeful that if they haven’t made their mind up, they will give Greg Ballard a really good look and get on his website and see what he stands for,” she said. “Look into his record and understand what a great candidate he would be and a great secretary of state he would make.”
A letter to the editor on her endorsement is in the Ferdinand News.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Republican gubernatorial nominee Gregg Hull announces plan to phase out New Mexico’s income tax
description: New Mexico’s Republican gubernatorial nominee, former Rio Rancho Mayor Gregg Hull, on Monday announced his plan to gradually phase out the state’s personal income tax if elected governor on Nov. 3. Speaking from his Albuquerque campaign headquarters, Hull said he hopes to accomplish the four-step plan over the course of four years.
text:
Gregg Hull, New Mexico's Republican gubernatorial nominee and former Rio Rancho mayor, on Oct. 5, 2026, announced his plan to phase out the state's income tax if elected governor. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)New Mexico’s Republican gubernatorial nominee, former Rio Rancho Mayor Gregg Hull, on Monday announced his plan to gradually phase out the state’s personal income tax if elected governor on Nov. 3.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Speaking from his Albuquerque campaign headquarters, Hull said he hopes to accomplish the four-step plan over the course of four years. The plan’s first step would reduce income tax for a single filer with a $40,000 salary from $1,471 to $671, he said. Similarly, it would reduce annual income tax for a married couple filing jointly with a $200,000 income from $8,989 to $7,250.
In the plan’s fourth and final step, no New Mexicans would continue to pay a state income tax.
“If you want to raise people out of poverty, the best way to do that is improve their personal wealth,” he told reporters at a news conference.
While New Mexico ranks high nationally in terms of poverty and low in terms of wages, the state manages a sovereign wealth fund that’s on track to be the largest in the nation by the end of the decade. 
“Right here in one of the highest-poverty states in the country, we’re sitting on that type of wealth,” Hull said.
New Mexico Election 2026: New Mexico governor

Hull said he and his team crafted the plan while assuming that the state’s social services, such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Medicaid, would continue at their current levels. Moving from one step of his plan to the next would require approval from the Legislature and would have to meet several benchmarks to ensure the reduction in income tax revenue doesn’t adversely affect the state’s ongoing programs.
For example, Hull said the plan cannot progress from one step to another if the state’s general fund reserves dip below 25% of the state’s current expenses. If the Legislature were to block his proposal, Hull said he would prioritize legislation to eliminate the remaining state income tax on Social Security benefits and qualifying military retirement pay.
He said he would not seek to institute additional taxes to replace the state’s lost income tax revenue and that he would seek to limit state spending.
“What we’re doing, first and foremost, is looking at controlling spending. We’ve seen the spending growth far exceed personal income growth. We need to bring that back into check,” he said. “That, really, is creating an imbalance in the ability to pay for these programs.”
While Hull said he wants to rein in the state’s spending, he added that he is not “looking to target” or cut programs — although he said he wants to rectify the state’s high SNAP error rate. He said his income tax plan would help state leaders ensure “that our existing programs can be appropriately funded before we add additional programs.”
Hull will face Democrat Deb Haaland, a former U.S. Department of the Interior secretary and member of Congress, in the Nov. 3 general election. Early voting begins Tuesday at county clerk’s offices across the state and will expand to alternate voting locations on Oct. 17.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Arguments set in court case challenging 4 North Dakota legislative candidates
description: The North Dakota Supreme Court has scheduled oral arguments for later this month in a court case challenging the eligibility of four Republican legislative candidates. Three Republican Party officials, two of whom lost their primary elections in June, want the court to essentially invalidate the candidacies and overturn the potential general election victori[...]
text:
North Dakota Supreme Court Chief Justice Lisa Fair McEvers, center, speaks during a hearing on Oct. 2, 2026. The other justices, from left, are Jon Jensen, Jerod Tufte, Douglas Bahr and Mark Friese. 
Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)The North Dakota Supreme Court has scheduled oral arguments for later this month in a court case challenging the eligibility of four Republican legislative candidates.
Three Republican Party officials, two of whom lost their primary elections in June, want the court to essentially invalidate the candidacies and overturn the potential general election victories of four GOP House nominees. They are Blaine DesLauriers, Terry Goerger, Tim Mihalick and Steve Sauter, who are running in districts in the Bismarck, Minot and Richland County areas. 
The challengers are District 25 GOP Chair Matt Evans, outgoing Rep. Jeff Hoverson, R-Minot, and District 7 GOP Executive Committee member Douglas Pearson. Evans and Hoverson lost their primaries to DesLauriers, Goerger and Mihalick.
Lawsuit challenges legality of 4 North Dakota legislative candidates

The challengers allege Secretary of State Michael Howe’s office treated candidate petitions inconsistently, allowing some to amend or correct incomplete petition signer information but rejecting others’ petitions. The challengers ultimately want the four seats declared vacant and filled by appointment, a method that would favor them. Correspondence between Prichard and state election officials in court documents indicates that candidates were allowed to make corrections but not if they submitted last-minute petitions.
Citizens Alliance of North Dakota is leading the court case. Former state Rep. Brandon Prichard leads the conservative group.
The court on Friday scheduled oral arguments by videoconference for Oct. 21. Court filings from both sides are due Oct. 15. 
Justices Douglas Bahr and Jerod Tufte are disqualified in the case. It’s unclear why. 
Absentee voting began last month in North Dakota’s November general election. 
Election-related challenges aren’t unusual for the court. In 2020 alone, the court took an initiated measure off the general election ballot, removed a Democratic-NPL statewide candidate due to a residency dispute, and determined who got to fill the seat of a legislative candidate who died during fall voting.
Howe has declined to comment on the Citizens Alliance case, citing the pending litigation. Sauter previously told the North Dakota Monitor he followed the law and trusts Howe’s office.
Prichard has said the secretary of state “cannot invent extra-statutory curing rules for favored candidates while strictly rejecting citizens’ petitions for minor technical omissions.”
The case shows the divisions within North Dakota’s dominant Republican Party, particularly over how candidates get on the ballot, whether by party endorsement or petition signatures.
The court on Wednesday denied a case brought by Michael Coachman, a frequent candidate who sought to get on the November ballot as an independent running for secretary of state. Coachman came up short of enough signatures after Howe’s office rejected some due to incomplete information. The court’s one-page order did not elaborate on its reasoning.

title: Tiverton abutters ask a Superior Court judge to intervene in Sapowet Cove oyster farm dispute
description: One month after the Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council (CRMC) failed to decide the fate of a proposed oyster farm in Tiverton, project opponents are asking a judge to step in. The Sept. 24 complaint filed in Providence County Superior Court against both the CRMC and applicants John and Patrick Bowen argues the council’s […]
text:
Sapowet Cove is shown on the western shore of Tiverton in the Sakonnet River. (Google Earth image)One month after the Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council (CRMC) failed to decide the fate of a proposed oyster farm in Tiverton, project opponents are asking a judge to step in.
The Sept. 24 complaint filed in Providence County Superior Court against both the CRMC and applicants John and Patrick Bowen argues the council’s failure to take action amounts to an illegal abuse of its authority. The application for the 1-acre oyster farm was submitted in late 2019, yet the seven-member council has yet to decide whether objections over its impact on boating, fishing and recreation can stop it from happening.
On Aug. 25, the council met to accept its hearing officer’s determination that a 2024 state law limiting development along the Sakonnet River did not stop the project review from advancing because the law was not retroactive.
In accepting the determination, however, the seven-member council made clear it was not issuing a final decision on the project, allowing the quasi-judicial hearing process to continue. Because it was not a final decision, there was not yet an opportunity for objectors to appeal under the state’s Administrative Procedures Act. 
A group of neighbors who own properties near the proposed oyster farm site argue they should not have to wait any longer before taking their case to a judge.
“Requiring Appellants to proceed through a full evidentiary hearing before obtaining judicial review of that threshold legal determination would therefore be futile and would not provide an adequate remedy within the meaning of [state law],” the complaint states. 
Laura Dwyer, a spokesperson for the CRMC, acknowledged requests for comment on the appeal, but did not immediately provide a response Monday.
The proposed oyster farm has become the poster child for what critics say is an inefficient and unfairly drawn-out coastal review process. John and Patrick Bowen, brothers who live in Little Compton, filed the application to set up 200 bottom cages a few hundred feet from the shoreline in December 2019. Nearby property owners, fishermen and the state aquaculture association joined together in opposition to what they allege would interfere with fishing, boating and public recreation.
The dispute made its way to Mark Krieger, CRMC hearing officer, in 2023, soon after Gov. Dan McKee appointed him to the position. An initial hearing was held in 2024, but the schedule was scratched in July 2025 after three groups of nearby property owners filed a motion, asking Krieger to dismiss the case based on the 2024 law limiting area waterfront development.
The complaint notes that almost two years have passed since initial arguments, well past the 60-day deadline required by state law. 
And the CRMC’s acceptance of Krieger’s determination, without a final decision or even a clear timeline for when that decision will come, amounts to an “abuse of discretion” of its authority, the complaint states.
John Bowen expressed frustration with the nearly seven-year wait for a decision, but blamed the delay on opposition groups rather than the CRMC.
“I’d rather have them get it right than rush to a decision or be pressured,” he said of the coastal regulatory review. 
Yet John Bowen said he and his brother are still committed to the project, which they envision as a side gig to their respective jobs as an aquaculture coordinator and carpentry teacher, both in Massachusetts. The pair plan to sell oysters direct-to-consumer and to local restaurants, in addition to offering educational visits for students. 
John Bowen said he was “dismayed” that he and his brother were named as defendants in the complaint, which centers on the state’s coastal review process — something applicants do not control.
“If the state is trying to encourage aquaculture, a process that allows applicants to be sued strictly for following the process is disheartening,” John Bowen said.
Marisa Desautel, the attorney representing three sets of property owners in the complaint, declined to comment.
The appeal asks a judge to toss Krieger’s determination that the 2024 law does not apply to the project, while affirming the property owners’ right to appeal even without a final decision by the CRMC.

text:
First-of-its-kind event inspired by Delaware-filmed mockumentary “The Conspiracists” will feature Bigfoot calls, tin foil hats, games, vendors and a movie screening
WILMINGTON — Bigfoot believers, UFO skeptics, comic fans and anyone willing to ask “what if?” will have a place to gather in Wilmington later this month.
ConCon, a conspiracy-themed convention inspired by the Delaware-filmed comedy mockumentary “The Conspiracists,” will be held Sunday, Oct. 18, at the Siegel Jewish Community Center.
Organizers describe the event as a lighthearted celebration of the fascination surrounding conspiracy theories rather than an effort to prove or disprove them.
“ConCon isn’t about whether conspiracy theories are true. It’s about why they’ve captured our imagination for generations,” said Christopher Bruce of Wilmington-based King Creative. “Through comedy, games, pop culture, interactive exhibits, unique vendors, and a movie that brings it all together, ConCon transforms curiosity into a shared adventure that everyone can enjoy.”
The convention runs from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., followed by a screening of “The Conspiracists” and a cast and creator question-and-answer session from 5 to 7 p.m. Ticketing information lists the overall event through 7:30 p.m. Ticket Tailor
Among the scheduled attractions are a tin foil hat-building station, Bigfoot Calling Championship, kids foil fashion show and “Real or Fake?” interactive game show.
A vendor hall will feature comics, collectibles, independent artists and other attractions. Attendees also will have opportunities to meet artists, puppeteers and creators connected to the movie.
From movie screen to real convention
ConCon essentially brings to life the fictional convention at the center of “The Conspiracists.”
The comedy follows siblings trying to create an all-inclusive conspiracy convention as their plans begin falling apart and an even larger conspiracy may be developing around them.
The movie was filmed almost entirely in Delaware and prominently features local locations, including the Hotel du Pont, The Grand and the Siegel JCC itself. The Conspiracists
Directed by Michael Perrie Jr. and produced by Uncultured Swine and King Creative, the film had its world premiere Jan. 8 at The Grand in Wilmington. BroadwayWorld
The production also relied heavily on Delaware cast members, crew members, businesses and locations, an approach filmmakers have said was intended to make Delaware part of the story rather than simply a stand-in for somewhere else. Town Square Delaware LIVE
Three ticket options
Organizers are offering three levels of admission.

The $10 Civilian Pass includes access to the vendor hall and daytime programming, including contests, the tin foil hat station, photo opportunities and scavenger hunt.
The $15 Conspiracist Pass adds reserved seating for the evening movie screening, access to the cast Q&A and additional raffle entries.
The $25 Classified Access ticket includes the daytime and movie activities, early entry, VIP movie seating, a post-panel group photo with the cast and a giveaway that organizers say will be revealed at the event.

The official ticket listing confirms that ConCon will be held Sunday, Oct. 18 — correcting a reference to Saturday contained later in the event announcement. Ticket Tailor

text:
Gov. Kim Reynolds has appointed former state Rep. Jon Dunwell to serve on the Iowa Utilities Commission. (Photo of the IUC by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch, inset photo courtesy of Iowa Legislature, photo illustration made with Canva)Gov. Kim Reynolds announced Monday she was appointing former Iowa Rep. Jon Dunwell, a Republican from Newton, to serve on the Iowa Utilities Commission. 
Dunwell fills the spot after the Sept. 4 resignation of Erik Helland, who was appointed to the role in May 2023. 
The Iowa Utilities Commission is responsible for approving utility rates in the state and permitting utility infrastructure projects, including energy generating facilities and pipelines. The IUC has faced increased public attention in recent years due to its role in approving a controversial carbon sequestration pipeline.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Dunwell was not seeking reelection to his position in the House, but officially resigned his seat Monday to take the role as IUC commissioner.
Dunwell, who currently serves the pastor of Gateway Church Monroe and director of outreach and engagement at The Family Leader, said he is grateful to Reynolds for the new opportunity. 
“Iowans depend on the work of the Iowa Utilities Commission every day, and I’m honored to serve them,” Dunwell said. 
Dunwell joins IUC chair Sarah Martz and commissioner Joshua Byrnes. 
Reynolds said, in a news release, she appreciates Dunwell’s “steady leadership style” and ability to “foster strong relationships.” While in the House, Dunwell was vice chair of the Administration and Rules Committee and the Ways and Means Committee. 
“Having had the opportunity to work with him, I’ve seen firsthand how he thoughtfully considers all sides of an issue,” Reynolds said in the release. “I’m confident that as a member of the Iowa Utilities Commission he will successfully balance growth and development opportunities with the importance of protecting ratepayers.” 
Earlier this year, the House voted to ban the use of eminent domain for carbon sequestration pipelines. According to the roll call, Dunwell was one of 28 representatives to vote no on the bill, which did not advance to the floor in the Senate. Dunwell was among yes votes the previous year for a similar bill and another that would have restricted carbon sequestration pipelines in the state. 
Dunwell’s appointment, which is subject to approval from the Senate, will fill the remainder of Helland’s term, which expires April 30, 2029, according to IUC.

As Alaska heads into the general election, the Alaska Beacon, Alaska Public Media, KTOO and the Anchorage Daily News have an updated voter guide. Just like we did for the primary election, we worked together to build a guide to help Alaskans make informed choices when they vote, and you can find it in the same place as our guide for the primary election.
Our 2026 Alaska Voter Guide is not intended to replace debates, forums and public statements. It’s an additional tool intended to inform voters about candidates’ positions and to hold them accountable once elected.[Voter Guide: 2026 Voter Guide Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
We hope it’s a useful resource as Alaskans make their picks for governor, U.S. House, U.S. Senate and the Legislature. Early voting begins Monday, Oct. 19, and Election Day is Nov. 3.
To build the guide, we asked you earlier this year what you wanted us to ask candidates, and formulated questions based on the responses we got.
It’s part of our commitment to the “citizens agenda” type of coverage, where our reporting is focused on what candidates believe and how they would affect things if elected, rather than on who’s ahead in the polls.
We began reaching out to candidates this summer for our primary guide, and we’ve updated the questions for the races for governor, U.S. House and U.S. Senate because the fields have narrowed so dramatically. 
For the governor’s race, all four candidates responded. For the U.S. House and Senate races, we received responses from three of the four candidates. 
While it isn’t everyone — and we’ll continue pursuing answers — we’re proud to say that this questionnaire is the most complete one that you can find anywhere in Alaska.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: AI apocalypse? Most Louisiana candidates for Congress stay vague on regulation
description: Most candidates running for Congress in Louisiana agree there should be some federal regulations placed on artificial intelligence. But at this point they are mostly offering generalities, without providing specifics about any limitations they would favor.  Their remarks come amid mounting concerns about AI safety. Lead tech executives, including Microsoft f[...]
text:
Louisiana candidates for U.S. Senate and two competitive U.S. House races, in the 5th and 6th districts, said some guardrails on the artificial intelligence industry are warranted, but most weren't specific about what restrictions they would support. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)Most candidates running for Congress in Louisiana agree there should be some federal regulations placed on artificial intelligence. But at this point they are mostly offering generalities, without providing specifics about any limitations they would favor. 
Their remarks come amid mounting concerns about AI safety. Lead tech executives, including Microsoft founder Bill Gates, have warned that artificial intelligence could upend the job market and pose significant threats to public safety and infrastructure unless it is safely contained. 
The Illuminator sought feedback on potential AI regulation from the two candidates for U.S. Senate and in the two competitive U.S. House races, for the 5th District and 6th District seats. 
In general, Republican candidates were more apprehensive about AI constraints, a position President Donald Trump and U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Benton, share. Democrats expressed more concern about the impact of artificial intelligence, particularly on the job market and the economy. 

“When you’re listening and especially the piece that I heard from Bill Gates, it’s frightening,” said state Rep. Pat Moore, D-Monroe, who is running for Congress in the 5th District. 
Davis: Tax AI for jobs taken 
While most candidates did not provide details about what they would want from AI regulation, three outlined some restrictions they would like to propose. 

Democrat Lindsay “Rubia” Garcia, who is running in the 6th District, said she would support cybersecurity testing and protections for personal data. Disclosure for when people are interacting with artificial intelligence and reporting serious security breaches should also be required, she said.

“People should also have a meaningful way to challenge consequential decisions made using AI, such as decisions about employment, housing or access to services,” Garcia wrote in an email.

State Rep. Michael Echols, R-Monroe, part of the 6th District field, wants to impose strict trade rules regarding selling the technology that helps power artificial intelligence. He said he does not think such sales to China should be allowed, citing national security concerns. 

“I want to make sure that America is the leader in this, and then we protect that intellectual capital here as well as the intellectual physical assets that create that capital,” Echols said. 

Jamie Davis, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, said companies that use artificial intelligence to cut jobs should not receive a tax break for doing so. 

“A company that replaces a human job with an AI job, I think that … company should have to pay the taxes for that human job,” Davis said. 
Congresswoman Julia Letlow, R-Baton Rouge, the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate, provided a written response to questions about her stance on AI concerns. She did not provide specifics about what she would support in terms of AI regulation. 
“Government has a responsibility to protect Americans and put common-sense guardrails in place without overregulating this technology or allowing China to win the global AI race,” Letlow said in her statement.
A threat to humanity?

In addition to Gates saying that artificial intelligence could cause “a billion” deaths, a former researcher for two of the most high-profile AI companies issued a similar warning. Jacob Coxon, who has worked with OpenAI and Anthropic, said people inside the industry believe AI could threaten humanity by the end of the decade, the Associated Press reported.

There have been several incidents of AI agents attempting to hack or scrap government websites in recent weeks, according to AP, and reports on the technology “going rogue” and acting autonomously without human direction. But some of the candidates feel the fears are overblown. 
“We do need to have some safeguards in place to make sure there are no unintended consequences, but, no, I do not think AI is going to imperil human existence,” said state Rep. Gabe Firment, R-Pollock, a 5th District candidate. 
Letlow and Chauna Banks, a Democrat in the 6th District race, also said they doubted AI poses a true threat to humankind. 
Echols said Congress should proceed with caution when it comes to artificial intelligence, but he added that he didn’t put much stock in warnings from Gates, whose reputation he considers tarnished since his relationship with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein has come to light. 
“I’ve never looked at Bill Gates as the moral code for America,” Echols said. 
Garcia and Pat Forbes, a Democrat running in the 6th District, said they don’t have the expertise to determine whether artificial intelligence could threaten humanity. But both expressed concern about the impact it could have on the economy by eliminating jobs on a large scale. 
“I am not against data centers. I’m not against AI,” Forbes said. “But we have to make sure the economic benefits are not just going to 10 wealthy people.” 
Banks said she doesn’t believe workforce upheaval would be enough reason for the federal government to place more regulations on the AI industry. 
“I don’t know any industry we stop because of job loss,” Banks said.

Banks, Firment and Louisiana Board of Regents chair Misti Cordell, a Republican running in the 5th District, said they are wary of holding AI companies legally liable for harm the technology could cause. 
U.S. Sens. Josh Hawley, R-Missouri, and Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Connecticut, jointly introduced legislation that would allow AI companies to be sued when their products become autonomous and engage in harmful activity. 

“An industry that’s just starting out, we don’t want the lawyers to feed off of it too soon,” Cordell said. 
State Sen. Stewart Cathey, R-Monroe, was the only major 5th District candidate who did not respond to phone calls or text messages for this story. 
Sen. Rick Edmonds, R-Baton Rouge, who is seeking the 6th District seat, also could not be reached. One of his opponents, state Sen. Blake Miguez, R-New Iberia, declined to be interviewed.
