description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahomans have until Friday to complete their voter registration for the Nov. 3 general elections if they haven’t yet done so. The same deadline applies to anyone needing to update their registration with a different name or address. Those seeking to register to vote for the first time or update their registration […]
text:
Voters mark their ballots in the Oklahoma County Election Board on June 11 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahomans have until Friday to complete their voter registration for the Nov. 3 general elections if they haven’t yet done so.
The same deadline applies to anyone needing to update their registration with a different name or address.
Those seeking to register to vote for the first time or update their registration can do so online through the Oklahoma Voter Portal or in person at their county election board.
The deadline to request an absentee ballot is 5 p.m. Oct. 19. A county election board must receive a voter’s mailed absentee ballot by 7 p.m. on election night for it to count. Any hand-delivered absentee ballots must arrive at the voter’s county election board by close of business on the Monday before the election.
A blackout period on switching political parties, which ran from April 1 to Aug. 31, is now over, meaning registered voters can also change their party affiliation.
The Nov. 3 General Elections are open to voters of any party, as well as independents.
These elections will decide Oklahoma’s next governor, U.S. senator, U.S. representatives, lieutenant governor, attorney general, state superintendent, state treasurer, and commissioners of labor, insurance and corporation.
Depending on where they live, Oklahomans’ ballots could include a state House or Senate race and county elections. Voters must decide on Nov. 3 whether to keep sitting Oklahoma Supreme Court justices and state appeals court judges in office.
Two state questions will appear on all ballots. 
State Question 845 would change rules for making appointments to the Judicial Nominating Commission. 
State Question 847 will reduce how much a property’s assessed value can increase each year, impacting property tax rates.
Early voting runs from Oct. 28-31. Polls are open on Nov. 3 from 7 a.m. until 7 p.m.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Judge dismisses Lutheran church challenge to Tennessee law making it a crime to harbor immigrants
description: A Tennessee law that makes it a felony to “harbor” immigrants without legal status remains enforceable after a federal judge last week dismissed a legal challenge brought by Lutheran churches.  The law defines human smuggling as intentionally concealing, harboring or shielding from detection, for financial gain, any individual known to have illegally entered[...]
text:
A federal judge on Sept. 20. 2026 dismissed a challenge to Tennessee's human smuggling law brought by Lutheran churches. Rev.  Rick Roberts, pastor of St. John’s  Lutheran Church in Donelson and Rev. Matt Steinhauer, interim pastor of St. Andrews Lutheran Church in Franklin, knelt in front of lawmakers debating a bill to deny an education to some immigrant children during the spring 2025 session of the Tennessee Legislature.  (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
A Tennessee law that makes it a felony to “harbor” immigrants without legal status remains enforceable after a federal judge last week dismissed a legal challenge brought by Lutheran churches. 
The law defines human smuggling as intentionally concealing, harboring or shielding from detection, for financial gain, any individual known to have illegally entered or remained in the United States.
It includes in the definition of human smuggling — a felony punishable by up to six years in prison — any attempt to transport an individual without legal status in an effort to conceal them from law enforcement, including immigration agents. 
Days before the law took effect in July 2025, the Southeastern Synod of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, along with a Nashville landlord and a father whose son-in-law is an asylum seeker living in his household, filed suit. 
They contended the law was an unconstitutional usurpation of federal powers to exclusively enforce immigration law and violated the First Amendment’s rights of the Synod congregations, which provide shelter and services to immigrants regardless of immigration status, often paid for by charitable contributions. The plaintiffs also argued the law was overly vague.
Suit seeks to block Tennessee law that makes it a crime to “harbor” certain immigrants

In dismissing the lawsuit last week, Chief District Judge William Campbell, Jr. ruled the churches, landlord and father-in-law lacked legal standing to challenge the law, because they could not show an immediate threat they would be prosecuted under its language.
Campbell, nominated to the bench by President Donald Trump in 2017, cited state attorneys’ assurances that the law applies only to “for-profit” operations that knowingly harbor or transport immigrants without legal status, not churches that accept charitable contributions to provide services that align with their faith. 
State attorneys also said that a violation of the law occurs not only by providing shelter but to do so with an “intent to conceal.” 
The judge conceded that the state’s interpretation of the law presented in court is not explicitly stated in the law’s language. 
“The court has serious misgivings that the defendant’s interpretation is not supported by the statutory language, particularly with regard to the purported ‘intent to conceal’ requirement and whether the statute requires knowledge of illegal status or knowledge of an ICE determination of illegal status,” Campbell wrote.
Even so, he concluded the plaintiffs had not met their legal hurdle to demonstrate they had the right to challenge the law, because they could not demonstrate they were likely to be prosecuted under it.

text:
Arkansas Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders gives her State of the State address in the House of Representatives chamber at the Arkansas State Capitol in Little Rock, Arkansas on Wednesday, April 8, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)A special election to fill state Senate District 18 has been moved up three weeks to Dec. 15, Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders announced Monday.
Sanders previously set Jan. 5, 2027, as the date of the special general election for the seat that had been held by former Republican Sen. Jonathan Dismang. In setting the new date, the Republican governor cited a state law that requires she do so in the event that only one or two candidates have filed for the nomination of a party holding a primary. 
Two people — Camille Feyen, a Democrat, and Will Moore, a Republican — filed to run in their parties’ respective primaries to replace Dismang, who stepped down last month to take a job with Arkansas Electric Cooperatives. 
Sanders had previously set Nov. 3 as the date for the special primary elections. Under the new schedule, county election commissioners must certify the results of the primary on Wednesday.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Senate District 18 covers White County and parts of Faulkner and Cleburne counties. The winner of the Dec. 15 special election will serve the remainder of Dismang’s term, which ends in January 2029. 
Two other candidates, Steven McClelland and Trevor McGarrah, filed to run as independents. 
Dismang’s resignation from the Senate kicked off the latest in a series of legislative special elections in 2026 as a result of deaths, new jobs and arrests. Not including Dismang’s former seat, five other vacancies have been filled or are in the process of being filled in both chambers since January.
With the vacancy, Republicans hold a 27-6 majority in the Senate. Senate District 1’s seat, previously held by Republican Sen. Ben Gilmore, is also empty.
Dismang, the former co-chairman of the Joint Budget Committee and an architect of the state’s hybrid Medicaid expansion, served in the Legislature for nearly two decades.
Sanders has previously run into legal issues for how she has handled scheduling special elections. She was successfully sued twice last year over lengthy timelines to fill vacancies in Senate District 26 and House District 70 after she set the dates for June 2026.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Farish Street gets breath of fresh air with new green space
description: A sign displayed in front of the newly built Farish Street Green space on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
More than a year after breaking ground, Jackson residents and city officials gathered Monday morning to celebrate the opening of Farish Street Green and Urban Forest, a project that has transformed a once-vacant lot in one of the city’s historic neighborhoods into a cooling green space intended to combat extreme heat.
Along North Farish Street, young sycamores, maples and sumacs are beginning to spread their branches over grass, walking trails and lounge areas, replacing a landscape that offered little refuge from the summer heat.
A sign with information regarding greenry sits infront of the new Farish Street Urban Forest on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today
The project grew out of research begun by the nonprofit 2C Mississippi in late 2020 to examine extreme heat in Jackson. Data gathered by volunteers from Jackson State University and the University of Mississippi Medical Center found that parts of downtown could be more than 10 degrees hotter during the summer than areas on the city’s outskirts. The findings helped spur plans to add trees and green space along Farish Street.
It was made in partnership with Tree Urban Design, Jackson Community Design Center and the Jackson Redevelopment Authority — costing around $500,000, according to Tree Urban Design Architect Travis Crabtree. 
“If you’re sitting there thinking, I hope this wraps up before it gets too hot. That’s the whole point,” Ward 7 Councilmember Kevin Parkison said to the crowd. 
The project is a part of an effort to eliminate urban heat islands — which suffer from higher heat temperatures because of asphalt and concrete. The addition of trees and other greenery aims to create shaded areas and reduce ambient temperatures.
Various city officials, volunteers and nonprofit workers gather for the ribbon cutting of Farish Street Green on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. The new green space in downtown Jackson is meant to offer a shaded canopies to beat the high heat in Jackson. Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today
2C Mississippi founder Dominika Parry said the alarmingly high heat in the area, alongside the historical significance of the area, made it easy to choose where to place the green space.
The project will continue to monitor temperature and humidity in the area over the next two years using stationary and handheld sensors. The findings will be used to help develop future projects to reduce Jackson’s urban heat islands, if data shows the tree canopies lower the area’s temperature, Parry said.
“The idea for 2C Mississippi is to provide as many projects as there is a demand,” Parry said in an interview Friday.
This is not the final project the 2C Mississippi and Tree Urban Design are working with the city to tackle.
2C Mississippi is using its resources to green areas for flood control near the Jackson Zoo. Tree Urban Green has been working alongside the city of Jackson and the Jackson River District Partnership to revitalize a 30-acre landfill near Old Brandon Road into a riverfront park.Tree Urban Design has also announced plans in conjunction with developer Gabriel Padro to revitalize the abandoned YMCA building in the greater Belhaven area into a mixed residential recreational space. The City Council approved rezoning the area in August. 
A tree covered trail replaces a previously dilapidated parking lot on Farish Street on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. The Urban Forest aims to reduce heat in the area by planting greenery. Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today
The 9-acre space will cost $60 million to redevelop.
“We’re planning some new exciting improvements that should be hopefully starting early this fall or early this spring,” Crabtree said.
Farish Street Green’s opening marks a new chapter for the historic district in downtown Jackson that was once the hub of Black-owned businesses  — with hopes that the revitalization will help the city’s efforts to breathe new life into the area. 
“Projects like this can help create momentum and encourage additional investment and contribute to continued monopolization to Farish Street and downtown Jackson,” city spokesperson Nic Lott said at the green space’s ribbon cutting.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa researcher warns higher vape tax could drive people back to cigarettes
description: As states increasingly implement taxes on alternative smoking products, research from a Des Moines University professor showed the policies could lead people to reach for cigarettes instead — impacting more than just themselves. Des Moines University Assistant Professor of Public Health Jason Semprini found in a study of state taxes on items like vapes and [[...]
text:
A Des Moines University researcher has published a study showing $1 e-cigarette taxes can lead to higher rates of secondhand smoke exposure. (Photo by Douglas Sacha/Getty Images)As states increasingly implement taxes on alternative smoking products, research from a Des Moines University professor showed the policies could lead people to reach for cigarettes instead — impacting more than just themselves.
Des Moines University Assistant Professor of Public Health Jason Semprini found in a study of state taxes on items like vapes and e-cigarettes and secondhand smoke exposure that increasing the tax by $1 on average increases a child’s chances of exposure to secondhand smoke by 16%.
“As vape taxes went up, exposure to cigarette smoke in the house also increased, so, kind of a negative consequence to this well-intentioned policy,” Semprini said. “Unfortunately, we have to consider both intended and unintended consequences.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Semprini’s report, published in the International Journal of Drug Policy, states that electronic nicotine delivery systems like e-cigarettes and vapes have contributed to declines in smoking cigarettes and “although not without risks or health concerns, contain fewer toxicants than combustible cigarettes.” However, taxes and regulations on the products “appear to inadvertently increase smoking rates.”
Where previous research in this area has shown that policies aimed at vaping reduce the practice while pushing some people back to smoking cigarettes, Semprini said no one before him had focused on nonsmokers who live with people who smoke or vape.
Using data from the National Survey of Children’s Health, Semprini said he compared trends of smoking in the house to instances of vape tax implementation and increases. The correlation he found between tax increases and smoke exposure was only present among households where the adults do not have an education beyond high school.
“It’s children who live in a house of lower-educated adults or parents who are bearing the major burden of this vape tax policy,” Semprini said.
According to U.S. Census data, more than 44% of Iowans hold at least an associate’s degree, and the American Lung Association reports a smoking rate among Iowa adults at 14.7%.
Taxation policies vary between the more than 34 states with taxes on electronic nicotine delivery systems, according to an article from the Tax Foundation showing taxes by state as of January 2026. Semprini said states can have multiple reasons for taxing these products, from wanting to curb use among young people to seeking a new revenue stream from sales.
In Iowa, Gov. Kim Reynolds signed a law in May imposing a 5-cent tax on vapes and other alternative nicotine products, with revenue going to the state’s healthcare trust fund and to pediatric cancer research.
Semprini said the 5% tax is “really unlikely to change behavior,” but if the Iowa Legislature and state governor ever decide to increase that tax, he would expect to see a similar response in the state that he’s seen nationally through his research.
“It kind of adds to the regressiveness of these types of taxes,” Semprini said. “Lower-income people have to pay more out of their own pockets relative to their income if they don’t change their behavior, and then it’s those people who are of lower socioeconomic status, lower education, their children who are bearing the negative effects of secondhand smoke exposure, which is a major predictor of future cigarette smoking.”
The researcher’s next focus in this area is on older adults and reducing smoking among the population, Semprini said.
Lung cancer will cause the highest number of cancer deaths in Iowa this year out of all cancer-caused deaths, according to the 2026 Cancer in Iowa report. Semprini said that in Iowa, where radon measurements are higher, those who smoke or are exposed to secondhand smoke see their risk of developing lung cancer go up 20 times compared to those who don’t smoke.
“It’s really important knowing our cancer rates, knowing that lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer mortality in Iowa, to not inadvertently cause people to go back to smoking cigarettes,” Semprini said. “We should be doing the opposite, and we should be doing that through the lens that it’s not just people who smoke, but also people who are exposed to smoking.”

title: State regulators to allow part of NextEra’s political past to be examined in Dominion merger case
description: The Virginia State Corporation Commission will allow documents detailing an internal investigation into NextEra Energy’s failed attempt to acquire Jacksonville, Florida’s public utility to be included in deliberations of the company’s $67 billion proposed merger with Dominion Energy.   “I find the requested information is discoverable in the instant case, al[...]
text:
Virginia State Corporation Commission allows new documents in the Dominion-NextEra merger case. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)The Virginia State Corporation Commission will allow documents detailing an internal investigation into NextEra Energy’s failed attempt to acquire Jacksonville, Florida’s public utility to be included in deliberations of the company’s $67 billion proposed merger with Dominion Energy.  
“I find the requested information is discoverable in the instant case, although the Commission will ultimately decide the admissibility of any information offered into the record as evidence,” Chief Hearing Examiner Mathias Roussey Jr. wrote Oct. 2, adding that the utility must furnish the requested information within four days. 
The order comes after energy policy advocacy group Clean Virginia, an intervenor in the merger case, argued that NextEra’s alleged political ties and attempts to take over other utilities should be examined during the case’s discovery process.
Before the evidentiary hearings – where attorneys take the stand to question witnesses, present evidence and present their key arguments on either side of the case — lawyers are sifting through documents and other information to help build their case and submit it to the SCC.
Clean Virginia and the two groups said NextEra’s previous actions and that of its former leadership — including the $150 million settlement NextEra agreed to pay in June to resolve a dispute over whether the company lied about its involvement in political interference schemes in Florida — should be allowed to be mentioned in this case. 
Clean Virginia pressed for the energy company to reveal several other items from its past dealings, as well, and called for further clarifications on enforcement mechanisms for the merger conditions.
“A public utility and any entity that controls it is more than the people who keep the lights on, and the responsibilities of its management and board are far broader,” said Clean Virginia Executive Director Brennan Gilmore. 
“How NextEra’s leadership responded to serious allegations about Florida Power & Light’s use of corporate resources to influence elections and target officials goes directly to how it would govern Dominion,” Gilmore added.
Clean Virginia’s lawyer also argued in a Sept. hearing that a major part of the merger filing hinges on NextEra’s track record, core values, and corporate governance – which the group said included the political activities.
While Dominion’s lawyer Joe Reid argued in a September hearing that NextEra’s actions under the company under previous leadership weren’t relevant due to a large turnover in staffing in recent years, on Friday the SCC granted part of Clean Virginia’s motion to bring some of these items to light.
‘A different deal on the table’: AG Jay Jones asks SCC to reset the clock on Dominion-NextEra merger

Roussey denied other requests by Clean Virginia, including a call for a half decade’s worth of the company’s spending on public opinion campaigns. 
The SCC is also weighing Attorney General Jay Jones’ request to reset the clock on the merger timeline due to the latest amendment to the proposal from NextEra and Dominion in mid-September. 
The amendment expanded portions of the proposal, including extending the customer bill credit from two years to four and building an office building in downtown Richmond. If the motion is approved, the merger case would stretch into the spring. 
Presently, regulators must approve or reject the merger by Jan. 11.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Collins applauds G7 oil release, says it will help Mainers struggling with costs
description: U.S. Sen. Susan Collins is applauding the news that the Group of Seven European nations will release 50 million barrels of diesel and 50 million barrels of crude oil over the next four months.  The release is expected to lower energy costs, which have soared as the war in Iran restricts the flow of diesel […]
text:
Roughly half of Maine households use heating oil as their primary heating source. (Photo by gmnicholas/ Getty Images)U.S. Sen. Susan Collins is applauding the news that the Group of Seven European nations will release 50 million barrels of diesel and 50 million barrels of crude oil over the next four months. 
The release is expected to lower energy costs, which have soared as the war in Iran restricts the flow of diesel and crude oil onto global markets and Russia has implemented an export ban on diesel after Ukrainian attacks on refineries. 
“I applaud this announcement, which will increase the supply of diesel, which can also be used to heat homes this winter, and crude oil, putting immediate downward pressure on gasoline and diesel prices,” Collins said in a statement Friday. “This will help to lower costs for Americans heating their homes and fueling up cars and trucks, farmers and other businesses producing and transporting goods, and households purchasing the everyday products they depend on.”
In a letter to President Donald Trump last month, Collins and Sen. Angus King urged the federal government to release supply from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve. 
According to the latest data from the Maine Department of Energy Resources, the average statewide price of heating oil was $5.96 per gallon on Sept. 28, up roughly 80% from last year. That is down slightly from Sept. 21, when the average price reached a record high of $6.02. 
“Maine’s reliance on imported heating fuels means our households remain exposed to volatility in global oil markets, putting added pressure on families as we head into winter with record high prices,” Celina Cunningham, acting commissioner of the Maine Department of Energy Resources, said in a statement Thursday. 
Roughly half of Maine households use heating oil as their primary heating source. That number is down from 70% of households in 2010, according to the department. 
On Friday, the Maine Democratic Party criticized Collins for voting to extend the war five times.
“The risks to our troops and our families were clear the moment that President Trump started this reckless war with Iran — yet Susan Collins voted five times against stopping it,” Maine Democratic Party spokesperson Misha Linnehan said in a statement. “Now, families are paying record prices to heat their homes this winter, and there’s no end to the war in sight.”

name: Delaware
title: Claymont Man Arrested After Customers’ Cars Stolen From Wilmington Repair Shop
description:
The Delaware State Police arrested 25-year-old Tzair Bryant, of Claymont, Delaware, and is seeking a second suspect after two customer vehicles were stolen during a burglary at an auto repair […]
The post State Police Arrest Claymont Man and Seek Second Suspect in Wilmington Auto Shop Burglary appeared first on Delaware State Police - State of Delaware.
text:
Police say two suspects broke into Penny Hill Service and Repair Center, stole customers’ keys and drove away in two vehicles; a second suspect remains at large
WILMINGTON, Del. — Delaware State Police have arrested a 25-year-old Claymont man and are searching for a second suspect after two vehicles belonging to customers were stolen during a burglary at a Wilmington-area auto repair shop.
Troopers were called about midnight Sept. 26 to Penny Hill Service and Repair Center, 517 Philadelphia Pike, for a burglary in progress.
When officers arrived, they found broken glass in a garage door and searched the business, but the suspects had already fled.
Investigators said a man and woman forced their way into the repair shop and stole keys belonging to customers who had left their vehicles there for service. The pair then allegedly used the keys to steal two of those vehicles.
The Delaware State Police Criminal Investigations Unit took over the investigation.
Four days later, on Sept. 30, Wilmington police received information that one of the stolen vehicles was near East Eighth and North Buttonwood streets.
Officers located the vehicle and took Tzair Bryant, 25, of Claymont, into custody. Police said Bryant was carrying the keys to the stolen vehicle.
Wilmington police contacted Delaware State Police detectives, who responded and identified Bryant as the male suspect in the Penny Hill burglary, according to state police.
Bryant was taken to Delaware State Police Troop 1 and charged with third-degree burglary, possession of burglar tools, two counts of motor vehicle theft, second-degree conspiracy and criminal mischief under $1,000.
All of the charges except criminal mischief are felonies.
Bryant was arraigned in Justice of the Peace Court and committed to the Delaware Department of Correction in lieu of $3,100 secured bail.
State police said they are continuing to investigate and are seeking the second suspect, described as a woman.
TO GO BOX

What: Delaware State Police investigation into a burglary and theft of two customers’ vehicles from Penny Hill Service and Repair Center
Where: 517 Philadelphia Pike, Wilmington
When: About midnight Sept. 26
Arrested: Tzair Bryant, 25, of Claymont
Charges: Third-degree burglary; possession of burglary tools; two counts of motor vehicle theft; second-degree conspiracy; criminal mischief under $1,000
Status: One suspect arrested; police are seeking a second suspect
Information: Anyone with information about the burglary or the second suspect should contact Delaware State Police.


Detectives continue to investigate this incident and ask anyone with information relevant to the case to contact Detective M. Kerrigan by calling (302) 365-8487. Information may also be provided by sending a private Facebook message to the Delaware State Police or contacting Delaware Crime Stoppers at 1-800-847-3333.
If you or someone you know is a victim or witness of a crime or has lost a loved one to a sudden death and needs assistance, the Delaware State Police Victim Services Unit / Delaware Victim Center is available to offer you support and resources 24 hours a day through a toll-free hotline at 1-800-VICTIM-1 (1-800-842-8461). name: Source New Mexico
title: 2 New Mexico GOP lawmakers continued paying canvasser accused of harassing Democrat, documents show
description: Two Republican state lawmakers seeking reelection continued to employ a New Mexico campaign canvasser accused of harassing their Democratic colleague even after another GOP candidate fired the man over his behavior, campaign finance records show.
text:
New Mexico state Reps. Luis Terraza (R-Silver City) and Jenifer Jones (R-Deming) paid Adalberto Rodrguez, above, a canvasser accused of harassment, more than $8,000 between July and September 2026, according to Secretary of State’s Office records. (Screenshot of video courtesy Heath Haussamen)
Two Republican state lawmakers seeking reelection continued to employ a New Mexico campaign canvasser accused of harassing their Democratic colleague even after another GOP candidate fired the man over his behavior, campaign finance records show.
Last month, New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva (D-Las Cruces) accused Adalberto Rodriguez, whom her Republican opponent hired as a canvasser, of harassing her and her husband at public events.
At several public events between April and July, Silva said Rodriguez approached her and her husband, independent journalist Heath Haussamen, while brandishing a tripod and a phone or camera and filming. Rodriguez can be seen on several videos Silva provided calling the lawmaker “baby” or “princess” and repeatedly insulting Haussamen’s testosterone levels and appearance as he tries to intervene.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Silva and Haussamen filed a police report in late July regarding Rodriguez’s behavior, which she described as “disruptive, offensive and dangerous in its escalation.” The Doña Ana County Sheriff’s Office ultimately declined to bring charges. 
Silva’s Republican opponent Ben Luna, Jr. previously told Source NM he fired Rodriguez in July due to his behavior and because he wasn’t meeting his quota as a canvasser. Luna also said he reached out to fellow Republican candidates in New Mexico who hired Rodriguez in some capacity to tell them about Rodriguez’s misbehavior.
In a social media post in early September, Silva shared videos of the encounters and accused House Minority Floor Leader Rep. Gail Armstrong (R-Magdalena) of failing to intervene to ensure candidates’ safety. Armstrong, in a previous statement, told Source NM that she considered the matter to be “already-resolved” by the time it came to her attention.
However, recent Secretary of State’s Office filings show that two southern New Mexico lawmakers — Reps. Luis Terraza (R-Silver City) and Jenifer Jones (R-Deming) — continued to employ Rodriguez until at least September. 
Jones and Terrazas paid Rodriguez more than $8,000 between June 28 and Sept. 7, according to campaign finance reports. 
Terrazas paid Rodriguez more than $6,300 for unspecified “campaign contract labor” in seven installments between July 9 and Aug. 26. Jones paid Rodriguez nearly $1,900 on Sept. 1 for “campaign paraphernalia/misc.,” the documents show. 
Rodriguez did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment Monday, though he previously told Source NM that he deleted one of the videos he posted of his encounters with Haussamen and Silva.  Rodriguez controls social media accounts called “The Border Gazette.” The handle has roughly 75,000 Instagram followers and primarily contains posts regarding Mexico politics and sports. 
Terrazas declined to comment Thursday afternoon, saying he was heading into a debate with his Democrat opponent Raul Turrieta for the District 39 seat. He did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment Monday. 
Jones told Source NM that she was unaware that she’d hired or paid Rodriguez. 
New Mexico lawmaker accuses election opponent’s employee of harassing her at events

In an emailed statement Friday afternoon on behalf of Terrazas and Jones, Armstrong did not address Source NM’s questions about what services the lawmakers procured from Rodriguez or why they continued to employ him.
“This is a blatant attempt by Source New Mexico and Sarah Silva to distract from the growing scrutiny of Silva’s critical support for Project Jupiter,” Armstrong said, referring to the controversial data center project in Doña Ana County. 
Both Terrazas and Jones have successfully held their seats in recent elections despite serving districts in which Democrats outnumber Republicans. Democrats currently outnumber Republicans 42-26 in the state house. 
Sila Avcil, campaign manager for Jones’ District 32 opponent Democrat Laura Parra, told Source NM on Friday that she was immediately concerned for her candidate after seeing Jones’ financial reports. 
“Our immediate reaction was just being appalled at the fact that she had hired someone like that knowingly after another Republican had just fired him for harassment,” she said. “Right after that, we were slightly concerned for Laura’s safety.”
Avcil said she and Parra ultimately opted not to hire additional security, but that they are “keeping an eye on the situation.” They have not seen Rodriguez at any campaign events or other public appearances, Avcil said. 
Turrieta, Terrazas’ opponent, also told Source NM he has not had any safety concerns.
Still, Silva told Source NM on Friday that Rodriguez continuing to serve on campaign shows that Armstrong continues not to take the matter seriously.
“Leader Armstrong and my opponent had both said at the time that this was taken care of,” Silva said. “Clearly, it wasn’t taken care of, and that bothers and worries me.”
Early voting begins Tuesday. Election Day is Nov. 3.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Commute chaos as WA ferries cancels dozens of runs as workers out sick
description: Numerous Washington state ferry sailings were canceled Monday as many workers called in sick and their replacements declined to fill in for them, according to state officials. Thirteen of the ferry system’s 18 vessels transporting travelers and commuters across Puget Sound were out of commission Monday morning, according to the Washington State Department of[...]
text:
The state ferry Tokitae, seen here approaching Whidbey Island. (Photo by Tom Banse)Numerous Washington state ferry sailings were canceled Monday as many workers called in sick and their replacements declined to fill in for them, according to state officials.
Thirteen of the ferry system’s 18 vessels transporting travelers and commuters across Puget Sound were out of commission Monday morning, according to the Washington State Department of Transportation.
The Seattle-Bainbridge Island, Edmonds-Kingston, Fauntleroy-Vashon Island-Southworth triangle and Port Townsend-Coupeville routes were all out of service Monday. Others remained afloat with reduced service. At the Clinton terminal, drivers were waiting an estimated three hours to cross the water to Mukilteo. And the Point Defiance-Tahlequah route may be out of service following the 12:10 p.m. sailing due to the crew shortage.
This came after 23 engine room employees called in sick, and the workers qualified to replace them declined to fill in, according to the transportation department. Without them, the boats can’t sail. 
The engine room workers are represented by the Marine Engineers’ Beneficial Association union. Work stoppages or strikes among ferry workers are prohibited under state law. The union didn’t immediately comment.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Members have long complained of uncompetitive wages and a reliance on overtime that drives burnout. A survey of 80-plus members in June found more than 60% were either somewhat or very likely to retire or leave the ferry system for another job. Over half reported poor morale among their colleagues.
The ferry agency countered that chief engineers have a base salary of $157,000 that can rise to $350,000 with overtime, retirement accrual and paid time off. 
“We expect our employees to return to work as soon as possible,” the ferry system said on social media.
Gov. Bob Ferguson, who has pushed heavily for more reliable ferry service in his first term, said he’s been meeting with Washington State Ferries leadership. 
“I understand thousands of Washingtonians are deeply impacted by what’s happening with our ferries,” he said in a Monday morning statement. “More details to come on how we’re going to resolve this situation.”
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

name: Michigan Advance
title: For U-M pro-Palestinian protesters, consequences linger after charges were dropped
description: Though their state-level criminal charges were dropped, pro-Palestinian activists at the University of Michigan say they still face repercussions for protesting. Former students and organizers say arrests and disciplinary actions tied to demonstrations have continued to affect their ability to be present on campus, find work and move beyond accusations that[...]
text:
U-M police officer watches over pro-Palestinian student protestors from the steps of the Rackham School of Graduate Studies on Oct. 7, 2024. (Photo by Charles H.F. Davis III with permission)Though their state-level criminal charges were dropped, pro-Palestinian activists at the University of Michigan say they still face repercussions for protesting.
Former students and organizers say arrests and disciplinary actions tied to demonstrations have continued to affect their ability to be present on campus, find work and move beyond accusations that were ultimately dismissed.
A nearly monthlong pro-Palestinian encampment at the University of Michigan in spring 2024 was cleared by police on May 21. The raid resulted in four arrests.
Salma Hamamy, a 2024 U-M graduate and former president of the pro-Palestinian Students Allied for Freedom and Equality, called the police response “brutal.” 
“They were just grabbing anyone that they could get their hands on,” she said. “The people who were arrested were ultimately charged with felonies.” 
Hamamy characterized the arrests as “a political tactic to repress the student movement, and to make an example out of a few when there were hundreds who were physically there in support and thousands across the state of Michigan.”
U-M Police confront pro-Palestinian activists as they break up the encampment on the Ann Arbor campus on May 21, 2024 (Screenshot of TAHRIR Coalition video)
Amy Doukoure, staff attorney at CAIR-Michigan, added that while pro-Palestinian protesters were charged for trespassing, the same treatment was not given to pro-Israel protesters who were also present. 
“They were allowed to stand and actually mock the pro-Palestinian protesters as they were being dispersed. I think that’s a very glaring example of the fact that they have been treated significantly different than other forms of speech,” Doukoure said. 
When asked about allegations that the university had criminalized protesting, a university spokesperson declined to comment, citing ongoing litigation.
While charges connected to the encampment raid and other pro-Palestinian demonstrations were later dropped by Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel’s office, several people who were charged in the course of their pro-Palestinian activism at the University of Michigan say there have been continued effects long afterward. 
Arrests, bans and disciplinary actions followed protests
Hamamy was among 40 students arrested on Nov. 17, 2023 during a demonstration at the Ruthven Administration Building. 
Protesters hosted an eight-hour sit-in, demanding a meeting with administrators and then-President Santa Ono to call for the university to divest its financial holdings from companies and entities associated with Israel. 
According to a Sept. 2026 report from the ACLU, more than 50 police vehicles from at least 10 police departments were dispatched to address the protest. “Multiple individuals reported being physically harmed by police officers on the scene, with one student reporting that a police officer ripped off her hijab,” the report stated. 



Quotation







The charges are never individual. They are always a part of a broader tactic to suppress a community, a movement of people. What they fail to understand is while they can charge a few, they can’t stop the movement.


– Salma Hamamy, a 2024 U-M graduate and former president of the pro-Palestinian Students Allied for Freedom and Equality


“Criminal charges at the state level ordered by the attorney general were an unprecedented escalation against divestment. It was an overreach, a political overreach,” Hamamy said. “It was designed to punish and suppress voices protesting genocide.” 
Hamamy claimed that the charges were ultimately dropped by the attorney general’s office through public mobilization and media coverage. 
When contacted for comment, Michigan Department of Attorney General Press Secretary Danny Wimmer linked a September 2024 press release describing each charge. 
“Many of those charged were not students, and none were charged for protesting. The alleged criminal conduct is described in our office’s release. Charges filed included trespassing and resisting or obstructing a police officer,” Wimmer said in an email. “The police action to clear the encampment occurred in May 2024, and cases arising were only referred to our office in June.” 
‘A campus should not be lawless’: AG charges 11 people involved in University of Michigan protests

In addition to being charged, Hamamy was also barred from entering campus for a year, ending in Oct. 2025. 
“I think students seeing that their fellow classmates can now be kicked out and prohibited from stepping on any campus property on a campus that they once contributed to is extremely isolating. I think it’s dehumanizing,” Hamamy said. 
A campus ban also removes a student from their community, Liz Jacob, lead staff attorney at the Sugar Law Center for Social and Economic Justice, added. 
“It’s not only meant that they couldn’t go to campus protests or be a part of organizing, but it also took them out of their dining halls, their libraries, and their classrooms,” Jacob said. “Being cut off from those spaces can be really isolating.” 
Eaman Ali, a 2025 University of Michigan graduate and former organizer with the pro-Palestinian TAHRIR Coalition, also experienced repercussions for her activism, which included protesting at the University of Michigan Museum of Art in May 2024.
In April 2025, Ali said she received a notice from the university’s human resources office alerting her that she had been suspended from her campus job. A few days later, Ali and eight other students were terminated. While the university contends the terminations were due to “violent conduct” and not merely for participating in the protest, attorneys representing the fired workers in a federal lawsuit deny there was any violence. That case is still pending.
In addition to losing her job, Ali received notification after graduating that she was also facing academic disciplinary charges and was barred from future employment by the university and its affiliates, which has impacted her ability to find work in Michigan. 
A university hiring ban for protesting was unprecedented and can strongly affect students’ ability to find work, Jacob said.
“The University of Michigan is one of the state’s biggest employers. That’s a really egregious sanction,” Jacob said. “Being cut off from those opportunities has a lot of downstream impacts on someone’s life that could not only really impact their ability to get a job in the state, but also to really meaningfully build a career in the fields that they choose.” 
Eaman Ali speaks at a press conference on Jan. 29, 2026 calling for an end to ongoing disciplinary charges against University of Michigan students and alumni who took part in anti-genocide and divestment demonstrations in 2024.   (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Criminal charges followed campus activism
Hiab Teshome, an M.D.-Ph.D. candidate at the University of Michigan and president of the Graduate Employees Organization, also faced disciplinary charges after being accused of using university funds to buy laptops for a student organization.
According to the court records, a felony complaint was filed against Teshome on June 4 and a complaint was issued by the office of Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit on June 11. Savit is the Democratic nominee for Michigan attorney general. 
During her arraignment on June 26, Teshome said she learned that university police had sought bond conditions that would have effectively imposed a campus ban. Although the request for a total ban was unsuccessful, she was barred from the Ruthven Administration Building, where the Board of Regents meets.
“The campus bans have been used as a tool here at the University of Michigan as a way to repress movement. The university arbitrarily will give these trespass bans to individuals and target individuals with these trespass bans in order to prevent people from going on campus and organizing,” Teshome said. 
The charges were dismissed on Aug. 6. According to Drop Site News, the charges were dropped after it was determined that while Hiab was a co-signer on the laptop purchases, “she did not actually make the purchase, and never possessed the devices. Another member of the club used the laptop and was reimbursed for it.” Hiab claims that despite what was essentially a misunderstanding, she was targeted for prosecution because of her pro-Palestinian activism. 
“The community came together throughout the summer to make sure the courts understood that these charges were ridiculous and insane,” Teshome said. “The first time it was presented to the court, it immediately fell apart.”
The Washtenaw County Prosecutor’s Office said the case was handled like any other matter. 
“It was dismissed, like similar cases on the docket that day, following the court’s receipt of information indicating that repayment had been made by Ms. Teshome’s co-defendant,” Alyssa Fountain, an administrative assistant with the department, said in an email. “As with any case, our office handles cases based solely on the evidence that is presented to us.”
Hiab Teshome at a protest on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor. (Photo provided by Hiab Teshome)
Hamamy said that while criminalization impacts individual protesters, it also has lingering effects on the university community and that the police and disciplinary responses were used as a “fear-mongering tactic” to quell future protests. 
“These charges were not about what did or didn’t happen on the ground. It was entirely to suppress, to discriminate, to be a type of overreach, and to push and suppress voices protesting genocide because they did not want the status quo to be impacted,” she said. 
Doukoure, the CAIR attorney, said that disproportionate government action creates a “community sense” that there’s something wrong with the viewpoint.
“They become criminalized in ideology, which then stigmatizes them. You create a hierarchy within the community because what government action is, it legitimizes one specific ideology,” Doukoure said. “If you’re saying a group is not legitimate and they’re criminal because of their speech, you’re legitimizing that specific viewpoint, which is exactly why we have freedom of speech protected under the Constitution to keep the government from being the arbiter of what is true and honest exchange of ideas.”
Ali said the tactics are about limiting protests and minimizing the movement.
“All of these things are laying the groundwork for future movements to be even more repressed and silenced and so that really is an untold legacy almost that is really disheartening,” Ali said. 
Despite the challenges, Ali said her colleagues have not expressed remorse for their activism. 
“I haven’t met anybody who regrets protesting for Palestine. I think our conscience has always been very clear that regardless of retaliation, we’re right to protest and we are right to call attention to the genocide in Gaza,” Ali said, referencing the ongoing military actions by Israel in Gaza, which multiple international organizations have called a genocide against the Palestinian people. 
TAHRIR Coalition stages a “die-in” demonstration on the U-M Diag in March 2024 to recognize Palestinians killed by ongoing Israeli military operations. (Photo by Charles H.F. Davis III with permission)
Ali said that the criminalization and disciplinary actions against protesters demonstrate a political attempt to silence pro-Palestinian sentiment. 
“This really isn’t about me as an individual or any of us who were fired or blacklisted or what have you. This really is about an institution that is trying to protect its profits and its own interests in investing in the genocide and in the apartheid state of Israel and really, they will do just about anything to ensure that that goes unchallenged,” Ali said. 
The university’s investment portfolio provides context for the financial interests Ali and other protesters point to.
The University of Michigan’s investments are not entirely public, but its annual endowment profile shows the fund was valued at $21.2 billion as of June 30, 2025.
A report published by the TAHRIR Coalition examined the university endowment and its alleged ties to Israeli companies. Data the report uncovered showed in fiscal year 2022, the university held $36.9 million in forward foreign-exchange contracts involving the Israeli shekel, which the authors described as a “direct connection” to the Israeli state. It also identified investments in companies including Boeing, Lockheed Martin, Airbnb and Hewlett Packard Enterprise, and claimed the endowment funded $6 billion in 333 Israeli companies and $5.7 billion in 241 defense-related companies.
The university has disputed those characterizations. In a 2024 Regents statement, Regent Michael Behm said the endowment has no direct investments in Israeli companies and that less than 0.1% is invested indirectly in them. The Regents reaffirmed their decision not to divest from companies linked to Israel, saying investment decisions would be based on “financial factors such as risk and return.”
But for the activists interviewed for this story, the fight over investments is only one part of a broader struggle over how U-M responds to dissent.
Hamamy agreed, focusing on the larger movement instead of individual arrests.
“The charges are never individual. They are always a part of a broader tactic to suppress a community, a movement of people. What they fail to understand is while they can charge a few, they can’t stop the movement,” Hamamy said. 
“The University of Michigan has a long history of trying to repress activism, and we’ve seen it so strongly in the past three years with the pro-Palestine movement,” Teshome added. 
Jacob said that while university reaction has seemingly escalated since the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel, the protest actions themselves are similar to other movements. 
“The student movement for Palestine, which has also been on the campus for decades, has adopted many of those really common protest tactics like sit-ins, marches, even encampments,” Jacob said. “But there has been a big departure with the university’s response.”
According to the ACLU report, “undercover investigators surveilled pro-Palestinian groups and followed them both on and off” the Ann Arbor
campus. Additionally, the ACLU said students reported that “investigators cursed at students, made threats, and, in one documented incident, drove a vehicle toward a student who was forced to jump away to avoid injury.”
Federal charges filed against U-M protesters
On June 10, the Department of Justice indicted eight pro-Palestinian activists associated with the University of Michigan for “their alleged roles in conspiracies to threaten University of Michigan leaders, law enforcement, and businesses,” according to a Justice Department press release. In addition to allegations of conspiracy to transmit threats, some of the defendants also were charged with witness intimidation and destruction of property.
Doukoure said the indictment was concerning due to its classification of constitutional rights as criminal. 
“The indictment itself is troubling because it wraps in free speech and political ideology in a way that intends to paint that free speech and the topic of that speech as inherently dangerous or criminal because it is pro-Palestinian,” Doukoure said. “I don’t think I’ve ever read a criminal indictment that talks about lawful activity as a precursor for the criminal indictment the way this does.”
Mariam Odeh speaking to pro-Palestinian protestors in front of the 15th District Court Building in Ann Arbor on Sept. 20, 2024. Odeh was later charged by the DOJ in 2026 for allegedly taking part in a conspiracy to “threaten University of Michigan leaders, law enforcement, and businesses”. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance).
Hamamy, Ali and Teshome said they viewed the charges as a continuation of the politicization of the pro-Palestinian movement. 
“The charges are not a reflection of what did or did not occur, but rather a reflection of the Trump administration’s war with the Palestine solidarity movement,” Hamamy said. “The Trump administration has moved to crush the movement domestically, whether it be through ICE abductions or attempted deportations of international students or lawsuits against the university and the weaponization of protections to cut federal funding.” 
Hamamy said that while university, state and federal charges are important to pay attention to, they also divert attention from the subject of the protests.
“The charges are distraction from real violence, real crimes against humanity, that Israel continues to perpetrate every day,” Hamamy said. 
She characterized the police and university pushback, including the charges against her, as a marker of victory.
“Something that comes along with the pushback is understanding that it occurs because we have been successful in advocating for the Palestinian people and advocating for people to be liberated throughout the world. The suppression is a measure of our commitment and our success in the movement, not a measure of our failure,” Hamamy said.

text:
The New Mexico Senate Democratic Caucus elected Sen. Linda Trujillo (D-Santa Fe), pictured during Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham's final State of the State address on Jan. 20, 2026, to serve as the new Senate Majority Leader. (Photo by Kate Russell for Source NM)New Mexico Senate Democrats met over the weekend to elect their party’s chamber leaders ahead of the upcoming 2027 legislative session.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Caucus members met behind closed doors Sunday to nominate incumbent Sen. Mimi Stewart (D-Albuquerque) for another term as Senate president pro tempore. Stewart will face an election for the title in January, when the legislative session convenes. The full Senate votes on the election of the president pro tempore, while each party’s caucus can select its floor leaders and whips ahead of the lawmaking session.
The caucus selected three other leaders who will not need to go to a full election in January. Caucus members chose state Sen. Linda Trujillo (D-Santa Fe) as the new Senate majority leader and Sen. Cindy Nava (D-Bernalillo) as the new Senate majority whip. They also reelected Sen. Leo Jaramillo (D-Española) to his post as majority caucus chair.
Trujillo first won election to the state Senate in 2024, though she previously held elected seats on the Santa Fe Public Schools Board of Education and in the state House of Representatives, where she cosponsored legislation to create the state Early Childhood Education and Care Department. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham had previously appointed her as superintendent of the New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, where Trujillo oversaw the implementation of legislation that created the state’s recreational cannabis industry.
“I am honored and humbled that my colleagues have placed their trust in me to serve as Majority Leader,” Trujillo said in a statement. “New Mexicans sent us to Santa Fe to solve real problems like strengthening our schools, protecting the health and safety of our communities and building an economy that works for every family in this state. I am excited and ready to get to work alongside this united caucus to deliver on our shared commitment to the people of New Mexico.”
Trujillo replaces Sen. Peter Wirth (D-Santa Fe), who in June announced that he wouldn’t seek reelection to his seat in the Senate.
Nava, the Bernalillo Democrat, will replace Sen. Michael Padilla (D-Albuquerque) as majority whip after he declined to seek another term in that leadership position.
The changes come as lawmakers prepare for a 60-day legislative session under a new governor. Former U.S. Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, a Democrat, faces former Rio Rancho Mayor Gregg Hull, a Republican, in the Nov. 3 general election. Early voting begins Tuesday at county clerk’s offices, before expanding to alternate voting locations on Oct. 17.
Lawmakers have announced their plans to craft legislation around implementing a statewide data center moratorium, overhauling the state’s troubled child welfare agency and updating New Mexico’s decades-old consumer protection law in the upcoming session.

name: WyoFile
title: Judge jails man in moose abuse case and warns: Wyoming values wildlife
description:
Former state livestock brand inspector appeared stunned as he received a harsher sentence than his plea deal called for.
The post Judge jails man in moose abuse case and warns: Wyoming values wildlife appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A Uinta County judge issued a stark warning Friday when he sentenced three men for abusing an infirm moose in the second high-profile animal cruelty case in western Wyoming courts this year.
“Wildlife of Wyoming belongs to the people of Wyoming,” 3rd District Court Judge James Kaste said during a court hearing Friday in Evanston. “You do this kind of nonsense in Wyoming, where we value our wildlife, you’re going to jail.” 
Kaste then jailed one of the men, who had agreed to a plea deal that did not call for time behind bars. Uinta County rancher and former state livestock brand inspector Justin Martin appeared stunned as he was immediately taken into custody to serve a 30-day sentence at the Uinta County Detention Center.
Last December, prosecutors charged the 55-year-old Martin with two felony counts of cruelty to animals, accessory before the fact, in connection to the mistreatment of moose twice in May 2021.
His son Range Martin, 24, and a third man, Kylan Platt, 23, of Malad City, Idaho, were each charged with a single felony count of cruelty to animals. 
In one incident, authorities say Range Martin lassoed an unhealthy and likely blind cow moose around her neck and dragged her through high and dense sagebrush before the animal collapsed. Prosecutors also accused Platt of roping, riding and aggressively spurring a moose — not definitively determined to be the same moose — on Justin Martin’s 5,000-acre M Arrow Ranch north of Bear River, a small town near the border with Utah.  
Justin Martin encouraged and celebrated the behavior, saying “All right now, spur that son of a bitch … spur on him!” as he filmed the Platt incident. When he shared the footage with several friends and family members, via text and email, he told one friend “Looks like he was ran down a little. That’s good s—. Not many kids can say they have rode a moose,” authorities say. 
The three men initially pleaded not guilty to felony animal cruelty charges and faced the prospect of prison time before accepting plea deals this summer. In the cases of Range Martin and Platt, the judge mostly followed the terms of their plea agreements, sentencing them to three years of supervised probation under a state law that allows first-time offenders to avoid felonies on their permanent record if they stay out of trouble. 

Former state livestock brand inspector Justin Martin was booked into the Uinta County Detention Center immediately following his Oct. 2 sentencing for felony cruelty to animals, accessory before the fact, for encouraging and documenting the abuse of a cow moose on two separate occasions in May 2021. Despite accepting a plea deal to avoid jail time, Martin was sentenced to serve 30 days behind bars. (Uinta County Sheriff’s Office)

Justin Martin, faced a suspended prison sentence in favor of supervised probation. But on Friday, Kaste ordered the older of the three defendants to serve jail time. Kaste also increased his supervised probation from two to three years. 
The judge also sentenced all three men to 576 hours of mandatory community service, which Kaste said was “the most productive thing I can do,” suggesting an array of opportunities. “You could do something for the Game and Fish,” he said. 
While Kaste dismissed the monetary fines outlined in their respective plea agreements, each man will pay $275 in court-related fees and costs. 
The case drew swift and inevitable comparisons to another recent animal cruelty case in Wyoming. Cody Roberts ignited international outrage after running down a wolf with a snowmobile in February 2024. The injured wolf’s mouth was taped shut when Roberts brought the suffering animal to the Green River Bar in Daniel. In photos, Roberts posed alongside the animal before shooting it behind the bar. 
The Wyoming Game and Fish Department initially issued Roberts a $250 fine for the incident before Sublette County Prosecutor Clayton Melinkovich, amid global anger over the act, chose to pursue a grand jury indictment. Roberts eventually pleaded guilty to felony animal cruelty and accepted a plea agreement of 18 months of supervised probation. Roberts never spent time in jail. 
The terms of Justin Martin’s plea agreement were identical to and determined by the Roberts’ case, special prosecuting attorney Gaston Gosar said. “That’s how we came to these terms,” Gosar told the court during Friday’s sentencing hearing.  
Gosar recalled how retired 3rd Circuit Court Judge Michael Greer assessed the crimes during a Feb. 20 preliminary hearing: The men’s conduct served “no other goal than the sheer joy of dominating and domineering a weak and vulnerable animal.” As the case progressed, Gosar said he’d “heard a lot of whitewashing and minimization” of the three men’s actions. 
When Range Martin changed his plea on June 22, he said he came across the moose as he was “moving cows and checking gates” and that it was interfering with his operation.
“I roped it … I tried to drag it out of the way,” he said, of pulling the feeble moose by its neck.
Justin Martin and his son Range Martin, right, talk to an attorney, left, for their fellow defendant Kylan Platt at the Uinta County Courthouse. (Bryon Glathar)
Platt, too, said his encounter occurred while he and Justin Martin were “out fixing fence, moving cows,” and that he “needed to move the moose” because she was in the way of relocating cattle, but he later admitted “we didn’t have the cows there yet.”
“I got on her, that’s when we took some videos, turned her loose. That was about it,” Platt said during his June 30 change of plea proceeding. He insisted the moose wasn’t as sickly as previously reported by Game and Fish investigators because “she was relatively healthy enough to run around,” he said, suggesting “she was far from dying — I didn’t burn her [or] start her on fire.”
Wyoming Game and Fish Department Game Warden Heather Sterling, who investigated the men, refuted their version of events at Friday’s sentencing. Sterling said that having “extensively reviewed the footage,” there were no fences located nearby and “there are no cattle visible for the duration of the video” as Range Martin and Platt initially stated. 
Sterling said that Justin Martin, who’d served as a Wyoming Livestock Board brand inspector for 16 years, “was supposed to be a respected member of the community … part of his job was to assist enforcement officers in livestock investigations, this includes animal welfare cases.
“He was trusted to guide others in the respectful treatment of animals,” Sterling said. “This treatment of that cow moose is unacceptable.”
State Livestock Director Steve True fired Justin Martin following his July 17 change of plea to guilty. “This is absolutely irresponsible behavior unbefitting a brand inspector,” Gov. Mark Gordon said in a statement afterwards. “I hold brand inspectors to a very high standard. Mr. Martin is no longer an employee of the state of Wyoming.”
The moose incidents were not the initial reason Justin Martin was on wildlife investigators’ radar. “This was a series of knowing, deliberate acts against a valued wildlife species,” Sterling said.
Prior to changing his plea, Justin Martin’s attorney filed a motion to suppress the video evidence for what was then his upcoming trial. During that proceeding, Sterling testified that the moose footage was discovered during a separate July 2022 investigation regarding Justin Martin allegedly granting an outfitter permission to hunt on a neighbor’s land in January of that year. Martin’s neighbor, however,  repeatedly and adamantly refused to allow hunting access.
In an effort to convince the landowner to drop trespassing charges against the outfitter, Justin Martin attempted to mediate a $1,000 payment between the parties. 
According to Sterling’s testimony, the outfitter shot an elk on the property which bordered Utah. The mortally wounded elk subsequently traveled into Utah, and the outfitter abandoned it there, where it suffered for up to two days until a conservation officer from the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources responded to euthanize it. That case was dismissed with prejudice last year, Sterling confirmed to WyoFile.  
Defense attorney Joe Hampton argued Justin Martin’s constitutional rights were violated when authorities discovered the moose footage after seizing his phone for that investigation. Game and Fish Wildlife Investigator Daniel Beach testified he’d inadvertently discovered the videos — which were created outside the date parameters detailed in the initial search warrant — while searching through Justin Martin’s phone for evidence related to the hunting incident. 
Gosar, however, successfully argued the plain view doctrine, which allows officers to seize visible evidence. Kaste agreed, saying “I can tell from the thumbnail there’s a guy riding a moose.” 
Justin Martin’s guilty plea was entered conditionally as he is awaiting the Wyoming Supreme Court’s ruling on Kaste’s decision to allow the video evidence. If he prevails at the high court, his conviction could be overturned.
Until then, Justin Martin will remain a convicted felon, meaning he will be unable to possess firearms. None of the defendants will be allowed to hunt, trap or fish, including shed hunting, during their three-year probation term.
“You shouldn’t have the privilege of taking wildlife here in Wyoming if you mistreat it,” Kaste said. 


Range Martin walks through the Uinta County Courthouse on Friday. (Amanda Manchester for WyoFile)


Kylan Platt walks through the Uinta County Courthouse on Friday. (Amanda Manchester for WyoFile)


“I’m the adult,” Justin Martin said in court Friday. “I apologize for wasting time and money. I tried my best to offer the best restitution. My apologies for any of this happening.” Prior to the sentencing, he had made two $3,750 donations to the Wyoming Game and Fish Department’s Wildlife Damages and Wildlife Crossing entities. 
Platt, who was 17 at the time of the crime, declined to speak during sentencing. Range Martin, who was 18 in May 2021, told the court, “I’m just sorry that I did what I did. I don’t like being in trouble and I’ll never do it again.” 
Platt’s attorney, J. Craig Abraham, informed the judge that his client has received death threats throughout the case, which Kaste publicly condemned. Range Martin later told WyoFile that he, too, had received similar threats. 
“You don’t take advantage of a creature who is more vulnerable than you,” the judge said, making clear it’s the responsibility of men to protect defenseless creatures. “The moose was not yours to do with what you will — it’s not your plaything.”
Admonishing Justin Martin in particular, Kaste told the court:  “Our wildlife matters — we will protect it — that is the message you should have sent those boys that day.”

title: ‘A political prisoner’: Roebling Bridge ICE protestor now faced with felony charge, arrested
description: More than a year after a Northern Kentucky protest at Roebling Street Bridge over federal immigration officials’ arrest of an Ohio cleric, a protester was arrested Monday morning on an upgraded charge.  Benjamin Potash, a Louisville lawyer representing Taylor Marshall, told the Kentucky Lantern that his client’s arrest and detainment at the Kenton County Det[...]
text:
The Roebling Bridge in January 2021. (Photo by Sarah Ladd)More than a year after a Northern Kentucky protest at Roebling Street Bridge over federal immigration officials’ arrest of an Ohio cleric, a protester was arrested Monday morning on an upgraded charge. 
Benjamin Potash, a Louisville lawyer representing Taylor Marshall, told the Kentucky Lantern that his client’s arrest and detainment at the Kenton County Detention Center “is totally aberrant to me.” 
Marshall had initially been charged with a felony, but that was amended down to a misdemeanor charge of failure to disperse. 
Potash said he and his client accepted this charge, but then Commonwealth’s Attorney Rob Sanders “went behind my back and indicted the matter in front of a grand jury, and secretly indicted Taylor Marshall for felony riot.” 
Sanders was not available by phone when the Lantern called his office Monday morning and he has not yet responded to an email sent around noon seeking comment. 
Marshall, 33, was among the roughly 100 people who protested at the bridge after United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained former Cincinnati Children’s Hospital chaplain Ayman Soliman in the summer of 2025. Soliman was later released. 
ICE releases Ohio hospital chaplain. Case for detention unclear

Following the 15 arrests — journalists covering the protest were also arrested — several people filed lawsuits against the city of Covington and police. One lawsuit alleging excessive force including photos of Brandon Hill’s bruises after a police officer “repeatedly punched” him, LINKNKY previously reported. 
Marshall has a bond of $2,500 and is set to be arraigned Monday afternoon. Marshall is also charged with obstructing governmental operations, resisting arrest and disorderly conduct, which are misdemeanor charges. 
Potash said it’s unusual for a person to be arrested for a protest this long after the event. 
“This is a year old,” he said. “This does appear to be political in nature, and I would consider Taylor to be a political prisoner.” 
This story may be updated.

description: North Dakota lawmakers and state officials announced Monday a proposal that would award yearly bonuses to teachers to boost recruitment and retention. Estimated bonuses for the first year would be about $3,400 per teacher, if lawmakers support the proposal during the 2027 legislative session. The Support Teachers and Youth Succeed stipend, or STAYS, would us[...]
text:
Rep. Mike Nathe, R-Bismarck, speaks during a press conference at the Capitol on Oct. 5, 2026, announcing a proposal for an annual teacher bonus. Others photographed, from the left, are Rep. Jim Jonas, R-West Fargo, Sen. Brad Bekkedahl, R-Williston, and Rep. David Richter, R-Williston. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota lawmakers and state officials announced Monday a proposal that would award yearly bonuses to teachers to boost recruitment and retention.
Estimated bonuses for the first year would be about $3,400 per teacher, if lawmakers support the proposal during the 2027 legislative session.
The Support Teachers and Youth Succeed stipend, or STAYS, would use 10% of the earnings from the Common Schools Trust Fund, divided evenly among the state’s full-time public and private school teachers. The fund is valued at $718 million for the 2025-27 biennium. 
The bonuses, awarded each fall, would increase as the fund’s earnings increase, said Rep. Mike Nathe, R-Bismarck.
“The teacher shortage in North Dakota is an urgent, statewide workforce issue and it deserves a statewide response,” Nathe said during a press conference at the Capitol.
Bonuses would be capped at 25% of a teacher’s salary, he said.
The proposal is backed by Gov. Kelly Armstrong’s office and Superintendent of Public Instruction Levi Bachmeier.
“The hardest part of this job is stepping into classrooms that are empty and have been repurposed into storage rooms because they can’t hire an ag teacher,” Bachmeier said Monday.
Task force adopts recommendations to better recruit, retain teachers

He said he just visited a school in Nelson County that didn’t have a science teacher and students were doing their science class coursework online, which can make it hard to participate in science labs.
“We know the science of learning is clear, the quality of the instructor standing in front of the classroom, pushing students to engage in meaningful, hands-on learning is the single greatest predictor of learning,” he said. “So, we have to fill these classrooms.”
The bill is expected to be introduced when  lawmakers convene in January.
North Dakota teacher pay ranked 41st in the nation in 2024-25, according to the National Education Foundation. 
This story will be updated.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.
