title: North Carolina’s Latino leaders celebrate heritage, focus on voter engagement ahead of midterms
description: Latino leaders gathered outside North Carolina’s legislative building Thursday to celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month and look ahead to the future. America Juarez-Maldonado with Carolina Migrant Network said it would be easy to feel anger and despair, especially at a time that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have wrongfully detained and arreste[...]
text:
America Juarez-Maldonado with Carolina Migrant Network said she came to the legislature to let others know that Latinos are resilient, and will not allow hate or fear to write their story. (Photo courtesy of ProgressNC) Latino leaders gathered outside North Carolina’s legislative building Thursday to celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month and look ahead to the future.
America Juarez-Maldonado with Carolina Migrant Network said it would be easy to feel anger and despair, especially at a time that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have wrongfully detained and arrested many Latinos.
“Here’s what I find hardest to understand –some of the same people telling us we don’t belong have forgotten their own history,” said Juarez-Maldonado. “Their ancestors also arrived to this land with no papers without permission.”
Juarez-Maldondo and other Latinos highlighted their heritage on the same day that a new law went into effect that requires state law enforcement agencies to sign 287(g) agreements with ICE. Under the arrangement, designated officers within the State Bureau of Investigation, the State Highway Patrol, and the Alcohol Law Enforcement Division will conduct immigration status checks and other immigration enforcement activities.
At least 10 people detained at Columbus County checkpoint, NC advocacy group says

Juarez-Maldonado, an immigration rights organizer, said she came to the legislature to let others know that Latinos are resilient, and will not allow hate or fear to write their story.
“Love is the most powerful force we have,” she reminded those at the press conference.
After the monthly celebration of heritage and culture concludes, Juarez-Maldonado said caring people will stay engaged and push for a better tomorrow.
“Love shows up, love organizes. Love says stop detention centers here in North Carolina,” said Juarez-Maldonado. “Love says vote.”
 Finding inclusion, finding a voice
Luis Lozano said higher education was critical for him in finding his place in the world.
Lozano recalled being a student at N.C. State University in Raleigh and feeling so lonely that he had called his parents in Asheville to come pick him up. He was ready to drop out just two weeks into his freshman year of college.
By chance, he saw an invitation to a Latino Heritage Month event on campus.
“It might have just looked like a cookout, but to me, that space changed the direction of my life,” Lozano said.
He found not only people who looked like him, but people who shared his passion for creating change in our communities.
Now an organizer for La Fuerza NC, a nonprofit advocacy group, Lozano said he is committed to helping other young people find their voice and recognize that they, too, have the power to create change.
Lozano said rather than impose restrictions on diversity, equity, and inclusion programs, state legislators should listen to the next generation of leaders.
“Listen to the young North Carolinians who are telling you that belonging matters,” said Lozano. “Invest in programs and organizations that give young people a place to grow instead of creating more barriers to these opportunities.”
 ‘Prepare to participate’
Kiara Aranda, deputy director for the nonprofit LatinxEd, said there are more than 1.2 million Latinos who call North Carolina home, with about 300,000 children attending school here.
“We’re raising families, building businesses, working in hospitals and farms, and contributing to communities across the state,” Aranda said.
The statewide nonprofit is working to increase educational equity and post-secondary opportunities for Latino students, who may not see higher education as a possibility.
Aranda reminded the community of the importance of using their voice this fall.
“As you prepare to participate in this election season, we have to ask what our vote could mean for our ability to invest in the public services that our communities depend on,” she said.
Aranda said it’s especially important to understand the constitutional amendments. Promises to limit property tax increases and cap the state’s income tax may sound appealing but may also limit opportunities for future generations.
In a recent proclamation, Governor Josh Stein recognized Hispanic and Latino North Carolinians as one of the fastest-growing ethnic groups in North Carolina, making up approximately 12% of the state’s residents and 17% of children under 18.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama state representative, school board member charged with attempted human trafficking
description: An Alabama state representative and the former president of the Satsuma City Schools Board of Education were arrested Friday on charges of attempted human trafficking.  According to court documents filed Monday morning, Rep. Brett Easterbrook, R-Fruitdale, and Kory Wesley, the former president of the Satsuma City Schools Board of Education, were arrested by[...]
text:
Rep. Brett Easterbrook, R-Fruitdale, walks across the floor of the House of Representatives on Feb. 3, 2026, at the Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. Easterbrook and Kory Wesley, president of the Satsuma City Schools Board of Education, were arrested Friday afternoon on charges of attempted human trafficking, which prosecutors described as part of a sting operation. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)An Alabama state representative and the former president of the Satsuma City Schools Board of Education were arrested Friday on charges of attempted human trafficking. 
According to court documents filed Monday morning, Rep. Brett Easterbrook, R-Fruitdale, and Kory Wesley, the former president of the Satsuma City Schools Board of Education, were arrested by the Escambia County Sheriff’s Office Friday afternoon. The documents described the arrests as part of a sting operation, but did not provide further details. 
Messages seeking comment were left with the Escambia County Sheriff’s Office and Satsuma City Schools Monday morning. Attempts to reach Easterbrook were not successful. As of mid-Monday morning, neither Easterbrook nor Wesley had attorneys listed in court documents. 
Satsuma City Schools said in a statement posted to their website Monday that Wesley had resigned from the board on Sunday evening. The statement said the mayor and city council of Satsuma will move to fill the position, and that Satsuma City Schools “remains committed to its core values of growth, community and high expectations.”
Both men were initially charged with first-degree human trafficking, but prosecutors Monday moved to reduce the charges to attempted human trafficking, writing that because the operation was a sting, no victim was involved.  The charge carries a maximum penalty of up to 20 years in prison. 
Easterbrook was additionally charged with soliciting prostitution, and Wesley was charged with attempting to elude an officer. Both charges are a Class A misdemeanor, punishable by up to one year in county jail. They were released within an hour of being arrested.
Messages seeking comment were left with Alabama House Speaker Nathaniel Ledbetter, R-Rainsville. 
Easterbrook was first elected to the Alabama House in 2018. He served as vice chair of the House Insurance Committee, and also served on Agriculture and Forestry, Transportation & Utilities and the House Ways and Means General Fund committees. In the House, he mainly sponsored local bills and legislation related to construction. Easterbrook was not seeking re-election this year. 
Editor’s note: This is a developing story and will be updated with more information.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana tallies $13M boost off ‘blackout’ license plate sales, invests in BMV modernization
description: Indiana's Bureau of Motor Vehicles has sold more than 380,000 "blackout" license plates in the year since the minimalist design launched.
text:
The Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles began offering the "blackout" plate in August 2025. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana’s Bureau of Motor Vehicles has sold more than 380,000 “blackout” license plates in the year since the minimalist design launched — generating $12.9 million toward a five-year modernization plan for the agency, the governor’s office announced Monday.
Sales began last August of the plates with while numerals and letters on an all-black background. Hoosiers bought nearly 22,000 plates in the first month and more than 90,000 by the end of 2025.
The optional plate adds $45 to registration and annual renewal fees.
Gov. Mike Braun poses with a “GOVERNR” blackout license plate. (Photo courtesy of Indiana governor’s office)
“Hoosiers clearly like the blackout plate, and its success is helping us build a better BMV,” Gov. Mike Braun said. “I directed the BMV to modernize, improve customer service and find smarter ways to operate. (The revenue) is now helping us invest in the employees who serve Hoosiers and technology that makes doing business with the BMV faster and easier.”
So far this year, the agency has purchased new payment machines that accept tap-to-pay options and digital currency and added more 24/7 BMV Connect kiosks statewide. Pay raises are coming for many customer-facing employees.
“The blackout plate gave us an opportunity to offer Hoosiers something they wanted while generating revenue we can put directly back into improving the BMV,” agency Commissioner Kevin Garvey said. “More than 380,000 sales later, that approach is paying off. We’re investing in our people, modernizing our technology and making the BMV easier for Hoosiers to use.”
More changes are expected.
Braun, in an executive order last year, directed BMV to modernize its 20-year-old tracking and record support software — and other systems — over five years.
The agency had to complete a comprehensive review of its systems last year, with recommendations for improvements or replacements. The resulting report featured 13 initiatives, such as introducing an AI chatbot, sending automated personalized notifications to customers, upgrading branch cameras and even implementing digital driver’s licenses.

title: Amanda Rosa of Extreme Weather Survivors discusses Helene recovery and weather-related disasters
description: It’s been two years now since Hurricane-turned-Tropical Storm Helene devastated a large swath of the southeastern United States, including much of western North Carolina. But as anyone paying even a little attention is painfully aware, Helene was just one of a growing array of weather-driven disasters to impact our world in recent years. What’s more, […]
text:
Amanda Rosa of Extreme Weather Survivors It’s been two years now since Hurricane-turned-Tropical Storm Helene devastated a large swath of the southeastern United States, including much of western North Carolina. But as anyone paying even a little attention is painfully aware, Helene was just one of a growing array of weather-driven disasters to impact our world in recent years. What’s more, as the impacts of climate change and continued expansion of human development into once natural areas continues, the potential impacts of these disasters – storms, wildfires, floods, extreme heat, deadly air pollution, drought – are only going to get worse unless society takes several swift and decisive actions.
Of course, one necessary predicate to action is for average people and their leaders to fully grasp the severity of the problem and, in particular, the havoc that weather-driven natural disasters can wreak. And to this important end, a new nonprofit has emerged in recent years that aims to shed a light on these hard truths while at the same time providing a pathway for the millions of people impacted by extreme weather events to share their stories with similarly affected people, and find a measure of healing. The group, appropriately enough, is called Extreme Weather Survivors. And recently to mark the anniversary of the Helene disaster, the group was in western North Carolina to highlight the huge recovery challenges that remain. And this past week, Newsline caught up with the organization’s Director of Outreach, Amanda Rosa.
Click here to listen to the full interview with Amanda Rosa.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Democrat Cindy Holscher’s campaign for Kansas governor highlights distinctions from GOP rival
description: Democrat Cindy Holscher says her campaign for Kansas governor reflects the perspective of voters more accurately than Ty Masterson's GOP bid.
text:
Cindy Holscher, the Democratic nominee for Kansas governor, points to differences on healthcare, public schools and other issues illustrate the distinctions between her and Republican nominee Ty Masterson. This image from Aug. 27,2026, is of Holscher campaigning in Olathe. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Democratic gubernatorial candidate Cindy Holscher closed out a campaign interview by accepting the hypothetical challenge of trying to persuade a group of undecided Kansans to vote for her.
Holscher, who is challenging Republican nominee Ty Masterson on Nov. 3, slipped into campaign mode to emphasize her accomplishments as a member of the Legislature and the value of a governor working collaboratively at the Statehouse. She said the next governor must deliver for regular Kansans struggling to make ends and not kowtow to corporate elites or special-interest lobbyists.


“I have an ability to get things done,” she said on Kansas Reflector’s podcast. “I’m going to find people who will work with me, but I’m also going to draw the line on things that … aren’t good for Kansans. I’m the most successful Democrat in the Senate in terms of getting bills implemented, but I’m also more successful than 90% of the Republicans. My focus is on the people and making life better for them through impactful legislation and actions.”
Holscher, 57, is a member of the Kansas Senate and won a tough gubernatorial primary. She said that’s where similarities to Masterson ended.
Holscher resides in Overland Park, while he lives in Andover. She has touted abortion rights and Medicaid expansion. She argued for full funding of special education in K-12 public schools. She endorsed the idea of legalizing marijuana. Masterson rejected those positions.
The Democrat blamed President Donald Trump for driving up the cost of living with ill-advised tariffs and war. In the GOP’s August primary, Trump’s endorsement put Masterson over the top.
She helped build a coalition of legislators who voted to repeal Republican Gov. Sam Brownback’s 2012 law slashing state income taxes. Brownback’s tax policy cratered the state budget and prompted a sales tax increase, heavy borrowing and cuts to core services. In 2017, Masterson condemned the bipartisan bill — supported by Holscher — that ended the Brownback economic development strategy. Masterson has served as Senate president since 2021.
“The absolute concern here is that, as my opponent has said before, he feels the Brownback experiment didn’t go far enough,” Holscher said. “He wants to take over this state and, should he become governor, we will see something worse than the Brownback experiment. I tell people, you know, that’s a warning to us in terms of where he is and what he wants to do to Kansas.”
“He has been very hostile to public education, trying to defund our public schools. He has attacked voting rights. He keeps talking about property taxes, yet he’s been in charge for six years, has a supermajority … but hasn’t answered and hasn’t solved these issues of property tax,” she said.
 
Missouri farm roots
Holscher was born in Missouri, graduated from Slater High School and earned a degree at the University of Missouri. She was the granddaughter of tenant farmers. Her father served in the Marine Corps and held a union job. Her mother worked at a public school.
“A good union job and public education, those were the things that propelled my family upward out of poverty,” she said.
She has been married for more than 30 years to Greg Holscher, an engineer. She previously worked for Sprint. They settled in Kansas and sent their three children to Johnson County public schools.
“We’re very proud of the education our kids received. We have a lot of teachers out there that just pour themselves into our kids,” Holscher said.
In 2016, Holscher defeated Republican incumbent Rep. Amanda Grosserode to take a seat in the Kansas House. She served two terms before being elected to the Kansas Senate in 2020. She was reelected in 2024. In August, Holscher defeated state Sen. Ethan Corson and Overland Park Mayor Mayor Curt Skoog in the Democratic gubernatorial primary, despite Gov. Laura Kelly’s endorsement of Corson. Holscher defeated Corson by a margin of 48.7% to 38.6%, with Skoog trailing at 12.6%. The Democratic governor subsequently endorsed Holscher.
Since her election to the Legislature a decade ago, Holscher has conducted listening tours in areas outside her Johnson County district. Typically, those involved eight to 10 stops in communities that don’t often have elected Democrats taking part in forums. Last year, she said, the invitations rolled in. She did 80 town halls.
“People are upset about the high cost of living and the fact that this Legislature really hasn’t done anything to address those issues,” she said.
Holscher said she would welcome the opportunity to debate Masterson again before the November election. They appeared together in September at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson, but two television debates were called off by Masterson. No one-on-one debates have been scheduled.
 
Property tax reform
Holscher said Masterson didn’t like answering questions about his inability to enact a bill that dealt effectively with rising property taxes. During the 2026 session, Republican leadership in the House and Senate, both controlling two-thirds GOP majorities in their chambers, clashed on how to address the problem. In the end, no deal on property taxes survived the political gauntlet.
Masterson sought an amendment to the Kansas Constitution capping residential and commercial property valuation increases, while House Speaker Dan Hawkins, R-Wichita, favored a state law limiting the spending of local government.
“Even his own party members recognize that some of the bills he brought forward were just gimmicks, and they didn’t even support him. … This is a failure in terms of his ability to reduce property taxes to address the affordability crisis,” Holscher said.
She said the state should fully fund K-12 special education because deficits in the program compelled local school districts to raise property taxes to fill the budget gap. In addition, she said Kansas had to restrain property tax exemptions and “sweetheart” economic deals that shifted the property tax burden to homeowners.
Holscher said she opposed the 2022 constitutional amendment designed to limit abortion rights and the August amendment to compel election of justices to the Kansas Supreme Court. Both were rejected by Kansas voters. The amendments represented a type of political advocacy harmful to Kansans and likely to resurface if Masterson was elected governor, she said.
“If Kansans make him our governor, you can bet this will become a priority, and reproductive healthcare in Kansas will be eliminated,” she said.
Holscher voted for legislation authorizing negotiations to bring either the Kansas City Royals or Kansas City Chiefs franchises to Kansas. She opposed the final deal with the Chiefs, which Masterson helped negotiate, because she said it was too generous to the billionaire owners of the NFL franchise. The deal provided the Chiefs with $1.8 billion in state bonds to build a $3 billion stadium.
“I want to make sure that this is economically beneficial for our communities and our people,” Holscher said. “I feel like billionaires should be funding stadiums. It’s a big giveaway.”
During the campaign, Masterson has accused Holscher of being a socialist. He said her politics reflected a liberal ideology. In response, Holscher said it would have been impossible to win legislative races in toss-up districts if she was out of touch with Republican and Democratic voters.
“I am not a socialist. That tells me that person who is writing those ads doesn’t have a record to stand on,” Holscher said. “Republicans would not keep electing me if I was, you know, an extreme person.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: A Black community in Louisiana faces a future without a champion in Congress after redistricting
description: Rep. Cleo Fields, D-La., center, who represents Louisiana's 6th congressional district, is joined by members of the Congressional Black Caucus as they speak to reporters at the Capitol in Washington, April 29, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
SCOTLANDVILLE, La. — If you cross the Mississippi River on the Huey P. Long-O.K. Allen Bridge, pass the Exxon Refinery, then head north for a few minutes, you’ll find a pocket of Louisiana that’s unlike any other place in America’s never-ending battle over what it means to have equal representation.
Here is Scotlandville, which was once its own unincorporated town but is now part of Baton Rouge. It’s a nearly all-Black community of 10,000 people that has been, for the second time, shuffled around on the state’s congressional map to make it part of a majority white district. Both times it was during the term of the same representative.
A man rides his bicycle past a closed meat market in the Scotlandville section of Baton Rouge, La., Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Gerald Herbert
The first time was 1996, when a group of voters sued to redraw the lines. The second time was earlier this year, after the U.S. Supreme Court decided that a core part of the Voting Rights Act intended to protect minorities’ political rights was unconstitutional.
The ruling led to cascading changes around the American South, but the case originated in Louisiana — specifically the 6th Congressional District that included Scotlandville. This is where Democratic Rep. Cleo Fields, 63, grew up poor and attended local schools before graduating from nearby Southern University A&M, eventually climbing the ranks to the U.S. House.
Now he plans to leave Washington and return to the Legislature instead of running for reelection in a race that he sees little chance of winning because the district boundaries have been altered dramatically. Scotlandville will no longer be represented by a native son, someone who people believed instinctively understood their challenges and offered a direct line to power and influence in the nation’s capital.
“We’re back to where we were right after Reconstruction,” said Press Robinson Sr., 89, who has spent years working on issues involving the congressional map. “When they redistrict, they are not concerned about the effect it has on those of us who are people of color.”
The methods have changed over the years, he said, but the intent has not.
“They disenfranchise people of color and they’ve done it again,” Robinson said.
Fields’ career echoes legal battle for representation
Congressional districts are core to debates over racial equality in the South, where white leaders spent decades using gerrymandering to ensure Black people couldn’t gain enough power to elect their own representatives.
The Voting Rights Act signed by Democratic President Lyndon Johnson in 1965 was supposed to fix that. Among other things, it required states and jurisdictions with a history of racial discrimination to get approval from the U.S. Department of Justice before congressional maps could take effect. It also allowed people to sue to challenge laws and procedures that would deny them the chance to elect candidates of their choice.
That didn’t settle the issue, however, and there has been a series of legal battles since then. Fields’ political career has tracked those twists and turns over the years.
He first came to Congress in 1993 when Scotlandville was part of the 4th District, which had been redrawn to create a majority-Black seat. A federal court said in 1996 the boundaries that zigzagged from northwest portion of the state to the Baton Rouge area were unconstitutional.
Southern University students participate in the traditional Pretty Wednesday on campus during lunch time in the Scotlandville section of Baton Rouge, La., Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. Credit: AP Photo/Gerald Herbert
Scotlandville shifted to the 6th District, which was then predominantly white, and Fields became a state senator. But he had an opening to return to Washington when Robinson and other plaintiffs challenged how the state drew its maps following the 2020 census.
A 2023 court decision involving Alabama also affected Louisiana, requiring the state to draw new district lines to achieve fairer representation for minorities. The district became majority-Black again, and Fields won the seat in 2024.
Another wave of litigation was already starting, and the issue soon reached the U.S. Supreme Court once more. The new lawsuit by a group of non-Black voters dovetailed with a separate effort by President Donald Trump to push Republican-led states to redraw their maps to help his party keep control of Congress in this year’s midterms.
The high court’s conservative majority said Fields’ district was unconstitutional. Louisiana, Alabama and Tennessee raced to redo their U.S. House districts in time for the November elections.
In Alabama, Democratic Rep. Shomari Figueres is fighting to hold onto his seat, where Black voting age population dropped from 50% to 40% under the new political lines, according to an Associated Press analysis of the citizen voting age population in his redrawn district. In Tennessee, the majority Black district anchored by Memphis was split between three others.
Fields’ district went from being 53% Black to 25% in the new one. He announced in July that he wasn’t going to run for reelection.
Blocks from the main entrance to Southern University A&M, a small crowd hung around a convenience store, but people were unwilling to talk about politics, eyeing strangers suspiciously. One younger man said he didn’t know who represents the area on the city council, let alone in Congress.
Frank Levy, 56, the cashier, said people’s apathy created the political environment that allowed for gerrymandering to occur again.
“A lot of people don’t even think about politics like this,” he said. “They don’t understand.”
About five minutes away, Dakasha Caulfield Leonard, 48, sat in the chapel of Scott’s Bluff Morticians, a nearly century-old fixture in the business community. Leonard returned two years ago to take over the funeral home when her father, who purchased it in the 1990s, became ill. She is worried about what will happen when Fields is no longer in office.
“The community is small and everybody knows everybody. Cleo is a member of our community,” she said. “If he doesn’t speak up and carry our voices, there’s nobody else to do that for us.”
Scotlandville has struggled for investment
Scenic Highway is one of the main thoroughfares in Scotlandville, and it once featured family businesses and restaurants as part of a prosperous self-contained Black community.
It’s faded overtime. The centerpiece boulevard has become blighted by empty lots and vacant buildings.
But deeper into the community is the Louisiana Leadership Institute, a sprawling complex that includes a full-scale gymnasium, classrooms, a fine arts center, a football field and a stadium with artificial turf. A thousand-seat amphitheater is being built.
The campus is the legacy of Fields, who founded the institute as the Congressional Classroom in 1993, during his first stint in Washington, and secured a mix of public and private funding for it. Over the decades since, it has hosted government, civics and leadership classes, and it’s created opportunities to travel and experience art and music and see government work in Washington.
“I wanted to engage young people,” Fields said. “Everything you see with the institute is result of me being a member of Congress.” The goal, he said, was to bring the workings of the federal government and other experiences to kids who had grown up like him.
Anthony Kenney, District 2 councilman for the Baton Rouge Metropolitan Council, speaks in his office underneath a photo of him with former Vice President Kamala Harris, in the Scotlandville section of Baton Rouge, La., Monday, Sept. 14, 2026. Credit: AP Photo/Gerald Herbert
Baton Rouge Councilman Anthony Kenney Jr., 29, is one of the human legacies, taking advantage of the course offerings, training and opportunities at the center as a young student.
“Congressman Fields is someone I’ve known my entire life,” Kenney said. “I actually grew up in the Louisiana Leadership Institute. I was talking about civics, how to get involved in government, how to do policy, how to move legislation as a young child.”
Kenney is now responsible for improving the roads, plumbing, drainage and sidewalks around Scotlandville, describing it as essential for attracting new businesses.
He said it was “devastating” to see what happened to Fields.
“It’s important for us to have representation that not only is from here, raised here, but actually lived through that same experiences,” Kenney said.
____
Associated Press data reporter Hannah Recht in Washington contributed to this report.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Judge dismisses Trump administration lawsuit over West Orange synagogue protest
description: The ruling ends a lawsuit targeting pro-Palestinian protesters involved in a 2024 melee outside a West Orange synagogue.
text:
A federal judge has ruled that the Trump administration failed to support its claims against a group of pro-Palestinian protesters involved in a 2024 melee outside Congregation Ohr Torah in West Orange. (Photo by New Jersey Monitor)A federal judge last week dismissed the federal government’s civil suit against protesters whose demonstration outside a West Orange synagogue in 2024 devolved into a brawl, with the judge finding the Trump administration failed to support their claims against them.
Counts against individuals and organizations sued under a federal statute that bars physical obstruction or threats of force to interfere with free expression at a place of worship or reproductive health clinic could not stand because the government had failed to allege a claim under the Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act, the judge said.
“The FACE Act does not impose liability for disruptive, offensive, or hostile advocacy,” Judge Katharine Hayden ruled.
The federal government’s claims against Altaf Sharif for allegedly charging at Moshe Glick, the organizer of the Nov. 13, 2024, real estate event and memorial that was the protesters’ target, could not form the basis of a claim because they did not argue his force was aimed at stopping a religious observance, Hayden said.
The government had alleged Sharif charged Glick after the latter man batted aside a vuvuzela an unnamed protestor was blowing directly into his ear. Sharif’s alleged charge was interrupted by pepper spray deployed by David Silberberg, a worshipper who Sharif put into a headlock and released after Glick struck him with a flashlight.
Claims against Eric Camins were dismissed because his shout of “the Jew is here” against Silberberg did not plausibly solicit or facilitate the use of force against him, Hayden ruled.
“There needs be context to infer that ‘the Jew is here’ is a statement inciting violence. The complaint does not supply that,” the judge said.
Another protestor, Tova Fry, could not face charges for sending Glick a letter that demanded he cancel the event under the threat of legal action because the statute bars only threats of physical violence. She could not be sued for her presence at the Nov. 13, 2024, protest based on the complaint because it does not allege Fry, personally, did anything illegal there.
The statute requires more than being part of a group, or crowd of protesters, Hayden ruled.
“The complaint does not allege that Fry blocked a door, or stood in a walkway, or touched a worshiper, or blew a horn, or said anything to anyone at the synagogue,” the judge wrote.
The judge dismissed claims against Matt Dragon, who the government alleged led the protest, because the Trump administration’s complaint did not claim he employed force, obstructed access, or moved to interfere with worshippers. The complaint, the judge wrote, only notes he was there and told Fry where the entrance to the synagogue was.
The Party for Socialism and Liberation New Jersey and Americans for Palestine New Jersey, who publicized the protests outside Glick’s home and synagogue, could not face charges over social media posts noting the demonstrations because those posts did not include a threat of force, the judge wrote.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: New polling shows Morrisey at 31-45% approval; it could affect Republican candidates this fall
description: Election polling time is hot, and while Gov. Patrick Morrisey isn’t on the ballot this year, numbers in some key Senate districts reveal the governor is underwater in popularity.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey gives his State of the State address in the West Virginia Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia, on Wednesday, Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)Election polling time is hot, and while Gov. Patrick Morrisey isn’t on the ballot this year, numbers in some key Senate districts reveal the governor is underwater in popularity. 
Morrisey, a Republican, has been in office for roughly 21 months. The former West Virginia attorney general narrowly won a multi-person primary in 2024 with 33% of the vote.
Recent forecasts by State Navigate, a nonprofit focused on election forecasts in state races, showed Morrisey’s approval is at 45% and 31% in two different districts of the state.
“I would say that Morrissey is definitely underwater in West Virginia in approval,” said Chaz Nuttycombe, executive director of State Navigate.
The organization recently polled voters in the Northern Panhandle’s Senate District 1 along with Senate District 8 in Kanawha County, which includes parts of Clay, Jackson, Putnam and Roane counties.
In Senate District 8, 61% of respondents said they disapprove of the job Morrisey is doing compared to 31% who say they approve.
In Senate District 1, Morrissey’s approval is an even 45-45. 
“Pretty astonishing since he won this district by 33 points,” Nuttycombe said.
As we’re in the throes of campaign season, Nuttycombe pointed out that a Morrisey endorsement could have a negative impact on Republican candidates, especially those in tight statehouse races. 
As part of the State Navigate poll, Nuttycombe surveyed what he called the “Morrisey effect.” In District 8, he believes a Morrisey endorsement “would be toxic” ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3.
“If Morrissey is being mentioned in this race a lot or anything, I think especially with the amount of undecideds and how much they hate the governor, that that could be something,” he said. 
In District 8, 45% of respondents said they were less likely to vote for a candidate attached to Morrisey. The poll showed 40% of voters said Morrisey’s endorsement would have no effect on their vote. 
In District 1, nearly half of voters said Morrisey’s endorsement wouldn’t affect their vote and 32% said they were less likely to vote for a candidate endorsed by the governor. 
State Navigate polling in these districts also showed fewer than 50% of respondents approve of the job President Donald Trump is doing after he easily won West Virginia in the 2024 election.
In District 1, incumbent Sen. Laura Chapman, R-Ohio, faces a challenge from Democratic candidate Shawn Fluharty, who currently serves in the House of Delegates. (West Virginia Legislative Photography photos)
A closer look at two state Senate races
State Navigate uses a seat by seat analysis in its polling process. They’ve already predicted the GOP supermajority will hold in both West Virginia’s Senate and House of Delegates. 
At the end of September, State Navigate polled more than 800 voters in Senate District 1 and 8 through a text to online survey.
In District 1, incumbent and Morrisey-ally Sen. Laura Chapman, R-Ohio, faces a meaningful challenge from Democratic candidate Shawn Fluharty, who currently serves in the House of Delegates.
This could be one of November’s closet statehouse races and a potential Senate seat flip to blue. 
Chapman leads Fluharty by 5 points in the polling in the majority Red area, but the samples show more motivated voters are behind Fluharty. Independents account for 20% of the district’s electorate, and if they show up to vote in the midterm election, this polling shows they’re leaning toward Fluharty. 
Morrisey backed Chapman in May’s bitter Repubclian primary, and the governor has said it “will be one of the defining races in the (West Virginia) state Senate this year.” Morrisey was recently in the Northern Panhandle and publicly praised Chapman. 
Chapman has held the Senate seat since 2022. She won the 2022 election with nearly 60% of the vote against Democratic challenger Randy Swartzmiller.
Fluharty’s anti-Morrisey stance is a hallmark of his campaign, billing his race as himself versus the governor since he expects Morrsiey to target him in the coming weeks. Fluharty easily won his 2024 House election despite Trump’s popularity in the area at the time; he is now pulling around 12% of voters who recall backing Trump for president. 
“Fluharty is doing really well with Trump voters … He’s getting like 15% of Trump voters. It’s pretty good for a Democrat based in West Virginia,” Nuttycombe said.
Nearly half of the respondents in Senate District 1 said Morrisey’s endorsement wouldn’t affect their vote in the race; 32% of respondents said they’re less likely to vote for a candidate with Morrisey’s endorsement. 
Senate District 8 will have a new elected official after incumbent Sen. Kevan Bartlett, R-Kanawha, lost his primary to Lance Wheeler. 
Kim Hundley is the Democratic challenger in the race. 
Wheeler leads 46% over 40% over Hundley with 14% undecided.
Independents lean Republican in this district, but have soured on Republican leadership. Hundley would need roughly 72% of undecided voters to overtake Wheeler, according to State Navigate.  
A Morrisey endorsement could completely shift this race, according to Nuttycombe. The voters pushed away by Morrisey are exactly the ones Hundley needs to win. Among undecided voters alone, 26% say a Morrisey endorsement would make them much less likely to support a candidate.
The deadline to register to vote or update voter registration information is Oct 13. Early in-person voting runs Oct. 21-31.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi agencies ask for more money as lawmakers begin work on $7B budget
authors: Katherine Lin, Alex Rozier, Allen Siegler, and Gwen Dilworth
description: University of Southern Mississippi President Joseph Paul, from left, Mississippi University for Women Interim President C. Scott Tollison, Alcorn State University President Tracy Cook, Delta State University President Daniel Ennis and Mississippi Valley State University President Jerryl Briggs attend a Joint Legislative Budget Committee meeting Friday, Oct.[...]
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A panel of state lawmakers heard from 11 state agency leaders on Thursday and Friday about their proposed spending for fiscal year 2028.
Nearly every agency asked for more money as legislators begin the work of setting a more than $7 billion state budget.
The Joint Legislative Budget Committee will issue its recommendations and revenue estimate later this year, but the final budget will be set during the regular legislative session that begins in January.
A lawmaker reviews information from the Office of Student Financial Aid at a Joint Legislative Budget Committee meeting, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Rogelio V. Solis for Mississippi Today
For fiscal year 2027, which started July 1, lawmakers passed a $7.5-billion state-funded budget, part of a $29 billion total budget that includes federal money.
With state revenue expected to remain more or less flat over the next few years due to tax cuts and the economy, legislators are carefully watching spending and as Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann said multiple times in the hearings, lawmakers do not like running deficits.
Legislators had a lot of questions for the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency as it raised concerns about its coffers after recent disasters, such as Winter Storm Fern, which has become the state’s second most expensive disaster after Hurricane Katrina. They also had many questions for the state Institutions of Higher Learning, over a controversial new funding formula for universities.
Institutions of Higher Learning
IHL’s hearing was perhaps the most contentious hearing. Legislators pressed its leaders for over an hour and a half. The questions were primarily over the move toward a performance based funding model and whether the universities would fund to metrics such as graduation rates, student income after graduation and cost per student.  
IHL asked for an increase of $93 million for a total education and general fund request of around $561 million for the coming budget year. Legislators questioned IHL leadership about whether the additional money is needed, how much universities are spending per student and the financial health of the schools amid declining enrollment. They pushed for more funding to be tied to performance. Lawmakers made it clear that their priority is graduating more students and preparing them for the workforce.
Alfred Rankins Jr., senior executive director of the Mississippi Institutions of Higher Learning, back to the camera, addresses members of the Joint Legislative Budget Committee, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026, in Jackson.  Credit: Rogelio V. Solis for Mississippi Today
Legislators questioned the willingness of the agency’s board to find cost savings through shared resources and by turning around financially struggling schools, and asked what IHL would do if the Legislature approved the same funding as the current year. 
Alfred Rankins Jr., IHL’s senior executive director, defended IHL’s approach but said the board is committed to improvement and supporting the universities. 
Alfred Rankins Jr., senior executive director of the Mississippi Institutions of Higher Learning, center, confers with provosts David Shaw of Mississippi State University, left, and Noel Wilkin of the University of Mississippi before presenting the universities’ budget requests before the Mississippi Joint Legislative Budget Committee, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Rogelio V. Solis for Mississippi Today
The Office of Student Financial Aid is facing a “significant” deficit in fiscal year 2027 due, in part, to changes in federal student aid and increasing the number of eligible students. Earlier this year, the FAITH scholarship, which is given to former foster youth, faced a funding gap until the Woodward Hines Education Foundation stepped in with a one-time gift of $800,000.
MEMA says it ‘won’t make it to June’
The Mississippi Emergency Management Agency again raised alarms about its funding in a year that saw three federally declared disasters in the state — Winter Storm Fern in January, tornadoes in May and Tropical Storm Arthur in June. 
Mississippi Emergency Management Agency Executive Director Stephen McCraney speaks to the Joint Legislative Budget Committee, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Rogelio V. Solis for Mississippi Today
The agency’s “Disaster Assistance Trust Fund” is critically low — at about half its usual level — considering what future disasters may be around the corner, MEMA executive director Stephen McCraney said Thursday. 
The agency’s disaster trust fund — which includes money for the state’s match of federal disaster aid, mission assignments and payments to the National Guard — stood at $6.7 million, MEMA chief deputy Crystal Thompson said Thursday.
“I won’t make it to June,” McCraney said. “Not at this current burn rate.”
In the Fern recovery, the state has so far spent $86 million to match federal funding for  “other needs” aid, part of FEMA’s Individual Assistance program that covers costs for things such as funerals, hotel stays and childcare. FEMA covers 75% of the costs and the state pays the remaining 25%. 
The Legislature put another $20 million in the disaster trust fund this past session, but MEMA has already spent that money matching FEMA aid, the agency said. 
MEMA requested a $70 million budget for fiscal year 2028, nearly twice what it had estimated spending for the current year. 
Medicaid’s increasing price tag after COVID
The Division of Medicaid is asking for an additional $179 million for a total request of $1.3 billion from the state. The Legislature provided more money to Medicaid for this fiscal year but the division is still anticipating a deficit of $34 million. And the department’s request for the upcoming fiscal year could continue to change.
Cindy Bradshaw, executive director of the Mississippi Division of Medicaid, speaks to the Joint Legislative Budget Committee on Friday, Oct. 2, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Rogelio V. Solis for Mississippi Today
It is one of the state’s largest expenditures and about a quarter of the state’s population is enrolled in Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program. The number of people enrolled has decreased, but the end of increased federal COVID money means that the cost to the state continues to rise even as enrollment has dropped.
Child Protection Services requests large increase
The Department of Child Protection Services requested an increase of about $52 million for a total of over $200 million in state funds. 
The agency wants to add 47 attorney positions, partly due to recent Youth Court reforms the Legislature passed during a special session. Around $34 million of the additional money would go to contractual services, including contractors to handle the agency’s large caseload. 
Andrea Sanders, executive director of the Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services, left, speaks to the Joint Legislative Budget Committee, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Rogelio V. Solis for Mississippi Today
One of the requirements of the Olivia Y lawsuit, a federal consent order focused on the safety of children in care of the state’s long-troubled foster system, is for the department to request enough money to meet the lawsuit’s safety standards. Hosemann said that for the past two years the agency has run an annual deficit of $35 million.
“We want them to budget realistically, particularly Child Protective Services,” Hosemann said, “We’re wanting them to be funded to adequately do their job and we don’t need for them to be short funded and have to come up with $35 million at the end of the year.” 
Despite deficit, court system lowers its request
Legislators acknowledged there have been many changes in state courts over the last year, including the recent Youth Court Reform Act. 
The Administrative Office of Courts has added contractors to handle intake from Youth Courts and will add nine new Youth Court judges next year.
The office is anticipating a deficit of nearly $3 million this year. The office, which includes the state Supreme Court, youth and electronic courts and court interpreters, said this is due to the system coming under oversight of the state Personnel Board and not receiving enough funding.  
Despite changes to the office and this year’s deficit, the overall budget request for the next fiscal year is $6 million less than the previous year for a total of close to $34 million.
Demand increases for mental health services
Mississippians’ unmet mental health needs continue to be critical. The state’s suicide death rate has risen in recent years while the national number has declined, according to federal health data.  
Wendy Bailey, the Department of Mental Health’s director, requested roughly $10 million more than the Legislature gave the department for the current year. 
Wendy Bailey, executive director of the Mississippi Department of Mental Health, speaks to the Joint Legislative Budget Committee, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Rogelio V. Solis for Mississippi Today
She said $4.5 million of the additional request would be for the department to fund community services for 200 people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. After Bailey told lawmakers that about 2,700 Mississippians were on a waiting list for the program, Hosemann asked why Bailey hadn’t requested more money. He asked a similar question after Bailey said the beds were full at a Brookhaven intellectual and developmental disability youth home.
Bailey responded that plenty of substance use, mental health and disability problems in the state are not being funded. 
“There are many, many more things I can add to the budget request,” Bailey said. “This is not an area that we are seeing a decrease in demand of services.”
Office of Workforce Development wants to expand
Accelerate Mississippi, the state office of workforce development, wants to expand its programs in the coming budget year.
The agency requested over $7 million, an increase of $2.5 million. The additional money would go to increasing staffing and covering increased costs of services to train more workers and meet industry demand in the state. 
Health Department requests no increase
Dr. Dan Edney, Mississippi’s state health officer, requested level funding, no major increase, for the Mississippi State Department of Health for the third year in a row. The department requested a budget of over $90 million from the state.
State Health Officer Dr. Daniel Edney presents the Mississippi State Department of Health’s budget request to the Joint Legislative Budget Committee, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Rogelio V. Solis for Mississippi Today
Edney said the agency has worked to reduce overhead on operations in order to maintain services in spite of significant inflationary pressure in healthcare. 
Edney said the agency hopes to allocate more of its money to developmental support and services for young children and their families, even as it maintains its current funding level. 
Public Safety wants salary increases
The Department of Public Safety requested a budget increase of around $30 million from about $167 million to $197 million. 
Most of the money would go to salary increases and making salaries for sworn officers competitive at a base of $65,000.
Mississippi Department of Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell speaks to the Joint Legislative Budget Committee, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Rogelio V. Solis for Mississippi Today

name: Alaska Beacon
title: After years of problems, Alaska plans to outsource payroll for 14,000 public employees
description: By the end of 2027, as many as 14,000 Alaska state workers could be paid by someone outside the state. After years of trouble within the payroll department within the Alaska Department of Administration, the agency is planning to outsource the state’s public employee payroll to an outside company. Proposals from interested companies were due […]
text:
The Alaska State Office Building in Juneau, the state capital, is seen on Feb. 16, 2023. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)By the end of 2027, as many as 14,000 Alaska state workers could be paid by someone outside the state.
After years of trouble within the payroll department within the Alaska Department of Administration, the agency is planning to outsource the state’s public employee payroll to an outside company.
Proposals from interested companies were due Thursday, and in an internal letter, DOA Commissioner Paula Vrana said “it likely will be several weeks before a final decision is made.”
Vrana implied that if the proposals aren’t affordable or are otherwise unfavorable, the state will not proceed with outsourcing. 
“As of now, we are exploring what options are available to the state and what value may be realized by this approach,” she wrote. “The final decision will be based on the proposals we receive.”
Vrana wrote that the department will begin talking with unions “to explore the options for transfers/placements of employees displaced by outsourcing” and if DOA does choose to outsource, “we will also work with the vendor to include as many existing state payroll employees as possible in their staffing plan.”
The state’s payroll department has struggled with staffing issues for years, leading to times when employees missed paychecks or encountered other problems with their pay. 
In April, DOA published a request for information from companies that might be interested in providing “comprehensive payroll processing” for the state.
A three-page feasibility study dated Sept. 28 states that payroll work involves 78 employees in different agencies; all would be affected by outsourcing.
According to the state’s formal request for proposals, it is prepared to pay $4 million per year for a company to handle payroll. It currently spends about $10 million per year on payroll employees and functions, the feasibility study stated. 
According to the study, in fiscal year 2025, state employees filed more than 1,500 “notice of pay problem” reports, and reducing the number of problems could make employees in other departments happier.
The first outsourced paychecks would come to a handful of departments on April 1, 2027, and other departments would be transferred to the outsourced payroll company through the rest of the year.
The outsourcing company would have to use the state’s existing payroll software programs, the document states, and the work would have to be done in the United States, but the contractor could get a waiver from the state that would allow payroll work to be done in a foreign country.
“The goal is not to change the system used to process payroll but to make payroll processing more efficient and ensure the state’s existing systems and processes are supported by qualified contracted professionals who can maintain continuity, reduce errors, and uphold the state’s obligations to its employees and the public,” the document states.
DOA provided a copy of the RFP documents to the Beacon this week; they were not previously published on the state’s public notice system, and the two public employee unions whose members would be affected by the outsourcing said they also had not previously seen the documents.
The Beacon asked DOA for an interview with Vrana or someone else involved with the outsourcing decision but was turned down.
In response to a written question asking why the department is planning to outsource, a spokesperson said by email: “Ensuring that employees are paid correctly and on time is the essential duty of payroll. Challenges stemming from high turnover and persistent vacancies within the Department have resulted in pay problems for some state employees. The administration has determined that outsourcing payroll may both provide significant recurring cost-savings to the State and improve services to its employees. However, no final decision on outsourcing payroll will be made until responses to the RFP issued earlier are evaluated.”
Jeff Kasper is the business manager of the Alaska Public Employees Association, which represents payroll workers. He’s not a fan of outsourcing. 
“It usually costs more and doesn’t provide the efficiencies that you’re looking for. When you’re talking about public services, you’re essentially having the public pay more for something that’s probably not as good,” he said. 
Kasper isn’t convinced that the Department of Administration has done enough to fix the problems that have deterred Alaskans from working for the payroll department.
“If people aren’t applying for jobs and accepting jobs, it’s usually because it doesn’t pay enough or it doesn’t provide benefits or it’s bad working conditions. This one could be all three, and I don’t think any of them have been addressed,” he said.
The state’s own feasibility study acknowledged those problems.
“Payroll processing occurs on a bi-weekly basis and does not have down time. This work environment and the entry level pay range are likely reasons for low retention and high staff turnover,” the study concluded.
As of last month, the study said, 58% of all payroll positions in the state are vacant, and it can take as long as a year of training before a new worker is capable of working independently.
MaryAnn Ganacias is the interim executive director of the Alaska State Employees Association, whose members are paid by the payroll department. 
“Alaskans deserve to know what the problem is with the state and what they’re trying to solve by privatizing payroll,” she said. 
Ganacias said state money spent outside Alaska is money that doesn’t benefit Alaskans.
“We need to do better investing in our own employees here in Alaska, and not outsourcing where the money actually goes,” she said.
Kasper said he doesn’t think the timeline described in the state’s RFP follows collective bargaining agreements or is realistic.
“The union’s not just gonna sit down and let this happen,” he said. “We don’t think the state has been following the process that’s in the contract.”
Kasper said his union’s contract with the state requires a 30-day consultation period before any outsourcing takes place, and even though the state’s RFP calls for a contract in November, he doesn’t think one is likely before Gov. Mike Dunleavy leaves office in the first week of December. 
Kate Sheehan, policy adviser for the Department of Administration, said by email in response to Kasper’s comments, “The State engaged the Confidential Employees Association (CEA) on September 25th, and we have entered into the 30-day period for the union to submit any alternate plans to be considered during this process. DOA does not intend to contract out prior to the Union’s response and analysis of their input.”
