name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington needs this aging state ferry to keep running and running
description: When the Washington state ferry Tillikum entered service in 1959, Albert Rosellini was in his first term as governor and Dwight Eisenhower was in his second as president.  The showy tail fins of Chevrolet and Plymouth sedans on its car deck could have made a killer whale jealous. The auto-and-driver fare to cross Puget Sound […]
text:
The 67-year-old Tillikum is the longest-serving Washington state ferry in active operation. It was expected to retire years ago, but can’t due to the shortage of working boats in the state fleet. (Photo by Tom Banse)When the Washington state ferry Tillikum entered service in 1959, Albert Rosellini was in his first term as governor and Dwight Eisenhower was in his second as president. 
The showy tail fins of Chevrolet and Plymouth sedans on its car deck could have made a killer whale jealous. The auto-and-driver fare to cross Puget Sound was $1.75.
Back then, the Tillikum was one of three Evergreen State-class ferries. Around a decade ago, the other two were decommissioned. However, that won’t happen anytime soon for the Tillikum. It must sail long past its expected retirement date because Washington State Ferries is so short on vessels, it cannot afford to let go of a single boat. Decommissioning is now projected in 2033 for this remarkably long-lived ferryboat. 
“She’s a sweetheart,” said Captain Justin McCaughan of the boat he and the crew affectionately call the “Tilly.”
“She’s a little underpowered, but she is fairly maneuverable,” continued McCaughan during an interview in the teak-trimmed pilothouse. “She’s more reliable than a lot of our newer boats because she is simpler.”
McCaughan said he trusted this “moving piece of history” to last until new boats join the fleet. The controls and instruments in the pilothouse have been repeatedly modernized. But the mates at the helm go gentle on the throttles to protect the ancient machinery down below. 
“Because we want to keep her around, we take it easy on this boat,” McCaughan said as the ferry chugged toward Friday Harbor. “So, we are not using maximum power unless we really need maximum power. We try to bring the throttles up slowly.”
The 87-car, 310-foot Tillikum was constructed in 1958 by the long-defunct Puget Sound Bridge and Drydock Company. Its drive motors were salvaged from a surplus World War II Navy ship. Replacement parts to keep it running sometimes have to be fabricated from scratch at the ferry system’s maintenance yard or are stripped from Tilly’s   mothballed sibling, the Klahowya.
Only one active vehicle ferry in America is older. The SS Badger, which was launched in 1953, sails daily during the warmer half of the year across the midsection of Lake Michigan. The 410-foot, coal-burning steamship is a floating, moving National Historic Landmark. The Tillikum burns conventional diesel for propulsion.
Wearing earplugs, oiler Earl Clark stands beside one of the two engines of the ferry Tillikum. (Photo by Tom Banse)
The view from the engine room
Below the Tillikum’s car deck, the vintage engines and diesel generators make a deafening din. Tight passageways wind past twisty pipes, conduits, valves and steel going every which way.
Inside a sound-insulated, air-conditioned engine control room, the chief engineer and two oilers monitor tiers of analog dials and gauges from the past century. Modern digital screens glow on another side of the room, mixed in with blinking instruments that could date to a mid-life overhaul in 1994.
The hull looks good and the ship’s steel, while old, “was done properly,” vouched Chief Engineer Alex Stamati.
“As long as they give us the time in drydock and maintenance money, we can keep the boat running,” said oiler Earl Clark. “The longer it lives, obviously the more expensive it is going to get.”
“She can last to 80 or 90 [years old] with proper maintenance, absolutely,” Stamati added.
So what about retirement?
The state ferry system is in a race against time to build new ferries before its aging vessels conk out. Five ferries now in operation are more than 50 years old. At 67, the Tillikum is the grande dame. 
So far, the state Legislature has only been able to scrape together enough money to order three new ferries due to their high price. The first of those hybrid-electric boats isn’t expected until 2030. The next vessels are due in 2031 and 2032.
“As we get closer to the first new ferry entering service in 2030, we’ll work with Gov. Bob Ferguson and the Legislature as they decide whether to follow past practice and retire an older vessel as each new one enters service, or invest in keeping our three oldest boats operating longer so we can begin growing the fleet sooner,” ferry system chief Steve Nevey told riders in a recent newsletter.
“We have 21 vessels today, down from 24 in 2015,” Nevey wrote. “One unexpected breakdown can cause a ripple effect across the system.”
Top brass at the ferry system prefer to add one or two relief vessels to the fleet before decommissioning aging boats, if possible. There is also public interest in restoring the long-suspended international run to Vancouver Island from Anacortes, which would require growing the fleet by another vessel.
“Put all of that together and 21 ferries aren’t enough. We need at least 24 to operate our current service,” Nevey said.
The upshot is that the Tillikum will likely be counted on well into her seventh decade. The most recent fleet planning document shared with state lawmakers shows its retirement happening in 2033.
The Tillikum has operated on nearly every Puget Sound route over the past six decades. Today, it’s the slowest member of the state fleet with a listed top cruising speed of 13 knots and is consigned to the San Juan Islands interisland circuit.
The Tillikum became the “big boat” on the Seattle-Bainbridge ferry route when it entered service n 1959. The Smith Tower, at top right, was still the tallest building in Seattle back then. (Photo courtesy of Washington State Archives)
Affection, frustration and amazement
The interisland service provided by the Tillikum evokes complex feelings among regular commuters. Some are “amazed” it is still running while others continue to be frustrated with unreliability on a vital route they consider a literal lifeline.  
The San Juans interisland service had the lowest rider satisfaction scores of all Puget Sound ferry routes in a survey conducted for the Washington State Transportation Commission earlier this year. The top reasons for dissatisfaction were late departures and arrivals. Other gripes included loading procedures and inadequate parking near the terminals.
“I don’t think it’s fair to equate the service dissatisfaction with the boat,” said frequent rider Justin Paulsen, the San Juan County Council Chair. “I think there’s a lot of love in the county for that boat.”
Across the first three quarters of this year, the Tillikum had 275 sailings completely cancelled out of 6,463 scheduled sailings. The most common cause of those cancellations was lack of sufficient crew. Mechanical problems on the aging ship accounted for 28% of the cancellations.
As much as county leaders praise the Tillikum, they still aspire to establish a competing interisland ferry. Paulsen said the goal is to provide an alternative to the state system that provides greater dependability. It’s unclear where the money to launch this new passenger-only service would come from.
Lopez Island author Iris Graville spent one or two days a week riding the Tillikum as the ferry system’s first writer-in-residence before the COVID-19 pandemic. The venerable boat remains her favorite. She described being charmed by 1950s-era touches such as its brass fixtures, elegant wooden slat benches and swivel chairs in front of a throwback mirrored makeup counter in the ladies room.
“She has those classic features that aren’t found in the newer vessels, like the brass railings and trim,” Graville said. “She just has more of a cozy feeling.”
Graville said she will miss the Tillikum whenever it finally retires, yet is also fully on board with the need to acquire cleaner, modern vessels. Like many San Juan County residents, she has her fingers crossed the aging boat will last until a replacement arrives.
“Anybody who knows any of the history of that vessel has to be wondering that very thing, can it really keep going?” Graville said in an interview. “We know there is usually a lifespan and a limit.”
Then and now. At left, Captain Theodore Thorson at the helm of the Tillikum in 1965. At right, Captain Justin McCaughan in the same pilothouse in late September 2026. (Photos  from Washington State Archives (left) and by Tom Banse)

name: Mississippi Today
title: Lettuce is safe to eat, says Mississippi epidemiologist, and food safety questions answered
description: Bagged lettuce and salads are displayed for sale at a grocery store chain in Minneapolis, Friday, July 31, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has posted a steady stream of food recalls, following a summer with historic rates of cyclospora-induced illnesses and several products with potential salmonella contamination. Mississippi Today talked to food safety experts to learn about top concerns, how food safety is addressed in Mississippi and how food systems are linked.
What are the active food recalls in Mississippi now?
Several active food recalls in Mississippi include some of Prime Line Distributor’s ready-to-eat pork products potentially contaminated with Listeria, Graziers raw milk cheeses from Sierra Nevada Cheese Company potentially contaminated with E. coli and raw meat products that were produced without federal inspection.
The recalls come in three classes, depending on the level of risk. Class I is for probable serious health risks, including death, such as E. coli or Listeria. Class II recalls have a remote chance of adverse health effects, and Class III recalls violate regulations but are unlikely to cause harm. 


Mississippians should know that recalls are very specific to certain brands, product names, use or freeze by dates and lot numbers, said Courtney Crist, a food safety specialist at the Mississippi State University. All information must match for a product to be considered part of the recall, she said, and one product being recalled does not mean every food of that category is unsafe. 
“Do not try to make a recalled food item safe,” she cautioned, recommending that consumers properly dispose of their purchases or return them for a refund. 
Should I be concerned about cyclospora in Mississippi?
Asked if Mississippians should be concerned about lettuce on their grocery shelves, State Epidemiologist Renia Dotson offered a succinct answer. 
“No, I don’t,” she said, while recommending people wash or scrub their fruits and vegetables as a general safety practice.   
On Sept. 11, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention declared an end to the multi-state cyclospora outbreak. Officials linked nearly 13,000 confirmed cases to this outbreak, the largest in modern U.S. history. 
Mississippi’s cyclospora cases, however, were not linked to the multi-state outbreak, according to the Mississippi State Department of Health. On July 15, the department temporarily made cyclosporasis a reportable disease in order to “do our part” and provide more data for the CDC investigation, Dotson said. Mississippi was previously one of three states, along with Idaho and Pennsylvania, that did not require clinicians or laboratories to report positive cases to the state Health Department. Dotson said Mississippi has not previously seen large numbers of the illness and that mandated reporting began, not due to increased cyclospora cases, but to contribute to the national database. 
On Aug. 22, Mississippi had 33 confirmed cases of cyclospora, Dotson said. For each confirmed case, nurses and a team of epidemiologists conducted an extensive interview with the affected person that included what they ate, where they ate it and when their symptoms started. 
“Each one seems to be an independent case on its own, and none of them trace back to the actual multi-state outbreak,” she said. 
Cyclosporasis tends to be a seasonal infection that runs from May to the end of August, Dotson said. Positive cases can emerge later because the disease can incubate for two or more weeks. 
Should I be concerned about salmonella in Mississippi?
Several recalls remain active for salmonella, a bacteria that causes illness year-round and has been reportable in Mississippi for decades.
“We’re always looking at salmonella,” Dotson said. 
Amid multi-state outbreaks of salmonella reported in jalapeno and eggs, Mississippi had some stores in the recall distribution chain but no confirmed cases linking salmonella to either outbreak, Dotson said. On Sept. 3, the CDC closed the investigation into potentially salmonella-contaminated eggs. The jalapeno investigation remains ongoing.
To test for clustered salmonella cases, state public health laboratories send samples through genomic sequencing and add it to a national CDC database called PulseNet. The amount of similar genetic sequences shows how closely bacterial samples are linked. If the samples reveal striking resemblances to a similar sequence, epidemiologists know it is connected to a certain outbreak.  
How can I keep myself safe from foodborne illnesses?
Experts recommended the following measures:

Stay up to date on food recalls through the FDA and USDA websites, or sign up for email alerts;
Pay attention to recall notices from grocery stores. If you have a shopper’s card at Kroger or Costco, for instance, you will get emails about their food recalls; 
Clean fruits and vegetables, even produce that is pre-washed;
Wash your hands, utensils, and kitchen surfaces often, including before food preparation and eating;
Separate raw meat, poultry, eggs and seafood from foods that are ready to eat, to help prevent cross-contamination;
Refrigerate and freeze foods promptly, such as by refrigerating perishable foods within two hours, or one hour if food is exposed to temperatures above 90°F;
Buy produce locally when possible, such as at farmer’s markets;
Be aware of your risk level. Young children, older adults, pregnant people and those with weakened immune systems have a higher risk of severe symptoms from foodborne illnesses.

Grocery shoppers who see a recalled product or concerning product on store shelves can scan the QR code on a Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce regulatory inspection sticker to report it, said Andy Gipson, the department’s commissioner. The red, white and blue stickers are placed throughout grocery stores and the checkout counter. 
What should I do if I think I am sick with a foodborne illness?
First, seek medical care, Dotson advises. From there, medical providers can offer tests for different foodborne illnesses. A cyclospora test is not included in the routine panel and has to be specifically asked for by the patient. 
Why have foodborne illnesses been so prominent this year? 
It’s hard to say whether food is getting less safe or not, but the whole food distribution system is under stress right now, said Barbara Kowalcyk, director of the Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security at George Washington University. 
“When you have a system under stress, failures do tend to happen more,” she said. The challenges start from the farms under stress from increased labor and fuel costs. They then spread all the way up the supply chain to distributors and escalating retail costs. Then, there’s public health agencies and regulatory agencies overseeing the safety of the food supply. 
As an example, Kowalcyk brought up the CDC’s parasitology group, once comprised of 11 staff members who were in charge of coordinating outbreak response across states and internationally. Part of the CDC team’s funding came from a different federal agency that was responsible for foreign aid and development, USAID. After the Trump administration cut USAID funds in early 2025, the CDC team was reduced to three staff members. 
Part of USAID’s work was funding water sanitation and hygiene programs in countries that import produce into the U.S. 
“And when you’re talking about cyclospora, you’re talking about contaminated agricultural water in all likelihood, or processing water,” Kowalcyk said. 
She thinks it’s important to understand that beyond the number of outbreaks, people should be aware of how quickly a response is mounted. Kowalcyk likens food safety to a fishnet. If the fishnet has big holes, it can only catch big fish, and not many. “Ideally you’ll have a strong fishnet with smaller holes so you can catch fish when they’re smaller, before they become a problem,” she said. 
 Who’s in charge of food safety in Mississippi?
Recalls are handled by two federal agencies. The FDA covers about 80% of the U.S. food supply, including fruits, vegetables, dairy, eggs, packaged foods, dietary supplements and seafood, except catfish. The U. S. Department of Agriculture, or USDA, handles recalled meat, poultry, processed egg products and catfish. However, most recalls are voluntary and come after the distributing company identified a health hazard in its product.  
The Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce has a team of about 200 food safety inspectors in grocery stores working with store managers to make sure recalled products have been taken off the shelves. 
“We’re the boots on the ground making sure that lettuce is not being offered for sale at the Dollar General if it’s under a recall,” Gipson said, as an example.
Meanwhile, the state Department of Health is in charge of restaurant and food facility inspections, conducted one to four times a year, depending on the facility’s risk level. 
Gipson emphasized that the level of food safety in the U.S. is the “gold standard.” 
“There’s no country that has the high level of food safety protocols that we have,” he said. “I feel very good about the safety of our food in Mississippi.” Gipson also encouraged Mississippians to shop for local food, which tends to be fresher than grocery store products.
In the most recent Global Food Security Index report, the U.S. ranked third out of 113 countries on the “Quality and Safety” pillar in 2022. Crist acknowledged this general safety with a caveat, saying, “The United States has many safeguards to protect its food supply, but no food system is completely free of risk.”
This story was produced with support from the Sarah Yelena Haselhorst Fund for Health Journalism.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri rejects optional hardship exceptions to Medicaid work requirements
description: Missouri will not use optional federal exemptions designed to help low-income people keep Medicaid coverage when they are hospitalized, travel for medical care or live in areas affected by disasters or high unemployment. The exceptions are optional in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which starting Jan. 1, 2027 will require states to verify that […]
text:
There were 344,669 MO HealthNet enrollees in the adult expansion group as of Sept. 25, according to the Department of Social Services. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, people in that group will have to show that they meet 80-hour monthly work requirements or qualify for an exemption to get or maintain coverage (Getty Images).Missouri will not use optional federal exemptions designed to help low-income people keep Medicaid coverage when they are hospitalized, travel for medical care or live in areas affected by disasters or high unemployment.
The exceptions are optional in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which starting Jan. 1, 2027 will require states to verify that adults ages 19 to 64 covered through Medicaid expansion work, attend school or volunteer 80 hours a month to get or maintain coverage.
The Missouri Department of Social Services says it aims to reduce paperwork and accommodate Missourians in some of these “short-term hardship” categories using other, mandatory exemptions in the federal law for caregivers and people who are “medically frail.” But advocates say the mandatory exemptions are likely to exclude some Missourians who would fall within the “short-term hardship” categories — and that where there is overlap, the mandatory exemptions require more verification.
In an email to The Independent, Baylee Watts, media director for the department, said that while the department will not use “separate, standalone” short-term hardship categories, “situations such as acute medical events and travel for specialized medical care will be accommodated under the department’s broader ‘medically frail’ and caregiver exemption pathways.”
Watts told The Independent the department wants to “limit the number of separate processes participants must navigate” and avoid “an additional, burdensome bureaucratic layer for participants” by forgoing short-term hardship exemptions.
The department also plans to verify compliance with work requirements based on one month within each six-month reporting period, Watts wrote, so that “a temporary disruption would not necessarily prevent someone from meeting the requirement.”
As reported by KFF earlier this year, the department initially planned to make exceptions for three of the four “short-term hardship events” in the federal law: extended travel to obtain medical treatment for oneself or a dependent, residence in an area with a federally declared disaster or emergency and inpatient or acute outpatient care in a hospital, nursing facility or intermediate care facility for people with intellectual disabilities. The department did not plan to make exceptions for residents of areas with high unemployment rates.
Watts said that after consulting with the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid, the department concluded that “circumstances outside of disasters can be effectively addressed through our existing plans for an exemption structure.”
According to a department webpage on Medicaid work requirements, the caregiver exemption will apply to parents or people caring for a child age 13 or younger and people who “regularly care for” someone with a disability and live with that person, are related to that person or provide 80 hours of care in a month.
Joel Ferber, director of advocacy at Legal Services of Eastern Missouri, said it’s unclear whether the “medically frail” exemption will accommodate people hospitalized for short-term acute medical events.
“It is speculative that the department’s definition of medical frailty will solve these problems since we haven’t seen their definition,” he said.
In a Sept. 22 email, Watts told The Independent the department “is continuing to finalize” its “process for identifying and verifying individuals who may qualify for the medically frail exclusion.”
Emily Kalmer, Missouri government relations director at the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network, told The Independent she is concerned the department’s decision not to grant short-term hardship exemptions will deprive low-income Missourians of options to keep the health insurance they need to detect and undergo treatment for cancer.
“We know people will lose coverage under this federal law,” Kalmer said. “It’s unclear right now how the state is going to be applying the medically frail exemption, and so we would like them to keep the options the federal law allows them as far as short-term hardship so that can be a tool if it’s needed.”
In the federal law, the “medical frailty” exemption includes people who are blind or disabled, have a substance use disorder, a “disabling mental disorder” or a “serious or complex medical condition.”
A federal rule issued by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid in June declined to include specific conditions like cancer in its definition of “serious or complex medical conditions,” saying the severity of a patient’s condition can vary over time.
 Bureaucratic barriers

Even if the department’s definition of “medically frail” encompasses acute medical events and medical travel, the federal rule instructing states how to implement the “medically frail” exemption is the target of multiple lawsuits arguing it creates an unlawfully high bar for people to qualify.
The rule, issued by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid in June, requires states to verify not only that they have a qualifying condition, but also that their condition impedes their ability to fulfill work requirements.
It’s unclear how much of the burden of proving eligibility will fall on applicants and enrollees. States are required to attempt to process Medicaid applications using information already available to them before requesting information from enrollees — a process known as ex parte verification. But Missouri only conducted 52.3% of Medicaid renewals that way in the first quarter of 2026, according to the Center for Children and Families at Georgetown University. That’s slightly below the national median of 54.8%.
The department also recently added new verification requirements for Missourians applying for or recertifying their eligibility for federal food assistance through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. Applicants and participants must provide documentation of shelter, utility and dependent care costs, as well as their financial resources, instead of being able to self-attest.
Ferber said it “does not ring true” for the department to say it wants to streamline processes for accessing public benefits “when the agency just added multiple new bureaucratic layers for SNAP applicants and participants.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Some Missouri Republicans are stressing independence from GOP in 2026 campaign ads
description: There are plenty of ways to tell when a political party is worried heading into an election. One is polling. President Donald Trump’s approval rating fell to 32% in a September Reuters/Ipsos poll, the lowest of his career, and sits in the mid-30s in national polling averages. Voters are especially unhappy about the cost of […]
text:
(Getty images).There are plenty of ways to tell when a political party is worried heading into an election.
One is polling. President Donald Trump’s approval rating fell to 32% in a September Reuters/Ipsos poll, the lowest of his career, and sits in the mid-30s in national polling averages. Voters are especially unhappy about the cost of living.
Another came in August, when Missouri voters demolished two priorities placed on the ballot by the Republican-controlled legislature. Amendment 4, which would have made it harder to pass initiative petitions, lost 80% to 20%. Amendment 5, aimed at replacing the state income tax with an expanded sales tax, lost 83% to 16%.
But maybe the clearest evidence can be found on your television and social media feeds.
Republicans are defending their two-thirds majority in the Missouri House this fall, and a series of new ads supporting GOP candidates in competitive districts has settled on a remarkably consistent message:
These Republicans aren’t afraid to stand up to Republicans.
Take Ben Keathley, the Republican incumbent from Chesterfield.
“Ben Keathley is the guy who asks why,” his ad says. “He broke with his own party. Not to be difficult. Because he actually read the bill.”
Or Philip Oehlerking, another Republican incumbent in St. Louis County.
“Oehlerking stood up to the lobbyists. He stood up to his own party bosses,” the narrator says, later adding that he “doesn’t answer to them. He answers to us.”
Then there’s Jeff Martin, the Republican running for an open House seat in Lee’s Summit.
He’s running “not for a party,” his ad says, but for families struggling with higher costs. And “when his own party gets it wrong, Jeff Martin will call them out.”
In St. Charles County, Republican Rep. Colin Wellenkamp is portrayed as “standing up to the big tech lobbyists and his own party’s leaders.”
And in Springfield, Republican Russ Gosselin promises to “always put people before politics.”
The ads have something else in common. They were all paid for by Citizens for a Better Government, a political action committee created this summer. So far, its only listed donor is the House Republican Campaign Committee, which gave $132,000 on Sept. 26.
In other words, the committee dedicated to electing Republicans to the Missouri House, chaired by House Majority Leader Alex Riley, is helping finance ads telling voters that its candidates are willing to defy Republicans.
Democrats are making almost exactly the opposite argument.
Their ads want voters thinking about the party in power. They don’t spend much time talking about being Democrats. Their argument is about Republicans — and what Republicans have done with their power in Jefferson City.
Cathy Summers, running for an open St. Louis County seat, points to the legislature’s repeal of the voter-approved paid sick leave law and its effort to overturn the abortion-rights amendment approved in 2024.
“We vote, they overrule us every time,” her ad says.
Matt Vitale, challenging Republican Rep. Brad Christ, hits the same themes and adds congressional redistricting.
“Every time working people won something at the ballot box, he took that, too,” Vitale’s ad says.
And Mary Ann Perkins, challenging Oehlerking, runs through a list of votes on sick leave, abortion rights and the initiative petition process before telling viewers: “When voters say yes, Oehlerking says no.”
None of this means Democrats are about to take control of the Missouri House.
Republicans won 111 of 163 seats in 2024. Two-thirds is 109, so Democrats don’t need anything resembling a takeover to change the balance of power. A net gain of three seats would end the GOP supermajority.
And Missouri remains a state where Republicans have controlled both legislative chambers since 2003.
But campaign ads are useful because they tell you what political professionals believe voters need to hear. Right now, Democrats in competitive House districts want voters thinking about what Republicans have done with nearly a quarter-century of legislative power.
Republicans, meanwhile, are spending money to tell those same voters something very different.
Yes, I’m a Republican. Just don’t confuse me with the Republicans you’re mad at.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: George Ayoub: Asking a lot not too much to ask
description: Nebraskans will remember a few years ago when a state senator made the case on the floor of the Legislature during a debate about school behavior that students were calling themselves “furries,” dressing the part and requesting litter boxes in public school bathrooms. This, the story went, was the result of some fiendish phenomenon in […]
text:
The U.S. Senate hearing room where former special counsel Jack Smith testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Sept. 29, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Nebraskans will remember a few years ago when a state senator made the case on the floor of the Legislature during a debate about school behavior that students were calling themselves “furries,” dressing the part and requesting litter boxes in public school bathrooms. This, the story went, was the result of some fiendish phenomenon in which our children fancied themselves felines and Fidos. 
He later apologized after realizing that the preposterous claim was … well … preposterous, proving yet again that confusing an assertion on Facebook or some other similarly situated social media with actual research rarely goes unpunished. 
I was reminded of Nebraska’s Furry Follies after the recent epic faceplant of U.S. Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.). Schmitt’s clanger was the result of concocting a conclusion for which he had the wrong premise. In the end, he clearly had no premise at all. 
At the risk of piling on, these are the details: During a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing, while trying to catch former Special Prosecutor Jack Smith in a lie, he mixed up the Atlanta Hawks men’s professional basketball team with the University of Iowa Hawkeye women’s basketball team, rendering his “Gotcha!” moment toothless and embarrassing. 
You might give a little slack to someone fooled on social media. It happens to all of us in the deep-fake, AI world in which we find ourselves. But a U.S. senator with a staff and researchers? Not so much, especially when his goal was not information but rather to attack the witness. 
Which, even despite his monumental airball, he did anyway, calling Smith a “total dirtbag,” giving the hearing the patina of an episode of “The Wire.” Not to be outdone, his fellow committee member, Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) — the recent guest of honor at Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ annual barbecue — went even further, forgoing actual questions surrounding Smith’s work as special prosecutor before closing with the wholly ignominious “You make me want to throw up in my mouth.” Other GOP senators joined the fray, too, attacking Smith as a liar, “villain” and serial abuser of power.
Perhaps these are serious people. After all, they are members of “the world’s greatest deliberative body,” the U.S. Senate. But you wouldn’t know it by some of the behavior in this hearing, because these were unserious responses to a serious matter, the investigation into the attempted undoing of an American election. 
Nor was the acrimony and ultimately empty show an isolated incident or, for that matter, new. Somewhere during the last couple of decades we have recalibrated our taste in political leaders, steering away from statesmanship, class and decorum and toward what gets clicks, raises money or, as we like to say, fires up the base. Yes, we’ve had exceptions, but we seem to have quit wringing our hands about the coarsening of American politics and culture. That’s because it’s already here.
With it comes a new construct for political leadership. At some point we decided one new litmus test for presidents, governors and other American leaders was someone you could have a beer or a cup of coffee with. Someone who could relate to us. 
Nothing wrong with that. 
About the same time we decided that “elite” was a bad word, and groups such as “East Coast elites” or “political elites” were bad people, representative of those whose power and position kept them out of touch with reality and who could care less about all of us “regular” Americans.
I would argue, however, that in our rush to “normalize” political officeholders and reduce the sway of the privileged, we discounted a few things too important to concede. Otherwise, anyone nursing a cold one at the corner tavern or a hot latte at your local Starbucks would be a good candidate for office. I say that not as an elite, but as someone who has apparently old-fashioned expectations of those who write laws and craft policies that affect my life.
Why not elect someone with elite intellect? Someone who is an elite problem solver? Someone who respects our Constitution and public institutions, the historical backbone of the nation? While we’re at it, how about giving a shot to someone whose compassion, empathy, open-mindedness, ability to handle criticism we would consider elite? Someone  with elite mental toughness, who also champions the power of diversity in people, ideas and thought. Finally, I’m a fan of all those “elites” out there who embrace science, make decisions with empirical data and can articulate their vision of how to employ all of the above in making our lives better.
You’re right. That’s a lot to ask. But we’re worth it.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Independent candidates hope to shake up status quo, give Oklahoma voters alternative option
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Frustration with mainstream political parties prompted a number of independents to file for office. A little over a dozen candidates, many of whom are fed up with partisan divides, will appear as independents on Oklahoma’s general election ballot in November. They hope their candidacy will give Oklahoma voters an alternative option to […]
text:
Voters mark their ballots in the Crown Heights Christian Church on June 16, 2026 in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Frustration with mainstream political parties prompted a number of independents to file for office.
A little over a dozen candidates, many of whom are fed up with partisan divides, will appear as independents on Oklahoma’s general election ballot in November.
They hope their candidacy will give Oklahoma voters an alternative option to the candidates running as nominees for the state’s three recognized political parties.
For two decades, Oklahoma’s Republican and Democrat parties have “pitted neighbor against neighbor,” said Robert Brooks, one of three independents running for governor against Republican Mike Mazzei and Democrat Cyndi Munson. 
“They’ve stirred up race relations,” Brooks said of Republicans and Democrats. “They have stirred up all kinds of nonsense.”
Robert Brooks (Provided photo)
People are hungry for leadership and unity, not division, he said.
As of Feb. 2, independents made up 20.4% of the state’s slightly more than 2.4 million voters, according to the Oklahoma State Election Board. 
Republicans composed 53.2% of Oklahoma voters while Democrats made up 25.3%. Almost 1% of voters identified as Libertarian.
Brooks, a Moore resident who has an insurance brokerage, said when he meets voters on the campaign trail and tells them he is an independent candidate, “they glow.” 
“They will just grin,” he said. “They will just smile. It is like their whole body language changes.”
Melissa Elder, a mental health therapist from Moore, is a registered independent running for Senate District 24. She’ll face Republican Jon Painter and Democrat Jonathan Morales in November. 
Republican Darrell Weaver, the incumbent, decided not to seek reelection and after making a failed bid for lieutenant governor was named Cleveland County sheriff.
“I’m just fed up with things not happening, and I felt like I needed to take action,” Elder said. “Running for office was the only way that I could, you know, put some energy behind doing something instead of just complaining.”
She described independents’ political beliefs as “a mixed bag.”
“People leave parties and register as independents for all different kinds of reasons and have all different kinds of ideas about political ideology,” she said.
Valentin Peña (Provided photo)
Elder, a former Democrat, said a lot of independents don’t see the party they align with as getting things done.
“We’ve opted out of playing that game,” she said.
Valentin Peña, a merchandiser for the Walton Corp. who lives in Lawton, said a dissatisfaction with politics at both the state and national level prompted him to run as an independent for Senate District 32. He’ll face Republican Curtis Erwin and Democrat Booker T. Newton. Incumbent Sen. Dusty Deevers, R-Elgin, lost his re-election bid in the primary.
“I was tired of seeing people not running on any of the policy positions I was looking for, so I decided to do it myself,” Peña said. “Because if there were no candidates I was going to be able to be willing to vote for, I was going to be a candidate I’d be willing to vote for.”
He said he hasn’t seen the progress he wanted from the current political system, which is dominated by Republicans and Democrats.
He also disagrees with the state’s closed partisan primary system, which restricts who can vote for candidates in those elections. In order to cast a ballot in a Republican, Democrat, or Libertarian primary, Oklahomans must be a registered voter of that party. Party leaders can decide to open the primary to registered independents. Democrats had previously opened their primaries to independents, but their primaries were closed this year.
“There’s no reason that we should have closed any kind of elections,” Peña said. “Who you decide to register as should not affect who you should be able to vote for.”
An initiative petition seeking to ask voters to open primaries was determined not to have collected enough valid signatures. But that decision is being challenged.
Robert Henri (Provided photo)
Like other independent candidates interviewed by Oklahoma Voice, Robert Henri said he is frustrated with the overarching role money plays in elections and believes there should be some tighter restrictions.
“It’s ridiculous,” said Henri, who is running for U.S. Representative in Oklahoma’s 5th Congressional District. 
Henri, an Edmond resident who runs a manufacturing facility, faces incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Stephanie Bice, Democrat Jena Nelson and fellow independent Austin Nieves.
Like other candidates, Henri said he is frustrated with the lack of progress under the current system and with the amount of money used to fund it.
“I feel like both sides are playing the same game,” Henri said. “They can scream and yell about their sides all they want, but at the end of the day, nothing is going to happen.”

name: WyoFile
title: Three sheriff’s offices sign up for jail mental health hold reimbursements under new Wyoming law
description:
The law allows the health department to pay jails for holding and treating people with mental illnesses while they await a bed at the state hospital. 
The post Three sheriff’s offices sign up for jail mental health hold reimbursements under new Wyoming law appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Three sheriff’s offices will be the first under a new law to receive reimbursements from the Wyoming Department of Health for lengthy mental health holds in their jails. 
Sheriff’s offices in Natrona, Laramie and Sheridan counties have finalized contracts with the health department and can now start billing the agency under a measure that went into effect in March. The department is also working with other interested counties and expects more participation in coming months, Monique McBride, the agency’s chief policy and communications officer, told WyoFile.
The new law allows the health department to pay jails for holding and treating people with mental illnesses until they’re evaluated to determine whether they can handle court proceedings, and to restore them to that capacity if needed. Lawmakers approved $5 million to pay for these reimbursements through 2028. 
The contracts offer two per-client, per-day reimbursements. The first is a $100 “holding payment,” which covers the cost of “security, housing, and baseline custodial care.” The second is a $250 “treatment payment.” The $250 covers the holding payment plus costs for inmate psychiatric treatment. 
The new measure gives law enforcement agencies flexibility over what treatment they offer and how they provide it, depending on the resources available locally. As a result, the mental health services of each agency are likely to be different. 
“A lot of good, independent work has been done, and we’re just trying to use this new law that passed and the resources that come with it to reinforce and further build that out,” Wyoming Department of Health Director Steffan Johansson said. 
Gov. Mark Gordon and the Legislature strongly supported the measure, which lawmakers considered after learning about the challenges jails face housing people with mental illnesses while they wait for a bed at the state-run psychiatric hospital in Evanston. 
Judges send more people to the Wyoming State Hospital than there are beds available. Such court orders have increased in recent years, both in Wyoming and nationwide, although the volume has recently stabilized a little in Wyoming, Johannson told WyoFile. Judges issue these orders both in criminal and civil courts. The new law addresses the criminal court side of the problem, when a person accused of committing a crime is found mentally incompetent to stand trial.
But the law isn’t “just about cutting checks” for jails holding inmates awaiting services at the state hospital, Johansson said. It’s a piece of a larger puzzle that is meant to work alongside other efforts to address mental health challenges throughout Wyoming’s justice system. “I think we have an agreement on the problem that we’re really trying to decompress and stabilize the entire system, which includes our state hospital, also their jails and their court systems.”
In 2025, the health department and law enforcement around Wyoming launched a pilot telepsychiatry program that gives officers smart-tablet access to trained clinicians working remotely. The program aims to help officers better interact with people who may be grappling with a mental health crisis. 
Law enforcement in Natrona, Laramie and Campbell counties are also participating in a pilot diversion program that connects people charged with low-level misdemeanors with community mental health treatment. These programs aim to intercept mental health challenges on the front end and get people out of the justice system more quickly. 
Johansson said the new law “can help bolster” these arrangements with law enforcement. “That’s what’s exciting to build out.” 
Staffing shortages at the state hospital have also contributed to the backlog of people waiting for competency evaluations and restoration. Lawmakers approved state employee raises this year, which included raises for health professionals at state facilities. Those salary boosts went into effect in July. Since then, Johansson said the health department has seen a “marked improvement” in recruiting for nurses and CNAs. Off the top of his head, he recalled six or seven health workers who had accepted state employee positions at the state hospital in the last month. “I think the driving factor there is the deal is better. We’re paying a more competitive wage for those folks.” 
While the volume of court orders has been relatively stable recently, wait times for admission to the state hospital have fallen, Johansson said. The average inpatient wait time for those ordered to the state hospital under Wyoming’s criminal statutes dropped in the past year from about four months on average to roughly three months. 
Whether these trends are indicative of a long-term shift remains to be seen. Johansson noted that the volume of court orders fluctuates from month to month. “We know that our courts and our jails and our hospitals are still seeing challenges with wait lists and wait times, so it is absolutely not solved, but the trend has been coming down,” Johansson said. 
The health department will share a report on facilities’ use of reimbursement contracts under the new law with the Joint Judiciary Committee by October 2027. Johansson said the department is in contact with other law enforcement agencies and expects more to participate in the coming months.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Sexual harassment gets you fired from most jobs. But the Oklahoma House prefers a softer approach.
description: If anyone in the private sector had sexual harassment claims substantiated by human resources they’d be out. Fired. Whatever terminology you prefer. That goes double if that employee also demonstrated such horrendously bad judgment that they were involved in a situation that resulted in a cup of urine being left on an assistant’s desk.  But […]
text:
The House Rules Committee listens to Rep. Danny Williams, R-Seminole, give a statement ahead of a vote to censure and take action against him following allegations of misconduct and sexual harassment. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)If anyone in the private sector had sexual harassment claims substantiated by human resources they’d be out. Fired. Whatever terminology you prefer.
That goes double if that employee also demonstrated such horrendously bad judgment that they were involved in a situation that resulted in a cup of urine being left on an assistant’s desk. 
But not in the Oklahoma House, where a committee stopped short of recommending expulsion for state Rep. Danny Williams.
That bipartisan group of lawmakers met behind closed doors for two days last month to hear testimony from witnesses and victims before determining that Williams, R-Seminole, had sexually harassed multiple women and urinated in that cup.
But rather than vote to discipline the 77-year-old by expelling him, this committee merely recommended the full House reprimand him — the equivalent of a public slap on the wrist.
They also recommended that Williams be stripped of all committee assignments and leadership posts, lose access to a legislative assistant and have no one-on-one contact with House staff. (They didn’t address how they’re going to protect his constituents from having one-on-one contact.)
This committee also suggested Williams complete “approved sexual harassment and toxic workplace training,” though apparently nobody can require him to do that.
They also called on him to resign and not seek reelection, but again that’s optional. So far, he hasn’t done those either.
Rather, Williams denied the claims and called the process unfair.
Despite the fact this is an HR issue and not a criminal trial, Williams complained that he “couldn’t challenge” those who accused him or “deal with false statements.”
He also denied urinating in the cup despite House Speaker Kyle Hilbert saying Williams was one of only two people working late that night that could have done it. (Even if he didn’t personally urinate in that cup, it’s not the job of William’s assistant to dispose of bodily fluids that belong in a toilet.)
Rep. Andy Fugate, D-Oklahoma City, said if any employee of a private business had faced the same accusations, they would have been terminated.
But Fugate said the House “is limited by its rules, procedures, and the reality of an election just weeks away.”
“The action taken today was all we had available, but it was not enough,” he said. “The House employees who came forward deserve better, and so do the people of Oklahoma.”
They certainly do.
The outcome of the committee hearing was an embarrassment. What was the point of expending the resources on this farce if they weren’t going to actually recommend anything substantive, enforceable and that actually protects the public from the behavior they allege Williams to have perpetuated?
To his credit, Hilbert had previously implemented some of the committee’s recommendations that included stripping Williams of his committee assignments and leadership posts and moving his office to the fifth floor. Hilbert later said he’ll permanently implement the rest of the recommendations, which include no one-on-one contact with House staff. He said he couldn’t force Williams to resign or to complete sexual harassment and toxic workplace training.
So this bipartisan committee left the room metaphorically wringing their hands, and lamenting that they tried their best – but saying those hands were also metaphorically tied.
They might want you to think that, but it’s not true.
Lawmakers have the power to expel each other with a two-thirds vote, but first they need to put on their big boy pants and muster up the guts to kick out one of their own.
While they shouldn’t use that power lightly, if any behavior calls for expulsion, sexual harassment seems to.
I mean, good Lord, the House committee reported that they substantiated the claims of multiple victims. There was even urine involved. Ew.
So that begs the question, why aren’t House members willing to expel their own?
In recent years, they’ve never expelled anyone. They came closest with former Republican Rep. Dan Kirby. A different House investigatory committee found he had sexually harassed an employee and rightly recommended expulsion. Kirby, who denied the accusation, resigned before the House could consider it.
It’s clear House leadership and some Republicans lack the political willpower to police their own membership and friends.
Don’t believe me? Rep. David Hardin, R-Stilwell, inexplicably voted against 2 of 3 disciplinary recommendations. The only one he supported was the do-nothing public reprimand.
Then after the hearing, Hilbert made this comment about Williams: “I think one of the most frustrating things about this is just not acknowledging what has happened, or not having remorse and just kind of doubling down. Because I think with a lot of these things, remorse would have went a long way. But unfortunately, that was not the choice that he chose to make, and so here we are today.”
“Remorse” doesn’t ever excuse sexual harassment. That committee should convene anytime there’s substantiated behavior that would get someone fired in the private sector, regardless of whether someone apologizes.
These aren’t children still learning appropriate behavior.
These are adults who are supposed to be overseeing billions of public dollars. Part of their job is ensuring the people employed in our Capitol are safe from unwanted sexual conduct regardless of whether the offender is an elected official.
The Capitol is also a place where tens of thousands of everyday Oklahomans visit their elected leaders. Oklahomans shouldn’t have to worry that someone is going to sexually harass them or wonder if lawmakers will sweep it under the rug to protect each other.
If lawmakers behave badly, Oklahomans should know there will be zero tolerance.
Sorry doesn’t cut it. Expulsion does.
We cannot let a good ol’ boys culture continue to thrive where there’s an attitude of “Gawrsh,” as Goofy likes to drawl when he’s surprised or dismayed, anytime an elected official behaves badly.
Williams’ accusers are probably still going to see him around the state Capitol, and this outcome is exactly why people are afraid to come forward.
Our Statehouse should not be allowed to operate like the worst fraternity houses that we see on the news where people are hazed, members are drunk and women are mistreated.
It seems like lawmakers’ motto is “voters will take care of problems.” 
Why should victims have to wait for relief? Why should voters have to do this? And what happens if voters don’t?
If a lawmaker wins reelection, they’ll turn back up like a bad penny. 
And now duly warned, taxpayers will be on the hook to pay to defend costly lawsuits for any future misconduct if lawmakers continue to refuse to protect us all from their colleagues.

title: What makes Yellowstone unique is at risk
authors: Andrew Hansen, Writers on the Range
description:
Following decades of expanding and protecting the wild lands that hold the ecosystem together, the Trump administration is working to fragment them, Writers on the Range contributor Andrew Hansen writes.
The post What makes Yellowstone unique is at risk appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

There’s a major reason that Yellowstone National Park attracts close to 5 million visitors every year. Yes, there are spectacular geysers and world-class trout rivers, but what’s unique about the national park is that it’s home to all the wild animals native to its area, from grizzly bears and wolves to elk, deer and bison. 
That they flourish is due to Yellowstone’s huge expanse of wildlands — you’d have to drive 1,000 miles to circle what’s called the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem.  
But new policies from Washington would dramatically reduce the size of these wildlands and threaten wildlife’s ability to survive.
Bigger is better for wildland ecosystems, a lesson learned soon after Yellowstone was established as the nation’s first national park in 1872.  When Gen. Philip Sheridan explored the region, he realized even then that the park was far too small to contain its migrating wildlife; he urged expanding the park. I’m an ecologist who has studied the region, and we know even better today that climate, soils and food sources vary enormously from place to place, causing wildlife to sometimes seek new ground.
Through the years, Congress has understood this pattern and acted. Federally protected lands around Yellowstone have been steadily enlarged, with national forests created in the late 1800s, designated wilderness areas created in the 1960s, along with wilderness study areas from the 1970s to 1980s, and inventoried roadless areas in the 1990s. 
The Yellowstone ecosystem now has as much — or more — lands protected for wildlife than anywhere else in the lower 48 states. These lands are needed to keep intact what makes Yellowstone unique.
Grizzly bears in Yellowstone. (Tom Murphy)
Protected federal lands have been the most important buffer against fragmented and developed private lands. In an Ecosphere paper, I reported that on privately owned land, vital signs of ecological health across greater Yellowstone had mostly deteriorated since 1970. But it was the opposite on protected federal lands, with most remaining stable or improving. 
As this disparity became widely known, conservation collaboratives have formed to maintain or restore wildlife habitat on large private ranches, while also helping rural homeowners and recreationists learn how to reduce their impacts on wildlife.  
For example, the Greater Yellowstone Coalition is using wildlife-friendly fencing to contain cattle while still allowing wildlife to migrate. The coalition also supports range rider programs to reduce predator impacts on cattle. And the Teton Conservation District provides “The Mountain Neighbor Handbook: A Local’s Guide to Stewardship in the Tetons” to new residents around Jackson.  
Now, this administration is promoting policies that harm, rather than help, the Yellowstone area. If enacted, these policies would:

Accelerate logging in national forests and expand access for motorized vehicles.
Open inventoried roadless areas to roadbuilding, logging and mining. 
Roll back protections for wilderness study areas.
Open the habitats of endangered species to development.

The Trump administration is telling us that these policy changes are needed to reduce fuels and protect communities from severe wildfires. The science shows otherwise. An analysis published in the International Journal of Wildland Fire in 2014 found that people’s lives and property are best protected by reducing fuels immediately around homes — not in remote wildlands that are critical for wildlife.
Stripping federal land protections would deliver a knife to the heart of what makes Yellowstone special. Unfortunately, the other great natural ecosystems across the country face the same loss of protections.
What can we do? Comment on the Roadless Rule before Oct. 6. We can also speak loudly and tell our elected representatives to halt the administration’s destructive policies. We can vote wisely in November to stop proposed rollbacks of federal land protections.
If we can block these threats, we can return to working collaboratively across ranchland associations, land trusts, conservation groups, local and tribal governments, recreationists, residents and visitors. We all know how precious wild country and wild animals are to this nation, and we’ve learned what it takes to keep wildlife thriving. 
We have to fight harder than ever now to keep intact the wild places we have left.

title: The mountain elite: Wyoming’s Lorna Corson, among the first Grand Canyon boatwomen
description:
She was small and shy and the boss wouldn’t hire her. So his wife did.
The post The mountain elite: Wyoming’s Lorna Corson, among the first Grand Canyon boatwomen appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Grand Canyon river guide Lorna Corson negotiated notorious rapids for more than four decades, keeping clients safe with her skills and knowledge. It took skill, determination and courage on the water. Clients have credited her safety lectures for saving their lives.
Yet one of the most fulfilling parts of her job was relating to her passengers and seeing them open up to the natural world, like the 300-pound city slicker.
After floating through the canyon his first time and enjoying the ambles and scrambles out of camps, “he started hiking — and came every single year for 30 years,” Corson said. “He got to half the weight he was.”
Guides can help passengers absorb the awe of a 6,000-foot deep gorge that stretches almost 300 miles. “Their values change,” Corson said of many clients. “I’ve seen people quit their jobs after one trip.
“Every guide appreciates how they made an impact on somebody’s life, created a life-altering experience. You hear it all the time. That’s pretty rewarding.”
Corson earned her way into the elite profession, among the first women to row clients through the Colorado River’s foam, frenzy and froth. She was an unlikely pioneer — only 5 foot 3 inches tall boasting a fighting weight of 120 pounds. On the oars of a large, inflatable raft capable of holding hundreds of pounds of gear and people, how could she possibly get through the V-wave at Lava Falls, the Charybdis holes of Crystal Rapid and the rock maze of Hance?
“I had to convince people that I could row the big ones. I don’t think anybody let me row Crystal till I had my own boat.”
She succeeded by reading the water and rowing smart for Arizona Raft Adventures, safeguarding thousands of visitors through the canyon’s storied sandstone walls.
“As soon as I rowed, it just felt intuitive,” Corson said. “It just really clicked for me.”
That was in 1977 when she was a 23-year-old trainee, and mentors were testing her skills. A child of a National Park Service family, she lived in Flagstaff.
“They were kind of judging your ability and whether they would trust you with their boat,” she said of the veteran, male guides. “I had to convince people that I could row the big ones.”
“I got to row Lava early,” she said of one famous rapid. “Crystal was the last one. I don’t think anybody let me row Crystal till I had my own boat.”
Being a woman guide was “very much a new thing,” Corson said. But guide Louise Teal’s 1978 all-women’s expedition was a breakthrough. “We didn’t have that many women boatmen but they shipped them in from Idaho and California.” Corson said. (A photograph of Corson is the cover of Teal‘s book “Breaking into the Current” about boatwomen in the Grand Canyon.)
Regardless, the company boss wasn’t impressed, Corson said.
“I was pretty introverted, and most guides tend to be extroverts. And my size — definitely he was not sure about that.”
His wife was. “She’s the one that actually hired me.”
Courson learned the character of the desert river – pool, drop, pool, drop and of the elusive seam between current and eddy.
“There’s a lot of slow water … it’s hard to see the currents, especially in the wind. Then there’s these huge eddies. If you get in an eddy, you can row your brains out and you won’t get anywhere. You can see very large, strong people struggling.”
Rapids present a different challenge — knowing where you want to go and then maneuvering.
“Where you enter the rapid is huge. (If) someone’s a foot left of you or right of you, they have a different run.”
Keeping the boat angled correctly is paramount, “especially if you’re entering a difficult rapid where you have to do a downstream ferry.
“You enter backwards and pull really hard at like 45 degrees to the current to get exactly where you want. Eventually you turn forward again to face the big waves.
“Because I was small, I felt like it was more imperative that I have my timing exactly right — the entry and my angle — so that I could make sure I was where I wanted to be without having to pull too hard.
“If you kind of hesitate on the entry a little bit longer and you’re bigger, maybe you can get where you want to be. But I felt like I had to be on it and have that perfect angle.”
In the tumult, there’s a sweet spot to pull or push on the oars to reorient or move the raft.
“If you’re on the peak [of a wave} and you take a couple strokes, you’re going to pivot very quickly. If you’re in the trough, you’re going to have to work a lot harder to because there’s so much more resistance on the boat.”
“If you get in an eddy, you can row your brains out and you won’t get anywhere. You can see very large, strong people struggling.”
Reading water and rowing came naturally, “more than anything else I’ve done in my life.” But passengers couldn’t see her abilities and were hesitant to ride with her “because I was young and female.
“In the end it was just the opposite,” Corson said of her career. “I don’t know why. Things did change. Maybe (it was) just being older. As soon as they hear you’ve been working down there for decades, that gives some confidence.”
When Corson got hired, other boatwomen began appearing on the scene. “It made the dynamics of the whole trip better for the passengers and the boatmen and the boatwomen. It was just much more balanced.”
Flagstaff was too big a city and decades ago an “inner voice” told her to move north. Wyoming had the “perfect climate” and few people. “Once I got here, it was obvious that it was where I wanted to be.
“Right away it felt safe in many ways,” Corson said. “I like Wilson and the mountains, of course.”
Today, Jackson Hole embraces women guides. “I think it’s pretty liberated that way now because it’s a town or community where people are playing a lot. But [it] was a while — decades, in the making. I don’t think it was [liberated] 45 years ago at all.”
Corson also is a carpenter and cabinetmaker, in business with her husband Norm Larson. It was hard to convince people in that profession that she was capable. It was harder than breaking into the Grand Canyon current.
“Carpenters were more old-style, more traditional … it’s a totally male-dominated field.”
After decades, people still don’t get it, she said.
“I’ve been doing carpentry for 40 years, but people always ask me what Norm is doing. We’re partners, and we have been for a long time, and we both work in the shop, and it’s our business. That always seemed kind of strange. Even people I know well still go, ‘What’s Norm working on?’
“I got a lot of recognition as a boatwoman, but I got hardly any as a carpenter, and I’m a big part of our business.
“I’m surprised,” she said.
A geology major in college, Corson is an avid rock climber, embracing the physical challenge, enjoying the movement and “a little bit of adrenaline.” With Larson, she’s completed exceptional routes, including on the dominating Lotus Flower Tower in Canada’s Northwest Territories.
“I like it more and more,” she said of rock climbing. At 72, “it’s getting physically harder.”
“We don’t care how hard we’re playing or what anybody else is doing,” she said, “It just feels good.”

title: Supporters and opponents of Idaho’s abortion rights initiative, Prop 1, have raised millions
description: Two Idaho political action committees, or PACS, on both sides of the proposed abortion rights initiative, Proposition 1, have spent $1.3 million combined, and raised nearly $7.5 million total. The ballot measure’s supporters have outpaced its opponents in both fundraising and spending so far.  So far, the main PAC supporting the measure has out-raised the […[...]
text:
Photos of the official petition for a ballot initiative to restore abortion access in Idaho, which were submitted to Attorney General Raúl Labrador’s office. (Photo courtesy of Melanie Folwell)Two Idaho political action committees, or PACS, on both sides of the proposed abortion rights initiative, Proposition 1, have spent $1.3 million combined, and raised nearly $7.5 million total. The ballot measure’s supporters have outpaced its opponents in both fundraising and spending so far. 
So far, the main PAC supporting the measure has out-raised the primary PAC that’s opposing the ballot measure — the measure’s supporters’ Idahoans United for Women and Families PAC had collected around $4.9 million as of Sept. 29 from more than 3,000 donors, while the measure’s opponents of the Too Extreme for Idaho PAC brought in about $2.5 million from 83, according to the Idaho Secretary of State campaign finance database. 
Just over $12,300 has been contributed from church-affiliated groups to both sides of the issue, according to an Idaho Capital Sun analysis of campaign finance data. 
In August, Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador published an opinion that allows churches to spend money supporting or opposing ballot initiatives without disclosing their donors — as long as they don’t ask congregants to donate specifically about the measure, Boise State Public Radio reported. 
The majority of independent expenditures — money spent without coordination with a campaign to support or oppose the ballot measure — were made in opposition to the ballot measure. County Republican Party central committees made most of these expenditures.
The measure’s supporters have not yet raised as much as the PAC formed in 2023 to campaign for a ballot initiative that would’ve made Idaho’s primary elections non-partisan and use top-four ranked choice voting Idahoans for Open Primaries raised more than $5.6 million, most of which originated out of state. 
More than $4.4 million was spent on independent expenditures to support the ranked choice voting initiative, and around $553,000 was spent in opposition, according to the Secretary of State data dashboard. That measure failed to pass, with nearly 70% of voters voting against it, the Sun previously reported. 



What would Idaho’s Proposition 1 do? 
The initiative would repeal Idaho’s abortion bans, enumerate rights related to reproductive healthcare such as access to contraceptives and IVF, and provide liability protection to doctors providing reproductive healthcare. 
Idaho’s existing laws ban nearly all abortions, with exceptions to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors who perform abortions face felony penalties and minimum prison sentences, licensing penalties, or could be sued in civil court for a minimum of $20,000 by family members of the aborted fetus. 




 PAC opposing Prop 1 raises more than $2.5 million 

The PAC Too Extreme for Idaho opposes the voter initiative. 
The committee, chaired by Katherine Heffner, has raised around $2.5 million and spent nearly $169,000. Nearly all of the money was contributed by Idaho individuals or companies, with $5,100 coming from out of state. 
Its top donors are Angela and James Harrison of Garden City, who have contributed $1 million total. The Harrisons co-founded a charitable foundation, Angels Among Us, and helped establish Idaho’s first Catholic radio station, Salt & Light. 
Dorothy Rebholtz, widow of the late Agri Beef Co co-founder Robert Rebholtz Sr., contributed another $300,000 to the Too Extreme for Idaho PAC. 
Other anti-abortion committees, the Right to Life of Idaho PAC and ID Family PAC, contributed a total of $71,561 to Too Extreme. 
Groups attached to Catholic organizations have contributed $7,161 to the PAC, campaign finance reporting shows. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise contributed $2,000, and Catholic fraternal groups, called Knights of Columbus Councils, from around the state contributed the rest.  
Most of the PAC’s spending has gone toward surveys and polls, totalling $94,142.The group has also spent nearly $52,500 on broadcast and other types of advertising, including production and preparation of advertising, according to campaign finance data. 
 PAC supporting Prop 1 brings in nearly $5 million 

The Idahoans United for Women and Families PAC, formed by the group that gathered signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot and wrote the initiative, has brought in around $4.9 million, campaign finance data shows as of Sept. 29. 
Idahoans United was created in 2024 to explore a ballot initiative to restore and protect access to abortion and reproductive healthcare, after members expressed frustration that legislators would not add an exception to Idaho’s strict abortion ban to protect the health of the mother, the Idaho Capital Sun reported at the time.  
The PAC, chaired by the Meridian OB-GYN Becky Uranga, has spent more than $1.1 million. 

The biggest contributor, donating $650,000 to the Idahoans United PAC, is the D.C.-based Government That Works PAC, which has contributed to races nationwide. The national PAC is the top donor to a PAC supporting the Texas U.S. Senate candidate, Democrat James Talarico, the Texas Tribune reported. 
Ketchum resident Jill Grossman, founder of a foundation that supports nonprofits in Idaho and the San Francisco Bay Area, contributed $254,000 to the Idaho PAC. 
McCall residents Kristine and Jeff Stoddard, who own real estate and construction companies, provided $252,000 to the committee. Minnesota billionaire heiress and equestrian Gwendolyn Sontheim and billionaire businessman and former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg each contributed $250,000. 
Most of the money, or about $3.9 million, came from individual people, while the remaining $1 million came from companies, according to the data. 
In total, $3.2 million of the contributions originated from Idaho individuals and organizations, and $1.7 million came from out-of-state. 
Just over $5,100 came from three church-affiliated groups: Northwest Intermountain Synod, a Lutheran church in Spokane; the Boise Jewish Congregation Ahavath Beth Israel’s Social Action Team; and Boise Unitarian Universalist Fellowship. 
The PAC has spent the most money for management services to Campaign Associates LLC, totalling $631,504.75. The LLC is an entity formed in 2025 by Idahoan’s United’s lead organizer Melanie Folwell to house payroll for the organization’s staff, Folwell told the Idaho Capital Sun. 
The committee has also spent nearly $155,000 on broadcast and other types of advertising, such as yard signs. 
 Groups independently spend more than $29,000 to oppose measure

As of Sep. 30, groups and individuals reported $29,142.79 in total on advertising, brochures, yard signs and more to oppose the measure.
However, there may be more expenditures both for and against the initiative that were not captured in this analysis, because the groups enter the name of the measure when reporting spending, and there were inconsistent entries in the state campaign reporting database — for example some people wrote “Proposition 1,” and others used its title “Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act.”
Republican Party central committees in Ada, Blaine, Bonner and Bonneville counties have reported spending over $9,000 to oppose the measure. The Idaho GOP has been a vocal opponent of the measure. 
In a July press release announcing a statewide effort to oppose the initiative, party leaders wrote that Prop 1 “directly attacks Idaho’s pro-life pro-family values by legalizing abortion in Idaho.” 
The Citizens Alliance of Idaho, a PAC that supports hardline conservative candidates, has also spent nearly $8,300. Moscow-based Forged Construction spent around $4,500. 
Idaho state Sen. Brandon Shippy, R-New Plymouth, also reported spending $1,000 on “preparation and production of advertising” to oppose the measure. 
Idaho Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates reported spending about $250 to support the measure.
