name: Colorado Newsline
title: Boulder, fossil-fuel companies face off at the Supreme Court in high-stakes climate case
description: Attorneys representing two Colorado local governments are set for a high-stakes legal showdown over climate change Monday at the U.S. Supreme Court, where they’ll ask justices to allow Boulder’s lawsuit seeking monetary damages from two fossil fuel companies to proceed in state court. With help from the Trump administration, the two companies, Suncor Energy[...]
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on April 9, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Attorneys representing two Colorado local governments are set for a high-stakes legal showdown over climate change Monday at the U.S. Supreme Court, where they’ll ask justices to allow Boulder’s lawsuit seeking monetary damages from two fossil fuel companies to proceed in state court.
With help from the Trump administration, the two companies, Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil, have asked the court to step in and quash the lawsuit, which was filed in 2018 by Boulder County and the city of Boulder. The plaintiffs are seeking monetary damages under state tort law “for the substantial role (the companies) played and continue to play in causing, contributing to and exacerbating climate change.”
Monday’s Supreme Court hearing in the case, known as Suncor v. Boulder, follows another unprecedented summer of record heat, extreme drought conditions and destructive wildfire activity impacting communities across Colorado. Boulder’s suit is one of more than 30 similar cases filed to date by state and local governments nationwide as human-caused climate change, mostly the result of fossil-fuel combustion, pushes average global temperatures to dangerous new highs.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“This case is really about who’s going to bear the costs of all of these accelerating effects that we’re experiencing on the front lines here in Colorado,” Chris Winter, an environmental attorney and executive director of the Getches-Wilkinson Center at the University of Colorado School of Law, said in an interview. “Are those costs just going to fall on the shoulders of all of the taxpayers and citizens and our local governments? Or is the oil industry going to be at least partially responsible for their role in contributing to this crisis?”
Exxon and Suncor, a Canadian oil giant that operates Colorado’s only fossil fuel refinery, argue that federal law preempts Boulder’s efforts to hold the companies accountable in state court. The defendants have tried and failed repeatedly to have the case dismissed or removed to federal court, most recently in May 2025, when the Colorado Supreme Court issued a ruling allowing the case to proceed.
Soon after that ruling, however, the companies asked the U.S. Supreme Court, where conservatives hold a 6-3 majority, to step in. Their petition asks the nation’s highest court to rule that federal statute “precludes state-law claims seeking relief for injuries allegedly caused by the effects of interstate and international greenhouse-gas emissions on the global climate.”
In February, justices agreed to hear the case, which is set to be among the most closely watched proceedings on the court’s docket for the 2026-27 term, and one of its highest-profile climate change decisions ever. A ruling from the court could have profound consequences for the dozens of other lawsuits seeking climate-related damages from fossil fuel companies, as scientists warn that catastrophic impacts from higher temperatures will continue to accelerate.
The view from aboard a Colorado National Guard helicopter, in which Gov. Jared Polis on Dec. 31, 2021, got a flyover tour of Boulder County neighborhoods destroyed by wildfires the previous day. (Hart Van Denburg/CPR, pool)
In an unusual move, President Donald J. Trump’s administration filed an unsolicited brief in support of Suncor and Exxon’s petition shortly after it was filed, urging the court to overturn the Colorado Supreme Court’s decision, which it called “contrary to the Constitution.” Alongside petitioners and respondents, U.S. Solicitor General John Sauer will be given time during Monday’s oral arguments to represent the Trump administration’s position in support of the companies.
“We’ve seen this administration really bend over backwards to serve the interests of the fossil-fuel industry, and this case is just one of many examples,” Winter said. “A lot of us who watch the court and have studied these issues for a long time are quite troubled by some of the legal arguments this administration has used, to try to undercut the ability of the states to protect (their) citizens, and to insulate the oil industry from liability for its actions.”
Alito’s recusal
In another unusual development, Justice Samuel Alito, one of the Supreme Court’s most conservative members, recused himself from further proceedings in the case last week.
Though the court’s announcement did not explain why, environmental advocates had called for Alito’s recusal because he owns stock in at least two oil companies. He previously stepped aside from a separate environmental case involving the oil industry in January of this year.
Critics say Alito’s abrupt recusal, announced just days before oral argument, raises the question of why he nonetheless participated in the court’s deliberations over whether to take up the case in the first place. Known as granting a writ of certiorari, that process requires at least four of the court’s nine justices to agree to accept a petition. The court does not release such votes publicly.
“We don’t know whether Alito’s vote made the difference, and that uncertainty is precisely the problem,” Alexandra Nagy, organizing director of the nonprofit Consumer Watchdog, said in a statement last week. “The Court is preparing to hear a case of enormous national consequence after one of the justices who participated in granting review concluded days before the hearing that he should no longer participate. If Alito was the fourth vote, this case should be dismissed.”
In their petition, Suncor and Exxon raise the specter of “potentially crushing monetary liability” imposed on fossil fuel companies for what they repeatedly refer to as the “alleged harms” of climate change.
The Suncor oil refinery in Commerce City is one of Colorado’s largest sources of air pollution. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
“The requested damages in any one case could reach into the billions,” attorneys for the companies wrote. “And if claims such as Boulder’s are allowed to proceed, every political jurisdiction in the Nation could bring a similar suit against any subset of the world’s fossil-fuel producers.”
Attorneys for Boulder’s city and county governments say it’s far too early for the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case — which, despite having been filed eight years ago, has not even proceeded to the trial stage amid the protracted jurisdictional challenges made by the companies. Neither the Constitution nor any legislation passed Congress preempts the state’s authority to try the case under tort law, they argue.
“Unwilling to let either the federal legislative or the state judicial process play out, (Suncor and Exxon) have run to this Court at the case’s outset, claiming that something implicit in the Constitution resolves the debate,” Boulder’s attorneys wrote in a response to the court.
“The conservative justices, and conservative line of thinking, usually interprets the Constitution in a way that protects the authority of the states, unless there’s been a very explicit grant of limited authority to the federal government that’s found in the text of the Constitution,” Winter said. “But this case flies directly in the face of that typical way of looking at the Constitution — because there’s nothing in the text of the Constitution that says states are preempted in this field.”

 Catching Our Eye

• We’ve all been there… The Ohio Newsroom’s Kaitlin Thorne digs into “The challenge of growing colossal pumpkins inside Ohio’s prisons”
Behind barbed-wired fences and multiple security checks sits a small patch of land in the center of the Belmont Correctional Institution in southeast Ohio’s Belmont County.
The growing season is over, so it doesn’t look like much now, but just a few weeks ago it was home to a colossal pumpkin weighing 1,700 lbs.
The pumpkin-growing tradition dates back to 2022, when Mansfield Correctional Institution issued a challenge: grow the biggest pumpkin in a prison yard. The Larry Stewart Giant Pumpkin Challenge, in its fifth year, now involves correctional institutions across the state.
• Notes from the underground. The Cincinnati Enquirer’s Sydney Franklin reports, “Cincinnati firms chosen to plan next steps on reviving subway tunnels”
The effort to revive Cincinnati’s abandoned subway tunnels is not over. And some of the world’s leading design and engineering experts have vied to study how to repurpose them, a sign that this could be more than a city daydream.
Over-the-Rhine-based Woolpert Inc. was ultimately chosen to lead the study for $284,073.
City records obtained by The Enquirer reveal that Woolpert and its team have likely been working on the feasibility study throughout this year. The final study is estimated to be done by early 2027.
• Delay tactics. Jonathan Walsh from News5Cleveland reports, “A man has lived in a $4.5 million mansion for 15 years while fighting foreclosure — now he’s facing eviction”
Louis Telerico has been living in a 17,000-square-foot home in Barrington Estates, an exclusive residential area in Aurora, near the 17th green of a golf course.
A foreclosure on the property began in August 2011. Court records show Telerico filed numerous motions over the years, including multiple bankruptcies, appeals, and other filings. The foreclosure took 14 years before the bank finally acquired the property in 2025, then sold it to investment company ERADAL.
At a recent eviction hearing, a magistrate approved the eviction of Telerico. However, Telerico’s attorney, Mark Graziani, indicated the situation may not be fully resolved.
Telerico told News 5 he plans to live in the house until he dies and said he believes he will be able to secure financing.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: What I learned from reading over 200 Alabama political campaign sites
description: We here at Alabama Reflector take state government reporting seriously. That’s why we released this comprehensive guide to Alabama’s elections last week. To get that guide together, or to address some unresolved Catholic guilt, I read more than 200 web and Facebook pages. All hosted by state officials or those aspiring to join their ranks. […]
text:
Voters wait in line at First Baptist Church during Election Day on Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024 in Huntsville, Ala. (Eric Schultz for Alabama Reflector)We here at Alabama Reflector take state government reporting seriously. That’s why we released this comprehensive guide to Alabama’s elections last week.
To get that guide together, or to address some unresolved Catholic guilt, I read more than 200 web and Facebook pages. All hosted by state officials or those aspiring to join their ranks.
Journalism is glamorous.
The material was not scintillating. Politicians try to position themselves in the center of their voters’ moods, and there’s almost never anything original or surprising in their material. There’s far too much awfulness about immigrants and transgender people. And there seem to be just three presentations for an Alabama politician, according to their campaign photos: Stranded in the woods with your family; stranded in the woods with a firearm and exiting a church laughing, presumably after the rangers found you.
And these sites can’t tell us the whole story about a candidate or a campaign. You need to see what candidates say to voters and what they shove into their mailboxes. 
Still, across all those URLs, some patterns emerged.
Everyone hates the grocery tax: The levy never won a popularity contest. But legislative candidates on both sides of the aisle are committed to reducing or repealing the 2% state tax on groceries.
They might have the chance next year. Rep. Danny Garrett, R-Trussville, the chair of the House Ways and Means Education Committee, is drawing up a bill to abolish the levy in the next session. Budget issues could make that complicated. But if politicians keep their promises, the grocery tax may be on borrowed time.
Democrats seeking a state minimum wage: Alabama lacks a state minimum wage, meaning it defaults to the federal wage of $7.25 an hour, unchanged since 2009. When Birmingham tried to set its own minimum wage in 2016, the business community got Republican lawmakers to crush it.
So it’s notable to see many Democratic candidates calling for Alabama to set its own wage floor. The party hasn’t ignored the issue in the past. Sen. Robert Stewart, D-Selma, this year introduced a $10-an-hour minimum wage bill. It went nowhere in the Republican-controlled Legislature, even though it exempted businesses with fewer than 50 employees. Still, among Democrats, the issue never went front-and-center like Medicaid expansion or a lottery. It’s certainly a lot less appealing to the powerful Business Council of Alabama.  
Republicans are almost certain to hold onto the Legislature next year, so minimum wage measures will likely remain aspirational. But it’s a sign of where the caucus might go in the future.
Republicans (mostly) forget Trump: The crowds around the Alabama Republican Party’s altar to Donald Trump have thinned out. There are still plenty of people worshipping at the president’s feet. But after a decade of Trump’s will being the only issue for Alabama Republicans, the president’s cratering popularity may finally be catching up to him. 
Many GOP candidates went to Trump’s Mobile rally on Friday to pay their respects, including Tommy Tuberville, the gubernatorial nominee. But Tuberville, once a human kazoo for the president, has yet to mention him in a general election ad. Further down the ballot, many if not most Republican legislative candidates avoid talking about him.
Trump won’t lack fans in the next legislative session. But far fewer Republicans seem compelled to follow him.
Candidate mismatches: Democrats drew candidates to more legislative races this year than in 2022. That’s a hopeful sign for the party. But many of those candidates are first-timers. They have a lot of enthusiasm and little experience getting votes. That won’t end well in deep-red regions with entrenched incumbents.
Do Republicans also have first-time candidates? Of course. But it’s a different dynamic for the majority party. The GOP has locked down far more districts and can put a dominant organization behind those venturing into less congenial areas. The Democrats, once again, are driving and building the car at the same time. Keeping the vehicle on the road will be an accomplishment.
To become more competitive in those state contests, the Democrats will need to make major investments in local races — particularly county commissions, which have produced several state senators. Enthusiastic candidates will help get Alabama Democrats back to political relevance. Becoming relevant will require candidates who know how to bring voters with them. 
Competition decreases silliness: It’s hard to say how Huntsville-area legislative races will go. The city and surrounding areas have been edging toward Democrats for years. But Republicans have organization and the power of incumbency. That’s made for some potentially tight contests.
From here, it appears the competitiveness has focused candidates on actual issues, like housing prices and infrastructure. I’m sure that’s not the whole story: I can’t tell you what flyers are hitting people’s inboxes. And I’m skeptical that seriousness can be sustained to Election Day.
But after going through hundreds of political websites, and seeing a lot of issues pages littered with irrelevancies, it’s refreshing to see some earnestness. 
And it’s a reminder that politicians can improve our lives or damage them. So we better have candidates who understand that. The stakes are always high.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: What I learned about West Virginia’s future after driving 10,800 miles
description: As a child, my grandmother and mother told me stories about Point Pleasant, West Virginia. One told of a legendary curse attributed to Shawnee Chief Cornstalk. Years later, his grave at Tu-Endie-Wei State Park called me back there. As I stood before his grave, more than the story of Cornstalk came through to me. And […]
text:
The Chief Cornstalk memorial marker at Tu-Endie-Wei State Park in Point Pleasant, West Virginia. (Photo courtesy of Brian Neal Bollinger)As a child, my grandmother and mother told me stories about Point Pleasant, West Virginia. One told of a legendary curse attributed to Shawnee Chief Cornstalk. Years later, his grave at Tu-Endie-Wei State Park called me back there. As I stood before his grave, more than the story of Cornstalk came through to me. And more than ever, I could hear my grandmother and mom in my mind. They had told me of his grave. And they had hinted that his story was more than the one they’d told me.
That hint led me to visit 25 reputedly haunted places across America, including sites featured by Reader’s Digest. Over nine days in August, I drove across the contiguous U.S. from one end to the other. At each place, I realized it was often a story that brought people to town. More importantly, through conversations with people living there, I learned much more than I could from any brochure.
West Virginians love a good story. For years, Ruth Ann Musick gathered ghost stories from around the state. She included them in her book, “The Telltale Lilac Bush and Other West Virginia Ghost Tales.” Every fall, Point Pleasant holds the Mothman Festival. I’ve gone there a few times, but more than anything, it was the story of Chief Cornstalk and his grave that stayed with me. 
In that moment, I realized his story meant a great deal to my grandmother, mom and me. Legend says he left a curse on his town. My grandmother and I heard his story, and we discussed it for years.
Often at workshops in this state, students and families ask me about our colleges. Some worry about cost. Others want to stay close to their hometown, their church or their family. Some want to give back to their hometown. In my conversations with students, I’ve realized that enrollment numbers tell us very little. What kind of world will my students find when they graduate? Is success possible here? Would they feel they were compromising by staying here?
In Man and Welch, I met people whose local economies were changing. Their stories are rich and could easily be the subject of a book. But more importantly, I think their stories ought to be more than what they are remembered for. Every day, people in these communities make decisions about work, school and family. They’re building their lives here. They would welcome visitors to their towns. And they want a say in decisions about their future.
I grew up in Parkersburg. Over the years, I’ve traveled to every county in West Virginia. And in every county, someone could point to something about their county that would be worth knowing. It would be valuable to preserve stories of people and places here. And more importantly, these stories should be told in all their richness, not just the parts that might interest outsiders.
To think about the future of any community, we should think beyond visitors who come here on the weekend. Instead, we could ask whether residents could live full, meaningful lives in their community throughout the year. That could start with asking residents what they think a visitor or a young person might want to know about their community. It could start with businesses in their community serving residents year-round, not just visitors. It could also start with helping students consider careers and education in their own community.
Each of these communities (Point Pleasant, Man and Welch) would have a different answer, depending on their history, their time and their circumstances. More important than any particular message about West Virginia is listening to each community on its own.
In their stories, they could tell us what they value about their community, what’s changed for them, and what they’d like to see. And once we heard their stories, we could make better decisions about our own communities. Through stories from my grandmother and my mother, I felt a desire to do more than they could.
After my 10,800-mile journey, I thought of the young people I meet in my workshops in West Virginia. I’d like them someday to see more of the world than they do now. And if they do decide to return, I hope they’ll have the opportunity to pursue the life they want.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Where you happen to be standing when angels pass by
description: At Standard & Poor’s in New York, I had young analysts with credentials far better than mine, MBAs from schools I could not have afforded to walk past. Every few months one of them would appear in my doorway and say, “Mr. Branscome, I’d like to discuss my career.” Because I liked them, I told […]
text:
Built in 1938 and renovated as recently as 2002, the Draper Building is one of the largest academic buildings on the Berea College Campus. It houses a variety of departments and programs, including Sustainability and Environmental Studies and Women's and Gender Studies. (Photo courtesy Crystal Wylie/Berea College)At Standard & Poor’s in New York, I had young analysts with credentials far better than mine, MBAs from schools I could not have afforded to walk past.
Every few months one of them would appear in my doorway and say, “Mr. Branscome, I’d like to discuss my career.”
Because I liked them, I told them the truth. “Your career is going to be far more random than you are prepared to accept. It depends mostly on where you happen to be standing when the angels of light and darkness pass by.”
They wanted a ladder. What I offered was a warning that the whole apparatus of planning is mostly ceremonial.
I have a case study, and most of it runs through Berea College, which recently announced that it will become the first college in the nation to offer every student a completely free education.
The teacher who knew a place existed
I started at the one-room Vinson School in Carroll County, Va., seven grades around a potbellied stove in the Blue Ridge Mountains.
The year I entered fourth grade, Velma Bowman Horton arrived with a fierce belief that mountain kids could go somewhere. I was a hillside farmer’s boy headed for the furniture plants in Galax or Pulaski.
Years later, as guidance counselor at Hillsville High School, Mrs. Horton knew my mother and I had no money. She also knew something few in Carroll County knew. There was a college in Kentucky, founded in 1855 by abolitionists as the first integrated, coeducational college in the South, that charged no tuition and put every student to work.
That is the whole hinge. Not encouragement, just information.
I arrived in Berea in August 1964 with $300 earned pitching hay and digging culvert ditches for the highway department. I never gave the college another cent, and when I graduated in 1968 they owed me $600 for the extra labor hours I had worked as a student teacher.
The barn
One morning, while we cleaned manure out of our barn, my grandfather, who had built a bigger dairy himself, said, “Jimmy, you could make a good living on this place.”
I heard a prison sentence and decided in that instant to go to college.
Neither of us could have known that Carroll County’s 100 dairy farms would dwindle to none. A few months ago, my second cousin shut down the last one.
I thought I was refusing manure. I was actually leaving ahead of a collapse I could not have named. Being right and being wise are almost impossible to tell apart from the inside.
What I asked for, and what I got
On my Berea application I asked to work at the college-owned Berea Citizen. Berea put me there, not to write, but to melt lead for the typesetting machines at 16 cents an hour.
My junior year I was moved to work for Dr. James Y. Holloway, a Yale-trained theologian who edited Katallagete, the journal of the Committee of Southern Churchmen. The group helped ministers who had been run out of their pulpits for supporting desegregation.
I copyedited manuscripts by Father Thomas Merton, Rep. John Lewis and Fannie Lou Hamer. I was 20 years old, from a one-room school, marking up Merton’s punctuation for beer money.
Holloway later asked me to write an article about the mountains. I called it “Annihilating the Hillbilly.” The Appalachian Movement Press sold thousands of copies as a pamphlet. Fifty-eight years later I published a book with a similar title.
A sidewalk in front of Boone Tavern
In 1968, I was admitted to Johns Hopkins on a full scholarship to study philosophy. It was the most orderly thing that had ever happened to me, and I gave it up. With a doctorate in philosophy, I would be driving an UBER today.
Bill Best, a Berea professor, was walking past Boone Tavern when he ran into Paul Nachtigal, who was recruiting for a Ford Foundation leadership program and wanted an Appalachian. Best said my name.
I was not on that sidewalk. I traded a funded doctorate for one year of foundation money with nothing waiting at the end of it. That was not a shrewd bet. It only looks like judgment because of how it came out. Ford sent me to the Appalachian Regional Commission for a month in January, 1969 and I became a staff member for two years where I met Sharen, my wife of 56 years.
Rooms I was not in
Lobbying for strip mine regulation in Kentucky, I got myself thrown out of a U.S. House hearing for insisting that citizens whose land was being destroyed be allowed to testify.
A New York Times reporter named Ben Franklin was in the room. He later told the editors of the Times Magazine that the fellow they’d thrown out might be able to write. My cover story ran in December 1971, and I have been a journalist ever since.
Six years later, the Washington Post called David Hawpe at the Courier-Journal looking for someone to cover the mine workers’ democracy movement. Hawpe gave them my name. I was not on that call either.
The thing I did not believe in
By 1990 I was running stock research and the index business at Standard & Poor’s. Nate Most at the American Stock Exchange wanted a fund built on the S&P 500 that would trade all day like a single stock. Jack Bogle of Vanguard, who invented index investing, had told him it would not work.
I signed the license. Nobody else at S&P would, partly because everyone was already calling the product “Spiders.”
Neither Most nor I thought SPY, the nation’s first exchange-traded fund, would amount to much. It launched in January 1993 with $6.5 million and nearly got shut down. Today it holds more than $800 billion.
I did not see the future. I signed a piece of paper five other people had declined to sign. I was promoted to Managing Director, probably because S&P earns a very handsome fee on all those assets.
What Berea has to do with it
In 1973 the sociologist Mark Granovetter found that opportunities come less through close friends than through acquaintances at the edge of your life, who have access to rooms you don’t. Bill Best was not my mentor. Ben Franklin had covered me once. Hawpe was a competitor.
Now count the institutions. Mrs. Horton knew Berea existed. Berea’s labor program put me at Holloway’s desk. Best was Berea faculty, and Boone Tavern is Berea property. Mike Clark, who hired me at the Highlander Center in 1972 and introduced me to Tom Gish at The Mountain Eagle, was a Berean a class ahead of me.
Six of my first eight accidents route through one small college in Madison County. I did not notice for 40 years.
That is what an institution is for. Randomness is distributed evenly. The ability to convert it is not.
A college that charges nothing and puts a farmer’s son in a room with a Yale theologian is not guaranteeing outcomes. It is standing you somewhere the angels are likely to pass.
The ones who went to Galax
My classmates at Hillsville High in 1964 were as quick as I was. Several were quicker.
Some went to the furniture plants in Galax and Pulaski. The plants went to China. Carroll County offered its children two honorable futures in 1964 and has since closed both.
The difference between them and me is not talent or grit. One woman knew about one college in Kentucky, and she told me.
So when a Berea student asks me what to plan for, I say plan for very little. Stay where the traffic is, keep the kind of reputation that makes people say your name when you are absent, and be ready to be wrong about what you wanted.
And when it turns out well, resist believing you did it. Somebody stood you there.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Sen. Julie Raque Adams gets $620K in outside help from GOP committees
description: FRANKFORT – Since early last May, Republican outside groups have spent more than $620,000 to help reelect Julie Raque Adams to another term in the Kentucky Senate. That’s nearly twice as much help as any other candidate on the Kentucky ballot this year – Republican or Democrat – has gotten from outside groups, according to […]
text:
Sen. Julie Raque Adams, R-Louisville, speaks to a legislative committee,
March 12, 2025. (LRC Public Information)FRANKFORT – Since early last May, Republican outside groups have spent more than $620,000 to help reelect Julie Raque Adams to another term in the Kentucky Senate.
That’s nearly twice as much help as any other candidate on the Kentucky ballot this year – Republican or Democrat – has gotten from outside groups, according to the list of “independent expenditures” on the Kentucky Registry of Election website.
The expenditures for advertising to help Adams’ campaign come from five Republican or conservative groups. But the lion’s share of this support has come from GOPAC – a nonprofit political committee which has had a strong presence in Kentucky for years.
Adams, a Republican who represents the 36th Senate District in Louisville, may seem an unlikely candidate for needing outside help. She has demonstrated her popularity at the polls by winning three straight elections to her Senate seat, and two elections before that to the Kentucky House. She chairs the Senate’s Licensing and Occupations Committee, and her own campaign committee reported last month it has $451,000 in cash on hand.
But last April, a Kentucky Lantern story revealed that Adams was paid $80,500 since 2023 by an inactive political committee she headed – a political committee called Kentucky Strong that has been funded exclusively by lobbying interests in recent years. In fact the $80,500 paid to Adams was the only spending that Kentucky Strong had done in the prior three years, according to a report it filed with the Internal Revenue Service.
The flow began late in the primary
The independent expenditures for Adams began a month after the Lantern story: GOPAC reported in early May it spent $230,000 on digital media and texting services supporting Adams. Also in May, the Kentucky Conservative Fund reported making $90,934 in independent expenditures supporting Adams.
Adams routed her opponent in the May 19 Republican primary capturing 80 percent of the vote. She faces Democrat Sarah Cole McIntosh, a former member of the Jefferson County Board of Education in November.
The flood of outside spending to help Adams resumed in late August: GOPAC came through with an additional $169,158; the Republican State Leadership Committee spent $74,500; Commonwealth Conservative Coalition, $40,000; and Americans for Prosperity $17,627.
Adams did not reply to an email from Kentucky Lantern asking questions about her support from the Republican groups and for an update on the activity of a revived Kentucky Strong. She could not be reached by the Lantern through the Republican Party of Kentucky or the state Senate majority offices.
Despite Adams’ massive edge in money, Democrats say the unique circumstances of this election – such as Trump’s plunging popularity – give McIntosh a shot at winning.
“Republican Super PACs are spending big to try to bail out Sen. Julie Raque Adams because voters will hold her accountable for her failed leadership in Frankfort,” said Kentucky Democratic Party Director of Communications Nat Turner.
The Lantern could not reach GOPAC by phone, and GOPAC did not respond to an email.
Independent expenditures
Independent expenditures are payments by groups or individuals for advertising that advocate the election or defeat of a candidate. There is no limit on the amount of an independent expenditure, nor is there a limit on how much a donor can contribute to a super PAC that makes independent expenditures. However, the law requires that these expenditures not be made in coordination with the campaign being helped by the expenditure.
Kentucky law requires independent expenditures be reported to the state election registry. As of Friday, the registry’s website listed 358 independent expenditures so far for the 2026 Kentucky elections in races of all sorts (magistrate, school board, county judge executive, etc.) Most of them have been for candidates for the Kentucky legislature.
Adams has received far more help than any Kentucky candidate from the spending of these outside groups this year – $622,220. The candidate receiving the next most help so far this year is Republican State Rep. Kim Holloway, of Mayfield, who has benefitted from $336,041 in advertising from independent spenders. (The vast majority of that – $312,000 – came from the Kentucky Conservative Fund in the primary.)
Republican Ky. Rep. Kim Holloway speaks on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, at the annual St. Jerome Picnic in Fancy Farm, Ky. (Austin Anthony / Kentucky Lantern)
While some outside groups – particularly the Kentucky Conservative Fund – have made many such expenditures for many candidates in Kentucky this year, GOPAC has bought independent advertising only for Adams.
GOPAC
GOPAC  Inc. is a large national Republican committee based in Arlington, Virginia. It was created in 1979 to help train and elect Republicans to state and local offices. It is a nonprofit organized under Section 527 of the IRS Code. Like Kentucky Strong it must report its contributions and expenses to the IRS. The independent expenditures to support Adams this year came from its affiliated PAC called GOPAC Election Fund, which files its contributions and spending with the Federal Election Commission. The FEC website shows GOPAC Election Fund has reported $23.9 million in receipts between Jan. 1, 2025 and Aug. 31, 2026, with 84 percent of the receipts coming from GOPAC Inc.
GOPAC has had close ties to Kentucky for several years. Former Senate Majority Leader Damon Thayer, a Georgetown Republican and friend of Adams, was an active member of GOPAC’s Legislative Leaders Advisory Board before he retired as a legislator at the end of 2025. Currently, the GOPAC website lists Kentucky Senate Majority Leader Max Wise and House Majority Leader Steven Rudy as members of the advisory board.
And GOPAC gets a steady flow of donations from Kentucky, according to its reports posted on an IRS website. Since Jan. 1, 2025: Churchill Downs has contributed $230,000; Sazerac Company, of Louisville, $90,500; Frankfort lobbying firm Top Shelf Lobby, $35,000; another Frankfort lobbying firm McCarthy Strategic Solutions, $25,000; lobbying firm Commonwealth Alliance, $15,000; lobbying firm HCM Governmental Relations of Lexington, $15,000; the Kentucky Association of Health Care Facilities, $10,0000; Yum Brands, of Louisville, $10,000.
It has many larger out-of-state donors, but many of them have a strong lobbying presence in Frankfort. Its biggest donors include tobacco interests (Reynolds American, Altria Client Service, PMI Global). It also gets large contributions from the gambling sector, pharmaceutical interests, the alcoholic beverage industry and others. And one of Kentucky Strong’s major funders that has a strong lobbying presence in Frankfort, Charter Communications, of St. Louis, has contributed $240,000 to GOPAC since the beginning of 2025.
Kentucky Strong 
On April 6, the Lantern revealed that the only expenses of Kentucky Strong during the prior three years were 12 payments to Adams totaling $80,500. Over roughly the same period, Kentucky Strong was funded exclusively by interests that actively lobby the Kentucky General Assembly, including $50,000 from Revolutionary Racing, which operates Sandy’s Racing & Gaming in Ashland; $25,000 from Churchill Downs; $15,000 from Charter Communications; and $15,000 from LG&E and KU Energy.
Kentucky Strong Inc. was founded in 2015 by Adams and two other Republican women from Louisville. Its initial tax return filed with the Internal Revenue Service said it is “dedicated to training Republican women to seek and hold public office.” It hoped to match the success recruiting female candidates of a nonprofit started by Democratic women in 2009 called Emerge Kentucky.
Adams told the Lantern last spring that she was doing lots of work to earn her pay, which she said covered out-of-pocket expenses as she drove to meetings to encourage both prospective candidates as well as Republican women already in office. She said she created training materials, travelled to speaking engagements and media appearances and did all of Kentucky Strong’s fundraising. Yet she did not respond to an emailed question last spring asking to identify any specific large, out-of-pocket expenses in recent years, nor did she  identify a candidate who ran for office because of the recruitment and training by Kentucky Strong.
Last spring, Kentucky Strong had no online presence, no website, no Facebook page. It was labeled “inactive” by the Kentucky Secretary of State’s office because it had not filed a required annual corporation report since 2018. (However, it had filed reports of its donations and expenses with the IRS during this period. Those reports were the basis of the Lantern story.)
After the Lantern story was published an official of the Louisville Democratic Party filed a complaint against Adams with the Legislative Ethics Commission. But that complaint was dismissed by the commission.
And Kentucky Strong is again showing signs of life. A Google search will reveal that its website is up and includes an application women can fill out to participate in a leadership training program. The site also features endorsements of two incumbent Republican state representatives – Kim Moser and Kim Banta – and a cover article giving numbers that show the underrepresentation of Republican women in public office in Kentucky.
Kentucky Strong’s most recent report filed with the IRS this summer shows that in the spring it paid expenses for digital advertising, reestablishing its website and social media presence, and fees paid to the Secretary of State’s office to restore its status as an active corporation.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky Court of Appeals race becoming another partisan judicial battleground
description: This story first appeared onLouisville Public Media. It’s republished here as part of the Appalachian News Exchange reporting partnership to strength Kentucky journalism. Fifty years ago, a constitutional amendment approved by Kentucky voters was implemented that dramatically reformed the state’s judicial system, including changing all judicial races from pa[...]
text:
A photo on the campaign website of Judge Will Moynahan features him standing in a courtroom next to Gov. Andy Beshear (left), who is supporting him in his Kentucky Court of Appeals race. (Moynahan campaign website)This story first appeared onLouisville Public Media. It’s republished here as part of the Appalachian News Exchange reporting partnership to strength Kentucky journalism.
Fifty years ago, a constitutional amendment approved by Kentucky voters was implemented that dramatically reformed the state’s judicial system, including changing all judicial races from partisan to nonpartisan.
For the third consecutive election cycle in Kentucky, that principle of a nonpartisan judiciary is being challenged in a high-profile race, with Republican and Democratic officials lining up to support and contribute money to opposing candidates.
Court of Appeals Judge Will Moynahan was appointed to his central Kentucky district last year by Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, and is running to hold onto that seat this fall. He faces Fayette Circuit Judge Lucy VanMeter, who has served two four-year terms in that county position.
In June, a nonpartisan judicial watchdog group voiced its concerns about the race, as Beshear attended a campaign fundraiser for Moynahan and appears in a photo with the judge on his campaign website. Much like the criticism and concerns the group raised in other high-profile judicial races in 2022 and 2024, the Kentucky Judicial Campaign Conduct Committee issued a statement warning that these actions blur the important distinction between partisan politics and judicial elections.
“Partisan politicians shouldn’t raise money for Kentucky judicial candidates, and judicial candidates should not use endorsements by partisan politicians, implied or explicit,” said KJCCC chair Charles Boteler on behalf of the nonpartisan committee, which has advocated for the integrity of judicial campaigns for 20 years.
Since that statement in June, the race between Moynahan and VanMeter has drawn even more partisan activity, with Beshear’s super PAC stepping up its support and more than a dozen Republican state lawmakers contributing to VanMeter, including several in leadership positions.
Boteler told Kentucky Public Radio this week that the trend on both sides is concerning, especially if partisan PAC spending reaches the level of hundreds of thousands of dollars, as it did in the 2022 and 2024 races for Kentucky Supreme Court races.
“Politics and law are similar, but they’re not the same,” Boteler said. “And we fear that an increased partisanship in the selection of judges in Kentucky will weaponize the judiciary and make it more like the partisan branches of government.”
In 2022, the KJCCC criticized partisan campaigning in a Supreme Court race that drew huge spending from partisan PACs, as well as the race for a key Franklin Circuit Court position, which broke a record with more than $1 million of spending.
The group also criticized both sides of a Supreme Court race in 2024, where Beshear’s super PAC and another affiliated group spent $500,000 on ads to support the election of Supreme Court Justice Pamela Goodwine — whose win created the vacancy that allowed Beshear to appoint Moynahan to the Court of Appeals. An impeachment petition was later filed by a GOP official against Goodwine, who argued she should have recused herself from a case due to the spending by the Beshear PACs and another PAC that received $300,000 from teachers unions.
Boteler says such partisan activity and spending on judicial races remains a concern, whether it is by Republicans or Democrats.
“If someone has raised a whole lot of money for you and then has an issue before the court, that has to be a concern, especially if it’s connected to partisan divides,” Boteler said.
Beshear’s political operation backs Moynahan
Judge Moynahan’s campaign was not just boosted by Beshear’s presence at a fundraiser, but also received financial contributions from In This Together — the governor’s PAC — and other current and former Democratic officials.
In This Together PAC had already contributed the maximum $2,200 to Moynahan’s primary election account late last year, and pitched in another $3,500 to his general election account in August — the new and higher maximum donation, per a new state law that went into effect this summer.
Additionally, Kentuckians for Good Judges — the PAC that spent a half million dollars on ads to elect Goodwine in 2024 — was reactivated last week in a filing by its chairman Eric Hyers, the top political strategist of Beshear and In This Together. Kentuckians for Good Judges indicated it will spend money to help elect Moynahan, but has not yet reported any contributions or spending.
Asked about the concern of the KJCCC, Hyers fully stood by the governor’s involvement in the race.
“Now more than ever, the country needs good judges who follow the rule of law,” Hyers said. “Governor Beshear believes that Judge Moynahan is one such judge and he has the governor’s full endorsement.”
In an interview with Kentucky Public Radio, Judge Moynahan said he has a long track record of nonpartisan service in the military and federal court system, and would not let Beshear’s support affect his judgment on the bench.
“I’m grateful for the confidence Gov. Beshear placed in me, but I don’t serve a particular governor or political party or any constituency,” Moynahan said. “I serve the people of Kentucky, and my responsibility is to apply the law fairly and impartially in every case that comes before me.”
Asked about the controversy over Goodwine from the past year and if he would recuse from cases where the governor was a party, Moynahan said he would “certainly recuse if it was required, or if there was an appearance of any impropriety, or any case that people thought I had some kind of predetermined view of a case.”
Moynahan added that recusals are fairly easy when it comes to the Court of Appeals, as panels of three judges are selected for cases out of the 14 appellate judges. He said that he believes he could preside over a case fairly where the governor’s administration was a party, but would review potential recusal “in a more in-depth fashion” if Beshear was personally a party to a lawsuit.
He had no comment on the 13 Republican state lawmakers donating to his opponent’s campaign.
There are 14 different Court of Appeals judges in Kentucky, with two each in seven districts. They preside over cases appealed from circuit court, with their rulings sometimes appealed up to the Supreme Court. Beshear is extremely popular among voters in this central Kentucky district of eight counties surrounding Lexington, where he won reelection by a wide margin in 2023.
Beshear is not the only current elected Democratic official to aid Moynahan, as his filings show that Congressman Morgan McGarvey of Louisville hosted a campaign fundraiser for him in April.
Moynahan also received a $3,500 contribution in August from Democratic Majority Action PAC, which is run by Amy McGrath, a three-time Democratic candidate for federal office in Kentucky. Another $12,000 has been contributed by the PACs of labor unions that typically give to Democrats, including $2,200 from the Jefferson County teachers’ union.
Former two-term Democratic state auditor Crit Luallen also hosted a Moynahan fundraiser, as did close relatives of a former Beshear cabinet official and the executive director of the Kentucky Democratic Party. More than a dozen former Democratic elected officials also contributed to Moynahan, as well as some of the top Democratic donors in recent years, such as Louisville philanthropist Christy Brown, University of Kentucky trustee Todd Case and attorneys Jon Rabinowitz and Hans Poppe.
Only two current Democratic state lawmakers have made small contributions to Moynahan’s campaign, including Sen. Reginald Thomas of Lexington, who gave $250 to both Moynahan and VanMeter.
Moynahan’s campaign had raised a total of $436,000 as of the most recent filing deadline in early September, which is slightly behind the $468,000 raised by VanMeter’s campaign.
Republican lawmakers back VanMeter
Judge VanMeter’s campaign haul has been aided by 13 contributions coming directly from state lawmakers in the Republican supermajority.
Fayette County Circuit Judge Lucy VanMeter. (Kentucky Administrative Office of the Courts)
This includes $1,000 contributions in August from Republican Senate President Robert Stivers and House Speaker David Osborne. Other members of GOP leadership to contribute to VanMeter are Rep. Steven Rudy of Paducah ($1,000) and Sen. David Givens of Greensburg ($2,200).
In addition to the other state lawmakers, two attorneys for House Republicans contributed, as did Frankfort lobbyist John McCarthy, who also serves in leadership with the Republican Party of Kentucky.
Asked if the GOP lawmakers’ contributions to VanMeter creates a potential conflict, a spokesperson for the Senate Republican majority said it does not rise to the same level as Beshear’s activity in the race.
“President Stivers does not believe his contribution, by itself, creates a conflict,” the GOP statement read. “He and the General Assembly expect every judge to decide cases impartially, including those involving the legislature or governor. Kentucky’s courts have hardly been a rubber stamp for the General Assembly.”
The GOP statement went on to cite the controversy over the spending in the Goodwine race and her failure to recuse from a key case, adding that Beshear “has openly endorsed a Supreme Court candidate and participated in fundraising for judicial candidates, including Judge Moynahan in this race. That involvement belongs in any discussion about appearances.”
VanMeter’s campaign did not return a request for comment on partisan contributions in her race, but previously commented to the Kentucky Lantern in a story about concerns over Beshear’s support for Moynahan. The campaign said judicial elections “are not about partisan politics: they are about experience, integrity, and a commitment to the fair administration of justice,” adding that she will serve “with fairness and impartiality, regardless of political affiliation.”
In contrast to Moynahan’s list of donors, the VanMeter campaign has been able to pull in donations from several bipartisan former officials in the Lexington area. These Democratic donors include former state auditor Adam Edelen, former secretary of state Alison Lundergan Grimes, former state representative and Kentucky Democratic Party leader (and Grimes’ father) Jerry Lundergan, and former state representatives Kelly Flood and R.J. Palmer.
Another unique aspect of VanMeter’s donor list is that it includes four former justices of the Kentucky Supreme Court — including, unsurprisingly, her husband, former Chief Justice Laurance VanMeter.
In addition to receiving $500 contributions from former Justices Lisabeth Hughes, Mary Noble and John Minton, the latter two justices are profiled speaking about their support for VanMeter in two campaign videos that are more than a minute long.
Minton and Noble both stressed VanMeter’s experience in state courts as both an attorney and judge, but another campaign video featuring former prosecutor Lou Anna Red Corn and defense attorney Burl McCoy added a message about ignoring politics.
“In a race that’s nonpartisan, your vote shouldn’t be about politics,” they said in turns. “It should be about who has the right experience.”
‘The new normal’
In an interview with Kentucky Public Radio, former Chief Justice John Minton said he is concerned about the continuing trend of politics bleeding into judicial races, as nonpartisan elections were “one of the pillars” of the constitutional judicial reform 50 years ago.
“I am concerned about the injection of big money from partisan sources into judicial races, that sort of transforms this into some sort of political contest,” Minton said. “This ought to be about the qualifications of the candidate, regardless of her or his political affiliation.”
Minton noted that he, Noble and Hughes are not regarded as hard right conservatives or Republicans, and they’re choosing to back VanMeter because they’ve seen her commitment in the courtroom, “regardless of how she may be registered politically.”
While Moynahan does have less experience in Kentucky state courtrooms, he does have a diverse legal background, which began after he served 40 combat missions as a fighter pilot in the Navy. Moynahan served as a clerk for the Sixth Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals, then as a federal prosecutor for the decade leading up to his appointment by Beshear.
Asked about the critique that he has less experience in state courts, Moynahan countered that he has more experience in appellate courts, where he clerked at the federal level for five years.
Boteler, the chair of the judicial watchdog group KJCCC, says he fears that the partisan money creeping into the Court of Appeals race is “the new normal” for high-profile judicial races in Kentucky, but is hopeful his group can create awareness of the issue and lead to a possible solution in the coming years.
“I don’t know that there’s that much we can do to clear the waters in this current Court of Appeals race in central Kentucky, but as chair of our committee, I hope that we can begin a discussion in Kentucky about judicial selection,” Boteler said.
In states with fully partisan judicial races, some have become national races with overtly political messaging and a jaw-dropping amount of spending. There’s no better example than the Wisconsin Supreme Court race from last year, in which $144.5 million was spent, including nearly $50 million by near-trillionaire Elon Musk.
“I don’t know why we would want to partisanize judicial elections now when we look at all the partisan wars that are going on in this country,” Boteler said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Perriello seeks another 5th District upset as McGuire leans on Trump
description: Democrats are looking to an old winner for a new opening in Virginia’s 5th Congressional District, where former U.S. Rep. Tom Perriello is trying to repeat the upset that briefly put the Republican-leaning seat in his party’s hands 18 years ago. Perriello, who defeated longtime Republican incumbent Virgil Goode in 2008, faces first-term U.S. Rep. […]
text:
From left: U.S. Rep. John McGuire, R-Goochland, Democrat and former U.S. Rep. Tom Perriello, and independent Cooke Costa Harvey are competing to represent Virginia’s 5th Congressional District in the Nov. 3 election. (Photos courtesy of campaigns; photo of Perriello by Markus Schmidt/Virginia Mercury) Democrats are looking to an old winner for a new opening in Virginia’s 5th Congressional District, where former U.S. Rep. Tom Perriello is trying to repeat the upset that briefly put the Republican-leaning seat in his party’s hands 18 years ago.
Perriello, who defeated longtime Republican incumbent Virgil Goode in 2008, faces first-term U.S. Rep. John McGuire, R-Goochland, in the Nov. 3 election. Independent Cooke Costa Harvey is also on the ballot. 
Perriello served one term before losing to Republican Robert Hurt in 2010. Republicans have held the seat ever since, although the district’s boundaries have changed considerably since Perriello last represented it. 
Today, the 5th District stretches from Charlottesville and Albemarle County through Lynchburg and Danville to the North Carolina border, while reaching east toward the Richmond suburbs. It takes in university-centered communities, parts of rural Southside and heavily Republican suburbs and exurbs. 
Recent elections show the challenge Perriello faces in his contest to oust McGuire. 
President Donald Trump carried the district by about 12% in 2024. That year, McGuire defeated Democrat Gloria Witt 57.3% to 42.3%. Even during Democrats’ strong statewide showing last year, Gov. Abigail Spanberger received 46.3% of the vote in the district, according to election data by the Virginia Public Access Project. 
A new Washington Post-Schar School poll suggests a closer contest this fall. Conducted Sept. 23-28, the survey found McGuire leading Perriello 51% to 45% among likely voters. The margin of error for likely voters in the district was 4.6%. 
David Richards, a professor and chair of the political science department at the University of Lynchburg, said the district’s Republican lean still gives McGuire an advantage, but turnout could matter more than large numbers of voters changing sides. 
“The numbers are still on McGuire’s side, and Perriello has a huge climb still, but the final vote may be uncomfortably close,” Richards said. 
For McGuire, Richards added, the danger would be Republican voters staying home. Perriello needs strong Democratic participation while also reaching voters in the middle. 
 McGuire ties his record to Trump

McGuire, a former U.S. Navy SEAL, came to Congress after several years in Virginia politics.  
In a 2024 interview, McGuire described a childhood spent partly in foster care around Central Virginia before his grandparents took him and his sister in. After leaving the Navy, McGuire returned to Virginia in 1998 and founded SEAL Team PT, a fitness business. He and his wife, Tracy, live in Goochland County.
He later served in the House of Delegates and briefly in the state Senate, before challenging then-U.S. Rep. Bob Good in the 2024 Republican primary.
That contest became a fight over loyalty to Trump after Good had endorsed Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis for president. Trump backed McGuire, who ultimately defeated Good by 370 votes after a recount. 
McGuire’s campaign did not respond to a request for an interview for this story. 
During a September telephone rally with Trump, McGuire drew on his military background while making the case for his first term in Congress. 
“As a Navy SEAL veteran, there are many ways to serve. We work as a team to get things done, and we do that in the General Assembly and now in Congress,” he said. 
McGuire credited his team and the Trump administration with helping negotiate roughly $20 billion in investment in the district and about 7,000 new jobs. He also said his office had returned more than $10 million owed to constituents by the federal government. 
He has defended Republicans’ 2025 tax-and-spending law, pointing to deductions for tips, overtime and seniors as well as a $50 billion rural health program. Virginia’s share of the funding totaled $189 million. 
The five-year Rural Health Transformation Fund was created alongside Medicaid reductions that health policy researchers have warned could put additional pressure on rural providers. 
“If Democrats win, like the president said, they will undo all of that,” McGuire said. 
Trump, in turn, praised McGuire as a reliable supporter of his agenda. 
“John McGuire has been a rock solid vote for strong borders, low taxes, low regulations, strong military, and supporting our vets,” Trump said. 
The president also attacked Perriello as a “left-wing radical lunatic who spent years working for George Soros.” Perriello previously led the U.S. operation of Open Society Foundations, the philanthropic network founded by Soros. 
McGuire has gone further himself, calling Perriello a “communist” while arguing that his policies would increase taxes, government spending and energy costs.  
Energy has become another dividing line in the race. 
McGuire supported legislation passed by the House aimed at shielding residential customers from some electricity costs associated with data centers. He also said local communities should decide where the facilities are built. 
 Perriello campaigns on affordability and independence

Perriello grew up in Albemarle County and graduated from Yale College and Yale Law School.
After leaving Congress in 2011, he held several diplomatic and foreign policy posts under Democratic administrations, including serving as a special envoy for the Great Lakes region of Africa and the Democratic Republic of Congo. 
He ran unsuccessfully for the Democratic nomination for Virginia governor in 2017. 
In an interview with The Mercury in Richmond last week, Perriello pointed to the new Washington Post-Schar School poll as evidence that his reach exceeds the Democratic base in his district.  
“We’re really building a broad coalition of common sense, and you can feel it at the door, and you can see it in the early vote numbers,” he said. 
His campaign has put affordability near the center of its argument against McGuire. 
Perriello said some of his first priorities in Congress would be ending the war in Iran, reclaiming congressional authority over tariffs and reversing federal healthcare changes that he says are pushing costs higher. 
“We’ve got to get to universal affordable care, whether that’s through Medicare for all or another plan,” he said. “But I don’t think that’s going to happen in the next two years.”
More immediately, he wants Congress to restore enhanced Affordable Care Act premium subsidies and protect Medicaid. The enhanced subsidies expired at the end of 2025, while Republicans’ tax-and-spending law made separate changes to Medicaid eligibility and financing that Virginia health leaders say could force 600,000 Virginians off the program.
Perriello also referred to his first stint in Congress when talking about politically difficult votes. 
He supported the Affordable Care Act in 2010, a vote that became a major issue in his unsuccessful reelection bid later that year. 
His argument now is that members of Congress should be willing to take those risks rather than simply follow their party of president. 
“A member of Congress does not work for the president. A member of Congress works for the people in the district,” Perriello said.
Data centers give the candidates another issue on which to make that case. 
Perriello criticized tax provisions in Republicans’ 2025 law that allow businesses to deduct certain investments more quickly, arguing that they benefit data center developers while Washington does too little to protect workers from automation. The provisions are available more broadly to businesses and are not limited to data centers. 
He also said local communities should decide whether to welcome the facilities and negotiate protections for residents. 
Perriello opposes the Valley Link transmission line, which would run across Central Virginia toward Northern Virginia as utilities respond to rising electric demand, much of it associated with data center growth. 
Asked about McGuire’s ideological attacks, Perriello returned to the pocketbook issues he has emphasized throughout his campaign. 
“This doesn’t bring down diesel costs. It doesn’t bring down gas prices,” he said. 
 Harvey rejects two-party system

Independent Harvey, a Delaware native who has lived in Amherst County since 2012, says voters deserve an alternative to both major parties. 
Harvey has worked in engineering, surveying and wilderness therapy with at-risk youth. He has never held political office and says he would serve only one term and accept no monetary donations. 
In a phone interview with The Mercury Friday, Harvey blamed partisan division for congressional failures on immigration reform, war and government funding.
“I am for a unified America, I am for the collaboration of ideas,” he said. 
Harvey said he supports eliminating tax incentives for data centers and backing communities that oppose them, citing residents’ concerns about water and electricity costs. 
“If they don’t want a data center in their community, I would support them,” he said.
Early voting is underway through Oct. 31. Election Day is Nov. 3. Read The Mercury’s voter guide to learn more about the candidates and stakes of the congressional races. 
Virginia’s 5th Congressional District stretches across Central and Southside Virginia, including Charlottesville, Lynchburg and Danville, and reaches east into communities near Richmond. (Map courtesy of Supreme Court of Virginia)

title: Virginia localities weigh 1% sales tax for school construction as voters decide on expansion
description: Six years ago, the city of Danville in Virginia’s Southside region struggled to raise funds for school construction and modernization across 15 schools, with nearly a quarter of its population, around 42,000, living in poverty. But since the state authorized the city to levy an additional sales and use tax of up to 1% for […]
text:
A view from the front entrance of the renovated Gloucester County High School, which opened in September 2025. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Six years ago, the city of Danville in Virginia’s Southside region struggled to raise funds for school construction and modernization across 15 schools, with nearly a quarter of its population, around 42,000, living in poverty.
But since the state authorized the city to levy an additional sales and use tax of up to 1% for school rehabilitation and voters agreed to the measure seven years ago, the future has changed for students, staff and local leaders.
 
Virginia follows the Dillon Rule, which limits local governments to powers the state explicitly grants. Adopted by the Virginia Supreme Court in 1896, the rule means cities, towns and counties often must ask the General Assembly for authority to change taxes or regulations. For example, localities can set property tax rates, but cannot change the sales tax rate without state approval.


“It’s been great so far,” said Michael Adkins, Danville’s assistant city manager and chief financial officer. 
“Based on the receipts we’re getting each month, we’re easily able to take care of the debt service on those 20-year bonds,” he added. “And we have a little leftover, so we were able to accumulate the excess 1% sales tax for specific projects or contingency funds for the school renovations and construction that have been going on here.”
Across the commonwealth, 47 localities hope for similar success, if not better, when voters decide next month whether to adopt the 1% tax and allow those revenues to support school construction and modernization costs. 
Records obtained by The Mercury show mixed results in the nine localities including Danville that Virginia’s legislature authorized to impose the 1% tax beginning in 2019. Those areas have generated $119 million total, state tax records show.
Despite the monetary benefits for schools, support for the tool isn’t unanimous statewide. 
 Concern around increased taxes

In York County, where voters will consider approving the tax, some residents are urging voters to reject the measure, arguing that it’s unnecessary because some localities, including York and Chesterfield County, already pay a significant amount in sales and use taxes.
According to the Department of Taxation, York County pays 7%, along with Williamsburg and James City County, representing the highest rate in the commonwealth. The next highest rate is 6.3%, for localities such as the city of Danville, and the counties of Charlotte, Gloucester, Halifax, Henry, Northampton, Patrick and Pittsylvania.
Steve Kennedy, a volunteer with the VOTE NO referendum committee, said voters in York and elsewhere should “100%” oppose the measure.
“Beyond the overall tax burden, the sales tax is highly regressive and hits low-income households the hardest,” Kennedy said, arguing that those same people are already struggling in a “stagflationary economy created by politicians’ spending and Federal Reserve policy.”
Kennedy added that before York County asks taxpayers to approve a new 1% sales tax and potentially take on decades of debt, it should prove that the money is truly necessary, that existing revenues have been used responsibly and that the projected sales-tax revenue is realistic.
A “No More Taxes York County” sign is posted outside a home in York County. (Photo courtesy of No New Taxes York County Committee)
Mecklenburg, one of the nine localities with state-approved authority, has not put the matter to voters after receiving authorization, largely because they were not in favor of raising taxes, according to the Board of Supervisors’ records in 2021.
In August 2021, the county considered researching state and federal money that could help pay for new school construction. At that time, Mecklenburg estimated it would need about $6 million per year in debt payments to move forward with new school construction.
However, interest died down because the board did not want to raise taxes to pay for the projects, plus the county had already invested in newer additions to the three elementary schools. 
Officials were concerned that replacing the schools would mean losing that investment. The committee recommended waiting a year before asking voters to approve it.
No action has been taken in the ensuing five years since former state Sen. Frank Ruff successfully proposed the change in 2020
“We did not and will not need to impose the additional 1% sales tax authority bestowed upon us and our neighboring localities thanks to the generosity of Senator
Ruff,” Alex Gottschalk, administrator for Mecklenburg County, said in a statement to the Mercury.  “Therefore, we generate zero dollars of revenue and have made zero dollars of expenditures related to this tax and revenue streams derived from such tax authority.”
 Danville’s success

In the shortest time span among the authorized localities, the city of Danville has collected more revenue than the others, with $30,739,149 in tax revenue for school construction costs through fiscal year 2025, after starting the tax in fiscal year 2023.
One takeaway from the city’s success is that it already established a significant sales-tax base of about $11 million per year, according to Adkins. In addition, the city has also attracted tourists, nonresidents and regional shoppers. 
The city has also seen increased economic activity associated with the casino, although gaming taxes are separate from the sales tax. That’s helped attract tourists, nonresidents and regional shoppers. 
“If you’re not a retail hub, it’s just going to take time,” Adkins said. “That 1% will add up. … It helps to offset your debt service if you decide to issue bonds to do some school construction … (but) certainly they’ll make a difference.”
The city invested $88 million to overhaul the 370,000-square-foot George Washington High School, which features a new gym, cafeteria, a renovated auditorium, expanded career and technical education classrooms, and remote central security systems.
Funds also went to renovating John M. Langston Campus into a modern learning facility that houses Galileo Magnet High School, RISE STEM Academy, and the administrative central offices.
The county also constructed a state-of-the-art elementary school, Arnett Hills, replacing the adjacent, aging G.L.H. Johnson Elementary School.
 ‘Significant impact’ in Gloucester

Gloucester County has used the 1% tax tool to generate $22,183,901 in revenue through fiscal year 2025, beginning in fiscal year 2022.
Like Danville, Gloucester is considered a retail hub in the Middle Peninsula region, and its sales tax benefits from residents’ and surrounding communities’ shopping there.
Gloucester has dedicated its revenues to projects focused on modernizing and improving school facilities, safety, accessibility and infrastructure, including the renovation of Gloucester High School.

George Bains, interim administrator for Gloucester County, said the investment has already made a noticeable mark on the school system.
“The 1% school sales tax has already made a significant impact here in Gloucester by supporting major renovations to our high school,” Bains said. “Not only did the renovations address basic functions of the building — they allow our students to take pride in our flagship school.”
Bains said other renovation projects supported by the sales tax revenue are in the works and will “ensure all Gloucester County students have classrooms and facilities that are modern, secure, and provide optimal learning environments.”
The county has also used the funds to replace an aging HVAC and air quality systems, repave high-traffic areas and lots, replace outdated and unsafe playgrounds, upgrade athletic fields and redesign school traffic loops.
 A ‘very fortunate’ Halifax

Halifax County, the first to receive state authorization, has collected $20,857,413 in tax revenue since implementing the tax in fiscal year 2021.
Former Republican Del. James Edmunds II pushed for the authorization as the county faced “very little opportunities to generate tax revenue,” he said to a House finance subcommittee in 2019. 
After the county raised the property tax rate to remodel the elementary schools and middle school, Edmunds said constructing a new high school would have been too much for the county’s tax rate to cover.
Ultimately, lawmakers endorsed the measure.
A view of the walking track and wall pad installation at Halifax County High School. (Courtesy of Halifax County Public Schools)A view of the auditorium at Halifax County High School. (Courtesy of Halifax County Public Schools)A view of the auditorium at Halifax County High School. (Courtesy of Halifax County Public Schools)
“Halifax is very fortunate to have been the first to initiate the 1% sales tax and our goal is to use it in the most fiscally responsible way possible to maximize the impact for all of our schools,” Halifax Schools Superintendent Amy Huskin said 
Halifax opened its new high school last year and is developing a new athletic complex. The county’s 1% sales tax, along with county funds, is being used to repay a portion of the high school’s debt service. The county has not yet drawn from the sales-tax account, but it is expected to begin doing so soon.
The school board also has other projects lined up in its Capital Improvement Plan. A full assessment of school assets is underway to determine priority needs and the best use of available funding. 
 Other successes, what’s next

In Charlotte, Henry, Northampton, Patrick and Pittsylvania counties, the 1% sales tax tool has also proved successful. 
Henry County, one of the first areas to get approval, raised $22,212,783 in tax money for school construction through fiscal year 2025. Collections began in fiscal year 2021. Since then, Henry County has paid for improvements to sports facilities, heating and cooling systems, roofs, accessibility, and electrical systems throughout the district generating about $5.5 million annually in local capital revenue.

Virginia voters in participating localities could decide whether to authorize an additional 1% local sales tax. In Planning District 8, which covers localities in Northern Virginia, the new revenue could fund not only school construction and modernization but also transportation projects, including support for Metro and other local transit systems. Only the city of Fairfax has put the matter to voters.

Between fiscal years 2022 and 2025, Northampton County collected $7,888,115 in tax money for school construction. The county set aside $91 million to expand and update its middle and high schools, to be finished next year, and $20 million to replace heating and cooling systems at its two elementary schools.
Patrick County collected $5,926,293 in tax money for school construction through fiscal year 2025. Collections started in fiscal year 2022. The biggest project was a $1.2 million update to its high school.
Through fiscal year 2025, Pittsylvania County raised $6,753,163, which varies slightly from the state’s record by about $5,000 in tax money for new school capital infrastructure. Collections began in fiscal year 2024. The biggest project was improving security and safety systems at 15 elementary and middle schools across the area, costing around $6 million.
In Charlotte County, from fiscal year 2022 through fiscal year 2025, the county collected $3,125,311 in tax money to pay for school construction.
Most of it went to new building work, including early planning and design for Randolph Henry High School, worth nearly $1 million.
According to a 2022 report to the state, a review of the high school found accessibility issues, uneven and cracked sidewalks and other items requiring remediation. Records show the school has been open since 1939, with improvements and a significant addition in 1968 — nearly 60 years ago. 
The remaining funds were used to fix the shared bathroom at Phenix Elementary School, install tile floors in the high school’s cafeteria and hallway, and remove asbestos around the school.
Early voting runs through Oct. 31 and Election Day is Nov. 3, when residents in all Virginia localities will decide whether to adopt the 1% sales tax for school construction and modernization needs.
